A line through $O$ intersects the circle $B_iOB_{i+3}$ again at $C_i$ for $i = 0, 1, 2$. Let $\ell_i$ be the tangent to the circle $B_iOB_{i+3}$ at $C_i$. The lines $\ell_i$ and $\ell_j$ intersect at point $D_k$, where $\{i, j, k\} = \{0, 1, 2\}$. Prove that the three circles $B_iOB_{i+1}$ and the circle $D_0D_1D_2$ share a point in the plane.

Let $A_0, A_1, \dots, A_5$ be six distinct points on a circle with center $O$, and let $B_i$ be the midpoint of $A_iA_{i+1}$, $i = 0, 1, \dots, 5$. A line through $O$ intersects the circle $B_iOB_{i+3}$ again at $C_i$ for $i = 0, 1, 2$. Let $\ell_i$ be the tangent to the circle $B_iOB_{i+3}$ at $C_i$. The lines $\ell_i$ and $\ell_j$ intersect at point $D_k$, where $\{i, j, k\} = \{0, 1, 2\}$. Prove that the three lines $\ell_0, \ell_1, \ell_2$ and the circle $D_0D_1D_2$ share a point in the plane.

positive_text:
Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $a, b: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions with finite support on the interval $[-N, N]$. Define $c: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
c(n) = \max \{a(k)b(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} c(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (a(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (b(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

negatives.text:
Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
h(n) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} f(k)g(n-k)
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
h(n) = \max \{f(k) + g(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \geq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

Let $N$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f, g: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ be functions such that $f(n) = g(n) = 0$ for all $|n| \geq N$. Define $h: \mathbb{Z} \to [0, \infty)$ by
$$
h(n) = \max \{f(k)g(n-k) : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}
$$
for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} h(n) \leq \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (f(n))^p \right)^{1/p} \left( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (g(n))^q \right)^{1/q}
$$
for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1$.

positive_text: Find all positive integer quadruplets $(a, b, c, d)$ such that $$ 13^b + 12^a - 14^c = 2013^d. $$

negatives.text: Find all positive integer quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ such that $$ 12^x + 13^y + 14^z = 2013^t. $$
Find all positive integer quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ such that $$ 12^x + 13^y - 14^z = 2014^t. $$
Find all positive integer quadruplets $(x, y, z, t)$ such that $$ 12^x + 13^y - 14^z = 2013^{t+1}. $$

positive_text: \text{Let } a, b, c, x, y, z \text{ be positive real numbers such that} \quad (a - x)(b - y)(c - z) = abc - xyz. \text{ Prove that} \quad (a + x)(b + y)(c + z) \geq 8abc.

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c, x, y, z \text{ be positive real numbers such that} \quad (a + x)(b + y)(c + z) = abc + xyz. \text{ Prove that} \quad (a - x)(b - y)(c - z) \geq 8abc.
\text{Let } a, b, c, x, y, z \text{ be positive real numbers such that} \quad (a - x)(b - y)(c - z) = abc + xyz. \text{ Prove that} \quad (a + x)(b + y)(c + z) \geq 8abc.
\text{Let } a, b, c, x, y, z \text{ be positive real numbers such that} \quad (a - x)(b - y)(c - z) = abc - xyz. \text{ Prove that} \quad (a + x)(b + y)(c + z) < 8abc.

positive_text: In triangle $PQR$ with $PQ = PR$, $N$ is the midpoint of $QR$, and $K$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $N$ onto $PQ$. Let $S$ be a point on $PR$, and let $T$ be the intersection of the line through $Q$ parallel to $KS$ with the line through $R$ parallel to $PQ$. Prove that $NS$ bisects $\angle PST$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, and $H$ is the projection of $M$ onto $AC$. Let $D$ be an arbitrary point on $AC$, and let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $B$ parallel to $HD$ with the line through $C$ parallel to $AB$. Prove that $DM$ bisects $\angle ADE$.

In triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, and $H$ is the projection of $M$ onto $AB$. Let $D$ be an arbitrary point on $AC$, and let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $B$ parallel to $HD$ with the line through $C$ parallel to $BC$. Prove that $DM$ bisects $\angle ADE$.

positive_text: Let $XY$ be a diameter of a circle ($\omega$) with centre $O$. From a point $P$ on $XY$ such that $PX < PY$ we draw the circles ($\omega_1$) and ($\omega_2$) with diameters $PX$ and $PY$ respectively. Let $UV$ be an external common tangent of ($\omega_1$), ($\omega_2$) such that $U$ lies on ($\omega_1$) and $V$ lies on ($\omega_2$). The point $W$ is diametrically opposite to $U$ with respect to ($\omega_1$) and the tangent to ($\omega_1$) at $W$ intersects ($\omega_2$) at points $S, T$. If the line of the common chord of the circumcircles of the triangles $UVW$ and $STV$ intersects the circle ($\omega$) at the points $K, L$ and the circle ($\omega_2$) at the point $N$ (with $N$ closer to $L$), then prove that $KC = NL$.

negatives.text: Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle ($\omega$) with centre $O$. From an arbitrary point $M$ on $AB$ such that $MA < MB$ we draw the circles ($\omega_1$) and ($\omega_2$) with radii $AM$ and $BM$ respectively. Let $CD$ be an external common tangent of ($\omega_1$), ($\omega_2$) such that $C$ belongs to ($\omega_1$) and $D$ belongs to ($\omega_2$). The point $E$ is diametrically opposite to $C$ with respect to ($\omega_1$) and the tangent to ($\omega_1$) at the point $E$ intersects ($\omega_2$) at the points $F, G$. If the line of the common chord of the circumcircles of the triangles $CED$ and $CFG$ intersects the circle ($\omega$) at the points $K, L$ and the circle ($\omega_2$) at the point $N$ (with $N$ closer to $L$), then prove that $KC = NL$.

Let $AB$ be a diameter of a circle ($\omega$) with centre $O$. From an arbitrary point $M$ on $AB$ such that $MA < MB$ we draw the circles ($\omega_1$) and ($\omega_2$) with diameters $AM$ and $BM$ respectively. Let $CD$ be an internal common tangent of ($\omega_1$), ($\omega_2$) such that $C$ belongs to ($\omega_1$) and $D$ belongs to ($\omega_2$). The point $E$ is diametrically opposite to $C$ with respect to ($\omega_1$) and the tangent to ($\omega_1$) at the point $E$ intersects ($\omega_2$) at the points $F, G$. If the line of the common chord of the circumcircles of the triangles $CED$ and $CFG$ intersects the circle ($\omega$) at the points $K, L$ and the circle ($\omega_2$) at the point $N$ (with $N$ closer to $L$), then prove that $KC = NL$.

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that} \quad \sqrt{x^3 y + x^3 z} + \sqrt{y^3 z + y^3 x} + \sqrt{z^3 x + z^3 y} \geq \frac{4}{3}(xy + yz + zx)

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that} \quad \sqrt{a^3 b + b^3 c + c^3 a} + \sqrt{b^3 a + c^3 b + a^3 c} \geq \frac{4}{3}(ab + bc + ca)
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that} \quad \sqrt{a^4 b + a^4 c} + \sqrt{b^4 c + b^4 a} + \sqrt{c^4 a + c^4 b} \geq \frac{4}{3}(ab + bc + ca)
\text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers. Prove that} \quad \sqrt{a^3 b + a^3 c} + \sqrt{b^3 c + b^3 a} + \sqrt{c^3 a + c^3 b} \leq \frac{4}{3}(ab + bc + ca)

positive_text: Determine all non-decreasing functions $ g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for any real number $ a $ and any positive integer $ m $, $$ \left| \sum_{j=1}^{m} j (g(a + j + 1) - g(g(a + j))) \right| < D $$ where $ D > 0 $ is a constant independent of $ a $ and $ g(g(a)) $ denotes the composition $ g(g(a)) $.

negatives.text: Find all monotonic functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for every real number $ x $ and every natural number $ n $, $$ \left| \sum_{i=1}^{n} i (f(x + i + 1) - f(x + i)) \right| < C $$ where $ C > 0 $ is independent of $ x $.

Find all monotonic functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for every real number $ x $ and every natural number $ n $, $$ \left| \sum_{i=1}^{n} i (f(x + i + 1) - f^2(x)) \right| < C $$ where $ C > 0 $ is independent of $ x $ and $ f^2(x) = f(f(x)) $.

Find all monotonic functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that for every real number $ x $ and every natural number $ n $, $$ \left| \sum_{i=1}^{n} i (f(x + i + 1) - f^2(x + i + 1)) \right| < C $$ where $ C > 0 $ is independent of $ x $ and $ f^2(x) = f(f(x)) $.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, with $AB < CD$, and suppose that diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $F$, while $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at $E$. Let $K$ and $L$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $F$ to $AD$ and $BC$, respectively. Let $M$, $S$, and $T$ be the midpoints of segments $EF$, $CF$, and $DF$. Prove that the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $MKT$ and $MLS$ lies on the side $CD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, with $AB < CD$, and diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ intersecting at $F$. Let $E$ be the intersection of $AB$ and $CD$, and let $K$, $L$ be the projections of $F$ onto $AB$, $CD$ respectively. Let $M$, $S$, $T$ be the midpoints of $EF$, $CF$, $DF$. Prove that the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $MKT$, $MLS$ lies on the side $CD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, with $AB < CD$, whose diagonals intersect at $F$ and $AD$, $BC$ intersect at $E$. Let $K$, $L$ be the projections of $E$ onto $AD$, $BC$ respectively, and $M$, $S$, $T$ be the midpoints of $EF$, $CF$, $DF$. Prove that the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $MKT$, $MLS$ lies on the side $CD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, with $AB < CD$, whose diagonals intersect at $F$ and $AD$, $BC$ intersect at $E$. Let $K$, $L$ be the projections of $F$ onto the sides $AD$, $BC$ respectively, and $M$, $S$, $T$ be the midpoints of $EF$, $CF$, $DF$. Prove that the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $KMT$, $LSM$ lies on the side $CD$.

positive_text: Let $PQR$ be a triangle with $PQ < PR$. On the rays $QP$ and $RP$ we construct points $S$ and $T$ such that $PS = RT = PR$. Let $U, V$, and $W$ be the midpoints of $PS$, $RT$, and $PR$, respectively. Let $L$ and $O$ be the circumcenters of triangles $PQR$ and $UVW$. Suppose that the line $OL$ intersects $QT$ and $VW$ at $P_1$ and $Q_1$, respectively, and let $R_1$ be the intersection of $VW$ and $ST$. If a line through $P_1$ parallel to $OR_1$ intersects $ST$ at $X$, and a line through $P_1$ perpendicular to $XQ_1$ intersects $ST$ at $Y$, prove that $T$ is the orthocenter of triangle $P_1OY$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. On the rays $AB$ and $AC$ we construct points $F$ and $E$ such that $AF = AE = AB$. Let $M, N$, and $H$ be the midpoints of $AF, AE$, and $AB$, respectively. Let $K$ and $O$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABC$ and $MNH$. Suppose that the line $OK$ intersects $BE$ and $HN$ at $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively, and let $C_1$ be the intersection of $HN$ and $FE$. If a line through $A_1$ parallel to $OC_1$ intersects $FE$ at $D$, and a line through $A_1$ perpendicular to $DB_1$ intersects $FE$ at $M_1$, prove that $E$ is the orthocenter of triangle $A_1OM_1$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. On the rays $AB$ and $AC$ we construct points $F$ and $E$ such that $BF = CE = AB$. Let $M, N$, and $H$ be the midpoints of $BF, CE$, and $BC$, respectively. Let $K$ and $O$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABC$ and $MNH$. Suppose that the line $OK$ intersects $BE$ and $HN$ at $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively, and let $C_1$ be the intersection of $HN$ and $FE$. If a line through $A_1$ parallel to $OC_1$ intersects $FE$ at $D$, and a line through $A_1$ perpendicular to $DB_1$ intersects $FE$ at $M_1$, prove that $E$ is the orthocenter of triangle $A_1OM_1$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. On the rays $AB$ and $AC$ we construct points $F$ and $E$ such that $BF = CE = BC$. Let $M, N$, and $H$ be the midpoints of $BF, CE$, and $BC$, respectively. Let $K$ and $O$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ABC$ and $MNH$. Suppose that the line $OK$ intersects $BE$ and $HN$ at $A_1$ and $B_1$, respectively, and let $C_1$ be the intersection of $HN$ and $FE$. If a line through $A_1$ parallel to $OC_1$ intersects $FE$ at $D$, and a line through $A_1$ perpendicular to $DB_1$ intersects $FE$ at $M_1$, prove that $A$ is the orthocenter of triangle $A_1OM_1$.

positive_text: Let $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_m$ be a collection of $m \ge 3$ points in the Euclidean plane. Let $R$ be the radius of the smallest enclosing circle for all these points. Prove that there exist three points among them, say $P_i, P_j, P_k$, such that the radius of the smallest enclosing circle for just $P_i, P_j, P_k$ is equal to $R$.

negatives.text: Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ be points in the plane with $n \ge 3$. Define $r(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n)$ as the radius of the smallest circle that contains all of these points. Prove that there are indices $i, j$ such that $r(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n) = r(A_i, A_j)$.

Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ be points in the plane with $n \ge 3$. Define $r(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n)$ as the radius of the smallest circle that contains all of these points. Prove that there are indices $i, j, k$ such that $r(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n) = r(A_i, A_j, A_k, A_1)$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle XYZ$ be an acute triangle. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on segments $XZ$ and $XY$, respectively, satisfying $YZ^2 = YX \cdot YQ + PZ \cdot XZ$. As $P$ and $Q$ move, prove that the circumcircle of $\triangle XPQ$ always passes through a fixed point other than $X$.

Let $\triangle XYZ$ be a triangle with $XY < XZ$ inscribed into a circle $\omega$. The tangent of $\omega$ at the point $Z$ meets the line parallel to $XZ$ through $Y$ at the point $P$. The tangent of $\omega$ at the point $Y$ meets the line parallel to $XY$ through $Z$ at the point $Q$ and the tangent of $\omega$ at the point $Z$ at the point $M$. Suppose that the circumcircle $\omega_1$ of triangle $YPZ$ meets $XZ$ at the point $U$ and the circumcircle $\omega_2$ of triangle $YQZ$ meets $XY$ at the point $V$. Prove that the lines $UV$, $YZ$, and $XM$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$ inscribed into a circle $c$. The tangent of $c$ at the point $C$ meets the line parallel to $AB$ through $B$ at the point $D$. The tangent of $c$ at the point $B$ meets the line parallel to $AC$ through $C$ at the point $E$ and the tangent of $c$ at the point $C$ at the point $L$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $BDC$ meets $AB$ at the point $T$ and the circumcircle of triangle $BEC$ meets $AC$ at the point $S$. Prove that the lines $ST$, $BC$, and $AL$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$ inscribed into a circle $c$. The tangent of $c$ at the point $C$ meets the line parallel to $AC$ through $B$ at the point $D$. The tangent of $c$ at the point $B$ meets the line parallel to $AB$ through $C$ at the point $E$ and the tangent of $c$ at the point $C$ at the point $L$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $BDC$ meets $AC$ at the point $T$ and the circumcircle of triangle $BEC$ meets $AB$ at the point $S$. Prove that the lines $ST$, $AB$, and $AL$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$ inscribed into a circle $c$. The tangent of $c$ at the point $C$ meets the line parallel to $AC$ through $B$ at the point $D$. The tangent of $c$ at the point $B$ meets the line parallel to $AB$ through $C$ at the point $E$ and the tangent of $c$ at the point $C$ at the point $L$. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $BDC$ meets $AB$ at the point $T$ and the circumcircle of triangle $BEC$ meets $AC$ at the point $S$. Prove that the lines $ST$, $BC$, and $AL$ are concurrent.

positive_text:
Let triangle $KLM$ be acute with $KL 
eq KM$ and circumcircle $\Omega$. The bisector of $\angle LKM$ intersects $LM$ and $\Omega$ at $N$ and $O$ respectively. A circle with diameter $NO$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $R 
eq O$. Point $S$ lies on $KR$ such that $SL = SM$, and $U$ and $V$ are feet of perpendiculars from $S$ to $KL$ and $KM$ respectively. Let $G$ and $G'$ be the orthocenters of $\triangle KLM$ and $\triangle KUV$ respectively. $KG$ meets $\Omega$ again at $Z$. If $KG'$ and $GG'$ intersect the circle with diameter $KG$ again at points $W$ and $X$ respectively, prove that the lines $KX$, $GW$, and $RZ$ are concurrent.

negatives.text:
Let triangle $PQR$ be acute with $PQ 
eq PR$ and circumcircle $\Lambda$. The bisector of $\angle QPR$ intersects $QR$ at $S$ and $\Lambda$ at $T$. A circle with diameter $ST$ intersects $\Lambda$ again at $U 
eq T$. Point $V$ lies on $PU$ such that $VQ = VR$, and $W$ and $X$ are feet of perpendiculars from $V$ to $PQ$ and $PR$ respectively. Let $J$ and $J'$ be the centroids of $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle PWX$ respectively. $PJ$ meets $\Lambda$ again at $Y$. If $PJ'$ and $JJ'$ intersect the circle with diameter $PJ$ again at points $Z$ and $A$ respectively, prove that the lines $PA$, $JZ$, and $UY$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Let $b_0$ be a given positive integer. For each $n \ge 1$, define $b_n$ to be the smallest positive integer such that $b_0 + b_1 + \dots + b_n$ is a multiple of $n$. Show that there exists a positive integer $M$ such that $b_{n} = b_{n+1}$ for all $n \ge M$.

negatives.text: Let $d_0$ be a positive integer. For each $n \ge 1$, define $d_n$ to be the smallest positive integer such that $d_0 + d_1 + \dots + d_n$ is a multiple of $n$, but $d_n$ is not equal to any of $d_0, d_1, \dots, d_{n-1}$. Prove that the sequence $\{d_n\}$ eventually becomes constant.

Let $e_0$ be a positive integer. For each $n \ge 1$, define $e_n$ to be the smallest positive integer such that $e_0 + e_1 + \dots + e_n$ is a multiple of $n$. Prove that the sequence $\{e_n\}$ is bounded.

positive_text: Let $\triangle XYZ$ ($YZ > XZ$) be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\omega$ centered at $M$. The tangent to $\omega$ at $Z$ intersects the line $XY$ at the point $W$. The circumcircles of triangles $YZW$, $MZW$ and $MX Y$ intersect the ray $ZX$ (beyond $X$) at the points $U$, $V$ and $L$, respectively, such that $V \in (LX)$ and $L \in (UV)$. The line $VW$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $YLZ$ at the point $S$, so that $V$ and $S$ are in different halfplanes with respect to $YL$. Prove that $SY = SL$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ ($BC > AC$) be an acute triangle with circumcircle $k$ centered at $O$. The tangent to $k$ at $C$ intersects the line $AB$ at the point $D$. The circumcircles of triangles $BCD$, $OCD$ and $AOB$ intersect the ray $CA$ (beyond $A$) at the points $Q$, $P$ and $K$, respectively, such that $P \in (AK)$ and $K \in (PQ)$. The line $PD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $BKQ$ at the point $T$, so that $P$ and $T$ are in the same halfplane with respect to $BQ$. Prove that $TB = TQ$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ ($BC > AC$) be an acute triangle with circumcircle $k$ centered at $O$. The tangent to $k$ at $C$ intersects the line $AB$ at the point $D$. The circumcircles of triangles $BCD$, $OCD$ and $AOB$ intersect the ray $CA$ (beyond $A$) at the points $Q$, $P$ and $K$, respectively, such that $P \in (AK)$ and $K \in (PQ)$. The line $PD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $BKQ$ at the point $T$, so that $P$ and $T$ are in different halfplanes with respect to $BQ$. Prove that $TB = TQ$ if and only if $\angle ABC = 60^\circ$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ ($BC > AC$) be an acute triangle with circumcircle $k$ centered at $O$. The tangent to $k$ at $C$ intersects the line $AB$ at the point $D$. The circumcircles of triangles $BCD$, $OCD$ and $AOB$ intersect the ray $CA$ (beyond $A$) at the points $Q$, $P$ and $K$, respectively, such that $P \in (AK)$ and $K \in (PQ)$. The line $PD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $BKQ$ at the point $T$, so that $P$ and $T$ are in different halfplanes with respect to $BQ$. Prove that $TB = TQ$ assuming $AB = AC$.

positive_text: Let $ m $ be a positive integer and $ V = \{1, 2, \dots, m\} $. Let $ A $ be a nonempty subset of $ V $, and let $ r $ ($ r > 1 $) be the smallest common divisor of all elements of $ A $. Determine the minimum number $ t $ such that every subset $ B $ of $ V $ with $ |B| = t $, containing $ A $, has the property that the greatest common divisor of the elements of $ B $ is $ 1 $.

negatives.text: Let $ n $ be a positive integer and $ U = \{1, \dots, n\} $. Let $ S $ be a nonempty subset of $ U $ and let $ d $ ($ d \neq 1 $) be the smallest common divisor of all elements of $ S $. Find the smallest positive integer $ k $ such that for any subset $ T $ of $ U $, consisting of $ k $ elements, with $ S \subset T $, the least common multiple of all elements of $ T $ is equal to $ n $.

Let $ n $ be a positive integer and $ U = \{1, \dots, n\} $. Let $ S $ be a nonempty subset of $ U $ and let $ d $ ($ d \neq 1 $) be the smallest common divisor of all elements of $ S $. Find the smallest positive integer $ k $ such that for any subset $ T $ of $ U $, consisting of $ k $ elements, with $ S \subset T $, the greatest common divisor of all elements of $ T $ is equal to $ d $.

Let $ n $ be a positive integer and $ U = \{1, \dots, n\} $. Let $ S $ be a nonempty subset of $ U $ and let $ d $ ($ d \neq 1 $) be the smallest common divisor of all elements of $ S $. Find the smallest positive integer $ k $ such that for any subset $ T $ of $ U $, consisting of $ k $ elements, with $ S \subset T $, the greatest common divisor of all elements of $ T $ is strictly greater than $ 1 $.

positive_text: In triangle $ PQR $, where $ \angle Q $ is obtuse, let $ M $ be the centroid and $ N $ the orthocenter. Consider a circle $ \gamma $ with diameter $ PM $, and let $ \gamma $ intersect the circumcircle of $ PQR $ again at $ S \neq P $. If the tangent to $ \gamma $ at $ S $ intersects the circumcircle of $ PQR $ at $ T \neq S $, and $ PM = MN $, show that $ \angle NTP = 90^\circ $.

negatives.text: Let $ G $, $ H $ be the centroid and orthocentre of $ \triangle ABC $, with $ \angle B $ obtuse. Let $ \omega $ be the circle with diameter $ AG $. $ \omega $ intersects $ \odot ABC $ again at $ L \neq A $. The tangent to $ \omega $ at $ L $ intersects $ \odot ABC $ at $ K \neq L $. If $ AG = 2GH $, prove $ \angle HKG = 90^\circ $.

positive_text: In triangle $\triangle PQR$, where $PQ = PR$ and $\angle P = 45^\circ$, let $S$ be the center of the circumcircle $(\omega)$. Let $T$ be the midpoint of $QR$, and let $U$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to $PQ$. Using $R$ as the center and $RU$ as the radius, draw a circle that intersects $PR$ at point $V$ and the circle $(\omega)$ at two points $W$ and $X$, such that $W$ lies on the small arc $\widehat{QR}$ and $X$ on the small arc $\widehat{PR}$. Prove that the lines $WX$, $RS$, and $TV$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 90^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter, $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $D$ the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. Draw a circle centered at $C$ with radius $CD$, intersecting $AC$ at $F$ and the circumcircle at $Z$ and $E$, with $Z$ on arc $\widehat{BC}$ and $E$ on arc $\widehat{AC}$. Prove that $ZE$, $CO$, and $FM$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 45^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter, $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $D$ the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. Draw a circle centered at $C$ with radius $CD$, intersecting $BC$ at $F$ and the circumcircle at $Z$ and $E$. Prove that the lines $ZE$, $CO$, and $FM$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$ and $\angle A = 45^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter, $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $D$ the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $AC$. Draw a circle centered at $C$ with radius $CD$, intersecting $AC$ at $F$ and the circumcircle at $Z$ and $E$. Prove that the lines $ZE$, $CO$, and $FM$ are concurrent.

positive_text:
Let $a, b$ be functions from $\mathbb{Z}^+$ to $\mathbb{Z}$. A kangaroo starts at position $(0,0)$ on the integer grid. Each jump at step $n \ge 1$ is one of the eight vectors $(\pm a(n), \pm b(n))$ or $(\pm b(n), \pm a(n))$. Can the kangaroo always return to the origin $(0,0)$ infinitely often when
(a) $a, b$ are integer-coefficient polynomials in $n$?
(b) $a, b$ are arbitrary integer-valued functions on $\mathbb{Z}^+$?

negatives.text:
Let $f, g$ be functions from $\mathbb{Z}^+$ to $\mathbb{Z}$. Vlad jumps on the integer grid starting at $(0,0)$, and for each $n \ge 1$, his jump is $(\pm f(n), \pm g(n))$ or $(\pm g(n), \pm f(n))$, but only four of these are allowed (e.g., only the combinations with positive signs). Can he return to $(0,0)$ infinitely often when
(a) $f, g$ are integer-coefficient polynomials?
(b) $f, g$ are arbitrary integer-valued functions?

Let $f, g$ be functions from $\mathbb{Z}^+$ to $\mathbb{Z}$. Vlad starts at $(0,0)$ and for each $n \ge 1$, he jumps by $(\pm f(n), \pm g(n))$ or $(\pm g(n), \pm f(n))$, but now the jump vector is multiplied by $n$ (i.e., $\pm n f(n)$, etc.). Can Vlad return to $(0,0)$ infinitely often when
(a) $f, g$ are integer-coefficient polynomials?
(b) $f, g$ are arbitrary integer-valued functions?

Let $f, g$ be functions from $\mathbb{Z}^+$ to $\mathbb{Z}$. Vlad starts at $(0,0)$ and for each $n \ge 1$, his jump is one of the four vectors $(\pm f(n), 0)$ or $(0, \pm g(n))$. Can he return to $(0,0)$ infinitely often when
(a) $f, g$ are integer-coefficient polynomials?
(b) $f, g$ are arbitrary integer-valued functions?

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, let $I$ be the incenter and $O$ the circumcenter. Let $s_a$ be the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. A line is drawn through $I$ and is perpendicular to $IO$, intersecting side $BC$ at $P$ and the external bisector $s_a$ at $Q$. Prove that the segment $IQ$ is twice as long as segment $IP$.

negatives.text: Let $I$ be the incenter and $O$ the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle A$ is denoted $s_a$. A line through $I$ is perpendicular to $IO$ and intersects $BC$ at $P$ and $s_a$ at $Q$. Prove that $IQ = 2IP$.

Let $I$ be the incenter and $O$ the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. A line through $I$ is perpendicular to $IO$ and intersects $AB$ at $P$ and the external bisector of $\angle A$ at $Q$. Prove that $IQ = 2IP$.

Let $I$ be the incenter and $O$ the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$. A line through $I$ is perpendicular to $IO$ and intersects the internal angle bisector of $\angle A$ at $Q$ and the side $BC$ at $P$. Prove that $IQ = 2IP$.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ satisfy $PQ < PR$. Let $\gamma$ be a circle through $Q, R$, with $P$ inside $\gamma$. Points $M, N$ lie on $\gamma$ such that $\angle QMP = \angle PNR$, and $M$ is on the side of $PQ$ opposite to $R$, while $N$ is on the side of $PR$ opposite to $Q$. Prove that as $M, N$ move on $\gamma$, the line $MN$ passes through a fixed point.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB < AC$, and let $\omega$ be a circle through $B, C$ with $A$ inside $\omega$. Let $X, Y$ lie on $\omega$ such that $\angle XBA = \angle AYC$, and $X$ is on the opposite side of $AB$ to $C$, while $Y$ is on the opposite side of $AC$ to $B$. Prove that as $X, Y$ vary on $\omega$, the line $XY$ passes through a fixed point.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB < AC$, and let $\omega$ be a circle through $B, C$ with $A$ outside $\omega$. Let $X, Y$ lie on $\omega$ such that $\angle BXA = \angle AYC$, and $X$ is on the opposite side of $AB$ to $C$, while $Y$ is on the opposite side of $AC$ to $B$. Prove that as $X, Y$ vary on $\omega$, the line $XY$ passes through a fixed point.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB < AC$, and let $\omega$ be a circle through $B, C$ with $A$ inside $\omega$. Let $X, Y$ lie on $\omega$ such that $\angle BXA = \angle AY C$, and both $X$ and $Y$ lie on the same side of $AB$ as $C$. Prove that as $X, Y$ vary on $\omega$, the line $XY$ passes through a fixed point.

positive_text: Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be points in the plane such that triangle $ABC$ is acute and $AC > AB$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let the tangent at $A$ to $\Gamma$ meet $BC$ at a point $T$. If $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, and $R$ is the reflection of $A$ over $B$, then define a point $S$ such that $SABT$ is a parallelogram. Let $P$ lie on line $SB$ with $MP \parallel AB$. If $P$ lies on $\Gamma$, show that the circumcircle of triangle $STR$ is tangent to line $AC$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AC > AB$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangent from $B$ to $\Gamma$ intersects $AC$ at $T$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$ and let $R$ be the reflection of $A$ in $B$. Let $S$ be a point so that $SABT$ is a parallelogram and finally let $P$ be a point on line $SB$ such that $MP$ is parallel to $AB$. Given that $P$ lies on $\Gamma$, prove that the circumcircle of $\triangle STR$ is tangent to line $AC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AC > AB$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangent from $A$ to $\Gamma$ intersects $BC$ at $T$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $R$ be the reflection of $A$ in $C$. Let $S$ be a point so that $SABT$ is a parallelogram and finally let $P$ be a point on line $SB$ such that $MP$ is parallel to $AB$. Given that $P$ lies on $\Gamma$, prove that the circumcircle of $\triangle STR$ is tangent to line $AC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AC > AB$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangent from $A$ to $\Gamma$ intersects $BC$ at $T$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $R$ be the reflection of $A$ in $B$. Let $S$ be a point so that $SABT$ is a parallelogram and finally let $P$ be a point on line $SB$ such that $MP$ is parallel to $AC$. Given that $P$ lies on $\Gamma$, prove that the circumcircle of $\triangle STR$ is tangent to line $AC$.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $A$ intersects $BC$ at point $D$. A circle $\Omega$ is drawn with center at $D$ and radius $AD$, and it intersects the circumcircle again at a point $E$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $BC$. The line $BE$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $X$, and the line $CX$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $Y$. Prove that points $A$, $Y$, and $M$ lie on a straight line.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $B$ intersects $AC$ at point $D$. A circle $\Omega$ is drawn with center at $D$ and radius $BD$, and it intersects the circumcircle again at a point $E$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $BC$. The line $CE$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $X$, and the line $AX$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $Y$. Prove that points $A$, $Y$, and $M$ lie on a straight line.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $A$ intersects $BC$ at point $D$. A circle $\Omega$ is drawn with center at $D$ and radius $AD^2$, and it intersects the circumcircle again at a point $E$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $BC$. The line $BE$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $X$, and the line $CX$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $Y$. Prove that points $A$, $Y$, and $M$ lie on a straight line.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$. The tangent to the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $A$ intersects $BC$ at point $D$. A circle $\Omega$ is drawn with center at $D$ and radius $AD$, and it intersects the circumcircle again at a point $E$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AB$. The line $BE$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $X$, and the line $CX$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $Y$. Prove that points $A$, $Y$, and $M$ lie on a straight line.

positive_text: In triangle $PQR$, $J$ is the incenter. Points $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $J$ to $QR$, $RP$, and $PQ$, respectively. Let $M$ be the reflection of $X$ across line $PJ$, and let $N$ be the second intersection point of the circumcircles of triangles $QZM$ and $RYM$. If $\frac{1}{3}QR = RP - PQ$, prove that $YZ = 2MN$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, $I$ is the incenter. Points $D$, $E$, and $F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $I$ to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Let $K$ be the reflection of $D$ over line $AI$, and let $L$ be the second point of intersection of the circumcircles of triangles $BFD$ and $CEK$. If $\frac{1}{3}BC = AC - AB$, prove that $DE = 2KL$.

Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle with incenter $I$. Points $D$, $E$, and $F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $I$ to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Let $K$ be the reflection of $E$ over the line $AI$, and let $L$ be the second intersection of the circumcircles of triangles $BFK$ and $CEK$. If $\frac{1}{3}BC = AC - AB$, prove that $DE = 2KL$.

Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle with incenter $I$. Points $D$, $E$, and $F$ are the feet of the perpendiculars from $I$ to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Let $K$ be the reflection of $D$ over the line $AI$, and let $L$ be the second intersection of the circumcircles of triangles $BFK$ and $CEK$. If $\frac{1}{3}BC = AB - AC$, prove that $DE = 2KL$.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ have circumcircle $\Gamma$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of the arc $QR$ not containing $P$, and let $N$ be the midpoint of segment $QR$. Let $U$ be the second intersection of $PN$ with $\Gamma$, and let $T$ be the intersection of $PD$ with $QR$. Let $Y$ be the second intersection of the circumcircle of triangle $TND$ with $\Gamma$, and let $Y'$ be the reflection of $U$ over $N$. Let $P'$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $QR$, and let $W$ be the second intersection of $Y P'$ with $\Gamma$. If $Z' \in \Gamma$ with $Z' \neq Y$ is such that $PY = PZ'$, prove that $W$, $Y'$, and $Z'$ are collinear.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have circumcircle $\omega$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of the major arc $BC$ of $\omega$, and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $V$ be the other point of intersection of $AM$ with $\omega$, $F$ the point of intersection of $AE$ with $BC$, $X$ the other point of intersection of the circumcircle of $FEM$ with $\omega$, $X'$ the reflection of $V$ with respect to $M$, $A'$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ and $S$ the other point of intersection of $XA'$ with $\omega$. If $Z \in \omega$ with $Z \neq X$ is such that $AX = AZ$, then prove that $S$, $X'$ and $Z$ are collinear.

Let triangle $ABC$ have circumcircle $\omega$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of the minor arc $BC$ of $\omega$, and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $V$ be the other point of intersection of $AM$ with $\omega$, $F$ the point of intersection of $AE$ with $BC$, $X$ the other point of intersection of the circumcircle of $FEM$ with $\omega$, $X'$ the reflection of $V$ with respect to $M$, $A'$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ and $S$ the other point of intersection of $XA'$ with $\omega$. If $Z \in \omega$ with $Z \neq X$ is such that $AX^2 = AZ^2 + 1$, then prove that $S$, $X'$ and $Z$ are collinear.

Let triangle $ABC$ have circumcircle $\omega$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of the minor arc $BC$ of $\omega$, and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $V$ be the other point of intersection of $AM$ with $\omega$, $F$ the point of intersection of $AE$ with $BC$, $X$ the other point of intersection of the circumcircle of $FEM$ with $\omega$, $X'$ the reflection of $V$ with respect to $M$, $A'$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ and $S$ the other point of intersection of $XA'$ with $\omega$. If $Z$ is the point such that $AZ = AX$ and $\angle AZX = 90^\circ$, then prove that $S$, $X'$ and $Z$ are collinear.

positive_text: Show that there exists a real number $c < \frac{3}{4} $ such that for any function $f : \mathbb{N} \to [0,1]$, there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ with $m > n$ such that $$ |f(m) - f(n)| \le \frac{c}{m}. $$

negatives.text: Prove that there exists a real number $c < \frac{3}{4} $ such that for each sequence $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ satisfying $0 \le x_i \le 1$ for all $i$, there are infinitely many pairs $(m, n)$ with $m > n$ such that $$ |x_m - x_n| \le \frac{c}{m^2}. $$

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $g: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$,
$$
g(a^{2023} + g(a)g(b)) = a^{2023} + b g(a).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(x^{2023} + f(x)f(y)) = y^{2023} + x f(y).
$$

Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(x^{2023} + f(x)f(y)) = x^{2023} + f(x)f(y).
$$

Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that for all positive real numbers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(x^{2023} + f(x)f(y)) = x^{2023} + y^{2023}.
$$

positive_text: \text{Let } WXYZ \text{ be a convex quadrilateral with an incircle, and let } O \text{ be the intersection point of its diagonals } WY \text{ and } XZ. \text{ Let } J_1, J_2, J_3, J_4 \text{ be the incenters of } \triangle YOZ, \triangle XOW, \triangle WOY, \text{ and } XOZ, \text{ respectively. The circumcircle of } \triangle YJ_1J_2 \text{ intersects the sides } YW \text{ and } YZ \text{ at points } R \text{ and } S, \text{ respectively. The circumcircle of } \triangle WJ_3J_4 \text{ intersects the sides } WX \text{ and } WZ \text{ at points } L \text{ and } K, \text{ respectively. Prove that}$$WL + YS = WK + YR.$$

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a cyclic quadrilateral (i.e. inscribed in a circle), and let } X \text{ be the intersection point of its diagonals } AC \text{ and } BD. \text{ Let } I_1, I_2, I_3, I_4 \text{ be the incenters of } \triangle DXC, \triangle BXC, \triangle AXB, \text{ and } \triangle DXA, \text{ respectively. The circumcircle of } \triangle CI_1I_2 \text{ intersects the sides } CB \text{ and } CD \text{ at points } P \text{ and } Q, \text{ respectively. The circumcircle of } \triangle AI_3I_4 \text{ intersects the sides } AB \text{ and } AD \text{ at points } M \text{ and } N, \text{ respectively. Prove that}$$AM + CQ = AN + CP.$$

\text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a circumscribed quadrilateral and let } X \text{ be the intersection point of its diagonals } AC \text{ and } BD. \text{ Let } I_1, I_2, I_3, I_4 \text{ be the incenters of } \triangle DXC, \triangle BXC, \triangle AXB, \text{ and } \triangle DXA, \text{ respectively. The circumcircle of } \triangle CI_1I_2 \text{ intersects the sides } CB \text{ and } CD \text{ at points } P \text{ and } Q, \text{ respectively. The circumcircle of } \triangle AI_3I_4 \text{ intersects the sides } AB \text{ and } AD \text{ at points } M \text{ and } N, \text{ respectively. Prove that}$$AM + CQ = AN + CP + 1.$

\text{Let } ABCD \text{ be a circumscribed quadrilateral and let } X \text{ be the intersection point of its diagonals } AC \text{ and } BD. \text{ Let } I_1, I_2, I_3, I_4 \text{ be the incenters of } \triangle DXC, \triangle BXC, \triangle AXB, \text{ and } \triangle DXA, \text{ respectively. The circumcircle of } \triangle CI_1I_2 \text{ intersects the sides } CB \text{ and } CD \text{ at points } P \text{ and } Q, \text{ respectively. The circumcircle of } \triangle AI_3I_4 \text{ intersects the sides } AB \text{ and } AD \text{ at points } M \text{ and } N, \text{ respectively. Prove that}$$AM + CQ = AN + CP + MN.$$

positive_text: Let $PQRS$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $T$ inside the quadrilateral. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the segments $QR$ and $SP$, respectively. Let $Y$ be the point on the same side of the line $MN$ as the vertex $R$ such that $\triangle MNY$ is similar to $\triangle TPS$. Prove that $YR = YS$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$ inside the quadrilateral. Let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of the segments $BC$ and $AD$, respectively. Let $X$ be the point on the same side of the line $EF$ as the vertex $C$ such that $\triangle EXF$ and $\triangle AOB$ are similar. Prove that $XC = XD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$ inside the quadrilateral. Let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of the segments $BC$ and $AD$, respectively. Let $X$ be the point on the opposite side of the line $EF$ from the vertex $C$ such that $\triangle EXF$ and $\triangle BOA$ are similar. Prove that $XC = XD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$ inside the quadrilateral. Let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of the segments $BC$ and $AD$, respectively. Let $X$ be the point on the same side of the line $EF$ as the vertex $C$ such that $\triangle EXF$ and $\triangle BOA$ are congruent. Prove that $XC = XD$.

positive_text: Let triangle $\triangle UVW$ be acute with $UV < VW < WU$. Let $\omega$ be its circumcircle. Suppose there is a point $Y$ on $WU$ such that $UV = VY$ and $WY = VW$. Points $F, G \in \omega$ are such that $\angle UFG < 90^\circ$, $UF = FG$ and $VW = WG$. Let $R$ be the intersection of $UG$ with the tangent to $\omega$ at $V$, and let $S$ be the intersection of $UV$ with the tangent to $\omega$ at $W$. Prove that the foot of the perpendicular from $F$ onto $RS$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle RUV$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be acute with $AB < BC < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose there exists $X \in AB$ such that $AB = BX$ and $AX = BC$. Let $D, E \in \Gamma$ with $\angle ADB < 90^\circ$, $DA = DB$, and $BC = CE$. Let $P$ be the intersection of $AE$ with the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $B$, and let $Q$ be the intersection of $AB$ with the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $C$. Prove that the projection of $D$ onto $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle PAB$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be acute with $AB < BC < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Suppose there exists $X \in AC$ such that $AB = BX$ and $AX = BC$. Let $D, E \in \Gamma$ with $\angle ADB < 90^\circ$, $DA = DB$, and $BC = CE$. Let $P$ be the intersection of $AE$ with the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $C$, and let $Q$ be the intersection of $AB$ with the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $B$. Prove that the projection of $D$ onto $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle PAB$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 3$ be a natural number. On a circular table with $n$ seats labeled $0$ to $n-1$, Alice and Bob each choose a seat. Alice then moves first, and on the $k$-th move (for $k = 1$ to $2n$), Alice moves $k$ seats either clockwise or counterclockwise, while Bob always moves $1$ seat in either direction. If at any point after a move, both are at the same seat, Alice wins; otherwise, Bob wins. Determine for each $n$ who has a winning strategy.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be a natural number. On the vertices of a regular $n$-gon, Anna and Bob place their tokens. Anna moves first, and on her $k$-th turn, she moves $k^2$ positions clockwise or counterclockwise. Bob moves $1$ position clockwise or counterclockwise each turn. If the tokens ever meet, Anna wins. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine for each $n$ who has a winning strategy.

Let $n \ge 3$ be a natural number. On the vertices of a regular $n$-gon, Anna and Bob place their tokens. Anna moves first and on her $k$-th turn moves $k$ positions clockwise or counterclockwise. Bob, however, can only move in one fixed direction (say, clockwise) on his $k$-th turn. If the tokens ever meet, Anna wins. Otherwise, Bob wins. Determine for each $n$ who has a winning strategy.

positive_text: In an acute triangle $PQR$ with $PQ < PR$, let $K$ be the orthocentre, $\Omega$ the circumcircle, and $S$ the circumcentre. Let $N$ be the midpoint of $QR$, and let $E$ be a point such that $PEKS$ forms a parallelogram. Suppose a point $T$ lies on $\Omega$ on the opposite side of $EK$ from $P$ and satisfies $\angle ET K + \angle EKP = 90^\circ$. Let $Z$ be the midpoint of $ST$. Prove that if $NZ = SP$ then $SP = 2SK$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, orthocentre $H$, circumcircle $\Gamma$ and circumcentre $O$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $D$ be a point such that $ADOH$ is a parallelogram. Suppose that there exists a point $X$ on $\Gamma$ and on the opposite side of $DH$ to $A$ such that $\angle DXH + \angle DHA = 180^\circ$. Let $Y$ be the midpoint of $OX$. Prove that if $MY = OA$ then $OA = 2OH$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, orthocentre $H$, circumcircle $\Gamma$ and circumcentre $O$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $D$ be a point such that $ADOH$ is a parallelogram. Suppose that there exists a point $X$ on $\Gamma$ and on the opposite side of $DH$ to $A$ such that $\angle DXH + \angle DHA = 90^\circ$. Let $Y$ be the midpoint of $HX$. Prove that if $MY = OA$ then $OA = 2OH$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, orthocentre $H$, circumcircle $\Gamma$ and circumcentre $O$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and let $D$ be a point such that $ADOH$ is a parallelogram. Suppose that there exists a point $X$ on $\Gamma$ and on the opposite side of $DH$ to $A$ such that $\angle DXH + \angle DHA = 90^\circ$. Let $Y$ be the midpoint of $OX$. Prove that if $MY = 2OA$ then $OA = 2OH$.

positive_text:
Suppose $ F: \pi \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfies
$$
 F(P) + F(Q) + F(R) = F(O') + F(M) + F(K)
$$
for any acute triangle $ PQR $, where $ O' $ is the circumcenter, $ M $ is the centroid, and $ K $ is the orthocenter. Prove that $ F $ is constant.

negatives.text:
Let $ f: \pi \to \mathbb{R} $ be a function such that
$$
 f(A) + f(B) + f(C) = f(O) + f(G) + f(H)
$$
for any right triangle $ ABC $ with circumcenter $ O $, centroid $ G $, and orthocenter $ H $. Prove that $ f $ is constant.

Let $ f: \pi \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfy
$$
 f(A) + f(B) + f(C) = f(G) + f(H) + f(I)
$$
for any acute triangle $ ABC $ with centroid $ G $, orthocenter $ H $, and incenter $ I $. Prove that $ f $ is constant.

Let $ f: \pi \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfy
$$
 f(A) + f(B) + f(C) = f(O) + f(G) + f(H)
$$
for any triangle $ ABC $ (not necessarily acute) with circumcenter $ O $, centroid $ G $, and orthocenter $ H $. Prove that $ f $ is constant.

positive_text:
Let $ m $ be a positive integer. Determine all sequences $ (b_n)_{n \ge 1} $ of positive integers satisfying
$$
 b_{n+2}(b_{n+1} - m) = b_n(b_{n+1} + m)
$$
for all $ n \ge 1 $.

negatives.text:
Let $ k $ be a positive integer. Find all sequences $ (a_n)_{n \ge 1} $ of positive integers such that
$$
 a_{n+2}(a_{n+1} + k) = a_n(a_{n+1} - k)
$$
for all $ n \ge 1 $.

Let $ k $ be a positive integer. Find all sequences $ (a_n)_{n \ge 1} $ of positive integers such that
$$
 a_{n+2}^2(a_{n+1} - k) = a_n^2(a_{n+1} + k)
$$
for all $ n \ge 1 $.

Let $ k $ be a positive integer. Find all sequences $ (a_n)_{n \ge 1} $ of positive integers such that
$$
 a_{n+2}(a_{n+1} - k) = a_{n+1}(a_{n+1} + k)
$$
for all $ n \ge 1 $.

positive_text:
Find all functions $ g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that
$$
 g(a + b g(a)) + b = a b + g(a + b)
$$
for all real numbers $ a, b $.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) + y = x y - f(x + y)
$$
for all real numbers $ x, y $.

Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) + y = x y + f(x - y)
$$
for all real numbers $ x, y $.

Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that
$$
 f(x + y f(x)) + y = x y + f(x + y)
$$
for all real numbers $ x $ and all $ y > 0 $.

positive_text: Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be positive real numbers satisfying $x^2y + x^2z + y^2x + y^2z + z^2x + z^2y = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{xy + yz + zx}{1 + 2xyz} \le \frac{(x + y + z)^2}{4}.$$

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers with $a^2b + b^2c + c^2a = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{ab + bc + ca}{1 + 2abc} \le \frac{(a + b + c)^2}{4}.$$
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers with $a^2b + a^2c + b^2a + b^2c + c^2a + c^2b = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{ab + bc + ca}{1 + abc} \le \frac{(a + b + c)^2}{4}.$$
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive real numbers with $a^2b + a^2c + b^2a + b^2c + c^2a + c^2b = 1$. Prove that $$\frac{ab + bc + ca}{1 + 2abc} \le \frac{(a + b + c)^3}{4}.$$

positive_text: There are $n$ nodes in a network, where $n \geq 100$ is a positive integer. Some pairs of nodes are connected by bidirectional edges. For two nodes $A$ and $B$, a route is a sequence of distinct nodes $C_0, C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_k, C_{k+1}$, such that there are edges between $C_i$ and $C_{i+1}$ for every $0 \leq i \leq k$, with $C_0 = A$ and $C_{k+1} = B$. A longest route between $A$ and $B$ is a route with the maximum number of nodes. A shortest route is a route with the minimum number of nodes. If $A$ and $B$ are directly connected, that is the shortest route. Suppose that for any pair of nodes $A$ and $B$ in the network, there exist a longest route and a shortest route between them that share no intermediate nodes. Determine all possible numbers of edges in the network for a given $n$.

negatives.text: There are $n$ cities in a country, where $n \geq 100$ is a positive integer. Some pairs of cities are connected by (two-way) flights. For any two cities $A$ and $B$, there exists a path between them. Suppose that for any pair of cities $A$ and $B$, there exists a unique shortest path and a unique longest path between them that share no cities except $A$ and $B$. Find all possible numbers of flights in the country.

There are $n$ cities in a country, where $n \geq 100$ is a positive integer. Some pairs of cities are connected by (two-way) flights. For any two cities $A$ and $B$, there exists a path between them. Suppose that for any pair of cities $A$ and $B$, there exist a long path and a short path between them that share at most one intermediate city. Find all possible numbers of flights in the country.

There are $n$ cities in a country, where $n \geq 100$ is a positive integer. Some pairs of cities are connected by (two-way) flights. For any two cities $A$ and $B$, there exists a path between them. Suppose that for any pair of cities $A$ and $B$, there exist a long path and a short path between them such that the long path is exactly one city longer than the short path. Find all possible numbers of flights in the country.

positive_text: Let triangle $\triangle PQR$ have $PQ < PR$, and let $S$ be a point on side $PR$ such that $PS = \frac{PR - PQ}{2}$. Points $M$ and $N$ are on the line through $P$ parallel to $QR$ such that $QM = RN$ and line $PR$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle SMN$. Prove that the tangents to the circumcircle of $\triangle SMN$ at $M$ and $N$ intersect on line $QR$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be a point on the side $AC$ such that $AD = \frac{AB - AC}{2}$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are on the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ such that $BX = CY$ and line $AB$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$. Prove that the tangents to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$ at points $X$ and $Y$ meet on line $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be a point on the side $AC$ such that $AD = \frac{AC - AB}{2}$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are on the line through $B$ parallel to $AC$ such that $BX = CY$ and line $AC$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$. Prove that the tangents to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$ at points $X$ and $Y$ meet on line $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be a point on the side $AC$ such that $AD = \frac{AC - AB}{2}$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are on the line through $A$ parallel to $BC$ such that $AX = AY$ and line $AC$ is tangent to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$. Prove that the tangents to the circumcircle of $\triangle XDY$ at points $X$ and $Y$ meet on line $BC$.

positive_text: In triangle $\triangle XYZ$ with $\angle YXZ = 2\angle XYZ$ and $XY < XZ$, a point $M$ is located on segment $XZ$ such that $MZ = XY + XM$. Let $R$ be the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle XYM$, and let the line through $R$ parallel to $XY$ meet $YM$ at $N$. Prove that $XN$ passes through the midpoint of segment $YZ$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC = 3\angle CBA$ and $AB < AC$. A point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $PC = AB + AP$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle ABP$, and let the line through $O$ parallel to $AB$ intersect $BP$ at $Q$. Show that $AQ$ passes through the midpoint of segment $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC = 2\angle CBA$ and $AB < AC$. A point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $PC = AB - AP$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle ABP$, and let the line through $O$ parallel to $AB$ intersect $BP$ at $Q$. Show that $AQ$ passes through the midpoint of segment $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC = 2\angle CBA$ and $AB < AC$. A point $P$ lies on segment $AC$ such that $PC = AB + AP$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle ABP$, and let the line through $O$ perpendicular to $AB$ intersect $BP$ at $Q$. Show that $AQ$ passes through the midpoint of segment $BC$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle XYZ$ be an acute triangle with $XY < XZ$, inscribed in circle $\Gamma_1$ with center $O$. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle XYZ$ and let $M$ be the midpoint of $YZ$. Let $\Gamma_2$ be the circumcircle of $\triangle YHZ$. If the line $OH$ intersects $\Gamma_2$ at $K \neq H$, and the line $MK$ intersects $\Gamma_2$ again at $P \neq K$, show that the tangents to $\Gamma_1$ at $X$ and to $\Gamma_2$ at $P$ intersect on the circumcircle of $\triangle XKP$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in a circle $\omega_1$ with center $O$. Let $H$ be the orthocenter and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $\omega_2$ be the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BHC$. If the line $HO$ intersects $\omega_2$ at $K \neq H$, and the line $MP$ intersects $\omega_2$ at $P$ such that $P = K$, show that the tangent to $\omega_1$ at $A$ and the tangent to $\omega_2$ at $P$ intersect on the circumcircle of $\triangle APK$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in circle $\omega_1$ with center $O$. Let $H$ be the orthocenter and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $\omega_2$ be the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BHC$. If the line $OH$ intersects $\omega_2$ at $K \neq H$, and the line $MK$ intersects $\omega_2$ again at $P \neq K$, prove that the tangent to $\omega_1$ at $A$ and the tangent to $\omega_2$ at $K$ intersect on the circumcircle of $\triangle APK$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$, inscribed in a circle $\omega_1$ with center $O$. Let $H$ be the orthocenter and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let $\omega_2$ be the circumcircle of triangle $\triangle BHC$. If the line $OH$ intersects $\omega_2$ at $K \neq H$, and the line $MK$ intersects $\omega_2$ again at $P \neq K$, prove that the tangent to $\omega_1$ at $A$ and the tangent to $\omega_2$ at $P$ intersect on the circumcircle of $\triangle AHP$.

positive_text: Show that there are infinitely many natural number pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying $a^2 - 7b^2 = 1$.

negatives.text: Prove that the equation $x^2 - 7y^2 = -1$ has infinitely many solutions in natural numbers.
Prove that the equation $x^2 - 8y^2 = 1$ has infinitely many solutions in natural numbers.

positive_text: Let $x_{0} > 0$, $k > 0$ and $$x_{n+1} = \frac{x_{n} + k}{1 - x_{n} k}, \quad n = 0, 1, \ldots$$ Is it possible that $x_{0}, x_{1}, \ldots, x_{1989}$ are all positive, but $x_{1990} < 0$?

negatives.text: Let $a_{0} > 0$, $c > 0$ and $$a_{n+1} = \frac{a_{n} + c}{1 + a_{n} c}, \quad n = 0, 1, \ldots$$ Is it possible that the first 1990 terms $a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{1989}$ are all positive but $a_{1990} < 0$?

Let $a_{0} > 0$, $c > 0$ and $$a_{n+1} = \frac{a_{n}^2 + c}{1 - a_{n} c}, \quad n = 0, 1, \ldots$$ Is it possible that the first 1990 terms $a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{1989}$ are all positive but $a_{1990} < 0$?

Let $a_{0} > 0$, $c > 0$ and $$a_{n+1} = \frac{a_{n} + c}{1 - a_{n} c^2}, \quad n = 0, 1, \ldots$$ Is it possible that the first 1990 terms $a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{1989}$ are all positive but $a_{1990} < 0$?

positive_text: Let $@$ be a binary operation on real numbers such that $a @ b$ is a real number for all $a, b$. Construct an identity that holds for all real $a, b, c$ if $@$ is either commutative or associative, but may not hold otherwise.

negatives.text: Let $*$ be a binary operation on real numbers. Devise an identity involving $*$ that is always true if $*$ is both commutative and associative, and false if $*$ is only one of them.

positive_text: In quadrilateral $WXY Z$, suppose $|WZ| = |XY|$ and $\angle W + \angle X = 120^\circ$. Let $Q$ be a point such that $Q$ and $W$ lie on opposite sides of the line $YZ$ and triangle $QYZ$ is equilateral. Prove that triangle $QWX$ is also equilateral.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $|AD| = |BC|$ and $\angle A + \angle B = 90^\circ$. Let $P$ be a point outside the quadrilateral such that $P$ and $A$ lie on opposite sides of the line $DC$ and triangle $DPC$ is equilateral. Prove that triangle $APB$ is also equilateral.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $|AD| = |BC|$ and $\angle A + \angle B = 120^\circ$. Let $P$ be a point outside the quadrilateral such that $P$ and $A$ lie on the same side of the line $DC$ and triangle $DPC$ is equilateral. Prove that triangle $APB$ is also equilateral.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $|AD| = |BC|$ and $\angle A + \angle B = 120^\circ$. Let $P$ be a point outside the quadrilateral such that $P$ and $A$ lie on opposite sides of the line $DC$ and triangle $DPC$ is isosceles with $|DP| = |DC|$. Prove that triangle $APB$ is also equilateral.

positive_text: \text{Prove that there are no positive integers } a \text{ and } b > 1 \text{ such that } (k - 1)^{2k + 1} + k^{2k + 1} = a^{b}, \text{ where } k = 103.

negatives.text: \text{Find all positive integers } n \text{ and } m > 1 \text{ such that } 102^{1991} - 103^{1991} = n^{m}.
\text{Prove that there are no positive integers } n \text{ and } m > 1 \text{ such that } 102^{1990} + 103^{1990} = n^{m}.
\text{Prove that there are no positive integers } n \text{ and } m > 1 \text{ such that } 102^{1991} + 103^{1991} + 1 = n^{m}.

positive_text: Let $P(a, 1/a)$ and $Q(b, 1/b)$ lie on the hyperbola $y = 1/x$ with $0 < a < b$, and suppose the distance between $P$ and $Q$ is twice the length of $OP$. Let $R$ be the midpoint of $PQ$. Prove that the angle between the $x$-axis and $OP$ is three times the angle between the $x$-axis and $OR$.

negatives.text: Let $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$ lie on the curve $y = 1/x$ with $0 < x_1 < x_2$, and suppose $|AB| = |OA|$. Let $C$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Prove that the angle between the $x$-axis and $OA$ is three times the angle between the $x$-axis and $OC$.

Let $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$ lie on the curve $y = x$ with $0 < x_1 < x_2$, and suppose $|AB| = 2|OA|$. Let $C$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Prove that the angle between the $x$-axis and $OA$ is three times the angle between the $x$-axis and $OC$.

Let $A(x_1, y_1)$ and $B(x_2, y_2)$ lie on the curve $y = 1/x$ with $0 < x_1 < x_2$, and suppose $|AB| = 2|OA|$. Let $C$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Prove that the angle between the $x$-axis and $OA$ is equal to the angle between the $x$-axis and $OC$.

positive_text: Let $\lfloor x \rfloor$ be the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$, and let $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$. Find all real numbers $x$ satisfying $$ \lfloor x \rfloor \cdot \{x\} = 1991x. $$

negatives.text: Let $[x]$ be the integer part of $x$, and $\{x\} = x - [x]$. Solve the equation $$ [x] + \{x\} = 1991x. $$
Let $[x]$ be the integer part of $x$, and $\{x\} = x - [x]$. Solve the equation $$ [x] \cdot \{x\} = 1991. $$
Let $[x]$ be the integer part of $x$, and $\{x\} = x - [x]$. Solve the equation $$ [x]^2 + \{x\} = 1991x. $$

positive_text: \text{Let } \alpha, \beta, \gamma \text{ be the angles of an acute triangle. Prove that } \sin \alpha + \sin \beta > \cos \alpha + \cos \beta + \cos \gamma

negatives.text: \text{Let } A, B, C \text{ be the angles of an acute-angled triangle. Prove the inequality } \sin A + \sin B > \cos A + \cos B - \cos C
\text{Let } A, B, C \text{ be the angles of an acute-angled triangle. Prove the inequality } \sin A + \sin B + \sin C > \cos A + \cos B + \cos C
\text{Let } A, B, C \text{ be the angles of an acute-angled triangle. Prove the inequality } \sin A + \sin B > \cos A + \cos B + \cos^2 C

positive_text: Determine how many real values of $x$ satisfy the equation $k e^{t} = t^{3}$.

negatives.text: Find the number of solutions of the equation $a e^{-x} = x^{3}$.
Find the number of solutions of the equation $a e^{x} = x^{2}$.
Find the number of integer solutions of the equation $a e^{x} = x^{3}$.

positive_text:
Determine all quartic polynomials $ q(x) $ with the following properties:
(i) $ q(x) $ is even, i.e., $ q(x) = q(-x) $ for all $ x $.
(ii) $ q(x) $ is non-negative for all real $ x $.
(iii) $ q(0) = 1 $.
(iv) $ q(x) $ has precisely two local minima at $ x_1 $ and $ x_2 $, where the distance between them is $ 2 $.

negatives.text:
Find all quartic polynomials $ s(x) $ such that:
(i) $ s(x) = s(-x) $ for all $ x $.
(ii) $ s(x) \geq 0 $ for all $ x $.
(iii) $ s(0) = 1 $.
(iv) $ s(x) $ has exactly two local maximum points $ x_1 $ and $ x_2 $ with $ |x_1 - x_2| = 2 $.

Find all degree-4 polynomials $ t(x) $ such that:
(i) $ t(x) = t(-x) $ for all $ x $.
(ii) $ t(x) > 0 $ for all $ x $.
(iii) $ t(0) = 1 $.
(iv) $ t(x) $ has exactly two local minima $ x_1 $ and $ x_2 $ with $ |x_1 - x_2| = 1 $.

Find all fourth degree polynomials $ u(x) $ such that:
(i) $ u(x) = -u(-x) $ for all $ x $.
(ii) $ u(x) \geq 0 $ for all $ x $.
(iii) $ u(0) = 1 $.
(iv) $ u(x) $ has exactly two local minima $ x_1 $ and $ x_2 $ with $ |x_1 - x_2| = 2 $.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{Q}^{+}$ be the set of positive rational numbers. Prove that there exists a unique function $f: \mathbb{Q}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}^{+}$ satisfying:

(i) For all $0 < r < \frac{1}{2}$, $f(r) = 1 + f\left(\frac{r}{1 - 2r}\right)$.

(ii) For all $r$ such that $1 < r \leq 2$, $f(r) = 1 + f(r - 1)$.

(iii) For all $r$, $f(r) \cdot f\left(\frac{1}{r}\right) = 1$.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{Q}^{+}$ be the set of positive rational numbers. Suppose $f: \mathbb{Q}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}^{+}$ satisfies:

(i) If $0 < q < \frac{1}{2}$, then $f(q) = 1 + f\left(\frac{q}{1 + 2q}\right)$.

(ii) If $1 < q \leq 2$, then $f(q) = 1 + f(q - 1)$.

(iii) $f(q) \cdot f\left(\frac{1}{q}\right) = 1$ for all $q$.

Prove that $f$ is unique.

Let $\mathbb{Q}^{+}$ be the set of positive rational numbers. Show that there exists a unique function $f: \mathbb{Q}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}^{+}$ such that:

(i) If $0 < q < \frac{1}{2}$, then $f(q) = 1 + f\left(\frac{2q}{1 - 2q}\right)$.

(ii) If $1 < q \leq 2$, then $f(q) = 1 + f(q - 1)$.

(iii) $f(q) \cdot f\left(\frac{1}{q}\right) = 1$ for all $q$.

Let $\mathbb{Q}^{+}$ be the set of positive rational numbers. Suppose $f: \mathbb{Q}^{+} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}^{+}$ satisfies:

(i) If $0 < q < \frac{1}{2}$, then $f(q) = 1 + f\left(\frac{q}{1 - 2q}\right)$.

(ii) If $1 < q \leq 2$, then $f(q) = 1 + f(1 - q)$.

(iii) $f(q) \cdot f\left(\frac{1}{q}\right) = 1$ for all $q$.

Prove that $f$ is unique.

positive_text: \text{Let } a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} > 0 \text{ and } b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n} > 0. \text{ Prove that} \$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_{i} b_{i}} \geq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_{i} + b_{i})^{2}} \$$.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that for any positive } x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \text{ and } y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n} \text{ the inequality} \$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_{i} y_{i}} \geq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} - y_{i})^{2}} \$$ holds.

\text{Prove that for any positive } x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \text{ and } y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n} \text{ the inequality} \$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_{i} y_{i}} \geq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}^{2} + y_{i}^{2})} \$$ holds.

\text{Prove that for any positive } x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \text{ and } y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n} \text{ the inequality} \$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_{i}^{2} + y_{i}^{2}} \geq \frac{4 n^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i} + y_{i})^{2}} \$$ holds.

positive_text: Let $b = \sqrt[1992]{1992}$. Determine whether $$ b^{b^{b^{b}}} $$ is greater than $1992$.
Let $ f(x) = x^3 + p x^2 + q x + r $ be a cubic polynomial with $ q < 0 $ and $ p q = 9 r $. Show that $ f(x) $ has three distinct real roots.

negatives.text: Let $ f(x) = x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c $ be a cubic polynomial with $ b < 0 $ and $ a b = 3 c $. Prove that $ f(x) $ has three different real roots.
Suppose $ f(x) = x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c $ satisfies $ b > 0 $ and $ a b = 9 c $. Prove that $ f(x) $ has three different real roots.
Let $ f(x) = x^3 + a x^2 + b x + c $ be a cubic polynomial with $ b < 0 $ and $ a + b = 9 c $. Prove that $ f(x) $ has three different real roots.

positive_text: Define the operation $\star$ on integers by $a \star b = a + b - a b$. Determine all integer triples $(p, q, r)$ for which $(p \star q) \star r + (q \star r) \star p + (r \star p) \star q = 0$.

negatives.text: Let $a \circ b = a + b - a b$. Find all integer triples $(x, y, z)$ such that $(x \circ y) \circ z + (y \circ z) \circ x + (z \circ x) \circ y = 1$.
Let $a \circ b = a + b + a b$. Find all integer triples $(x, y, z)$ such that $(x \circ y) \circ z + (y \circ z) \circ x + (z \circ x) \circ y = 0$.
Let $a \circ b = a + b - a b$. Find all integer triples $(x, y, z)$ such that $(x \circ y) \circ z + (y \circ z) \circ x + (z \circ x) \circ y = -x - y - z$.

positive_text: Let $PQ$ and $RS$ be two perpendicular diameters of a circle $\mathcal{C}$. A line $\ell$ is tangent to $\mathcal{C}$ at point $Q$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be two points on $\mathcal{C}$, symmetric with respect to the diameter $RS$. Let $\ell$ intersect the lines $PX$ and $PY$ at points $X'$ and $Y'$, respectively. Prove that $|QX'| \cdot |QY'| = |PQ|^2$.

negatives.text: Let $NS$ and $EW$ be two perpendicular diameters of a circle $\mathcal{C}$. A line $l$ intersects $\mathcal{C}$ at point $S$. Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on $\mathcal{C}$, symmetric with respect to the diameter $EW$. Denote the intersection points of $l$ with the lines $NA$ and $NB$ by $A'$ and $B'$, respectively. Show that $|SA'| \cdot |SB'| = |SN|^2$.

Let $NS$ and $EW$ be two perpendicular diameters of a circle $\mathcal{C}$. A line $l$ touches $\mathcal{C}$ at point $S$. Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on $\mathcal{C}$, not necessarily symmetric with respect to the diameter $EW$. Denote the intersection points of $l$ with the lines $NA$ and $NB$ by $A'$ and $B'$, respectively. Show that $|SA'| \cdot |SB'| = |SN|^2$.

Let $NS$ and $EW$ be two perpendicular diameters of a circle $\mathcal{C}$. A line $l$ touches $\mathcal{C}$ at point $S$. Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on $\mathcal{C}$, symmetric with respect to the diameter $NS$. Denote the intersection points of $l$ with the lines $NA$ and $NB$ by $A'$ and $B'$, respectively. Show that $|SA'| \cdot |SB'| = |SN|^2$.

positive_text:
Let $\angle A, \angle B, \angle C$ be the angles of triangle $ABC$ with side lengths $x, y, z$ opposite to these angles, respectively. Show that
$$
x \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\angle B} + \frac{1}{\angle C}\right) + y \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\angle C} + \frac{1}{\angle A}\right) + z \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\angle A} + \frac{1}{\angle B}\right) \geq 2 \cdot\left(\frac{x}{\angle A} + \frac{y}{\angle B} + \frac{z}{\angle C}\right)
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the angles of a triangle opposite to its sides with lengths $a, b$ and $c$, respectively. Prove the inequality
$$
a \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\beta^2}+\frac{1}{\gamma^2}\right)+b \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\gamma^2}+\frac{1}{\alpha^2}\right)+c \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\alpha^2}+\frac{1}{\beta^2}\right) \geq 2 \cdot\left(\frac{a}{\alpha}+\frac{b}{\beta}+\frac{c}{\gamma}\right)
$$

Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the angles of a triangle opposite to its sides with lengths $a, b$ and $c$, respectively. Prove the inequality
$$
a \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\beta}+\frac{1}{\gamma}\right)+b \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\gamma}+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)+c \cdot\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta}\right) \geq 2 \cdot\left(\frac{a}{\alpha}+\frac{b}{\beta}+\frac{c}{\gamma} + 1\right)
$$

positive_text: Let $ f(x) $ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that there exist integers $ a $ and $ b $ with $ f(a) = 1 $ and $ f(b) = 3 $. Is it possible that $ f(x) = 2 $ has two distinct integer solutions?

negatives.text: Let $ p(x) $ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that both equations $ p(x) = 1 $ and $ p(x) = -3 $ have integer solutions. Can the equation $ p(x) = -2 $ have two different integer solutions?

Let $ p(x) $ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that both equations $ p(x) = 1 $ and $ p(x) = 3 $ have integer solutions. Can the equation $ p(x) = 2 $ have two different rational solutions?

Let $ p(x) $ be a polynomial with rational coefficients such that both equations $ p(x) = 1 $ and $ p(x) = 3 $ have integer solutions. Can the equation $ p(x) = 2 $ have two different integer solutions?

positive_text: \text{Let } p > 2 \text{ be a prime number and } \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{1}{k^3} = \frac{a}{b} \text{ where } a \text{ and } b \text{ are relatively prime. Prove that } p \mid a.

negatives.text: \text{Let } p > 2 \text{ be a prime number and } 1 + \frac{1}{2^{2}} + \frac{1}{3^{2}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{(p-1)^{2}} = \frac{m}{n} \text{ where } m \text{ and } n \text{ are relatively prime. Show that } m \text{ is a multiple of } p.

\text{Let } p > 2 \text{ be a prime number and } 1 + \frac{1}{2^{3}} + \frac{1}{3^{3}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{p^{3}} = \frac{m}{n} \text{ where } m \text{ and } n \text{ are relatively prime. Show that } m \text{ is a multiple of } p.

\text{Let } p > 2 \text{ be a prime number and } 1 + \frac{1}{2^{3}} + \frac{1}{3^{3}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{(p-1)^{3}} = \frac{m}{n} \text{ where } m \text{ and } n \text{ are relatively prime. Show that } n \text{ is a multiple of } p.

positive_text: Prove that for every integer $x \geq 5$, there are integers $y$ and $z$, with $z \geq y \geq x$, such that a triangle with side lengths $x, y, z$ is right-angled.

negatives.text: Show that for any integer $a \geq 5$ there exist integers $b$ and $c$, $c \geq b \geq a$, such that $a, b, c$ are the lengths of the sides of an acute triangle.
Show that for any integer $a \geq 5$ there exist integers $b$ and $c$, $c \geq b \geq a$, such that $a^2 + b^2 = c^2 + 1$.
Show that for any integer $a \geq 5$ there exist integers $b$ and $c$, $c \geq b \geq a$, such that $a, b, c$ are the lengths of the sides of a triangle with integer area.

positive_text:
Determine all real-valued functions $g$ defined on $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ such that:
(1) $g(1) = 1$,
(2) $g\left(\frac{1}{a+b}\right) = g\left(\frac{1}{a}\right) + g\left(\frac{1}{b}\right)$ for all $a, b, a+b \ne 0$,
(3) $(a+b) g(a+b) = ab g(a) g(b)$ for all $a, b, a+b \ne 0$.

negatives.text:
Find all real-valued functions $f$ defined on $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ such that:
(1) $f(1) = 1$,
(2) $f\left(\frac{1}{x+y}\right) = f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) + f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$ for all $x, y, x+y \ne 0$,
(3) $(x+y) f(x+y) = x y f(x) f(y)$ for all $x, y, x+y > 0$.

Find all real-valued functions $f$ defined on $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ such that:
(1) $f(1) = 1$,
(2) $f\left(\frac{1}{x+y}\right) = f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) + f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$ for all $x, y, x+y \ne 0$,
(3) $(x+y) f(x+y) = x y f(x) f(y)^2$ for all $x, y, x+y \ne 0$.

Find all real-valued functions $f$ defined on $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ such that:
(1) $f(1) = 2$,
(2) $f\left(\frac{1}{x+y}\right) = f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) + f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$ for all $x, y, x+y \ne 0$,
(3) $(x+y) f(x+y) = x y f(x) f(y)$ for all $x, y, x+y \ne 0$.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ have an external angle at vertex $R$, and let $m$ be the bisector of that external angle. If $M$ is the midpoint of segment $PQ$, and the line through $M$ parallel to $m$ intersects line $PR$ at point $S$, find the length of $|RS|$, given that $|PR|=7$ and $|RQ|=4$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, let $l$ be the bisector of the internal angle at $C$. The line through the midpoint $O$ of segment $AB$ parallel to $l$ meets the line $AC$ at $E$. Determine $|CE|$, if $|AC|=7$ and $|CB|=4$.

In triangle $ABC$, let $l$ be the bisector of the external angle at $C$. The line through the midpoint $O$ of segment $AB$ parallel to $l$ meets the line $BC$ at $E$. Determine $|CE|$, if $|AC|=7$ and $|CB|=4$.

In triangle $ABC$, let $l$ be the bisector of the external angle at $C$. The line through the midpoint $O$ of segment $AB$ parallel to $l$ meets the line $AC$ at $E$. Determine $|AE|$, if $|AC|=7$ and $|CB|=4$.

positive_text: Suppose $x$ and $m$ are positive integers such that $x^2 + m$ divides the product $(x - 1)(x)(x + 1)$. Prove that $m \geq x$.

negatives.text: Let $a$ and $k$ be positive integers such that $a^{2} - k$ divides $(a-1)a(a+1)$. Prove that $k \geq a$.
Let $a$ and $k$ be positive integers such that $a^{2} + k$ divides $(a - 1)(a + 2)$. Prove that $k \geq a$.
Let $a$ and $k$ be positive integers such that $a^{2} + k$ divides $(a - 1)^2 a^2$. Prove that $k \geq a$.

positive_text: Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be positive integers such that $x^2 + y^2 = z^2$, with $x$ and $z$ both odd, and $x$, $y$, and $z$ pairwise coprime. Show that $y + z$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive integers such that $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, with $a$ and $c$ both odd, and $a$, $b$, and $c$ pairwise coprime. Show that $b - c$ is a perfect square.
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be positive integers such that $a^2 - b^2 = c^2$, with $a$ and $c$ both odd, and $a$, $b$, and $c$ pairwise coprime. Show that $b + c$ is a perfect square.

positive_text: Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be real numbers such that $|x| \geq |y+z|$, $|y| \geq |z+x|$, and $|z| \geq |x+y|$. Show that $x+y+z=0$.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be real numbers such that $|a| \geq |b| + |c|$, $|b| \geq |c| + |a|$, and $|c| \geq |a| + |b|$. Prove that $a+b+c=0$.
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be real numbers such that $|a| \geq |b-c|$, $|b| \geq |c-a|$, and $|c| \geq |a-b|$. Prove that $a+b+c=0$.
Let $a$, $b$, and $c$ be real numbers such that $|a| \geq |b+c|$, $|b| \geq |c-a|$, and $|c| \geq |a+b|$. Prove that $a+b+c=0$.

positive_text:
Let $g$ be a function from the integers to the real numbers satisfying the identity
$$
g(x) = g\left(x^{2} + x + 1\right)
$$
for every integer $x$. Determine
(a) all such $g$ that satisfy $g(-x) = g(x)$,
(b) all such $g$ that satisfy $g(-x) = -g(x)$.

negatives.text:
Let $f$ be a function from the integers to the real numbers satisfying
$$
f(x) = f\left(x^{2} - x + 1\right)
$$
for all integers $x$. Find
(a) all even functions,
(b) all odd functions of this kind.

Let $f$ be a function from the integers to the real numbers satisfying
$$
f(x) = f\left(x^{2} + x - 1\right)
$$
for all integers $x$. Find
(a) all even functions,
(b) all odd functions of this kind.

Let $f$ be a function from the integers to the real numbers satisfying
$$
f(x) = f\left(x^{3} + x + 1\right)
$$
for all integers $x$. Find
(a) all even functions,
(b) all odd functions of this kind.

positive_text: Using each of the digits $1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$, and $9$ exactly once, construct a three-digit number $P$, two two-digit numbers $Q$ and $R$ with $Q < R$, and a single-digit number $S$. If $P + S = Q + R = 143$, how many such constructions are possible?

negatives.text: Using the digits $1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$, and $9$ exactly once, form a three-digit number $A$, two two-digit numbers $B$ and $C$, and a one-digit number $D$. If $A - D = B + C = 143$, how many such combinations are possible?

Using the digits $1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$, and $9$ exactly once, construct a three-digit number $A$, two two-digit numbers $B$ and $C$, and a one-digit number $D$. If $A + D = B - C = 143$, how many such combinations are possible?

Using the digits $1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8$, and $9$ exactly once, form a three-digit number $A$, two two-digit numbers $B$ and $C$, and a one-digit number $D$. If $A + D = B + C = 142$, how many such combinations are possible?

positive_text: Let $PQRS$ be a convex cyclic quadrilateral. Denote by $r_p, r_q, r_r, r_s$ the inradii of triangles $QRS$, $PRS$, $PQS$, and $PQR$ respectively. Show that $r_p + r_r = r_q + r_s$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral (not necessarily cyclic). Let $r_a, r_b, r_c, r_d$ be the inradii of triangles $BCD$, $ACD$, $ABD$, and $ABC$ respectively. Prove or disprove that $r_a + r_c = r_b + r_d$.

positive_text: Suppose $x, y, z, w$ are positive integers satisfying $xy = zw$. Show that $x + y + z + w$ is composite.

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c, d$ be positive integers such that $a^2 + b^2 = c^2 + d^2$. Prove that $a + b + c + d$ is not prime.
Let $a, b, c, d$ be positive integers such that $a + b = c + d$. Prove that $a + b + c + d$ is not prime.
Let $a, b, c, d$ be positive integers such that $ab = cd + 1$. Prove that $a + b + c + d$ is not prime.

positive_text: \begin{aligned} a_{1} & = 19, \\ a_{2} & = 95, \\ a_{n+2} & = \operatorname{lcm}(a_{n+1}, a_{n}) + a_{n}, \end{aligned} \text{for } n > 1. \text{ Find } \gcd(a_{1995}, a_{1996}).

negatives.text: \begin{aligned} b_{1} & = 19, \\ b_{2} & = 95, \\ b_{n+2} & = \gcd(b_{n+1}, b_{n}) + b_{n}, \end{aligned} \text{for } n > 1. \text{ Find } \gcd(b_{1995}, b_{1996}).
\begin{aligned} c_{1} & = 19, \\ c_{2} & = 95, \\ c_{n+2} & = \operatorname{lcm}(c_{n+1}, c_{n}) - c_{n}, \end{aligned} \text{for } n > 1. \text{ Find } \gcd(c_{1995}, c_{1996}).
\begin{aligned} d_{1} & = 19, \\ d_{2} & = 95, \\ d_{n+2} & = \operatorname{lcm}(d_{n+1}, d_{n}) + d_{n+1}, \end{aligned} \text{for } n > 1. \text{ Find } \gcd(d_{1995}, d_{1996}).

positive_text: Find all non-zero functions $ g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that $ g(a) g(b) = g(a - b) $ for all real numbers $ a $ and $ b $.

negatives.text: Find all non-zero functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that $ f(x) f(y) = f(x + y) $ for all real numbers $ x $ and $ y $.
Find all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $, not identically zero, such that $ f(x) + f(y) = f(x - y) $ for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R} $.
Find all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $, not identically zero, such that $ f(x) f(y) = f(x - y) + 1 $ for all real numbers $ x $ and $ y $.

positive_text:
a) Construct two infinite sets $X$ and $Y$ of non-negative integers such that every non-negative integer $n$ has a unique decomposition as $n = x + y$ with $x \in X$, $y \in Y$.

b) Show that in any such pair $(X, Y)$, one of the sets $X$ or $Y$ must consist only of multiples of some fixed integer $k > 1$.

negatives.text:
