\text{Let } PQR \text{ be a triangle with side lengths } PQ = r, QR = p, RP = q. Points } R_1, R_2 \text{ on } PQ, P_1, P_2 \text{ on } QR, Q_1, Q_2 \text{ on } RP \text{ are defined such that}\\
\begin{aligned}
\frac{RP_1}{p} &= \frac{RQ_2}{q} = \frac{p+q}{p+q+r}, \\
\frac{PQ_1}{q} &= \frac{PR_2}{r} = \frac{q+r}{p+q+r}, \\
\frac{QR_1}{r} &= \frac{QP_2}{p} = \frac{r+p}{p+q+r}.
\end{aligned}
\text{Show that the intersection points of lines } P_1R_2, R_1Q_2, Q_1P_2 \text{ lie on the circumcircle of } PQR.

negatives.text:
\text{In triangle } XYZ \text{ with sides } XY = z, YZ = x, ZX = y, points } Z_1, Z_2 \text{ on } XY, X_1, X_2 \text{ on } YZ, Y_1, Y_2 \text{ on } ZX \text{ satisfy}\\
\begin{aligned}
\frac{XZ_1}{x} &= \frac{XY_2}{y} = \frac{x+y}{x+y+z}, \\
\frac{YZ_1}{y} &= \frac{YX_2}{z} = \frac{y+z}{x+y+z}, \\
\frac{ZX_1}{z} &= \frac{ZY_2}{x} = \frac{z+x}{x+y+z}.
\end{aligned}
\text{Prove that the lines } X_1Z_2, Z_1Y_2, Y_1X_2 \text{ intersect at a point on the Euler circle of } XYZ.

\text{Let } LMN \text{ be a triangle with side lengths } LM = m, MN = l, NL = n. Points } N_1, N_2 \text{ on } LM, L_1, L_2 \text{ on } MN, M_1, M_2 \text{ on } NL \text{ are defined such that}\\
\begin{aligned}
\frac{NL_1}{l} &= \frac{NM_2}{n} = \frac{l+n}{l+m+n}, \\
\frac{ML_1}{n} &= \frac{MN_2}{m} = \frac{m+n}{l+m+n}, \\
\frac{LM_1}{m} &= \frac{LN_2}{l} = \frac{l+m}{l+m+n}.
\end{aligned}
\text{Prove that the lines } L_1N_2, N_1M_2, M_1L_2 \text{ intersect at a point on the angle bisector of } \angle LMN.

positive_text: \text{Show that } \frac{1}{a+b+1} - \frac{1}{(a+1)(b+1)} < \frac{1}{11} \text{ for all positive real numbers } a \text{ and } b.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x+y+1} - \frac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} > \frac{1}{11} \text{ for all positive } x \text{ and } y.
\text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x+y+1} - \frac{1}{(x-1)(y-1)} < \frac{1}{11} \text{ for all } x > 1, y > 1.
\text{Prove that } \frac{1}{x+y+1} - \frac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)} < \frac{1}{11} \text{ for all non-negative } x \text{ and } y.

positive_text: A square grid of size $n \times n$ with $n \ge 4$ is to be tiled with multiple layers of a 4-cell tile in the shape of a 3x2 rectangle missing one corner (rotations allowed). Determine all values of $n$ for which such a tiling is possible, with every cell covered the same number of times by tiles.

negatives.text: An $n \times n$ square with $n \ge 4$ is to be tiled with 4-cell tiles in the shape of a 2x2 square. Determine all values of $n$ for which such a tiling is possible.
A square grid of size $n \times n$ with $n \ge 4$ is to be tiled with 4-cell tiles shaped like a 3x2 rectangle with one interior cell missing. Determine all values of $n$ for which this is possible.

positive_text: Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be the graphs of the functions $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ and $f(x) = -\frac{1}{x}$, respectively. A line intersects $K_1$ at points $P$ and $Q$, and $K_2$ at points $R$ and $S$. The tangents to $K_1$ at $P$ and $Q$ meet at point $X$, and the tangents to $K_2$ at $R$ and $S$ meet at point $Y$. Show that $X$ and $Y$ are symmetric with respect to the origin.

negatives.text: Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be the graphs of the functions $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ and $f(x) = -\frac{1}{x} + 1$, respectively. A line intersects $K_1$ at points $P$ and $Q$, and $K_2$ at points $R$ and $S$. The tangents to $K_1$ at $P$ and $Q$ meet at point $X$, and the tangents to $K_2$ at $R$ and $S$ meet at point $Y$. Show that $X$ and $Y$ are symmetric with respect to the origin.

Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be the graphs of the functions $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ and $f(x) = -\frac{1}{x^2}$, respectively. A line intersects $K_1$ at points $P$ and $Q$, and $K_2$ at points $R$ and $S$. The tangents to $K_1$ at $P$ and $Q$ meet at point $X$, and the tangents to $K_2$ at $R$ and $S$ meet at point $Y$. Show that $X$ and $Y$ are symmetric with respect to the origin.

Let $K_1$ and $K_2$ be the graphs of the functions $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ and $f(x) = -\frac{1}{x}$, respectively. A line intersects $K_1$ at points $P$ and $Q$, and $K_2$ at points $R$ and $S$. The normals to $K_1$ at $P$ and $Q$ meet at point $X$, and the normals to $K_2$ at $R$ and $S$ meet at point $Y$. Show that $X$ and $Y$ are symmetric with respect to the origin.

positive_text: Two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ are defined by $y = \frac{1}{x}$ and $y = -\frac{1}{x}$. A line intersects $C_1$ at points $P$ and $Q$, and intersects $C_2$ at points $R$ and $S$. Let $O$ be the origin. Prove that the areas of triangles $OPR$ and $OQS$ are equal.

negatives.text: Two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ are defined by $y = \frac{1}{x^2}$ and $y = -\frac{1}{x^2}$. A line intersects $C_1$ at points $P$ and $Q$, and intersects $C_2$ at points $R$ and $S$. Let $O$ be the origin. Prove that the areas of triangles $OPR$ and $OQS$ are equal.

Two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ are defined by $y = \frac{1}{x}$ and $y = -\frac{1}{x}$. A line intersects $C_1$ at points $P$ and $Q$, and intersects $C_2$ at point $R$ only. Let $O$ be the origin. Prove that the areas of triangles $OPR$ and $OQP$ are equal.

Two curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ are defined by $y = \frac{1}{x}$ and $y = -\frac{1}{x}$. A line intersects $C_1$ at points $P$ and $Q$, and intersects $C_2$ at points $R$ and $S$. Let $O$ be the origin. Prove that the areas of triangles $OPQ$ and $ORS$ are equal.

positive_text: Let $P$ be a point on the curve $xy = 1$. Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be the points of tangency of the two lines through $P$ that are tangent to the curve $xy = -1$. Show that the line joining $P_1$ and $P_2$ is tangent to the curve $xy = 1$.

negatives.text: Let $P$ be a point on the parabola $y = x^2$. Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be the points of tangency of the two lines through $P$ that are tangent to the parabola $y = -x^2$. Show that the line joining $P_1$ and $P_2$ is tangent to the parabola $y = x^2$.

Let $P$ be a point on the hyperbola $xy = 1$. Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be the points of tangency of the two lines through $P$ that are tangent to the hyperbola $xy = -1$. Show that the line joining $P_1$ and $P_2$ is tangent to the hyperbola $xy = 1$ at the point $P$.

Let $P$ be a point on the hyperbola $xy = 1$. Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be the points of tangency of the two lines through $P$ that are tangent to the hyperbola $xy = -1$. Show that the line joining $P_1$ and $P_2$ is tangent to the hyperbola $xy = -1$.

positive_text: Determine all integers $n$ with $n < 60$ such that the set $S = \{n, n+1, \dots, 60\}$ can be divided into non-overlapping subsets where one element in each subset is the sum of the rest.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $n$ ($n < 60$) such that the set $M = \{n, n+1, \dots, 60\}$ can be partitioned into subsets where the sum of the elements in each subset is a perfect square.
Find all positive integers $n$ ($n < 60$) such that the set $M = \{n, n+1, \dots, 60\}$ can be partitioned into subsets where each subset has a product equal to one of its elements.

Find all positive integers $n$ ($n < 60$) such that the set $M = \{n, n+1, \dots, 60\}$ can be partitioned into subsets where one of the numbers is equal to the sum of all other numbers in the entire set.

positive_text:
Let $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$, $u$, $v$ be the side lengths $PQ$, $QR$, $RS$, $SP$ and the diagonals $PR$, $QS$ of a cyclic quadrilateral $PQRS$, respectively. Prove that
$$
\left(\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{q} + \frac{1}{s}\right)^2 \ge 8 \left(\frac{1}{u^2} + \frac{1}{v^2}\right).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $x$, $y$ denote the side lengths and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. Prove that
$$
\left(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{d}\right) \ge 4 \left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y}\right).
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $x$, $y$ be the side lengths and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$. Prove that
$$
\left(\frac{1}{a^2} + \frac{1}{c^2}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{b^2} + \frac{1}{d^2}\right) \ge 8 \left(\frac{1}{x^2} + \frac{1}{y^2}\right).
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $x$, $y$ be the side lengths and diagonals of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$. Prove that
$$
\left(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{c}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{d}\right)^2 \ge 8 \left(\frac{1}{x^2} + \frac{1}{y^2}\right).
$$

positive_text: \left(x^2 + \frac{z^2}{y^2}\right) \left(y^2 + \frac{x^2}{z^2}\right) \left(z^2 + \frac{y^2}{x^2}\right) \ge \frac{xyz}{\sqrt{3}} \left(x + \frac{1}{x}\right) \left(y + \frac{1}{y}\right) \left(z + \frac{1}{z}\right)

negatives.text: \left(a^2 + \frac{c^2}{b^2}\right) \left(b^2 + \frac{a^2}{c^2}\right) \left(c^2 + \frac{b^2}{a^2}\right) \ge \frac{abc}{\sqrt{2}} \left(a + \frac{1}{a}\right) \left(b + \frac{1}{b}\right) \left(c + \frac{1}{c}\right)

\left(a^2 + \frac{c^2}{b^2}\right) \left(b^2 + \frac{a^2}{c^2}\right) \left(c^2 + \frac{b^2}{a^2}\right) \ge \frac{abc}{\sqrt{3}} \left(a - \frac{1}{a}\right) \left(b - \frac{1}{b}\right) \left(c - \frac{1}{c}\right)

\left(a^2 + \frac{c^2}{b^2}\right) \left(b^2 + \frac{a^2}{c^2}\right) \left(c^2 + \frac{b^2}{a^2}\right) \ge \frac{abc}{\sqrt{3}} \left(a^2 + \frac{1}{a^2}\right) \left(b^2 + \frac{1}{b^2}\right) \left(c^2 + \frac{1}{c^2}\right)

positive_text: Let $p, q, r, s$ be real numbers satisfying $\sin p + q > \sin r + s$ and $p + \sin q > r + \sin s$. Prove that $p + q > r + s$.

negatives.text: Let $x, y, z, w$ be real numbers such that $\sin x + y > \sin z + w$ and $x + \sin y < z + \sin w$. Prove that $x + y > z + w$.
Let $m, n, p, q$ be real numbers such that $\sin^2 m + n > \sin^2 p + q$ and $m + \sin n > p + \sin q$. Prove that $m + n > p + q$.
Let $u, v, w, x$ be real numbers such that $\sin u + v > \sin w + x$ and $u + \sin v > w + \sin x$. Prove that $u + v < w + x$.

positive_text: Determine all real values of $a$ for which there exists a non-constant function $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $g(g(x)) = x g(x) - a x$ for all real $x$, and $g(x) = a$ for some real $x$.

negatives.text: Find all real numbers $a$ such that there exists a non-constant function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(f(x)) = x f(x) + a x$ for all real $x$, and $f$ takes the value $a$.
Find all real numbers $a$ such that there exists a non-constant function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(f(x)) = x f(x) - a x^2$ for all real $x$, and $f$ takes the value $a$.
Find all real numbers $a$ such that there exists a non-constant function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(f(x)) = x f(x) - a x$ for all real $x$, and $f(x) = a$ for all real $x$.

positive_text: Let $ ABC $ be an acute isosceles triangle with $ AB = AC $. Points $ D $ and $ E $ are placed on $ AB $ and $ AC $ respectively so that $ BD = AE $. A point $ P $ is chosen in the same half-plane as $ B $ and $ C $ with respect to line $ DE $, such that $ \angle PD E = \angle PE D = \angle BAC $. Prove that $ B $, $ C $, and $ P $ are collinear if and only if triangle $ ABC $ is equilateral.

negatives.text: Let $ ABC $ be an acute isosceles triangle with $ AB = AC $. Points $ D $ and $ E $ are placed on $ AB $ and $ AC $ respectively so that $ BD = AE $. A point $ P $ is chosen in the same half-plane as $ B $ and $ C $ with respect to line $ DE $, such that $ \angle PD E = \angle PE D = \angle BAC $. Prove that $ A $, $ C $, and $ P $ are collinear if and only if triangle $ ABC $ is equilateral.

positive_text: In triangle $ PQR $, points $ X $ and $ Y $ lie on $ PQ $ and $ PR $, respectively, such that $ XQ = XY $. The bisector of angle $ PQR $ intersects the circumcircle of $ PQR $ at $ Q $ and $ S $. The perpendicular from $ S $ to $ PR $ intersects segment $ XY $ at $ T $. Show that points $ P $, $ X $, $ T $, $ Y $ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Points $ K $ and $ N $ are marked on the sides $ AB $ and $ AC $ of triangle $ ABC $, respectively, such that $ KB = KN $. The bisector of the angle $ BAC $ meets the circumcircle of $ ABC $ at points $ A $ and $ R $. The perpendicular from $ R $ to $ AB $ intersects the segment $ BN $ at $ D $. Prove that the points $ A $, $ K $, $ D $, $ N $ are concyclic.

Points $ K $ and $ N $ are marked on the sides $ AB $ and $ AC $ of triangle $ ABC $, respectively, such that $ KB = KN $. The bisector of the angle $ ACB $ meets the circumcircle of $ ABC $ at points $ C $ and $ R $. The perpendicular from $ R $ to $ AC $ intersects the segment $ BN $ at $ D $. Prove that the points $ A $, $ K $, $ D $, $ N $ are concyclic.

Points $ K $ and $ N $ are marked on the sides $ AB $ and $ AC $ of triangle $ ABC $, respectively, such that $ KB = KN $. The bisector of the angle $ ACB $ meets the circumcircle of $ ABC $ at points $ C $ and $ R $. The perpendicular from $ R $ to $ AB $ intersects the segment $ BN $ at $ D $. Prove that the points $ A $, $ K $, $ D $, $ B $ are concyclic.

positive_text: Suppose a graph has $n$ vertices ($n \ge 4$) such that for any pair of vertices, there exists another vertex that is adjacent to neither of them. Determine the maximum number of edges this graph can have.

negatives.text: Suppose a graph has $n$ vertices ($n \ge 4$) such that for any pair of vertices, there exists another vertex that is adjacent to both of them. Determine the maximum number of edges this graph can have.

Suppose a graph has $n$ vertices ($n \ge 4$) such that for any pair of vertices, there exists another vertex that is adjacent to exactly one of them. Determine the maximum number of edges this graph can have.

Suppose a graph has $n$ vertices ($n \ge 4$) such that for any pair of vertices, there exists another vertex that is adjacent to at least one of them. Determine the maximum number of edges this graph can have.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ satisfy $PQ = 2PR$. Suppose points $S$ and $T$ lie on $QR$ and $PQ$, respectively, and the perimeter of trapezoid $RSPT$ equals $PQ + PR$. Construct point $S$ with compass and straightedge.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB = 2AC$. Suppose points $M$ and $N$ lie on $BC$ and $AB$, respectively, and the perimeter of trapezoid $CMNA$ is the sum of the lengths of the sides $BC$ and $AC$. Construct point $M$ using compasses and ruler.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB = 2AC$. Suppose points $M$ and $N$ lie on $BC$ and $AB$, respectively, and the area of trapezoid $CMNA$ is half the area of triangle $ABC$. Construct point $M$ using compasses and ruler.

Let triangle $ABC$ satisfy $AB = AC$. Suppose points $M$ and $N$ lie on $BC$ and $AB$, respectively, and the perimeter of trapezoid $CMNA$ is the sum of the lengths of the sides $AB$ and $AC$. Construct point $M$ using compasses and ruler.

positive_text: A trapezoid $PQRS$ ($PQ \parallel RS$) is inscribed into the parabola $y = x^2$. The line passing through the midpoints of $PQ$ and $RS$ intersects the parabola at two new points $X$ and $Y$. Prove that the distance from $X$ to the midpoint of $PQ$ is equal to the distance from $Y$ to the midpoint of $RS$.

negatives.text: A trapezoid $ABCD$ ($AB \parallel CD$) is inscribed into the parabola $y = x^2$. The line containing the midline $MN$ of this trapezoid is extended and intersects the parabola at points $K$ and $L$. Prove that the lengths of the segments $KM$ and $ML$ are equal.

A trapezoid $ABCD$ ($AB \parallel CD$) is inscribed into the cubic curve $y = x^3$. The line containing the midline $MN$ of this trapezoid meets the curve at points $K$ and $L$. Prove that the lengths of the segments $KM$ and $NL$ are equal.

positive_text: A straight line $ m $ intersects the right half of the hyperbola $ xy = 1 $ at two distinct points $ P $ and $ Q $. Two other lines $ m_1 $ and $ m_2 $, parallel to $ m $, intersect the left half of the same hyperbola at points $ R, S $ and $ T, U $, respectively. The line $ m_1 $ intersects the segments $ PT $ and $ QU $ at points $ X $ and $ Y $, respectively. Prove that $ XR = YS $.

negatives.text: A line $ l $ intersects the right branch of the hyperbola $ y = 1/x $ at points $ A $ and $ B $. Two lines $ l_1 $ and $ l_2 $, parallel to $ l $, intersect the right branch of the hyperbola at points $ C, D $ and $ E, F $, respectively. The line $ l_1 $ intersects the segments $ AE $ and $ BF $ at points $ G $ and $ H $. Prove that $ GE = HF $.

A line $ l $ intersects the right branch of the hyperbola $ y = 1/x $ at points $ A $ and $ B $. Two lines $ l_1 $ and $ l_2 $, perpendicular to $ l $, intersect the left branch of the hyperbola at points $ C, D $ and $ E, F $, respectively. The line $ l_1 $ intersects the segments $ AD $ and $ BC $ at points $ G $ and $ H $. Prove that $ GE = HF $.

A line $ l $ intersects the right branch of the hyperbola $ y = 1/x $ at points $ A $ and $ B $. Two lines $ l_1 $ and $ l_2 $, parallel to $ l $, intersect the left branch of the parabola $ y = x^2 $ at points $ C, D $ and $ E, F $, respectively. The line $ l_1 $ intersects the segments $ AD $ and $ BC $ at points $ G $ and $ H $. Prove that $ GE = HF $.

positive_text: We define two monic quadratic polynomials $f(x) = x^2 + p x + q$ and $g(x) = x^2 + r x + s$ as *amicable* if each has two distinct real roots and the numbers $x_1 + y_1$, $x_2 + y_2$ (with $x_1 < x_2$ the roots of $f$, $y_1 < y_2$ the roots of $g$) are the roots of $x^2 + (p + r)x + q + s$. Suppose $N$ is a set of at least three *amicable* polynomials. Show that every polynomial in $N$ has a root at $0$.

negatives.text: Let $P(x) = x^2 + a x + b$ and $Q(x) = x^2 + c x + d$ be two quadratic trinomials with distinct real roots. Suppose $x_1 + x_3$, $x_2 + x_4$ are the roots of $x^2 + (a - c)x + b + d$, where $x_1 < x_2$ are the roots of $P(x)$, $x_3 < x_4$ are the roots of $Q(x)$. Let $M$ be a set of at least three such trinomials with this property. Prove that $0$ is a root of every trinomial in $M$.

Two monic quadratic trinomials $P(x) = x^2 + a x + b$ and $Q(x) = x^2 + c x + d$ are called *linked* if they have distinct real roots and $x_1 + x_3$, $x_1 + x_4$ are the roots of $x^2 + (a + c)x + b + d$, where $x_1 < x_2$ are the roots of $P(x)$, $x_3 < x_4$ are the roots of $Q(x)$. Let $M$ be a set of at least three *linked* trinomials. Show that $0$ is a root of every trinomial in $M$.

Two quadratic trinomials $P(x) = x^2 + a x + b$ and $Q(x) = x^2 + c x + d$ are called *sociable* if each has distinct real roots and $x_1 + x_3$, $x_2 + x_4$ are the roots of $x^2 + (a + c)x + b - d$, where $x_1 < x_2$ are the roots of $P(x)$, $x_3 < x_4$ are the roots of $Q(x)$. Let $M$ be a set of at least three *sociable* trinomials. Prove that $0$ is a root of every trinomial in $M$.

positive_text: An empty $2n \times 2n$ grid is filled with white tiles. In each move, you can flip the color of any three adjacent tiles in a straight line, either horizontally or vertically (white becomes black, black becomes white). Determine all $n \ge 2$ such that the final configuration can be a checkerboard pattern.

negatives.text: An empty $2n \times 2n$ grid is filled with white tiles. In each move, you can flip the color of any two adjacent tiles in a straight line, either horizontally or vertically. Determine all $n \ge 2$ such that the final configuration can be a checkerboard pattern.

An empty $2n \times 2n$ grid is filled with white tiles. In each move, you can flip the color of any three consecutive tiles in a straight line, either horizontally or vertically. Determine all $n \ge 2$ such that the final configuration can be a fully black grid.

positive_text:
Consider a $(2k + 1) \times (2k + 1)$ grid, all of its squares initially white. In one operation, you can flip the color of any three consecutive squares in any row or column (flipping white to black and black to white). 

a) Prove that for any positive integer $k$ it is possible to achieve a checkerboard coloring with white corners.

b) Determine the smallest number of operations required to reach the checkerboard coloring with white corners when $k = 3$.

negatives.text:
Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table, all its unit cells being white. Per move it is allowed to change the color of any four consecutive cells in any row or in any column (white cell is replaced by black one and vice versa).

a) Prove that for any positive integer $n$ one can obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells.

b) Find the minimum number of the moves one needs to obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells if $n = 3$.

Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table, all its unit cells being white. Per move it is allowed to change the color of any three consecutive cells in any row or in any column (white cell is replaced by black one and vice versa), but only if the center cell of the three is white.

a) Prove that for any positive integer $n$ one can obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells.

b) Find the minimum number of the moves one needs to obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells if $n = 3$.

Given a $(2n + 1) \times (2n + 1)$ table, all its unit cells being white. Per move it is allowed to change the color of any three consecutive cells in any row or in any column (white cell is replaced by black one and vice versa), but only if the three cells form a diagonal in the row or column.

a) Prove that for any positive integer $n$ one can obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells.

b) Find the minimum number of the moves one needs to obtain the chess coloring of the given table with white corner cells if $n = 3$.

positive_text: Consider a $(2m + 1) 	imes (2m + 1)$ grid filled with white cells. In each move, you may toggle the color (white to black or black to white) of any three adjacent cells in the same row or column. Determine all values of $m$ for which it is possible to achieve a checkerboard pattern where the four corner cells are black.

negatives.text: Consider a $(2n + 1) 	imes (2n + 1)$ grid filled with white cells. In each move, you may toggle the color of any two adjacent cells in the same row or column. Determine all values of $n$ for which it is possible to achieve a checkerboard pattern where the four corner cells are black.

Consider a $(2n + 1) 	imes (2n + 1)$ grid filled with white cells. In each move, you may toggle the color of any three consecutive cells in the same row or column, but only in the middle row or column. Determine all values of $n$ for which it is possible to achieve a checkerboard pattern where the four corner cells are black.

Consider a $(2n + 1) 	imes (2n + 1)$ grid filled with white cells. In each move, you may toggle the color of any three consecutive cells in the same row or column. Determine all values of $n$ for which it is possible to achieve a checkerboard pattern where the four corner cells are white.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = BC$, and let $K$ and $M$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The circle through $C$, $K$, and $B$ intersects the line $BM$ again at point $N$. A line through $N$ parallel to $AC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $A_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $A_1BC_1$ is equilateral.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be isosceles with $AB = AC$, and let $K$ and $M$ be the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The circle through $C$, $K$, and $B$ intersects the line $BM$ again at point $N$. A line through $N$ parallel to $AB$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $A_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $A_1BC_1$ is equilateral.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = BC$, points $K$ and $M$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The circle through $C$, $K$, and $B$ intersects the line $BM$ again at point $N$. A line through $N$ parallel to the side $AC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $A_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $A_1BC_1$ is isosceles.

In triangle $ABC$ with $AB 
e BC$, points $K$ and $M$ are the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. The circle through $C$, $K$, and $B$ intersects the line $BM$ again at point $N$. A line through $N$ parallel to the side $AC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $A_1$ and $C_1$. Prove that triangle $A_1BC_1$ is equilateral.

positive_text: Let $ D $ be the midpoint of the hypotenuse $ EF $ of the right triangle $ EFG $. A point $ Q $ is located on the leg $ FG $ such that $ FQ : QG = 1 : 2 $. A line passing through $ G $ intersects the segments $ DE $, $ DQ $, and $ QF $ at points $ U $, $ V $, and $ W $, respectively. Prove that the angle bisector of $ QWV $ passes through point $ F $ if and only if the angle bisector of $ QVU $ also passes through $ F $.

negatives.text: Let $ M $ be the midpoint of the hypotenuse $ AB $ of the right triangle $ ABC $. Point $ P $ is chosen on the cathetus $ CB $ so that $ CP : PB = 1 : 2 $. The straight line passing through $ A $ meets the segments $ BC $, $ AP $, and $ PM $ at points $ X $, $ Y $, and $ Z $, respectively. Prove that the bisector of the angle $ PZY $ passes through point $ C $ if and only if the bisector of the angle $ PYX $ also passes through $ C $.

Let $ M $ be the midpoint of the hypotenuse $ AB $ of the right triangle $ ABC $. Point $ P $ is chosen on the cathetus $ CB $ so that $ CP : PB = 2 : 1 $. The straight line passing through $ B $ meets the segments $ AC $, $ AP $, and $ PM $ at points $ X $, $ Y $, and $ Z $, respectively. Prove that the bisector of the angle $ PZY $ passes through point $ C $ if and only if the bisector of the angle $ PYX $ also passes through $ C $.

Let $ M $ be the midpoint of the hypotenuse $ AB $ of the right triangle $ ABC $. Point $ P $ is chosen on the cathetus $ CB $ so that $ CP : PB = 1 : 2 $. The straight line passing through $ B $ meets the segments $ AC $, $ AP $, and $ AM $ at points $ X $, $ Y $, and $ Z $, respectively. Prove that the bisector of the angle $ PZY $ passes through point $ C $ if and only if the bisector of the angle $ PYX $ also passes through $ C $.

positive_text:
Determine all real values $ k $ such that there exists a bijective function $ g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying
$$
 g(g(t)) = t^2 g(t) + k t^2
$$
for all real $ t $.

negatives.text:
Determine all real values $ a $ such that there exists a bijective function $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying
$$
 f(f(x)) = x^2 f(x) + a x
$$
for all real $ x $.

Find all real numbers $ a $ for which there exists a function $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying
$$
 f(f(x)) = x^2 f(x) + a x^2
$$
for all nonzero real $ x $.

positive_text: Find the smallest prime number $ q $ such that the fractional part of $ \sqrt{q} $ is less than $ \frac{1}{501} $.

negatives.text: Find the smallest prime number $ p $ such that $ \{\sqrt{p} + 1\} < \frac{1}{501} $.
Find the smallest prime number $ p $ such that $ \{\sqrt{p}\} > \frac{1}{501} $.
Find the smallest prime number $ p $ such that $ \left\lfloor \sqrt{p} \right\rfloor < \frac{1}{501} $.

positive_text: \text{Let } n \ge 2 \text{ be an integer. Prove that} \quad \sum_{k=2}^n \frac{2^{k-2}}{k!} \le \frac{3}{2}.

negatives.text: \text{Let } n \ge 2 \text{ be an integer. Prove that} \quad \frac{1}{2!} + \frac{2}{3!} + \dots + \frac{2^{n-2}}{n!} \le 1.
\text{Let } n \ge 2 \text{ be an integer. Prove that} \quad \frac{1}{2!} + \frac{2}{3!} + \dots + \frac{2^{n-2}}{n!} < \frac{3}{2}.
\text{Let } n \ge 2 \text{ be an integer. Prove that} \quad \frac{1}{2!} + \frac{2}{3!} + \dots + \frac{2^{n-2}}{n!} \le \frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{2^n}.

positive_text: Three $n \times n$ squares are joined to form a composite shape $\Phi$ as depicted in the figure. Adjacent squares share an edge of length $1$. Determine all integers $n > 1$ such that $\Phi$ can be tiled completely using $1 \times 3$ and $3 \times 1$ tiles without overlap.

negatives.text: Three $n \times n$ squares form a figure $\Phi$ on the grid. If neighboring squares share a full edge of length $1$, determine all $n > 1$ for which $\Phi$ can be tiled with $2 \times 2$ square tiles.
A composite shape $\Phi$ is formed by three $n \times n$ squares joined at their edges. For which $n > 1$ can $\Phi$ be tiled with $1 \times 3$ tiles only (no $3 \times 1$ tiles allowed)?

Three $n \times n$ squares are connected to form a shape $\Phi$ as in the diagram. Determine all $n > 1$ for which $\Phi$ can be covered with $1 \times 3$ and $3 \times 1$ tiles, allowing overlapping.

positive_text: Let $PQRS$ be a convex quadrilateral with all its vertices lying on the curve $y = x^2$. Suppose that $PQRS$ is inscribed in a circle and that $PR$ is the diameter of this circle. If $U$ and $V$ are the midpoints of $PR$ and $QS$ respectively, determine the length of the projection of the segment $UV$ onto the $y$-axis.

negatives.text: The points $ABCD$ lie on the parabola $y = x^2$. It is given that $ABCD$ is cyclic and that $AC$ is a diameter of the circle. If $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AC$ and $BD$, respectively, find the length of the projection of $MN$ on the $x$-axis.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, with all vertices on the curve $y = x^2$. It is known that $AC$ is a diameter of the circle. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $AC$ and $BD$, respectively. Determine the length of the projection of the segment $MN$ onto the line $y = x$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with all vertices on the parabola $y = x^2$. It is given that $ABCD$ is cyclic and $AC$ is a diameter of the circle. If $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$, respectively, find the length of the projection of $MN$ on the $y$-axis.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be positive integers such that
$$
x^3 y^3 + y^3 z^3 + z^3 x^3 = xyz(x^3 + y^3 + z^3).
$$
Show that the product of at least two of $x$, $y$, and $z$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text:
Let $p$, $q$, and $r$ be positive integers such that
$$
p^3 q^3 + q^3 r^3 + r^3 p^3 = pqr(p^3 + q^3 + r^3 + 1).
$$
Prove that the product of some two of these numbers is the square of a positive integer.

Let $d$, $e$, and $f$ be positive integers such that
$$
d^3 e^3 + e^3 f^3 + f^3 d^3 = def(d^3 - e^3 + f^3).
$$
Prove that the product of some two of these numbers is a perfect square.

positive_text:
a) Determine all real values of $k$ for which the graph of $y = x^2 - k$ intersects the graph of $y = \frac{1}{x}$ in three distinct points.

b) Determine the set of centers of the circumcircles of these triples of intersection points as $k$ varies over all such real values.

negatives.text:
a) Find all real numbers $a$ such that the parabola $y = x^2 - a$ and the hyperbola $y = \frac{1}{x^2}$ intersect in three different points.

b) Find the locus of the centers of circumcircles of such triples of intersection points as $a$ varies.

a) Find all real numbers $a$ such that the parabola $y = x^2 + a$ and the hyperbola $y = \frac{1}{x}$ intersect in three different points.

b) Find the locus of the centers of circumcircles of such triples of intersection points as $a$ varies.

a) Find all real numbers $a$ such that the parabola $y = x^2 - a$ and the line $y = x$ intersect in three different points.

b) Find the locus of the centers of circumcircles of such triples of intersection points as $a$ varies.

positive_text:
Let $ f(x) = x^2 + cx + 8 $, where $ c 
eq 0 $, have distinct real roots $ r_1 $ and $ r_2 $. The expressions $ r_1 +  rac{1}{r_2} $ and $ r_2 +  rac{1}{r_1} $ are the roots of the monic quadratic polynomial $ h(x) $. Determine all values of $ h(1) $ such that $ h(1) = f(1) $.

negatives.text:
Let $ f(x) = x^2 + cx + 8 $, where $ c 
eq 0 $, have real roots $ r_1 $ and $ r_2 $. The numbers $ r_1 + r_2 $ and $ r_1 - r_2 $ are the roots of the monic quadratic polynomial $ h(x) $. Determine all values of $ h(1) $ such that $ h(1) = f(1) $.

Let $ f(x) = x^2 + cx + 8 $, where $ c 
eq 0 $, have real roots $ r_1 $ and $ r_2 $. The numbers $ r_1^2 $ and $ r_2^2 $ are the roots of the monic quadratic polynomial $ h(x) $. Determine all values of $ h(1) $ such that $ h(1) = f(1) $.

positive_text:
a) Find a positive integer $n$ such that there exist distinct positive integers $x$ and $y$ (both dividing $n$) for which $n = x^2 - p$ and $n = y^2 - q$, with $p, q$ also divisors of $n$.

b) Show that there are infinitely many such integers $n$.

negatives.text:
a) Find a positive integer $n$ such that there exist positive integers $x$ and $y$ (both dividing $n$) for which $n = x^2 + p = y^2 + q$, with $p, q$ also divisors of $n$.

b) Show that there are infinitely many such integers $n$.

a) Find a positive integer $n$ such that there exist positive integers $x$ and $y$ (both dividing $n$) for which $n = x^3 - p = y^3 - q$, with $p, q$ also divisors of $n$.

b) Show that there are infinitely many such integers $n$.

positive_text: Given two sequences $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$ and $(b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n)$ with $a_i \ge b_j$ for all $i, j$, define $P = \max_{1 \le i \le n}(a_i - b_i)$ and $G = \max_{1 \le i \le n} a_i - \min_{1 \le j \le n} b_j$. Prove that $P \le G \le nP$.

Find all functions $ g(x): \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying for all $ x \in \mathbb{R} $ the equation
$$
 x = \frac{3}{4}g(|x|) + |g(x)|.
$$

negatives.text:
Find all functions $ f(x): \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying for all $ x \in \mathbb{R} $ the equation
$$
 x = \frac{3}{4}f(x) + |f(x)|.
$$

Find all functions $ f(x): \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying for all $ x \in \mathbb{R} $ the equation
$$
 x = \frac{3}{4}f(|x|) - |f(x)|.
$$

Find all functions $ f(x): \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying for all $ x > 0 $ the equation
$$
 x = \frac{3}{4}f(x) + |f(x)|.
$$

positive_text: In a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$, let $O$ be the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Drop perpendiculars from $O$ to each side: $P$ on $AB$, $Q$ on $BC$, $R$ on $CD$, and $S$ on $DA$. Prove that $BD \ge SP + QR$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals intersecting at $O$. Drop perpendiculars from $O$ to each side as before. Prove that $BD^2 \ge SP^2 + QR^2$.

positive_text: \text{A collection of positive integers } \{b_1, b_2, \dots, b_m\} \text{ is called nice if } \gcd(b_j, S - b_j) > 1 \text{ for all } j = \overline{1, m}, \text{ where } S = \sum_{i=1}^m b_i. \text{Show that for any } c \in (0, 1) \text{ there is a threshold } M \text{ such that for all } K \ge M, \text{ there is a nice collection with at least } cK \text{ elements, all at most } K.

negatives.text: \text{Call a set } \{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} \text{ of positive integers good if } \gcd(a_k, a_{k+1}) > 1 \text{ for all } k = \overline{1, n-1}. \text{Prove that for each } c \in (0, 1) \text{ there exists a positive integer } M \text{ such that for any positive integer } K \ge M \text{ one can find a good set with at least } cK \text{ elements all elements of which do not exceed } K.

\text{Call the set } \{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} \text{ of positive integers good if } \gcd(a_k, \sum_{i \neq k} a_i) = 1 \text{ for each } k = \overline{1, n}. \text{Prove that for each } c \in (0, 1) \text{ there exists a positive integer } M \text{ such that for any positive integer } K \ge M \text{ one can find a good set with at least } cK \text{ elements all elements of which do not exceed } K.

\text{Call the set } \{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\} \text{ of positive integers good if } \gcd(a_k, \sum_{i \neq k} a_i) > 1 \text{ for at least one } k = \overline{1, n}. \text{Prove that for each } c \in (0, 1) \text{ there exists a positive integer } M \text{ such that for any positive integer } K \ge M \text{ one can find a good set with at least } cK \text{ elements all elements of which do not exceed } K.

positive_text: Let $P_1, \dots, P_n$ be points in the plane with rational coordinates such that the distance between any two of them is an integer. Show that there exist points $Q_1, \dots, Q_n$ with integer coordinates such that the distance between $Q_i$ and $Q_j$ equals the distance between $P_i$ and $P_j$ for all $i \ne j$.

negatives.text: Let $A_1, \dots, A_n$ be points in the plane with rational coordinates, all pairwise distances being rational. Prove that there exist points $B_1, \dots, B_n$ with integer coordinates such that $|B_iB_j| = |A_iA_j|$ for all $1 \le i < j \le n$.

Suppose $A_1, \dots, A_n$ are points in the plane with rational coordinates, all pairwise distances being integers. Prove that there exist points $B_1, \dots, B_n$ with integer coordinates such that $|B_iB_j| = 2|A_iA_j|$ for all $1 \le i < j \le n$.

Let $A_1, \dots, A_n$ be points in the plane with rational coordinates such that the square of the distance between any two points is an integer. Prove that there exist points $B_1, \dots, B_n$ with integer coordinates such that $|B_iB_j| = |A_iA_j|$ for all $1 \le i < j \le n$.

positive_text:
Given positive integers $ n $ and $ k \le n $. Imagine a triangular grid with side length $ n $, arranged so that the top row has 1 circle, the second row has 2 circles, ..., and the bottom row has $ n $ circles. Place tokens on the grid such that every line running in one of the three primary directions of the triangle (i.e., each of the $ 3n $ lines parallel to a side) has at most $ k $ tokens. Let $ T(k, n) $ be the maximum number of tokens that can be placed under this constraint.

a) Prove the following inequality:
$$
T(k, n) \le \left\lfloor \frac{k(2n + 1)}{3} \right\rfloor .
$$

b) Determine $ T(1, n) $ and $ T(2, n) $.

negatives.text:
Let $ n $ and $ k $ be positive integers with $ k \le n $. Consider a triangular grid with $ n $ rows, where the $ i $-th row contains $ i $ circles. You are to place tokens on this grid such that each of the $ 3n $ lines parallel to a side of the triangle contains at most $ k $ tokens. Let $ T(k, n) $ be the maximum number of tokens that can be placed under this condition.

a) Show that:
$$
T(k, n) \le \left\lfloor \frac{k(2n - 1)}{3} \right\rfloor .
$$

b) Find $ T(1, n) $ and $ T(2, n) $.

Let $ n $ and $ k $ be positive integers with $ k \le n $. Consider a triangular grid with $ n $ rows, where the $ i $-th row contains $ i $ circles. You are to place tokens on this grid such that each of the $ 3n $ lines parallel to a side of the triangle contains at most $ k $ tokens. Let $ T(k, n) $ be the maximum number of tokens that can be placed under this condition.

a) Show that:
$$
T(k, n) \le \left\lfloor \frac{k(2n)}{3} \right\rfloor .
$$

b) Find $ T(1, n) $ and $ T(2, n) $.

Let $ n $ and $ k $ be positive integers with $ k \le n $. Consider a triangular grid with $ n $ rows, where the $ i $-th row contains $ i $ circles. You are to place tokens on this grid such that each of the $ 3n $ lines parallel to a side of the triangle contains at most $ k $ tokens. Let $ T(k, n) $ be the maximum number of tokens that can be placed under this condition.

a) Show that:
$$
T(k, n) \le \left\lfloor \frac{k(2n + 1)}{2} \right\rfloor .
$$

b) Find $ T(1, n) $ and $ T(2, n) $.

positive_text:
Determine all real-coefficient polynomials $q(x)$ satisfying
$$
q(x+y-2 z)+q(y+z-2 x)+q(z+x-2 y)=3 q(x-y)+3 q(y-z)+3 q(z-x)
$$
for all real numbers $x, y, z$.

negatives.text:
Find all polynomials $p(x)$ with real coefficients such that
$$
p(a+b+2 c)+p(b+c+2 a)+p(c+a+2 b)=3 p(a-b)+3 p(b-c)+3 p(c-a)
$$
for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all polynomials $p(x)$ with real coefficients such that
$$
p(a+b-2 c)+p(b+c-2 a)+p(c+a-2 b)=p(a-b)+p(b-c)+p(c-a)
$$
for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all polynomials $p(x)$ with real coefficients such that
$$
p(a+b-2 c)+p(b+c-2 a)+p(c+a-2 b)=3 p(a)+3 p(b)+3 p(c)
$$
for all $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text: Determine all positive integer quadruples $(x, y, q, m)$ such that $q$ is prime and $$ x^{3} + y^{3} = q^{m} $$

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $(a, b, p, n)$ with $p$ prime such that $$ a^{3} - b^{3} = p^{n} $$
Find all positive integers $(a, b, p, n)$ with $p$ prime such that $$ a^{2} + b^{2} = p^{n} $$
Find all positive integers $(a, b, p, n)$ with $p$ prime such that $$ a^{3} + b^{3} = p^{n} + 1 $$

positive_text:
Two integers $a$ and $b$ satisfy $1 < a < b$. We define a pair $(a, b)$ to be a Lusben pair if the prime factorizations of $a$ and $b$ consist of the same set of primes, and the same is true for $a+1$ and $b+1$.
a. Find three Lusben pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \leqslant 14$.
b. Prove that there are infinitely many Lusben pairs.

negatives.text:
An ordered pair of integers $(p, q)$ with $1 < p < q$ is called a Benelux pair if $p$ has the same prime divisors as $q$, and $p-1$ has the same prime divisors as $q-1$.
a. Find three Benelux pairs $(p, q)$ with $p \leqslant 14$.
b. Prove that there are infinitely many Benelux pairs.

An ordered pair of integers $(a, b)$ with $1 < a < b$ is said to be a Benelux pair if $a$ has the same prime divisors as $b$, and $a^2$ has the same prime divisors as $b^2$.
a. Find three Benelux pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \leqslant 14$.
b. Prove that there are infinitely many Benelux pairs.

Two integers $x$ and $y$ with $1 < x < y$ are said to form a Benelux pair if $x$ and $y$ have the same prime divisors, and the prime factorizations of $x+1$ and $y$ are identical.
a. Find three Benelux pairs $(x, y)$ with $x \leqslant 14$.
b. Prove that there are infinitely many Benelux pairs.

positive_text:
Alice and Bob play a game where they choose a positive integer $N$. Alice writes $1$ on the board first. After that, if the last number written is $n$, the next player writes either $n+1$ or $2n$, provided the result is $\leq N$. The player who writes $N$ wins.

a. Who wins if $N = 2011$?

b. How many values of $N \leq 2011$ result in a win for Bob?

negatives.text:
Alex and Ben play a game with a positive integer $N$. Alex writes $1$ first, and then players alternately write $n+1$ or $n+2$, provided the result is $\leq N$. The player who writes $N$ wins.

a. Who has a winning strategy if $N = 2011$?

b. How many $N \leq 2011$ allow Ben to win?

Eva and Frank play a game with a positive integer $N$. Eva writes $1$ first, and then players alternately write $n+1$ or $n^2$, provided the result is $\leq N$. The player who writes $N$ wins.

a. Who has a winning strategy if $N = 2011$?

b. How many $N \leq 2011$ allow Frank to win?

positive_text: Find all quadruples $(x, y, z, w)$ of positive real numbers such that $xyzw = 1$, $x^{2012} + 2012y = 2012z + w^{2012}$, and $2012x + y^{2012} = z^{2012} + 2012w$.

negatives.text: Find all quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ of positive real numbers such that $ab cd = 1$, $a^{2012} - 2012b = 2012c + d^{2012}$, and $2012a + b^{2012} = c^{2012} + 2012d$.
Find all quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ of positive real numbers such that $ab cd = 1$, $a^{2012} + 2012b = 2012c + d^{2012}$, and $2012a + b^{2012} = c^{2012} - 2012d$.
Find all quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$ of positive real numbers such that $ab cd = 1$, $a^{2012} + 2012b = 2012c + d^{2012}$, and $2012a + b^{2012} = c^{2012} + 2012d^2$.

positive_text:
Suppose $ n \geq 4 $ people were seated around a circular table yesterday. Each person only recalls the identities of their two adjacent neighbors, but not the left-right order. Today, you must re-seat the same people around the same circular table such that everyone has the same two neighbors as yesterday, regardless of their left/right orientation. You can ask any person to reveal their two neighbors from yesterday. 

a. What is the minimum number $ f(n) $ of people you must ask in advance (i.e., without adaptive querying) to guarantee that you can reconstruct the correct seating?

b. What is the minimum number $ g(n) $ of people you must ask adaptively (i.e., with each query depending on previous answers) to guarantee that you can reconstruct the correct seating?

negatives.text:
Yesterday, $ n \geq 4 $ people sat around a round table. Each person remembers the identities of their two immediate neighbors and the left-right orientation. Today, you must reseat the same people around the same table with the same left-right neighbor relationships. You can ask any person to recall their left and right neighbor from yesterday. 

a. What is the minimal number $ f(n) $ of people you must ask in advance to guarantee a correct seating reconstruction?

b. What is the minimal number $ g(n) $ of people you must ask adaptively to guarantee a correct seating reconstruction?

Yesterday, $ n \geq 4 $ people sat around a round table. Each person remembers the identities of their two immediate neighbors, but not the left-right orientation. Today, you must reseat the same people around the same table such that each person has the same two neighbors as yesterday, and also that the seating is consistent with the direction of the original seating (i.e., the same cyclic order). 

a. What is the minimal number $ f(n) $ of people you must ask in advance to guarantee a correct seating reconstruction?

b. What is the minimal number $ g(n) $ of people you must ask adaptively to guarantee a correct seating reconstruction?

positive_text: Let $m \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A toad starts at position $0$ on the real number line and performs $m$ moves, each of distinct lengths $1, 2, \ldots, m$ in any order. When the toad is at a position $x \leqslant 0$, it must move right for its next jump; when at a position $x > 0$, it must move left. Determine the maximum integer $k$ such that the toad can choose an order of jumps to avoid all positions $1, 2, \ldots, k$.

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A frog starts at point $0$ and makes $n$ jumps of lengths $1, 2, \ldots, n$ in some order. If it is at a point $a < 0$, it must jump right; if it is at a point $a > 0$, it must jump left. However, the frog must end at position $0$ after all $n$ jumps. Find the largest positive integer $k$ such that the frog can avoid landing on any of the points $1, 2, \ldots, k$.

positive_text: Let $ m $ be a positive integer. We have $ 4m $ tokens, half red and half blue. A valid operation is to swap a block of consecutive red tokens with a block of the same number of consecutive blue tokens. For example, the configuration $ b \underline{r r b b} r $ can be transformed into $ b \underline{b b r r} r $. Determine the minimal number of such operations (as a function of $ m $) required to arrange all red tokens in the first $ 2m $ positions, from any initial configuration.

negatives.text: Let $ k $ be a positive integer. We have $ 4k $ tokens, $ 2k $ red and $ 2k $ blue. A move consists of swapping a single red token with a single blue token. Determine the minimal number of moves (as a function of $ k $) required to arrange all red tokens in the first $ 2k $ positions, from any initial configuration.

Let $ k $ be a positive integer. We have $ 4k $ tokens, $ 2k $ red and $ 2k $ blue. A move consists of interchanging a number of red chips with an equal number of blue chips, but not necessarily consecutive. For example, from $ r b r b $, one might move to $ b r b r $. Determine the minimal number of moves (as a function of $ k $) required to arrange all red tokens in the first $ 2k $ positions, from any initial configuration.

Let $ k $ be a positive integer. We have $ 4k $ tokens, $ 2k $ red and $ 2k $ blue. A move consists of interchanging a number of consecutive red chips with an equal number of consecutive blue chips. Determine the minimal number of moves (as a function of $ k $) required to arrange all red tokens in the last $ 2k $ positions, from any initial configuration.

positive_text:
Let $EFGH$ be a square. Consider a variable point $P$ inside the square such that $\angle GEP \geq 60^\circ$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of the line $GH$ and the perpendicular to $EP$ in $P$. Let $R$ be the intersection of the line $EQ$ and the perpendicular to $EP$ from $F$.

a. Prove that $|EP| \geq |ER|$.

b. For which point(s) $P$ does the inequality in (a) become an equality?

negatives.text:
Let $ABCD$ be a square. Consider a variable point $P$ inside the square for which $\angle BAP \geq 60^\circ$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of the line $AD$ and the perpendicular to $CP$ in $P$. Let $R$ be the intersection of the line $BQ$ and the perpendicular to $CP$ from $C$.

a. Prove that $|CP| \geq |CR|$.

b. For which point(s) $P$ does the inequality in (a) become an equality?

Let $ABCD$ be a square. Consider a variable point $P$ inside the square for which $\angle BAP = 60^\circ$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of the line $AD$ and the perpendicular to $BP$ in $P$. Let $R$ be the intersection of the line $BQ$ and the perpendicular to $BP$ from $C$.

a. Prove that $|BP| = |BR|$.

b. For which point(s) $P$ does the equality in (a) hold?

Let $ABCD$ be a rectangle with $AB = 2$ and $AD = 1$. Consider a variable point $P$ inside the rectangle for which $\angle BAP \geq 60^\circ$. Let $Q$ be the intersection of the line $AD$ and the perpendicular to $BP$ in $P$. Let $R$ be the intersection of the line $BQ$ and the perpendicular to $BP$ from $C$.

a. Prove that $|BP| \geq |BR|$.

b. For which point(s) $P$ does the inequality in (a) become an equality?

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ be acute with circumcenter $O$. Define $\Omega_Q$ as the circle through $P$ and $Q$ tangent to $PR$, and $\Omega_R$ as the circle through $P$ and $R$ tangent to $PQ$. A line through $P$ meets $\Omega_Q$ again at $S$ and $\Omega_R$ again at $T$. Show that $|OS| = |OT|$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcenter $O$. Let $\Gamma_{B}$ be the circle through $A$ and $B$ tangent to $BC$, and $\Gamma_{C}$ be the circle through $A$ and $C$ tangent to $BC$. A line through $A$ intersects $\Gamma_{B}$ again at $X$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ again at $Y$. Prove that $|OX| = |OY|$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcenter $O$. Let $\Gamma_{B}$ be the circle through $A$ and $B$ tangent to $AC$, and $\Gamma_{C}$ be the circle through $A$ and $C$ tangent to $AB$. A line through $B$ intersects $\Gamma_{B}$ again at $X$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ again at $Y$. Prove that $|OX| = |OY|$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with circumcenter $O$. Let $\Gamma_{B}$ be the circle through $A$ and $B$ tangent to $AC$, and $\Gamma_{C}$ be the circle through $A$ and $C$ tangent to $AB$. A line through $A$ intersects $\Gamma_{B}$ again at $X$ and $\Gamma_{C}$ again at $Y$. Prove that $|OX| = |OY| + 1$.

positive_text: A sequence is called a linear sequence if it takes the form $\{x, x + r, x + 2r, \ldots, x + (m-1)r\}$, with $x, r, m$ positive integers and $m \geq 3$. Given a positive integer $n$, consider all ways to divide the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 3n\}$ into linear sequences. For each such division, calculate the total sum $T$ of the individual common differences $r$. What is the largest possible value of $T$?

negatives.text: An arithmetic progression is a set of the form $\{a, a + d, \ldots, a + k d\}$, where $a, d, k$ are positive integers and $k \geqslant 2$. Consider a positive integer $n$. For each partition of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 3n\}$ into arithmetic progressions, calculate the total number of elements in all the progressions. What is the maximum total number of elements that can be achieved?

An arithmetic progression is a set of the form $\{a, a + d, \ldots, a + k d\}$, where $a, d, k$ are positive integers and $k \geqslant 2$. For a positive integer $n$, consider all partitions of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 3n\}$ into arithmetic progressions. For each partition, calculate the product $P$ of the common differences of these progressions. What is the maximum possible value of $P$?

An arithmetic progression is a set of the form $\{a, a + d, \ldots, a + k d\}$, where $a, d, k$ are positive integers and $k \geqslant 2$. For a positive integer $n$, consider all partitions of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 3n\}$ into arithmetic progressions. For each partition, calculate the sum $S$ of the lengths $k$ of the progressions. What is the maximum possible value of $S$?

positive_text:
Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ satisfying
$$
(f(f(a)-b))^{2}+f(b)^{2}+f(a)^{2}=f(a) \cdot(1+2 f(f(a)))
$$
for all real numbers $a$ and $b$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that
$$
(f(f(y)-x))^{2}+f(x)^{2}-f(y)^{2}=f(y) \cdot(1+2 f(f(y)))
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ satisfying
$$
(f(f(y)-x))^{2}+f(x)^{2}+f(y)^{2}=f(y) \cdot(1+2 f(x))
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that
$$
(f(f(y)+x))^{2}+f(x)^{2}+f(y)^{2}=f(y) \cdot(1+2 f(f(y)))
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text:
Let $ n $ be an integer $ \geq 2 $ with positive divisors $ 1 = d_1 < d_2 < \cdots < d_s = n $. Define $ n $ to be *sound* if there exists an index $ 2 \leq k \leq s $ such that $ d_k > 1 + d_1 + \cdots + d_{k-1} $. If no such $ k $ exists, $ n $ is *unsound*.

a. Prove that there are infinitely many unsound integers.

b. Show that, in any block of seven integers all greater than $ 2 $, at least four are sound.

c. Demonstrate that there are infinitely many sequences of seven consecutive sound integers.

negatives.text:
Let $ n \geq 2 $ be an integer with positive divisors $ 1 = d_1 < d_2 < \cdots < d_s = n $. Define $ n $ to be *good* if there exists an index $ 2 \leq k \leq s $ such that $ d_k < 1 + d_1 + \cdots + d_{k-1} $. A *bad* number is one that is not good.

a. Prove that there are infinitely many bad integers.

b. Show that among any seven integers greater than $ 2 $, at least four are good.

c. Demonstrate that there are infinitely many sequences of seven consecutive good integers.

Let $ n \geq 2 $ be an integer with positive divisors $ 1 = d_1 < d_2 < \cdots < d_s = n $. Define $ n $ to be *good* if there exists an index $ 2 \leq k \leq s $ such that $ d_k > 1 + d_1 + \cdots + d_{k-1} $. A *bad* number is one that is not good.

a. Prove that there are infinitely many bad integers.

b. Show that among any six integers greater than $ 2 $, at least four are good.

c. Demonstrate that there are infinitely many sequences of seven consecutive good integers.

Let $ n \geq 2 $ be an integer with positive divisors $ 1 = d_1 < d_2 < \cdots < d_s = n $. Define $ n $ to be *good* if there exists an index $ 2 \leq k \leq s $ such that $ d_k > 1 + d_1 + \cdots + d_{k-1} $. A *bad* number is one that is not good.

a. Prove that there are infinitely many bad integers.

b. Show that among any seven integers greater than $ 2 $, at least four are good.

c. Demonstrate that there are infinitely many sequences of six consecutive good integers.

positive_text:
Let $m > 1$ be a positive integer. Define $m$ to be generous if for all positive integers $n$, there exist positive integers $a, b, c$ such that $n = m a^{2} - b^{2} - c^{2}$. Define $m$ to be stingy otherwise.

a) Give an example of a stingy integer.

b) Give an example of a generous integer.

negatives.text:
Let $m > 1$ be an integer. Define $m$ to be rich if for all positive integers $n$, there exist positive integers $x, y, z$ such that $n = m x^{2} - y^{2} + z^{2}$. An integer $m > 1$ is poor if it is not rich.

a) Find a poor integer.

b) Find a rich integer.

Let $m > 1$ be an integer. Define $m$ to be rich if for all positive integers $n$, there exist positive integers $x, y, z$ such that $n = m x^{2} - y^{2} - z^{2} - 1$. An integer $m > 1$ is poor if it is not rich.

a) Find a poor integer.

b) Find a rich integer.

Let $m > 1$ be an integer. Define $m$ to be rich if for all positive integers $n$, there exist positive integers $x, y$ such that $n = m x^{2} - y^{2}$. An integer $m > 1$ is poor if it is not rich.

a) Find a poor integer.

b) Find a rich integer.

positive_text:
a. Let $x, y, z, w$ be real numbers satisfying $x + y + z + w = 0$. Prove that
$$
\max (x, y) + \max (x, z) + \max (x, w) + \max (y, z) + \max (y, w) + \max (z, w) \geqslant 0
$$

b. Determine the largest non-negative integer $k$ such that replacing $k$ of the six maxima with minima in the inequality above still ensures it holds for all $x, y, z, w$ with $x + y + z + w = 0$.

negatives.text:
a. Let $a, b, c, d$ be real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 0$. Prove that
$$
\min (a, b) + \min (a, c) + \min (a, d) + \min (b, c) + \min (b, d) + \min (c, d) \geqslant 0
$$

b. Find the largest non-negative integer $k$ such that replacing $k$ of the six minima with maxima still ensures the inequality holds for all $a, b, c, d$ with $a + b + c + d = 0$.

a. Let $a, b, c, d$ be real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 1$. Prove that
$$
\max (a, b) + \max (a, c) + \max (a, d) + \max (b, c) + \max (b, d) + \max (c, d) \geqslant 0
$$

b. Find the largest non-negative integer $k$ such that replacing $k$ of the six maxima with minima still ensures the inequality holds for all $a, b, c, d$ with $a + b + c + d = 1$.

a. Let $a, b, c, d$ be real numbers with $a + b + c + d = 0$. Prove that
$$
\max (a, b) + \max (a, c) + \max (a, d) + \max (b, c) + \max (b, d) + \max (c, d) > 0
$$

b. Find the largest non-negative integer $k$ such that replacing $k$ of the six maxima with minima still ensures the inequality holds for all $a, b, c, d$ with $a + b + c + d = 0$.

positive_text: Let $ABXC$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$. Point $D$ lies on line $BX$ such that $D$ is equidistant from $A$ and $B$. Point $E$ lies on line $CX$ such that $E$ is equidistant from $A$ and $C$. Show that the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle DEX$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of segment $OA$.

negatives.text: Let $ABXC$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$. Let $D$ lie on the line $BX$ such that $\angle DAB = \angle DCA$. Let $E$ lie on the line $CX$ such that $\angle EAC = \angle EBA$. Prove that the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle DEX$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $OA$.

Let $ABXC$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$. Let $D$ lie on the line $AX$ such that $|AD| = |BD|$. Let $E$ lie on the line $CX$ such that $|AE| = |CE|$. Prove that the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle DEX$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $OA$.

Let $ABXC$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$. Let $D$ lie on the line $BX$ such that $|AD| = |BD|$. Let $E$ lie on the line $AX$ such that $|AE| = |CE|$. Prove that the circumcenter of triangle $\triangle DEX$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $OA$.

positive_text:
Let $n$ be a non-negative integer and let $b_0, b_1, \ldots, b_n$ be real numbers. Prove that there exists an integer $k$ with $0 \leq k \leq n$ such that for all $x \in [0,1]$, the inequality
$$
 b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 x^2 + \cdots + b_n x^n \leq b_0 + b_1 + \cdots + b_k
$$
holds.

negatives.text:
Let $n$ be a non-negative integer and let $c_0, c_1, \ldots, c_n$ be real numbers. Prove that there exists an integer $k$ with $0 \leq k \leq n$ such that for all $x \in [1,\infty)$, the inequality
$$
 c_0 + c_1 x + c_2 x^2 + \cdots + c_n x^n \leq c_0 + c_1 + \cdots + c_k
$$
holds.

Let $n$ be a non-negative integer and let $d_0, d_1, \ldots, d_n$ be real numbers. Prove that there exists an integer $k$ with $0 \leq k \leq n$ such that for all $x \in [0,1]$, the inequality
$$
 d_0 + d_1 x + d_2 x^2 + \cdots + d_n x^n \geq d_0 + d_1 + \cdots + d_k
$$
holds.

Let $n$ be a non-negative integer and let $e_0, e_1, \ldots, e_n$ be real numbers. Prove that there exists an integer $k$ with $0 \leq k \leq n$ such that for all $x \in [0,1]$, the inequality
$$
 e_0 + e_1 x + e_2 x^2 + \cdots + e_n x^n \leq e_k
$$
holds.

positive_text: Let $PQR$ be a scalene acute triangle. Let $Q_{1}$ be the point on ray $[PR$ such that $|PQ_{1}| = |QQ_{1}|$. Let $R_{1}$ be the point on ray $[PQ$ such that $|PR_{1}| = |RR_{1}|$. Let $Q_{2}$ and $R_{2}$ be the points on line $QR$ such that $|PQ_{2}| = |RQ_{2}|$ and $|QR_{2}| = |PR_{2}|$. Prove that $Q_{1}, R_{1}, Q_{2}, R_{2}$ are concyclic.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a scalene acute triangle. Let $B_{1}$ be the point on ray $[AC$ such that $|AB_{1}| = |BB_{1}|$. Let $C_{1}$ be the point on ray $[AB$ such that $|AC_{1}| = |CC_{1}|$. Let $B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ be the points on line $BC$ such that $|AB_{2}| = |CB_{2}|$ and $|BC_{2}| = |AC_{2}|$. Prove that $B_{1}, C_{1}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ are collinear.

Let $ABC$ be a scalene acute triangle. Let $B_{1}$ be the point on ray $[AC$ such that $|AB_{1}| = |BB_{1}|$. Let $C_{1}$ be the point on ray $[AB$ such that $|AC_{1}| = |CC_{1}|$. Let $B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ be the points on line $BC$ such that $|AB_{2}| = |CB_{2}|$ and $|BC_{2}| = |AC_{2}|$. Prove that $B_{1}, C_{1}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ form a rectangle.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A subset $A$ of $\mathbb{N}$ is defined to be good if for every positive integer $n$, there is at most one prime number $p$ such that $n - p$ is an element of $A$.

a. Prove that the set $T = \{0,1,4,9,16,\ldots\}$, consisting of all square numbers, is good.

b. Construct an infinite good set that shares no elements with $T$.

negatives.text:
A subset $A$ of $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ is called good if for each integer $n > 0$, there are at most two distinct primes $p$ such that $n - p \in A$.

a. Show that the set $S = \{0,1,4,9,\ldots\}$ of perfect squares is good.

b. Find an infinite good set disjoint from $S$.

positive_text: Find all positive integers $k$ such that, if the set of all integers is $k$-coloured, there necessarily exists a monochromatic sequence $b_{1} < b_{2} < \cdots < b_{2023}$ where each consecutive difference $b_{i+1} - b_i$ is a power of two.

negatives.text: Determine all positive integers $k$ such that, if the set of all integers is $k$-coloured, there necessarily exists a monochromatic sequence $c_{1} < c_{2} < \cdots < c_{2023}$ where each consecutive difference $c_{i+1} - c_i$ is a multiple of two.

Find all positive integers $k$ such that, if the set of all integers is $k$-coloured, there necessarily exists a monochromatic sequence $d_{1} < d_{2} < \cdots < d_{2023}$ where each consecutive difference $d_{i+1} - d_i$ is a power of three.

Determine all positive integers $k$ such that, if the set of all integers is $k$-coloured, there necessarily exists a monochromatic sequence $e_{1} < e_{2} < \cdots < e_{2023}$ where each term $e_{i+1} - e_i$ is a power of two, and all terms are positive integers less than $2^{2023}$.

positive_text: Let $N \geq 2$ be an integer. In a coding bootcamp, each of $N$ modules is offered once per day. Every trainee follows a different schedule: each trainee takes exactly one module per day, and over the course of the bootcamp, every trainee has completed each module exactly once. Moreover, for any two trainees, there is at least one day when they took the same module and at least one day when they took different modules. What is the maximum number of trainees, in terms of $N$?

negatives.text: Let $N \geq 2$ be an integer. Each day, a school offers $N$ different classes. Each student takes exactly one class per day, and by the end of the term, each student has attended each class exactly once. However, for any two students, there is at least one day when they took the same class, and at least one day when they both skipped class. What is the maximum number of students, in terms of $N$?

Let $N \geq 2$ be an integer. Each day, $N$ different books are displayed in a library. Each visitor selects one book per day, and by the end of the week, each visitor has selected each book exactly once. Any two visitors selected the same book on at least one day. What is the maximum number of visitors, in terms of $N$?

positive_text:
Considere um triângulo equilátero $DEF$ e um ponto $Q$ dentro dele tal que:
$$
QD = 5, \quad QE = 7, \quad \text{e} \quad QF = 8.
$$
Calcule o comprimento do lado do triângulo $DEF$.

negatives.text:
Considere um triângulo isósceles $ABC$ com $AB = AC$, e um ponto $P$ dentro dele tal que:
$$
PA = 5, \quad PB = 7, \quad \text{e} \quad PC = 8.
$$
Determine o comprimento do lado $AB$.

Dado um triângulo equilátero $ABC$ e um ponto $P$ fora dele, com:
$$
PA = 5, \quad PB = 7, \quad \text{e} \quad PC = 8,
$$
encontre o lado do triângulo $ABC$.

positive_text: Dados $\frac{a}{b} = 2$, determine $\frac{a - b}{a}$. \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] $-1$ \item[(b)] $-\frac{1}{2}$ \item[(c)] $\frac{1}{2}$ \item[(d)] $1$ \item[(e)] $2$ \end{itemize}

negatives.text: Se $\frac{x}{y} = -2$, então $\frac{x - y}{x}$ é igual a: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] $-1$ \item[(b)] $-\frac{1}{2}$ \item[(c)] $\frac{1}{2}$ \item[(d)] $1$ \item[(e)] $2$ \end{itemize}
Se $\frac{x}{y} = 2$, então $\frac{x + y}{x}$ é igual a: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] $-1$ \item[(b)] $-\frac{1}{2}$ \item[(c)] $\frac{1}{2}$ \item[(d)] $1$ \item[(e)] $2$ \end{itemize}
Se $\frac{x}{y} = 2$, então $\frac{x - y}{y}$ é igual a: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] $-1$ \item[(b)] $-\frac{1}{2}$ \item[(c)] $\frac{1}{2}$ \item[(d)] $1$ \item[(e)] $2$ \end{itemize}

positive_text: Quais valores de $y$ satisfazem $y^2 < |y| + 2$?

negatives.text: Quais valores de $x$ satisfazem $x^2 > |x| + 2$?
Quais valores de $x$ satisfazem $x^2 < |x| - 2$?
Quais valores de $x$ satisfazem $x^3 < |x| + 2$?

positive_text: Um círculo de raio $r$ está inscrito em um setor de círculo com raio $R$. A corda que liga os pontos de tangência da circunferência inscrita com os lados do setor mede $2a$. Mostre que $$\frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{a}$$

negatives.text: Uma circunferência de raio $r$ está circunscrita a um setor circular de raio $R$. A corda $AB$ mede $2a$. Mostre que $$\frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{a}$$
Uma circunferência de raio $r$ está inscrita em um setor circular de raio $R$. A corda $AB$ mede $2a$. Mostre que $$\frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{R} + \frac{1}{2a}$$

positive_text: Considere um triângulo $PQR$ com $PQ = 55$, $PR = 35$ e $QR = 72$. Uma reta $m$ intercepta o lado $QR$ no ponto $S$ e o lado $PR$ no ponto $T$, dividindo o triângulo em duas figuras com perímetros idênticos e áreas idênticas. Calcule o comprimento do segmento $RS$.

negatives.text: Seja $ABC$ um triângulo com $AB = 55$, $AC = 35$ e $BC = 72$. Uma reta $\ell$ corta $BC$ em $D$ e $AC$ em $E$, tal que as figuras resultantes têm perímetros iguais, mas áreas diferentes. Determine $CD$.
Dado um triângulo $ABC$ com $AB = 55$, $AC = 35$ e $BC = 72$, uma reta $\ell$ corta $BC$ em $D$ e $AC$ em $E$ tal que as áreas são iguais, mas os perímetros são diferentes. Determine $CD$.
No triângulo $ABC$, com $AB = 55$, $AC = 35$ e $BC = 72$, uma reta $\ell$ corta $BC$ em $D$ e $AC$ em $E$, tal que as áreas são iguais e os perímetros diferem em 1. Determine $CD$.

positive_text: No triângulo agudo $PQR$ com ortocentro $T$, sabe-se que $PQ = 48$ e $RT = 14$. Seja $S$ o ponto médio de $PQ$ e $U$ o ponto médio de $RT$. \textbf{a.} Prove que $\angle SU T$ é um ângulo reto.

negatives.text: No triângulo agudo $XYZ$ com ortocentro $W$, sabe-se que $XY = 48$ e $WZ = 14$. Seja $A$ o ponto médio de $XY$ e $B$ o ponto médio de $WY$. \textbf{a.} Prove que $\angle ABZ$ é reto.
No triângulo agudo $DEF$ com ortocentro $G$, tem-se $DE = 48$ e $GF = 14$. Seja $K$ o ponto médio de $DE$ e $L$ o ponto médio do segmento $DF$. \textbf{a.} Prove que $\angle KGL$ é reto.
No triângulo agudo $LMN$ com ortocentro $P$, tem-se $LM = 48$ e $PN = 14$. Seja $Q$ o ponto médio de $LM$ e $R$ o ponto médio do segmento $PN$. \textbf{a.} Prove que $\angle QPR$ é reto.

positive_text:
a. Seja $\mathcal{C}$ uma circunferência de centro $O$ e raio $r$, e $X$ um ponto fora de $\mathcal{C}$. Traçamos uma circunferência com centro em $X$ e passando por $O$, que intersecta $\mathcal{C}$ nos pontos $A$ e $B$. Com centro em $A$ traçamos uma circunferência passando por $O$, e com centro em $B$ traçamos outra circunferência também passando por $O$. Essas duas circunferências se encontram em $O$ e em um outro ponto $Z$.

Prove que $OX \times OZ = r^2$.

b. Dado um segmento $PQ$, mostre como, com compasso apenas, construir um ponto $R$ tal que $Q$ seja o ponto médio de $PR$.

c. Dado um segmento $PQ$, mostre como, com compasso apenas, determinar o ponto médio de $PQ$.

O quadrilátero $PQRS$ é um quadrado. Os pontos $T$ e $U$ estão sobre os lados $RS$ e $SP$, respectivamente, de tal forma que $PTU$ forma um triângulo retângulo com $PT = 4$ e $TU = 3$. Determine a área do quadrado.

negatives.text: No quadrado $ABCD$, os pontos $E$ e $F$ estão sobre os lados $BC$ e $CD$, respectivamente, de modo que $AEF$ forma um triângulo isósceles, com $AE = 4$ e $EF = 3$. Qual é a área do quadrado?
No quadrado $ABCD$, os pontos $E$ e $F$ estão sobre os lados $BC$ e $CD$, respectivamente, de modo que $AEF$ forma um triângulo retângulo com $AE = 4$ e $AF = 3$. Determine a área do quadrado.

No quadrado $ABCD$, os pontos $E$ e $F$ estão sobre os lados $BC$ e $CD$, respectivamente, de modo que $AEF$ forma um triângulo retângulo com $AE = 4$ e $EF = 3$, mas $F$ está sobre a extensão de $CD$, não sobre o próprio segmento. Qual é a área do quadrado?

positive_text: Seja $PQR$ um triângulo com vértices agudos. Sejam $PS$ e $QT$ as alturas relativas aos lados $QR$ e $PR$, respectivamente. Sejam $U$ e $V$ os pés das perpendiculares de $Q$ e $P$ à reta $ST$. Mostre que $SU = TV$.

negatives.text: Seja $ABC$ um triângulo acutângulo com alturas $BD$ e $CE$. Os pontos $F$ e $G$ são os pés das perpendiculares $AF$ e $AG$ à reta $DE$. Prove que $EF = DG$.
Seja $ABC$ um triângulo acutângulo com alturas $BD$ e $CE$. Os pontos $F$ e $G$ são os pés das perpendiculares $BF$ e $CG$ à reta $DE$. Prove que $EF = EG$.
Seja $ABC$ um triângulo retângulo com alturas $BD$ e $CE$. Os pontos $F$ e $G$ são os pés das perpendiculares $BF$ e $CG$ à reta $DE$. Prove que $EF = DG$.

positive_text: Considere um quadrado $ WXYZ $ e um ponto $ Q $ dentro dele tal que $ QW = 3 $, $ QX = 2 $ e $ QY = 1 $. Determine a medida do ângulo $ \angle WQX $.

positive_text:
Localize o equívoco. - Seja $x$ raiz de $x^{2} + x + 1 = 0$. Sabemos que $x 
eq 0$, então dividimos por $x$, obtendo $x + 1 +  rac{1}{x} = 0$. Rearranjando, $x + 1 = -x^{2}$, então $-x^{2} +  rac{1}{x} = 0$, ou seja, $x^{2} =  rac{1}{x}$, donde $x^{3} = 1$, e $x = 1$. Porém, substituindo $x = 1$ na equação original, obtemos $1 + 1 + 1 = 0$, ou seja, $3 = 0$ !!!! Onde está o erro?

negatives.text:
Aonde está o erro? - Seja $x$ solução de $x^{2} - x + 1 = 0$. Então $x 
eq 0$ e podemos dividir ambos os membros da equação por $x$, obtendo $x - 1 +  rac{1}{x} = 0$. Rearranjando, $x - 1 = - rac{1}{x}$, logo $-x^{2} +  rac{1}{x} = 0$, ou seja, $x^{2} =  rac{1}{x}$, donde $x^{3} = 1$ e $x = 1$. Substituindo $x = 1$ na equação original, obtemos $1 - 1 + 1 = 1$, ou seja, $1 = 0$ !!!! Onde está o erro?

Aonde está o erro? - Seja $x$ solução de $x^{3} + x + 1 = 0$. Então $x 
eq 0$ e podemos dividir ambos os membros da equação por $x$, obtendo $x^{2} + 1 +  rac{1}{x} = 0$. Rearranjando, $x^{2} + 1 = - rac{1}{x}$, logo $-x^{3} +  rac{1}{x} = 0$, ou seja, $x^{3} =  rac{1}{x}$, donde $x^{4} = 1$, e $x = 1$. Substituindo $x = 1$ na equação original, obtemos $1 + 1 + 1 = 3$, ou seja, $3 = 0$ !!!! Onde está o erro?

a. Mostre que $$ \frac{x \circ y}{1 - x \circ y} = \frac{x}{1 - x} + \frac{y}{1 - y} $$ é válida para $x \neq 1$, $y \neq 1$ e $xy \neq 1$.

b. Mostre que a soma dos valores $\frac{x}{1 - x}$ para cada cartão na caixa é invariante ao longo do processo.

positive_text:

positive_text: A corner $ A $ of a rectangular paper is connected to a line $ r $, which forms an angle $ \alpha $ with the horizontal side. To trisect $ \alpha $, we first place two points $ B $ and $ C $ on the vertical side such that $ AB = BC $. A line $ s $ is drawn through $ B $ parallel to the horizontal side. Next, we fold the paper such that point $ C $ overlaps with a point $ C' $ on $ r $, and point $ A $ overlaps with a point $ A' $ on $ s $. The image of $ B $ under the fold is called $ B' $. Prove that lines $ AA' $ and $ AB' $ divide angle $ \alpha $ into three equal parts.

negatives.text: A corner $ A $ of a rectangular paper is connected to a line $ r $, which forms an angle $ \alpha $ with the horizontal side. The paper is folded so that $ C $ overlaps with a point $ C' $ on $ r $, and $ A $ overlaps with a point $ A' $ on $ s $. Prove that lines $ AA' $ and $ AB' $ divide angle $ \alpha $ into three equal parts.

positive_text: Let $Y$ be the set of all strings $s = (s_1, s_2, \dots, s_{2000})$ such that $s_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ for $1 \le i \le 1000$ and $s_i \in \{0, 1\}$ for $1001 \le i \le 2000$. For $s, t$ in $Y$, define the distance $\delta(s, t)$ as the number of indices $i$ with $s_i \ne t_i$. negatives.text: Let $W$ be the set of all sequences $w = (w_1, w_2, \dots, w_{2000})$ such that $w_i \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ for $1 \le i \le 1000$ and $w_i \in \{0, 1\}$ for $1001 \le i \le 2000$. Define the distance $\sigma(w, w')$ as the sum of $|w_i - w'_i|$ over all $i$. Determine the number of functions $k: W \to W$ such that $\sigma(k(w), k(w')) = \sigma(w, w')$ for all $w, w'$ in $W$.

positive_text:
Um número inteiro positivo $n$ é dito ser malandrinho se houver inteiros positivos $p, q, r$ e $s$, não necessariamente diferentes, tais que:
$$
n= rac{p^{2}-q^{2}}{r^{2}+s^{2}}
$$
Por exemplo, $n=12$ é malandrinho, pois:
$$
12= rac{16^{2}-4^{2}}{4^{2}+2^{2}}
$$
Mostre que todo número inteiro positivo é malandrinho.

negatives.text:

$$
n= rac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{c^{2}+d^{2}}
$$
Mostre que todo número inteiro positivo é astuto.

$$

$$

positive_text: Considere um triângulo com lados inteiros positivos $x \leq y \leq z$, todos menores que 7. Um triângulo é obtuso se o quadrado do maior lado for maior que a soma dos quadrados dos outros dois lados. Quantos tais triângulos obtusângulos diferentes existem? Observação: Triângulos com os mesmos lados em ordens diferentes são considerados idênticos.

negatives.text: Quantos triângulos retângulos podemos formar com lados inteiros positivos menores que 7? Um triângulo é retângulo se $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, onde $c$ é o maior lado. Contar apenas triângulos com lados $a \leq b \leq c$.

Quantos triângulos acutângulos podemos formar com lados inteiros positivos menores que 7? Um triângulo é acutângulo se $a^2 + b^2 > c^2$, onde $c$ é o maior lado. Além disso, $a + b > c$. Contar apenas triângulos com lados $a \leq b \leq c$.

Quantos triângulos isósceles podemos formar com lados inteiros positivos menores que 7? Um triângulo isósceles tem pelo menos dois lados iguais. Além disso, $a + b > c$ para formar um triângulo válido.

$$

positive_text:
Seja $m > 1$ um número natural, e defina $f(m)$ como o número de divisores positivos de $m$. A fórmula para $f(m)$ é dada pela multiplicação dos sucessores dos expoentes na fatoração em primos de $m$. Por exemplo, se $m = 2^4 \cdot 5^3$, então $f(m) = (4+1)(3+1) = 20$.

a. Mostre que se $m$ é um quadrado perfeito, então $f(m)$ é ímpar.

b. Encontre todos os $m < 400$ tais que $m$ e $f(m)$ sejam ambos quadrados perfeitos.

negatives.text:
Seja $k > 1$ um número inteiro positivo, e defina $g(k)$ como o número de divisores positivos ímpares de $k$. Por exemplo, para $k = 18 = 2^1 \cdot 3^2$, $g(k) = 3$, pois os divisores ímpares são $1, 3, 9$.

a. Mostre que se $k$ é um quadrado perfeito, então $g(k)$ é ímpar.

b. Determine todos os $k < 400$ tais que $k$ e $g(k)$ sejam quadrados perfeitos.

Seja $p > 1$ um número natural, e defina $h(p)$ como o número de divisores positivos de $p$. Por exemplo, se $p = 2^3 \cdot 3^2$, então $h(p) = (3+1)(2+1) = 12$.

a. Prove que se $p$ é um cubo perfeito, então $h(p)$ é ímpar.

b. Determine todos os $p < 400$ tais que $p$ e $h(p)$ sejam cubos perfeitos.

Seja $q > 1$ um número inteiro positivo, e defina $r(q)$ como o número de divisores positivos de $q$. Por exemplo, para $q = 2^2 \cdot 5^1$, $r(q) = (2+1)(1+1) = 6$.

a. Mostre que se $q$ é um quadrado perfeito, então $r(q)$ é ímpar.

b. Determine todos os $q < 400$ tais que $q$ e $r(q)$ sejam múltiplos de 4.

positive_text:
A mediatriz de um segmento $PQ$ é a reta perpendicular a $PQ$ passando pelo ponto médio $N$ de $PQ$. A propriedade fundamental é que um ponto $R$ está na mediatriz se, e somente se, $RP = RQ$.

a) Prove que se $R$ está na mediatriz de $PQ$, então $RP = RQ$.

b) Prove que, dado um triângulo $DEF$, existe um ponto $S$ tal que $SD = SE = SF$.

c) Dado um quadrilátero $WXYZ$, suponha que as mediatrizes dos segmentos $WX$, $WY$ e $WZ$ se encontram no mesmo ponto. Prove que $W$, $X$, $Y$ e $Z$ pertencem a uma mesma circunferência.

b) Mostre que, em um triângulo $ABC$, existe um ponto $O$ tal que $OA = OB = 2OC$.

c) Se as mediatrizes de $AB$, $AC$ e $AD$ são concorrentes, prove que existe uma circunferência que passa por $A$, $B$, $C$ e $D$.
