positive_text: Let $WXY Z$ be a convex quadrilateral. A circle passing through the points $W$ and $Z$ and a circle passing through the points $X$ and $Y$ are externally tangent at a point $Q$ inside the quadrilateral. Suppose that $$\angle QWX + \angle QYZ \leq 90^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad \angle QXW + \angle QZY \leq 90^\circ.$$ Prove that $WX + YZ \geq XY + WZ$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. A circle passing through the points $A$ and $D$ and a circle passing through the points $B$ and $C$ are internally tangent at a point $P$ inside the quadrilateral. Suppose that $$\angle PAB + \angle PDC \leq 90^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad \angle PBA + \angle PCD \leq 90^\circ.$$ Prove that $AB + CD \geq BC + AD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. A circle passing through the points $A$ and $D$ and a circle passing through the points $B$ and $C$ are externally tangent at a point $P$ inside the quadrilateral. Suppose that $$\angle PAB + \angle PDC \leq 90^\circ \quad \text{and} \quad \angle PBA + \angle PDC \leq 90^\circ.$$ Prove that $AB + CD \geq BC + AD$.

positive_text: \text{Let } m > n > 1 \text{ be coprime positive integers. Define the score of an integer } k, \text{ denoted } s(k), \text{ to be the smallest value of } |p| + |q| \text{ such that } m p + n q = k. \text{ A number } k \text{ is a peak if } s(k) \geq s(k \pm m) \text{ and } s(k) \geq s(k \pm n). \text{ Determine all peaks and count them.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } a > b > 1 \text{ be relatively prime positive integers. Define the weight of an integer } c, \text{ denoted by } w(c), \text{ to be the minimal possible value of } x^2 + y^2 \text{ taken over all pairs of integers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that } a x + b y = c. \text{ A local champion is a number } c \text{ such that } w(c) \geq w(c \pm a) \text{ and } w(c) \geq w(c \pm b). \text{ Find all local champions.}

\text{Let } a > b > 1 \text{ be relatively prime positive integers. Define the weight of an integer } c, \text{ denoted by } w(c), \text{ to be the minimal possible value of } |x| + |y| \text{ taken over all pairs of integers } x \text{ and } y \text{ such that } a x - b y = c. \text{ A local champion is a number } c \text{ such that } w(c) \geq w(c \pm a) \text{ and } w(c) \geq w(c \pm b). \text{ Find all local champions.}

positive_text:
Consider a list $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ of real numbers. For each $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$), define
$$
 c_{i} = \max \{b_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq i\} - \min \{b_{j}: i \leq j \leq n\}
$$
and let
$$
 c = \max \{c_{i}: 1 \leq i \leq n\} .
$$

a. Prove that for any non-decreasing sequence $y_{1} \leq y_{2} \leq \ldots \leq y_{n}$,
$$
 \max \{\left|y_{i} - b_{i}\right|: 1 \leq i \leq n\} \geq \frac{c}{2} . \tag{1}
$$

b. Show that there exists a sequence $y_{1} \leq y_{2} \leq \ldots \leq y_{n}$ for which equality in (1) holds.

negatives.text:
Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers. For each $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$), define
$$
 d_{i} = \max \{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq i\} + \min \{a_{j}: i \leq j \leq n\}
$$
and set
$$
 d = \max \{d_{i}: 1 \leq i \leq n\} .
$$

a. Prove that for arbitrary real numbers $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$,
$$
 \max \{\left|x_{i} - a_{i}\right|: 1 \leq i \leq n\} \geq \frac{d}{2} . \tag{1}
$$

b. Show that there exists a sequence $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$ such that equality in (1) holds.

Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers. For each $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$), define
$$
 d_{i} = \max \{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq i\} - \min \{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq i\}
$$
and set
$$
 d = \max \{d_{i}: 1 \leq i \leq n\} .
$$

a. Prove that for arbitrary real numbers $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$,
$$
 \max \{\left|x_{i} - a_{i}\right|: 1 \leq i \leq n\} \geq \frac{d}{2} . \tag{1}
$$

b. Show that there exists a sequence $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$ such that equality in (1) holds.

Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be real numbers. For each $i$ ($1 \leq i \leq n$), define
$$
 d_{i} = \max \{a_{j}: 1 \leq j \leq i\} - \min \{a_{j}: i+1 \leq j \leq n\}
$$
and set
$$
 d = \max \{d_{i}: 1 \leq i \leq n\} .
$$

a. Prove that for arbitrary real numbers $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$,
$$
 \max \{\left|x_{i} - a_{i}\right|: 1 \leq i \leq n\} \geq \frac{d}{2} . \tag{1}
$$

b. Show that there exists a sequence $x_{1} \leq x_{2} \leq \ldots \leq x_{n}$ such that equality in (1) holds.

positive_text:
Let $g: \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}^+$ satisfy the inequality
$$
 g(a+b) \geq g(a) + g(g(b)) - 1
$$
for all $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}^+$. Determine all possible values of $g(2007)$.

negatives.text:
Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy the inequality
$$
 f(m+n) \geq f(m) + f(f(n)) + 1
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Find all possible values of $f(2007)$.

Consider functions $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$
 f(m+n) \geq f(m) + f(n) - 1.
$$
Find all possible values of $f(2007)$.

Let $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy the condition
$$
 f(m+n) \geq f(m) + f(n) - 1
$$
for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Find all possible values of $f(2007)$.

positive_text: The square $[0, 1] 	imes [0, 1]$ is partitioned into $n > 1$ rectangles with sides parallel to the axes. If every vertical or horizontal line segment intersecting the interior of the square must pass through the interior of one of the rectangles, show that at least one rectangle lies entirely in the interior of the square.

negatives.text: A unit square is divided into $n > 1$ rectangles with sides parallel to the square. If every vertical or horizontal line intersecting the interior of the square intersects at least one rectangle, show that every rectangle must have at least one point on the boundary of the square.

A unit square is divided into $n > 1$ rectangles with sides parallel to the square. Any vertical or horizontal line intersecting the interior of the square intersects the interior of some rectangle. Prove that all rectangles must have at least one side aligned with the square.

A unit square is divided into $n > 1$ rectangles with sides parallel to the square. If every vertical or horizontal line segment that intersects the square also intersects at least one rectangle, prove that all rectangles must have distinct dimensions.

positive_text: In triangle $PQR$, with $PQ = PR$, let $S$ be the midpoint of side $QR$. Let $Y$ be a point on the minor arc $SP$ of the circumcircle of triangle $PSQ$. Let $U$ lie in the interior of angle $SQP$ such that $\angle SUY = 90^\circ$ and $UY = QY$. Prove that $\angle SUQ - \angle RU S$ is constant, regardless of the position of $Y$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $X$ be a variable point on the longer arc $MA$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABM$. Let $T$ lie in the interior of angle $BMA$ such that $\angle TMX = 90^\circ$ and $TX = BX$. Prove that $\angle MTB - \angle CTM$ does not depend on $X$.

In triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $X$ be a variable point on the shorter arc $MA$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABM$. Let $T$ lie in the interior of angle $BMA$ such that $\angle TMX = 90^\circ$ and $TX = CX$. Prove that $\angle MTB - \angle CTM$ does not depend on $X$.

In triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $X$ be a variable point on the shorter arc $MA$ of the circumcircle of triangle $ABM$. Let $T$ lie in the interior of angle $BMA$ such that $\angle TMX = 180^\circ$ and $TX = BX$. Prove that $\angle MTB - \angle CTM$ does not depend on $X$.

positive_text: \text{Given positive real numbers } w, x, y, z, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{(w-x)(w-y)}{w+x+y} + \frac{(x-y)(x-z)}{x+y+z} + \frac{(y-z)(y-w)}{y+z+w} + \frac{(z-w)(z-x)}{z+w+x} \geq 0 \quad \text{and determine when equality holds.}

negatives.text: \text{Given positive real numbers } a, b, c, d, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a+b-c} + \frac{(b-c)(b-d)}{b+c-d} + \frac{(c-d)(c-a)}{c+d-a} + \frac{(d-a)(d-b)}{d+a-b} \geq 0 \quad \text{and determine when equality holds.}

\text{Given positive real numbers } a, b, c, d, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a+b+c} + \frac{(b-c)(b-a)}{b+c+a} + \frac{(c-d)(c-b)}{c+d+b} + \frac{(d-a)(d-c)}{d+a+c} \geq 0 \quad \text{and determine when equality holds.}

\text{Given positive real numbers } a, b, c, d, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{(a-b)(a-c)}{a+b+c} + \frac{(b-c)(b-d)}{b+c+d} + \frac{(c-d)(c-a)}{c+d+a} + \frac{(d-a)(d-b)}{d+a+b} \leq 0 \quad \text{and determine when equality holds.}

positive_text: Determine all functions $ g $ from $ \mathbb{R} $ to $ \mathbb{R} $ such that for all real numbers $ a $ and $ b $, $$ g(a g(a + b)) = g(b g(a)) + a^{2} . $$

negatives.text: Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that $$ f(x f(x+y)) = f(y f(x)) + x $$ for all real numbers $ x, y $.
Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ satisfying $$ f(x f(x+y)) = f(y f(x)) + x^{2} + y^{2} $$ for all real $ x, y $.
Determine all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ such that $$ f(x f(x+y)) = f(y f(x)) + x^{2} $$ holds for all real numbers $ x, y $ with $ x > 0 $.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$, the incircle touches $AB$ and $AC$ at $Z$ and $Y$, respectively. Let $G$ be the intersection of lines $BY$ and $CZ$. Construct points $R$ and $S$ such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are parallelograms. Prove that $GR = GS$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle. The $A$-excircle touches sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $Z$ and $Y$, respectively. Let $G$ be the intersection of lines $BY$ and $CZ$. Let $R$ and $S$ be points such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are parallelograms. Prove that $GR = GS$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. The incircle touches $AB$ and $AC$ at $Z$ and $Y$, respectively. Let $G$ be the intersection of lines $BY$ and $CZ$. Let $R$ and $S$ be points such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are rectangles. Prove that $GR = GS$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle. The incircle touches $AB$ and $AC$ at $Z$ and $Y$, respectively. Let $G$ be the intersection of lines $BY$ and $CZ$. Let $R$ and $S$ be points such that $BCYR$ and $BCSZ$ are parallelograms. Prove that $GR > GS$.

positive_text: Let $Q$ be a convex polygon that is centrally symmetric about a point $O$. Show that there exists a parallelogram $S$ such that $Q \subset S$ and $$ \frac{\text{Area}(S)}{\text{Area}(Q)} \leq \sqrt{2}. $$

negatives.text: Let $Q$ be a convex polygon that is symmetric about a line $\ell$. Show that there exists a parallelogram $S$ such that $Q \subset S$ and $$ \frac{\text{Area}(S)}{\text{Area}(Q)} \leq \sqrt{2}. $$
Let $Q$ be a convex polygon that is symmetric about a point $O$. Show that there exists a rectangle $S$ such that $Q \subset S$ and $$ \frac{\text{Area}(S)}{\text{Area}(Q)} \leq \sqrt{2}. $$
Let $Q$ be a convex polygon that is symmetric about a point $O$. Show that there exists a parallelogram $S$ such that $Q \subset S$ and $$ \frac{\text{Area}(S)}{\text{Area}(Q)} \leq 1. $$

positive_text: \text{Let } n \geq 4 \text{ teams play a round-robin tournament with no ties. A set of four teams is called bad if one team is beaten by the other three, and each of those three teams has one win and one loss among themselves. Assume there are no bad sets in the tournament. For each team, let } a_i \text{ and } b_i \text{ be its number of wins and losses. Prove that } \sum_{i=1}^{n}(a_i - b_i)^3 \geq 0.

negatives.text: \text{In a round-robin tournament with } n \geq 4 \text{ players and no ties, a company of four is bad if one is defeated by the other three, and each of those three has one win and one loss against each other. Suppose there are no bad companies. Let } w_i \text{ and } \ell_i \text{ be the number of wins and losses. Prove that } \sum_{i=1}^{n}(w_i - \ell_i)^2 \geq 0.

\text{In a round-robin tournament with } n \geq 4 \text{ players and no ties, a company of four is bad if one is defeated by the other three, and each of those three has one win and one loss among themselves. Suppose there are no bad companies. Let } w_i \text{ and } \ell_i \text{ be the number of wins and losses. Prove that } \sum_{i=1}^{n}(w_i - \ell_i)^3 \leq 0.

positive_text:
Let $A_{1}, \ldots, A_{s}$ be arithmetic sequences of integers such that:
(i) every integer is in at least one sequence;
(ii) for each sequence, there exists an integer in it not in any other sequence.
Let $m$ be the least common multiple of the common differences of the sequences, with prime factorization $m = q_{1}^{\beta_{1}} \ldots q_{k}^{\beta_{k}}$. Prove that
$$
s \geq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \beta_{i}(q_{i} - 1)
$$

negatives.text:
Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers such that:
(i) each integer is in at least one progression;
(ii) each progression has a unique common difference not shared with any other.
Let $n$ be the least common multiple of the steps of these progressions, with prime factorization $n = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$. Prove that
$$
s \geq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}(p_{i} - 1)
$$

Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers such that:
(i) each integer is in at least one progression;
(ii) each progression has at least one integer not in any other.
Let $n$ be the product of the steps of these progressions, with prime factorization $n = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$. Prove that
$$
s \geq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}(p_{i} - 1)
$$

Let $P_{1}, \ldots, P_{s}$ be arithmetic progressions of integers such that:
(i) each integer is in at least one progression;
(ii) each progression has at least one integer not in any other.
Let $n$ be the least common multiple of the steps of these progressions, with prime factorization $n = p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} \ldots p_{k}^{\alpha_{k}}$. Prove that
$$
s \geq 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_{i}p_{i}
$$

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of side $AC$. Let the bisector of $\angle BAC$ meet the circumcircle of triangle $DBC$ at a point $E$ inside $ABC$. The line $BD$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $AEB$ again at a point $F$. Let $AF$ and $BE$ meet at $I$, and let $CI$ and $BD$ meet at $K$. Prove that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ instead of $AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ at a point $E$ inside triangle $ABC$. The line $BD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of side $AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ in a point $E$ inside triangle $ABC$. The line $BD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

Let $ABC$ be an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of side $AC$. The angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersects the circle through $D$, $B$, and $C$ in a point $E$ inside triangle $ABC$. The line $CD$ intersects the circle through $A$, $E$, and $B$ in two points $B$ and $F$. The lines $AF$ and $BE$ meet at a point $I$, and the lines $CI$ and $BD$ meet at a point $K$. Show that $I$ is the incenter of triangle $KAB$.

positive_text: Let $ P Q R S T U $ be a convex hexagon such that all of its sides are tangent to a circle $ \Gamma $ centered at $ M $. It is given that the circumcircle of triangle $ P R T $ has the same center as $ \Gamma $. Let $ X $ be the foot of the perpendicular from $ Q $ to $ R S $. Suppose that the perpendicular from $ Q $ to $ S U $ meets the line $ T M $ at a point $ Y $. Let $ Z $ be the foot of the perpendicular from $ Y $ to $ S T $. Prove that $ S X = S Z $.

negatives.text: Let $ A B C D E F $ be a convex hexagon all of whose sides are tangent to a circle $ \omega $ with center $ O $. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ A C E $ is tangent to $ \omega $. Let $ J $ be the foot of the perpendicular from $ B $ to $ C D $. Suppose that the perpendicular from $ B $ to $ D F $ intersects the line $ E O $ at a point $ K $. Let $ L $ be the foot of the perpendicular from $ K $ to $ D E $. Prove that $ D J = D L $.

Let $ A B C D E F $ be a convex hexagon all of whose sides are tangent to a circle $ \omega $ with center $ O $. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ A C E $ is concentric with $ \omega $. Let $ J $ be the foot of the perpendicular from $ B $ to $ C D $. Suppose that the perpendicular from $ B $ to $ D F $ intersects the line $ E O $ at a point $ K $. Let $ L $ be the foot of the perpendicular from $ K $ to $ D F $. Prove that $ D J = D L $.

Let $ A B C D E F $ be a convex hexagon all of whose sides are tangent to a circle $ \omega $ with center $ O $. Suppose that the circumcircle of triangle $ A C E $ is concentric with $ \omega $. Let $ J $ be the foot of the perpendicular from $ B $ to $ C D $. Suppose that the perpendicular from $ B $ to $ D F $ intersects the line $ E F $ at a point $ K $. Let $ L $ be the foot of the perpendicular from $ K $ to $ D E $. Prove that $ D J = D L $.

positive_text: Let $DEF$ be a triangle with $\angle DFE = 90^\circ$, and let $F_0$ be the foot of the altitude from $F$. Choose a point $Y$ in the interior of the segment $FF_0$, and let $P, Q$ be the points on the segments $DY, EY$ for which $EP = EF$ and $DP = DF$ respectively. Let $N$ be the intersection of $DQ$ and $EP$. Prove that $NP = NQ$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Choose a point $X$ in the interior of the segment $CC_0$, and let $K, L$ be the points on the segments $AX, BX$ for which $BK = AC$ and $AL = BC$ respectively. Denote by $M$ the intersection of $AL$ and $BK$. Show that $MK = ML$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BCA = 90^\circ$, and let $C_0$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$. Choose a point $X$ in the interior of the segment $CC_0$, and let $K, L$ be the points on the segments $AX, BX$ for which $BK = BC$ and $AL = AC$ respectively. Denote by $M$ the intersection of $AL$ and $BK$. Show that $MK = KC$.

positive_text: Given a set $S$ containing $2000$ distinct real numbers, show that there are two distinct pairs $x > y$ and $u > v$ such that $$ \left|\frac{x-y}{u-v} - 1\right| < \frac{1}{100000} $$

negatives.text: Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that $$ \left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}+1\right|<\frac{1}{100000} $$
Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that $$ \left|\frac{a-b}{c-d}-1\right|<\frac{1}{1000000} $$
Prove that in any set of $2000$ distinct real numbers there exist two pairs $a > b$ and $c > d$ with $a \neq c$ or $b \neq d$, such that $$ \left|\frac{a+b}{c-d}-1\right|<\frac{1}{100000} $$

positive_text: Let $N$ be a positive integer, and let $S$ be a subset of $\{1, 2, \ldots, N\}$. A representation of $N$ as a sum $N = b_1 + b_2 + \cdots + b_m$ with all $b_i \in S$ is called an $S$-decomposition. The number of distinct components in such a decomposition is the size of the set $\{b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_m\}$. A decomposition is minimal if no such decomposition with fewer summands exists. Show that any minimal $S$-decomposition of $N$ involves at most $\sqrt[3]{6N}$ distinct components.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and let $A$ be a subset of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is a representation $n = a_1 + \cdots + a_k$ with $a_i \in A$. The number of different parts is the number of distinct $a_i$. Suppose the partition is optimal, meaning it uses the smallest number of parts. Prove that any optimal $A$-partition of $n$ contains at most $\sqrt[3]{6n^2}$ different parts.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $A$ be a subset of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is a representation $n = a_1 + \cdots + a_k$ with $a_i \in A$. The number of different parts is the number of distinct $a_i$. An $A$-partition is optimal if it uses the fewest possible parts. Prove that any optimal $A$-partition of $n$ contains at most $\sqrt{6n}$ different parts.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $A$ be a subset of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An $A$-partition of $n$ into $k$ parts is a representation $n = a_1 + \cdots + a_k$ with $a_i \in A$. The number of different parts is the number of distinct $a_i$. An $A$-partition is optimal if it uses the fewest possible parts. Prove that any optimal $A$-partition of $n$ contains at most $\sqrt[3]{6(n-1)}$ different parts.

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular permutations of the set $\{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$, where rotations are considered the same. A permutation is called elegant if, for all four distinct elements $a, b, c, d$ in the set with $a + c = b + d$, the chords connecting $a$ and $c$ do not intersect the chords connecting $b$ and $d$. Let $M$ be the number of elegant circular permutations. Let $N$ be the number of pairs $(x, y)$ with $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$, $x + y \leqslant n$, and $\gcd(x, y) = 1$. Prove that
$$
M = N + 1.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular permutations of the set $\{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$, where rotations are considered the same. A permutation is called elegant if, for all four distinct elements $a, b, c, d$ in the set with $a + c = b + d$, the chords connecting $a$ and $c$ intersect the chords connecting $b$ and $d$. Let $M$ be the number of elegant circular permutations. Let $N$ be the number of pairs $(x, y)$ with $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$, $x + y \leqslant n$, and $\gcd(x, y) = 1$. Prove that
$$
M = N + 1.
$$

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. Consider all circular permutations of the set $\{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$, where rotations are considered the same. A permutation is called elegant if, for all four distinct elements $a, b, c, d$ in the set with $a + c = b + d$, the chords connecting $a$ and $c$ do not intersect the chords connecting $b$ and $d$. Let $M$ be the number of elegant circular permutations. Let $N$ be the number of pairs $(x, y)$ with $x, y \in \mathbb{N}$, $x + y = n$, and $\gcd(x, y) = 1$. Prove that
$$
M = N + 1.
$$

positive_text: In triangle $UVW$, suppose $\angle U > \angle W$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on line $VW$ with $\angle XUV = \angle YUV = \angle UWV$ and $V$ between $X$ and $W$. Let $Z$ be a point on segment $UY$ such that $XZ = XU$. If the ray $VZ$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $UVW$ again at $T$, prove that $UY = UT$.

Let $m \geqslant 2$ be an integer. An $m \times m$ grid is given, and $m$ pieces are placed such that each row and column contains exactly one piece. Determine the largest integer $k$ such that in every such arrangement, there exists a $k \times k$ subgrid that contains no pieces.

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. An $n \times n$ grid is given, and $n$ rooks are placed such that each row and column contains at least one rook. Find the largest integer $k$ such that in every such configuration, there exists a $k \times k$ subgrid with no rooks.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. An $n \times n$ grid is given, and $n$ rooks are placed such that each row and column contains exactly one rook. Find the largest integer $k$ such that in every such configuration, there exists a $k \times k$ subgrid that contains at least one rook.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. An $n \times n$ grid is given, and $n$ rooks are placed such that each row and column contains exactly one rook. Find the largest integer $k$ such that in every such configuration, there exists a $k \times k$ subgrid that contains exactly one rook.

positive_text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer, and consider a configuration of $n$ lines in general position in the plane (i.e., no two parallel, no three concurrent). These lines partition the plane into various regions, some of which are bounded. Let $\mathcal{R}$ be the set of all bounded regions. Prove that one can select $\lceil\sqrt{n / 2}\rceil$ lines and mark them as blue, such that no region in $\mathcal{R}$ is surrounded entirely by blue lines.

negatives.text: Suppose $n \geqslant 3$ lines are drawn in the plane, with no two parallel and no three intersecting at a single point. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of bounded regions formed by these lines. Prove that it is possible to colour $\lceil\sqrt{n / 2}\rceil$ of the lines red such that every region in $\mathcal{F}$ has at least one red side.

Consider $n \geqslant 3$ lines in the plane such that no two are parallel. These lines divide the plane into regions. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of bounded regions. Prove that it is possible to colour $\lfloor\sqrt{n / 2}\rfloor$ of the lines blue in such a way that no region in $\mathcal{F}$ has a completely blue boundary.

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute-angled, and let points $P$ and $Q$ be selected on side $BC$ such that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. Extend $AP$ beyond $P$ to a point $M$ such that $AP = PM$, and similarly extend $AQ$ beyond $Q$ to a point $N$ such that $AQ = QN$. Show that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute-angled, and let points $P$ and $Q$ lie on side $BC$ such that $\angle PAB = \angle BAC$ and $\angle QAC = \angle ABC$. Let $M$ and $N$ lie on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$ such that $AP = PM$ and $AQ = QN$. Prove that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, let points $P$ and $Q$ lie on the extension of side $BC$ beyond $C$ and $B$, respectively, such that $\angle PAB = \angle ACB$ and $\angle QAC = \angle CBA$. Let $M$ and $N$ be points on the rays $AP$ and $AQ$ such that $AP = PM$ and $AQ = QN$. Prove that the lines $BM$ and $CN$ intersect on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$.

positive_text: Let $\omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\omega$ again at point $M$. Let $\gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The internal bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\gamma$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. Let $R$ be the point on line $PQ$ such that $BR = MR$. Prove that $BR$ is parallel to $AC$.

negatives.text: Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The external angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $M$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The angle bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The point $R$ is chosen on the line $PQ$ so that $BR = MR$. Prove that $BR \parallel AC$.

Let $\Omega$ and $O$ be the circumcircle and the circumcenter of triangle $ABC$ with $AB > BC$. The internal angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ intersects $\Omega$ again at $M$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $BM$. The angle bisectors of $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$ intersect $\Gamma$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively. The point $R$ is chosen on the line $PQ$ so that $BR = MP$. Prove that $BR \parallel AC$.

positive_text: In a straight-line country with $n \geqslant 1$ settlements labeled from left to right, each settlement has a left-moving and a right-moving machine. The machines have distinct strengths. When a right-moving machine encounters a left-moving one, the stronger one pushes the weaker one out of the road. If a machine reaches the back of another machine, it pushes it out regardless of strength. For any two settlements $P$ and $Q$, with $Q$ to the right of $P$, we say $P$ can clear $Q$ if its right machine can pass through all intermediate machines to reach $Q$. Similarly, $Q$ can clear $P$ if its left machine can pass through all intermediate machines to reach $P$. Prove that there is exactly one settlement that cannot be cleared by any other.

negatives.text: In Lineland there are $n \geqslant 1$ towns arranged left to right. Each town has a left and a right bulldozer with all sizes distinct. When a right and left bulldozer meet, the smaller one is pushed off. If a bulldozer reaches the back of another, it is pushed off regardless of size. Let $A$ and $B$ be two towns, with $B$ to the right of $A$. Town $A$ can sweep $B$ if its right bulldozer can push off all bulldozers in between and reach $B$. Town $B$ can sweep $A$ if its left bulldozer can push off all bulldozers in between and reach $A$. Prove that there is exactly one town which cannot be swept away by any other, or show that such a town may not exist.

In Lineland there are $n \geqslant 1$ towns arranged left to right. Each town has a left and a right bulldozer, and all bulldozers have distinct sizes. When a right and a left bulldozer confront each other, the smaller one is pushed off the road. If a bulldozer reaches the back of another, it pushes it off regardless of size. Let $A$ and $B$ be two towns, with $B$ to the right of $A$. Town $A$ can sweep $B$ if its right bulldozer can reach $B$ by pushing off all bulldozers in between. Similarly, $B$ can sweep $A$ if its left bulldozer can reach $A$ by pushing off all bulldozers in between. Prove that there is exactly one pair of towns that cannot sweep each other away.

positive_text:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{S}$ is symmetric if for any two distinct points $X, Y \in \mathcal{S}$, there is a point $Z \in \mathcal{S}$ such that $XZ = YZ$. We say that $\mathcal{S}$ is non-concentric if for any three distinct points $X, Y, Z \in \mathcal{S}$, there is no point $Q \in \mathcal{S}$ such that $QX = QY = QZ$.

a. Prove that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a symmetric set of size $n$.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ is there a symmetric, non-concentric set of size $n$?

negatives.text:
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{P}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{P}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{P}$ such that $AC = 2BC$. We say that $\mathcal{P}$ is center-free if for any three distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{P}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{P}$ such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points?

Let $\mathcal{Q}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{Q}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{Q}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{Q}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say that $\mathcal{Q}$ is center-free if for any three distinct points $A, B, C \in \mathcal{Q}$, there does not exist a point $P$ in the plane (not necessarily in $\mathcal{Q}$) such that $PA = PB = PC$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points?

Let $\mathcal{R}$ be a finite set of points in the plane. We say that $\mathcal{R}$ is balanced if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{R}$, there exists a point $C \in \mathcal{R}$ such that $AC = BC$. We say that $\mathcal{R}$ is center-free if for any two distinct points $A, B \in \mathcal{R}$, there does not exist a point $P \in \mathcal{R}$ such that $PA = PB$.

a. Show that for all $n \geqslant 3$, there exists a balanced set consisting of $n$ points.

b. For which $n \geqslant 3$ does there exist a balanced, center-free set consisting of $n$ points?

positive_text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB > AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle. Let $H$ be the orthocenter, $M$ the midpoint of side $BC$, and $F$ the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$. Define points $Q$ and $K$ on $\Gamma$ such that $\angle AQH = 90^\circ$ and $\angle QKH = 90^\circ$. Show that the circumcircles of $\triangle KQH$ and $\triangle KFM$ are tangent.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB > AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $H$ be the orthocenter, $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $F$ the foot of the altitude from $A$. Let $Q$ and $K$ be points on $\Gamma$ such that $\angle AQH = 90^\circ$ and $\angle QKH = 90^\circ$. Prove that the circumcircles of $\triangle KQH$ and $\triangle KFM$ are congruent.

positive_text:
Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ for which the following holds: for any real numbers $p_{1}, q_{1}, p_{2}, q_{2}, \ldots, p_{n}, q_{n}$ with $\left|p_{k}\right| + \left|q_{k}\right| = 1$ for each $k$, there exists a sequence $s_{1}, s_{2}, \ldots, s_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} s_{k} p_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} s_{k} q_{k}\right| \leqslant 1
$$

negatives.text:
Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ such that for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $k$, there exists a sequence $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ for which
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right|^{2} + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right|^{2} \leqslant 1
$$

Find all integers $n \geqslant 3$ for which the following holds: for all real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $k$, there exists a sequence $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k} + \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k} \leqslant 1
$$

Determine all integers $n \geqslant 3$ for which the following holds: for any real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ with $\left|a_{k}\right| + \left|b_{k}\right| = 1$ for all $k$, there exists a sequence $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \in \{-1, 1\}$ such that
$$
\left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} a_{k}\right| + \left|\sum_{k=1}^{n} x_{k} b_{k}\right| < 1
$$

positive_text:
Let $k \geqslant 1$ be an integer. In the plane, there are $k+1$ line segments such that any two intersect in the interior, and no three are concurrent. A robot is placed at one endpoint of each segment. After each of $k$ intervals, the robot moves to the next intersection point along its segment. After $k$ intervals, all robots reach the endpoint opposite to their starting point.

a) Prove that if $k+1$ is odd then the robots can be placed so that no two ever share an intersection point.

b) Prove that if $k+1$ is even then there must be an interval when at least two robots share an intersection point, regardless of the placement.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer. In the plane, there are $n$ segments such that any two intersect in the interior, and no three intersect at the same point. Jeff places a snail at one of the endpoints of each segment and claps his hands $n$ times. Each time he claps, all snails move along their segments to the next intersection point. After $n$ claps, all snails reach the opposite endpoint.

a) Prove that if $n$ is odd then Jeff can always place the snails so that no two ever share an intersection point.

b) Prove that if $n$ is even then there must be a moment when some two snails share an intersection point, regardless of the placement.

positive_text: Let $g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that for all real numbers $a$ and $b$ with $(g(a)+b)(g(b)+a) > 0$, it holds that $g(a)+b = g(b)+a$. Prove that $g(a)+b \leqslant g(b)+a$ for all $a > b$.

negatives.text: Suppose $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfies the condition that for all $x, y$ with $(f(x)+y)(f(y)+x) < 0$, we have $f(x)+y = f(y)+x$. Prove that $f(x)+y \leqslant f(y)+x$ for all $x > y$.

positive_text:
Let $ n \geqslant 3 $ be an integer. Suppose $ \mathcal{P} $ and $ \mathcal{Q} $ are regular $ n $-gons in the plane. Show that the set of vertices of $ \mathcal{P} $ that lie in $ \mathcal{Q} $ or on its boundary form a single arc of $ \mathcal{P} $.
(In other words, there exists a line that separates the vertices of $ \mathcal{P} $ inside $ \mathcal{Q} $ from those outside.)

negatives.text: Let $ n \geqslant 3 $ be an integer. Suppose $ \mathcal{P} $ is a regular $ n $-gon and $ \mathcal{Q} $ is a regular $ (n+1) $-gon in the plane. Show that the vertices of $ \mathcal{P} $ that lie in $ \mathcal{Q} $ or on its boundary are consecutive.

Let $ n \geqslant 3 $ be an integer. Suppose $ \mathcal{P} $ is a regular $ n $-gon and $ \mathcal{Q} $ is a regular $ n $-gon rotated by an irrational multiple of $ \pi/n $ radians. Show that the vertices of $ \mathcal{P} $ that lie in $ \mathcal{Q} $ or on its boundary are consecutive.

Let $ n \geqslant 3 $ be an integer. Suppose $ \mathcal{P} $ is a regular $ n $-gon and $ \mathcal{Q} $ is a regular $ n $-gon scaled by a factor of 2. Show that the vertices of $ \mathcal{P} $ that lie in $ \mathcal{Q} $ or on its boundary are consecutive.

positive_text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$ be an integer, and let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}, y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ be distinct positive integers with $x_i, y_i \leq 5n$ for all $i$. If the sequence
$$
\frac{x_{1}}{y_{1}}, \frac{x_{2}}{y_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{x_{n}}{y_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression, show that all terms in the sequence are equal.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geqslant 2018$, and let $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{n}, q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}$ be distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{p_{1}}{q_{1}}, \frac{p_{2}}{q_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}}
$$
forms a geometric progression. Prove that all the terms are equal.

Let $n \geqslant 2018$, and let $m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n}, n_{1}, n_{2}, \ldots, n_{n}$ be distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{m_{1}}{n_{1}}, \frac{m_{2}}{n_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{m_{n}}{n_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression. Prove that the sequence is constant modulo $n$.

Let $n \geqslant 2018$, and let $u_{1}, u_{2}, \ldots, u_{n}, v_{1}, v_{2}, \ldots, v_{n}$ be distinct positive integers not exceeding $5n$. Suppose that the sequence
$$
\frac{u_{1}}{v_{1}}, \frac{u_{2}}{v_{2}}, \ldots, \frac{u_{n}}{v_{n}}
$$
forms an arithmetic progression. Prove that the sequence is strictly increasing.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $x$ and $y$,
$$
f(2x) + 2f(y) = f(f(x+y)).
$$

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a) + f(b)).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a) + b).
$$

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ be the set of integers. Determine all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$,
$$
f(2a) + 2f(b) = f(f(a) + f(f(b))).
$$

positive_text: \text{Let } n \geqslant 2 \text{ be a positive integer and } x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \text{ be real numbers with } x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{n}=0. \text{ Define the set } S \text{ by } S=\left\{(p, q)\left|1 \leqslant p<q \leqslant n,\left|x_{p}-x_{q}\right| \geqslant 1\right.\right\}. \text{ Prove that, if } S \neq \emptyset, \text{ then } \sum_{(p, q) \in S} x_{p} x_{q}<0.

negatives.text: \text{Let } n \geqslant 2 \text{ be a positive integer and } a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \text{ be real numbers such that } a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=1. \text{ Define the set } A \text{ by } A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right.\right\}. \text{ Prove that, if } A \neq \emptyset, \text{ then } \sum_{(i, j) \in A} a_{i} a_{j}<0.

\text{Let } n \geqslant 2 \text{ be a positive integer and } a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \text{ be real numbers such that } a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}=0. \text{ Define the set } A \text{ by } A=\left\{(i, j)\left|1 \leqslant i<j \leqslant n,\left|a_{i}-a_{j}\right| \geqslant 1\right.\right\}. \text{ Prove that, if } A \neq \emptyset, \text{ then } \sum_{(i, j) \in A} (a_{i}+a_{j})<0.

positive_text:
Let $Q(a, b, c)$ be a polynomial in three variables with real coefficients such that
$$
Q(a, b, c) = Q(a, b, a b - c) = Q(a, c a - b, c) = Q(b c - a, b, c)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $G(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
Q(a, b, c) = G\left(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2} - a b c\right)\right.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $R(x, y, z)$ be a polynomial in three variables with real coefficients such that
$$
R(x, y, z) = R(x, y, x y + z) = R(x, z x - y, z) = R(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $H(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
R(x, y, z) = H\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y z\right)\right.
$$

Let $S(x, y, z)$ be a polynomial in three variables with real coefficients such that
$$
S(x, y, z) = S(x, y, x y - z) = S(x, z x + y, z) = S(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $H(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
S(x, y, z) = H\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} - x y z\right)\right.
$$

Let $T(x, y, z)$ be a polynomial in three variables with real coefficients such that
$$
T(x, y, z) = T(x, y, x y - z) = T(x, z x - y, z) = T(y z - x, y, z)
$$
Prove that there exists a polynomial $H(t)$ in one variable such that
$$
T(x, y, z) = H\left(x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} + x y z\right)\right.
$$

positive_text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Alice has $n$ switches labeled $1$ through $n$, each in either an on or off state. She performs the following procedure repeatedly: if there are $k$ switches in the on state and $k > 0$, then she toggles the $k^{	ext{th}}$ switch; otherwise she stops. Let $\ell(S)$ be the number of steps until all switches are off. Prove that $\ell(S)$ is finite for all initial states $S$, and find the average of $\ell(S)$ over all $2^{n}$ possible initial states.

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins. He repeatedly does the following: if there are $k$ coins showing heads, then he flips the $(k+1)^{	ext{th}}$ coin (if it exists); otherwise he stops. Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps until all coins are tails. Prove that $\ell(C)$ is finite for all initial configurations $C$, and compute its average over all $2^{n}$ configurations.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Harry has $n$ coins. He repeatedly does the following: if there are $k$ coins showing heads, he flips the $k^{	ext{th}}$ coin only if it is showing heads; otherwise he stops. Let $\ell(C)$ be the number of steps until all coins are tails. Prove $\ell(C)$ is finite for all configurations $C$, and find its average over all $2^{n}$ configurations.

positive_text: In a network of $n \geqslant 2$ cities, each pair is connected by a one-way highway. A traveler wants to determine if there exists at least one city with at most one outgoing highway. They can query the direction of any highway between two cities. Show that it is possible to determine the answer with no more than $4 n$ queries.

negatives.text: In a country of $n \geqslant 2$ towns, each pair is connected by a one-way road. Alice wants to know if there is at least one town with at most one incoming road. The King of Hearts will tell her the direction of any road she asks about. Prove that she can determine the answer with at most $4 n$ queries.

Alice has a map of $n \geqslant 2$ towns where each pair is connected by a one-way road. She wants to know if there is at least one town with no outgoing roads. The King of Hearts will tell her the direction of any road she asks about. Prove that she can determine the answer with at most $4 n$ queries.

Alice has a map of $n \geqslant 2$ towns where each pair is connected by a one-way road. She wants to know if there is at least one town with at most one outgoing road. The King of Hearts will tell her the direction of any road she asks about. Prove that she can determine the answer with at most $2 n$ queries.

positive_text: Let $VWXYZ$ be a convex pentagon with $YZ = ZX$ and $\angle XZY \neq 2 \cdot \angle VZW$. Suppose that a point $Q$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $VQ = VY$ and $WQ = WX$. Prove that $Q$ lies on the diagonal $XZ$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(WYZ) + \operatorname{area}(VZX) = \operatorname{area}(VWZ) + \operatorname{area}(VWQ)$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC = 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AD$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = \operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP)$.

Let $ABCDE$ be a convex pentagon with $CD = DE$ and $\angle EDC \neq 2 \cdot \angle ADB$. Suppose that a point $P$ is located in the interior of the pentagon such that $AP = AE$ and $BP = BC$. Prove that $P$ lies on the diagonal $CE$ if and only if $\operatorname{area}(BCD) + \operatorname{area}(ADE) = 2 \cdot (\operatorname{area}(ABD) + \operatorname{area}(ABP))$.

positive_text: Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of all straight lines in the plane and let $g$ be a function assigning to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{F}$ a point $g(\ell)$ lying on $\ell$. Suppose that for every point $A$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ that all pass through $A$, the points $g\left(\ell_{1}\right), g\left(\ell_{2}\right), g\left(\ell_{3}\right)$, and $A$ are concyclic. Prove that there exists a unique point $Q$ such that $g(\ell) = Q$ for all lines $\ell$ that contain $Q$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function assigning to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ are colinear. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of all lines in the plane and let $f$ be a function assigning to each line $\ell \in \mathcal{L}$ a point $f(\ell)$ on $\ell$. Suppose that for any point $X$, and for any three lines $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ell_{3}$ passing through $X$, the points $f\left(\ell_{1}\right), f\left(\ell_{2}\right), f\left(\ell_{3}\right)$ and $X$ lie on a parabola. Prove that there is a unique point $P$ such that $f(\ell)=P$ for any line $\ell$ passing through $P$.

positive_text:
Let $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ be positive real numbers such that $p \geqslant q \geqslant r \geqslant s$ and $p + q + r + s = 1$. Show that
$$
(p + 2q + 3r + 4s) p^{p} q^{q} r^{r} s^{s} < 1
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Show that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{b} b^{c} c^{d} d^{a} < 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d > 0$ and $a + b + c + d = 1$. Show that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} \leq 1
$$

Let $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ be four real numbers such that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c \geqslant d$ and $a + b + c + d = 0$. Show that
$$
(a + 2b + 3c + 4d) a^{a} b^{b} c^{c} d^{d} < 1
$$

positive_text: For each positive integer $ k $, let $ A_k $ be a $ k \times k $ matrix where the entry at row $ r $ and column $ c $ is $ \left\lfloor\frac{rc}{k+1}\right\rfloor $. Find all $ k $ such that the total sum of the entries in $ A_k $ equals $ \frac{1}{4} k^2(k-1) $.

negatives.text: For every integer $ n \geqslant 1 $, consider the $ n \times n $ table with entry $ \left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n-1}\right\rfloor $ at the intersection of row $ i $ and column $ j $. Determine all $ n $ for which the sum of the $ n^2 $ entries is equal to $ \frac{1}{4} n^2(n-1) $.

For every integer $ n \geqslant 1 $, consider the $ n \times n $ table with entry $ \left\lfloor\frac{i + j}{n+1}\right\rfloor $ at the intersection of row $ i $ and column $ j $. Determine all $ n $ for which the sum of the $ n^2 $ entries is equal to $ \frac{1}{4} n^2(n-1) $.

For every integer $ n \geqslant 1 $, consider the $ n \times n $ table with entry $ \left\lfloor\frac{ij}{n+1}\right\rfloor $ at the intersection of row $ i $ and column $ j $. Determine all $ n $ for which the sum of the $ n^2 $ entries is equal to $ \frac{1}{4} n(n-1)^2 $.

positive_text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A number $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-rich if, given an unlimited supply of $n$ types of tokens $T_{1}, T_{2}, \ldots, T_{n}$, one can arrange $m$ of them in a circular pattern such that any block of $n+1$ adjacent tokens contains at least one token of each type. Prove that there are finitely many integers which are not $n$-rich. Determine the largest such integer.

negatives.text: Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A number $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-bright if, given infinitely many tiles of each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them in a circle so that in any group of $n$ consecutive tiles there is at least one tile of each colour. Prove that there are finitely many integers which are not $n$-bright. Find the largest such integer.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A number $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-luminous if, given infinitely many tiles of each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them in a circle so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive tiles there is at least one tile of colour $C_{1}$. Prove that there are finitely many integers which are not $n$-luminous. Find the largest such integer.

Let $n \geqslant 3$ be an integer. A number $m \geqslant n+1$ is called $n$-vivid if, given infinitely many tiles of each of $n$ colours $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots, C_{n}$, it is possible to place $m$ of them in a line (not a circle) so that in any group of $n+1$ consecutive tiles there is at least one tile of each colour. Prove that there are finitely many integers which are not $n$-vivid. Find the largest such integer.

positive_text:
Find the maximum number $N$ such that there exists an $N \times 100$ matrix $A$ with the following properties:
(i) Each row of $A$ is a permutation of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $i$ and $j$, there exists at least one column $k$ such that $|A(i,k) - A(j,k)| \geq 2$.

negatives.text:
Determine the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of integers with $N$ rows and 100 columns such that:
(i) Each row is a permutation of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $|T(r,c) - T(s,c)| \geq 1$.

Find the maximum $N$ such that there exists a table $T$ with $N$ rows and 100 columns, where:
(i) Each row is a permutation of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, there is a column $c$ such that $T(r,c) = T(s,c)$.

What is the largest $N$ for which there exists a table $T$ of size $N \times 100$ with the following properties:
(i) Each row is a permutation of $\{1, 2, \ldots, 100\}$.
(ii) For any two distinct rows $r$ and $s$, the number of columns $c$ with $|T(r,c) - T(s,c)| \geq 2$ is even.

positive_text: Given a polynomial $Q(x)$ with integer coefficients, define $Q^{1}(x) = Q(x)$ and $Q^{k+1}(x) = Q\left(Q^{k}(x)\right)$ for $k \geqslant 1$. Determine all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $Q(x)$ with integer coefficients for which the sequence $\{Q^{m}(1), \ldots, Q^{m}(n)\}$ modulo $n$ contains exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rceil$ distinct values for all $m \geqslant 1$.

negatives.text: For a polynomial $R(x)$ with integer coefficients, define $R^{1}(x) = R(x)$ and $R^{k+1}(x) = R\left(R^{k}(x)\right)$ for $k \geqslant 1$. Find all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $R(x)$ for which the numbers $R^{m}(1), \ldots, R^{m}(n)$ leave exactly $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rfloor$ distinct remainders modulo $n$ for all $m \geqslant 1$.

For a polynomial $T(x)$ with integer coefficients, define $T^{1}(x) = T(x)$ and $T^{k+1}(x) = T\left(T^{k}(x)\right)$ for $k \geqslant 1$. Find all positive integers $n$ such that there exists a polynomial $T(x)$ for which the numbers $T^{m}(1), \ldots, T^{m}(n)$ leave exactly $\left\lceil \frac{n}{2^{m}}\right\rceil$ distinct remainders modulo $2n$ for all $m \geqslant 1$.

positive_text:
Two types of tokens, red (denoted $R$) and blue (denoted $B$), are arranged in a row of $2n$ tokens, with exactly $n$ of each color. For a fixed $k$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$, a transformation is applied repeatedly: locate the largest block of consecutive tokens of the same color that includes the $k$-th token from the left, and move the entire block to the beginning of the row. For example, with $n=4$ and $k=4$, starting from $R R B B B R B R$, the transformation yields
$$
R R B B B R B R \rightarrow B B B R R R B R \rightarrow R R R B B B B R \rightarrow B B B B R R R R \rightarrow \cdots .
$$
Determine all pairs $(n, k)$ such that for all initial configurations, the process eventually results in at most one red token adjacent to a blue token.

negatives.text:
Suppose $2n$ coins are arranged in a row, $n$ of type $A$ and $n$ of type $C$. For a fixed $k$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$, repeatedly perform the following: identify the largest subsequence of coins of the same type that includes the $k$-th coin from the right, and move this subsequence to the left end of the row. For example, if $n=4$ and $k=4$, starting from $A A C C C A C A$, the transformation would be
$$
A A C C C A C A \rightarrow A A A C C C C A \rightarrow C C C C A A A A \rightarrow \cdots .
$$
Find all pairs $(n, k)$ such that the process eventually results in at most one $A$ adjacent to a $C$.

A sequence of $2n$ coins, $n$ of type $A$ and $n$ of type $C$, is arranged in a row. For a fixed $k$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$, repeatedly perform the following: identify the largest subsequence of coins of the same type that includes the $k$-th coin from the left, and move this subsequence to the right end of the row. For example, with $n=4$ and $k=4$, starting from $A A C C C A C A$, the transformation would be
$$
A A C C C A C A \rightarrow A A A C A C C C \rightarrow A A A A C C C C \rightarrow \cdots .
$$
Find all pairs $(n, k)$ such that the process eventually results in at most one $A$ adjacent to a $C$.

positive_text:
Let $PQR$ be an acute-angled triangle with $PR > PQ$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. A point $M$ lies on segment $QR$. The line through $M$ perpendicular to $QR$ meets the lines $PO$, $PR$, and $PQ$ at $U$, $S$, and $T$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $PST$ and $PQR$ intersect again at $N 
eq P$. Prove that if $OU = OM$, then $MN$ is tangent to the circle $PST$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. A point $D$ lies on segment $BC$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ meets the lines $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$ intersect again at $Z 
eq A$. Prove that if $OW = WD$, then $DZ$ is tangent to the circle $AXY$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. A point $D$ lies on segment $BC$. The line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meets the lines $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$ intersect again at $Z 
eq A$. Prove that if $OW = OD$, then $DZ$ is tangent to the circle $AXY$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AC > AB$, and let $O$ be its circumcenter. A point $D$ lies on segment $BC$. The line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ meets the lines $AO$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $W$, $X$, and $Y$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $AXY$ and $ABC$ intersect again at $Z 
eq A$. Prove that if $OW = OD$, then $DZ$ is perpendicular to the circle $AXY$.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ be given, and let $m$ and $n$ be two parallel lines intersecting the sides $QR$, $RP$, and $PQ$ at points $A_i$, $B_i$, $C_i$ for $i = 1, 2$. For each $i$, construct the triangle $\Gamma_i$ by taking the lines through $A_i$, $B_i$, and $C_i$ that are perpendicular to $QR$, $RP$, and $PQ$, respectively. Prove that the circumcircles of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ are tangent to each other.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ and two lines $\ell_{1}$, $\ell_{2}$ be given (not necessarily parallel). For $i=1,2$, let $\ell_i$ intersect the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_i$, $Y_i$, $Z_i$, respectively. Let $\Delta_i$ be the triangle formed by the lines through $X_i$, $Y_i$, $Z_i$ perpendicular to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$. Prove that the circumcircles of $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_2$ are tangent.

Let triangle $ABC$ and two parallel lines $\ell_{1}$, $\ell_{2}$ be given. For $i=1,2$, let $\ell_i$ intersect the lines $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ at $X_i$, $Y_i$, $Z_i$, respectively. Construct triangle $\Delta_i$ by drawing lines through $X_i$, $Y_i$, $Z_i$ perpendicular to the medians of triangle $ABC$. Show that the circumcircles of $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_2$ are tangent.

positive_text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{N}$; $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{N}$; and $z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots, z_{N}$ of $1, 2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{x_{k}}+\sqrt{y_{k}}+\sqrt{z_{k}}-2\sqrt{N}\right|<2023
$$
held for all $k=1,2,\ldots,N$.

negatives.text:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1, 2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}}+\sqrt{b_{k}}+\sqrt{c_{k}}-\sqrt{N}\right|<2023
$$
held for all $k=1,2,\ldots,N$.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1, 2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}}+\sqrt{b_{k}}+\sqrt{c_{k}}-2\sqrt{N}+1000\right|<2023
$$
held for all $k=1,2,\ldots,N$.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Prove that there exist three permutations $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{N}$; $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{N}$; and $c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_{N}$ of $1, 2, \ldots, N$ such that
$$
\left|\sqrt{a_{k}}+\sqrt{b_{k}}+\sqrt{c_{k}}-2\sqrt{N}\right|<\frac{1}{2023}
$$
held for all $k=1,2,\ldots,N$.

positive_text: Consider a triangle of circles with $n$ rows, where the $i^\text{th}$ row has $i$ circles. A warrior-path is defined as a sequence of circles starting from the top circle and moving at each step to one of the two circles directly beneath. Suppose one circle is marked in each row. Show that there exists a warrior-path that intersects at least $k$ marked circles, and find the largest such $k$ in terms of $n$.

negatives.text: Consider a triangle of circles with $n$ rows, where the $i^\text{th}$ row has $i$ circles. A warrior-path is defined as a sequence of circles starting from the top circle and moving at each step to one of the two circles directly beneath. Suppose two circles are marked in each row. Show that there exists a warrior-path that intersects at least $k$ marked circles, and find the largest such $k$ in terms of $n$.

Consider a triangle of circles with $n$ rows, where the $i^\text{th}$ row has $i$ circles. A warrior-path is defined as a sequence of circles starting from the top circle and moving at each step to one of the two circles directly beneath. Suppose one circle is marked in each row, and all marked circles are in the same column. Show that there exists a warrior-path that intersects at least $k$ marked circles, and find the largest such $k$ in terms of $n$.

positive_text: In triangle $ABC$ with $AC > BC$, let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ and $r$ the radius of $\omega$. Let $P$ be a point on $AC$ such that $CP = BC$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$. Let $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$, and choose a point $Q$ on the line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and the order is $S, P, Q$. If $E$ is the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CQ$ and the line through $B$ perpendicular to $DQ$, show that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > BC$, and let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Let $P$ be a point on segment $AC$ such that $CP = BC$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$. Let ray $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$, and let $Q$ lie on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and the order is $S, P, Q$. If $E$ is the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CP$ and the line through $B$ perpendicular to $DQ$, show that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC > BC$, and let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Let $P$ be a point on segment $AC$ such that $CP = BC$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $AB$. Let ray $BP$ intersect $\omega$ again at $D$, and let $Q$ lie on line $SP$ such that $PQ = r$ and the order is $S, P, Q$. If $E$ is the intersection of the line through $A$ perpendicular to $CQ$ and the line through $B$ perpendicular to $SP$, show that $E$ lies on $\omega$.

positive_text: Let $PQR$ be an acute triangle with $PQ < PR$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $PQR$, and let $T$ be the midpoint of the arc $QPR$ not containing $Q$. The altitude from $P$ to $QR$ intersects $QT$ and $\Gamma$ at $D$ and $F \neq P$ respectively. A line through $D$ parallel to $QR$ meets $PF$ at $M$, and let $\gamma$ be the circumcircle of triangle $QDM$. Let $\gamma$ intersect $\Gamma$ again at $X \neq Q$. Prove that the tangent to $\gamma$ at $X$ and the line $QT$ meet on the internal angle bisector of $\angle QPR$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$. Denote its circumcircle by $\Omega$ and denote the midpoint of $\operatorname{arc} ACB$ by $S$. Let the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ meet $CS$ and $\Omega$ at $D$ and $E \neq A$ respectively. Let the line through $D$ parallel to $BC$ meet line $CE$ at $L$ and denote the circumcircle of triangle $CDL$ by $\omega$. Let $\omega$ meet $\Omega$ again at $P \neq C$. Prove that the line tangent to $\omega$ at $P$, and line $CS$ intersect on the internal bisector of $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$. Denote its circumcircle by $\Omega$ and denote the midpoint of $\operatorname{arc} CAB$ by $S$. Let the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ meet $BS$ and $\Omega$ at $D$ and $E \neq A$ respectively. Let the line through $D$ perpendicular to $BC$ meet line $BE$ at $L$ and denote the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$ by $\omega$. Let $\omega$ meet $\Omega$ again at $P \neq B$. Prove that the line tangent to $\omega$ at $P$, and line $BS$ intersect on the internal bisector of $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $AB < AC$. Denote its circumcircle by $\Omega$ and denote the midpoint of $\operatorname{arc} CAB$ by $S$. Let the perpendicular from $B$ to $AC$ meet $BS$ and $\Omega$ at $D$ and $E \neq B$ respectively. Let the line through $D$ parallel to $AC$ meet line $BE$ at $L$ and denote the circumcircle of triangle $BDL$ by $\omega$. Let $\omega$ meet $\Omega$ again at $P \neq B$. Prove that the line tangent to $\omega$ at $P$, and line $BS$ intersect on the internal bisector of $\angle BAC$.

positive_text: Suppose integers $1, 2, \ldots, N$ are written on a board. Players Alice and Bob alternate turns, with Alice going first. On each turn, a player chooses a nonnegative integer $k$ and an integer $n$ on the board, then removes all numbers $s$ for which $2^k$ divides $n - s$. The game ends when the board is empty, and the player who removes the last number loses. Determine all $N$ for which Alice can force a win.

negatives.text: Let $N$ be a positive integer. Players Xavier and Yvonne take turns removing numbers from the board containing $1$ to $N$. On each turn, a player picks a number $n$ on the board and a nonnegative integer $k$, and removes all numbers $s$ such that $n - s$ is divisible by $2^k + 1$. The game ends when the board is empty, and the player who removes the last number loses. Determine all $N$ for which Xavier can force a win.

Let $N$ be a positive integer. Players start with numbers $1$ to $N$ written on a board. On each turn, a player selects a number $n$ and removes all numbers $s$ such that $n - s$ is divisible by $2^k$ for some fixed $k$. The game ends when the board is empty, and the player who removes the last number loses. Determine all $N$ for which the first player can force a win.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Construct point $E$ on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ so that $E$ is on the opposite side of $AD$ from $C$ and $AC = DE$. Construct point $F$ on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ so that $F$ is on the opposite side of $AD$ from $C$ and $BD = AF$. Show that the perpendicular bisectors of $BC$ and $EF$ meet on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA = 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of $AD$, and $AC = DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of $AD$, and $AC = DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of $BC$ and $DF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AC < BD < AD$ and $\angle DBA < 90^\circ$. Point $E$ lies on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$ such that $E$ and $C$ lie on the same side of $AD$, and $AC = DE$. Point $F$ lies on the line through $A$ parallel to $CD$ such that $F$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of $AD$, and $BD = AF$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of $BC$ and $EF$ intersect on the circumcircle of $ABCD$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $AB \parallel CD$ and $AB < CD$. Let $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at $P$. Let $X$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, different from $C$, such that $PX = PC$. Let $Y$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$, different from $D$, such that $PY = PD$. Let $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ$ is parallel to the bases $AB$ and $CD$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB \perp CD$ and $AB < CD$. Lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at a point $P$. Point $X \neq C$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ is such that $PC = PX$. Point $Y \neq D$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is such that $PD = PY$. Lines $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB$ parallel to $CD$ and $AB < CD$. Lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at a point $P$. Point $X \neq C$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ is such that $PC = 2PX$. Point $Y \neq D$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is such that $PD = 2PY$. Lines $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ$ is parallel to $AB$.

Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $AB$ parallel to $CD$ and $AB < CD$. Lines $AD$ and $BC$ intersect at a point $P$. Point $X \neq C$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ is such that $PC = PX$. Point $Y \neq D$ on the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$ is such that $PY = PD$. Lines $AX$ and $BY$ intersect at $Q$. Prove that $PQ$ is perpendicular to $AB$.

positive_text: Let $PQR$ be an acute triangle with $PQ < PR$, and let $\Omega$ be the circumcircle of $PQR$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on $\Omega$ so that $MN$ and $QR$ intersect on the external angle bisector of $\angle QPR$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Omega$ at $M$ and $N$ intersect at a point $S$ on the same side of $QR$ as $P$, and that $SM$ and $SN$ intersect $QR$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively. Let $K$ be the centre of the excircle of triangle $SDE$ opposite the vertex $S$. Prove that $PK$ bisects $\angle QPR$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the centre of the excircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the centre of the excircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB < AC$, and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ lie on $\Gamma$ so that $XY$ and $BC$ intersect on the external angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Suppose that the chords $X$ and $Y$ intersect at a point $T$ on the same side of $BC$ as $A$, and that $TX$ and $TY$ intersect $BC$ at $U$ and $V$, respectively. Let $J$ be the centre of the excircle of triangle $TUV$ opposite the vertex $T$. Prove that $AJ$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

positive_text: \text{Find all positive integer sequences } b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots \text{ such that, for any } 1 \leqslant i \leqslant j, \text{ the average } \frac{b_{i}+b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_{j}}{j-i+1} \text{ and the } (j-i+1)\text{th root of the product } \left(b_{i} b_{i+1} \cdots b_{j}\right)^{\frac{1}{j-i+1}} \text{ are both integers.}

negatives.text: \text{Determine all sequences } d_{1}, d_{2}, \ldots \text{ of positive integers such that for all } m \leqslant n, \text{ the arithmetic mean } \frac{d_{m}+d_{m+1}+\cdots+d_{n}}{n-m+1} \text{ and the } (n-m+1)\text{th power sum } d_{m}^{n-m+1} + d_{m+1}^{n-m+1} + \cdots + d_{n}^{n-m+1} \text{ are both integers.}

\text{Determine all sequences } f_{1}, f_{2}, \ldots \text{ of positive integers such that for all } m \leqslant n, \text{ the harmonic mean } \frac{n-m+1}{\frac{1}{f_{m}} + \frac{1}{f_{m+1}} + \cdots + \frac{1}{f_{n}}} \text{ and the geometric mean } \left(f_{m} f_{m+1} \cdots f_{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n-m+1}} \text{ are both integers.}

positive_text: Determine all integer triples $(x, y, z)$ such that $x + y + z = 24$, $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 210$, and $xyz = 440$.

negatives.text: Find all integer solutions to: $a + b + c = 24$, $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 210$, and $ab + bc + ca = 440$.
Find all integer solutions to: $a + b + c = 24$, $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 210$, and $abc = -440$.
Find all integer solutions to: $a + b + c = 24$, $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 210$, and $a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 440$.
