\text{Define } b_1 = \frac{1}{6} \text{ and } b_{n+1} = \frac{n+1}{n+2} \left( b_n + \frac{1}{2} \right) \text{ for } n \ge 1. \text{ Find } b_{2011}.
\text{Define } c_1 = \frac{1}{6} \text{ and } c_{n+1} = \frac{n+1}{n+3} \left( c_n + \frac{1}{2} \right)^2 \text{ for } n \ge 1. \text{ Find } c_{2011}.

positive_text: \text{Let } a_1 = 20, a_2 = 12. \text{ For } n \ge 1, \text{ define } a_{n+2} = a_n + a_{n+1} + 2\sqrt{a_n a_{n+1} + 121}. \text{ 1) Find } a_{10}. \text{ 2) Prove or disprove that all terms } a_n \text{ are integers.}

negatives.text: \text{Sequence } (x_1, x_2, \dots) \text{ is defined as } x_1 = 20, x_2 = 12, \quad x_{n+2} = x_n + x_{n+1} + 2\sqrt{x_n x_{n+1} - 121}, \text{ for } n \ge 1. \text{ 1) Compute } x_{10}. \text{ 2) Are all terms integers?}

\text{Sequence } (x_1, x_2, \dots) \text{ is defined as } x_1 = 20, x_2 = 12, \quad x_{n+2} = x_n + x_{n+1} + 2\sqrt{x_n x_{n+1} + 144}, \text{ for } n \ge 1. \text{ 1) Compute } x_{10}. \text{ 2) Are all terms integers?}

\text{Sequence } (x_1, x_2, \dots) \text{ is defined as } x_1 = 20, x_2 = 12, \quad x_{n+2} = x_n + x_{n+1} + 2\sqrt{x_n x_{n+1} + 121} + 1, \text{ for } n \ge 1. \text{ 1) Compute } x_{10}. \text{ 2) Are all terms integers?}

positive_text: Find all positive integers $k$ and primes $q \ge 5$ such that $$(2q)^k + 1$$ is the cube of an integer.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $n$ and primes $p \ge 5$ such that $$(2p)^n - 1$$ is a perfect cube.
Find all positive integers $n$ and primes $p \ge 5$ such that $$(3p)^n + 1$$ is a perfect cube.
Find all positive integers $n$ and primes $p \ge 5$ such that $$(2p)^n + 1$$ is a perfect square.

positive_text: \text{Determine the largest real number } a \text{ for which the inequality } \frac{p+1}{q} + \frac{2q+1}{r} + \frac{3r+1}{p} > a \text{ holds for all positive real numbers } p, q, r.

negatives.text: \text{Find the greatest real number } a \text{ such that for every positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ we have } \frac{x+1}{y} + \frac{2y+1}{z} + \frac{3z+1}{x} < a.
\text{Find the greatest real number } a \text{ such that for every positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ we have } \frac{x+1}{y} + \frac{2y+1}{z} + \frac{3z+1}{x} > a \cdot (x + y + z).

positive_text: In triangle $PQR$, with $PQ = PR$, a semicircle with diameter $ST$ is drawn on the base $QR$. This semicircle is tangent to $PQ$ and $PR$ at points $X$ and $Y$, respectively. The line $PS$ intersects the semicircle again at point $Z$. Prove that the line $ZT$ passes through the midpoint of the chord $XY$.

negatives.text: In isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, a semicircle of diameter $EF$ is drawn on the side $AB$, and it is tangent to $AC$ and $BC$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively. The line $AE$ intersects the semicircle at $P$. Prove that the line $PF$ passes through the midpoint of the chord $MN$.

In isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = AC$, a semicircle of diameter $EF$ is drawn on the side $BC$, and is tangent to $AB$ and $AC$ at points $M$ and $N$, respectively. The line $AP$ intersects the semicircle at point $E$. Prove that the line $PF$ passes through the midpoint of the chord $MN$.

positive_text: In triangle $PQR$, the internal angle bisector of $\angle P$ meets $QR$ at $S$, and the external angle bisector of $\angle P$ meets $QR$ at $T$. Let $\omega_1$ be the circumcircle of $PST$. The segment $PR$ intersects $\omega_1$ again at $U$. Let $\omega_2$ be the circumcircle of $PQU$, and the tangent to $\omega_2$ at $P$ meets $\omega_1$ again at $V$. Prove that $PU = PV$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, the internal bisector of $\angle A$ intersects $BC$ at $D$ and the external bisector of $\angle A$ intersects $BC$ at $E$. Let $C_1$ be the circumcircle of $ADE$. $AB$ intersects $C_1$ at $F$. Let $C_2$ be the circumcircle of $ACF$ and the tangent of $C_2$ at $A$ intersects $C_1$ at $G$. Prove that $AF = AG$.

In triangle $ABC$, the internal bisector of $\angle A$ intersects $BC$ at $D$ and the external bisector of $\angle A$ intersects $BC$ at $E$. Let $C_1$ be the circumcircle of $ADE$. $AC$ intersects $C_1$ at $F$. Let $C_2$ be the circumcircle of $ABF$ and the tangent of $C_2$ at $B$ intersects $C_1$ at $G$. Prove that $AF = AG$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be inscribed in circle $\omega$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$, and let $M$ be a point on $BD$ such that $DM = 2BM$. The line $AM$ intersects $BC$ at $E$, and the line $CM$ intersects $AB$ at $F$. The line $FE$ intersects $\omega$ again at $N$. Given that $\angle AMC = 90^\circ$, prove that quadrilateral $ADEF$ is cyclic if and only if $AN$ bisects $BC$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be inscribed in circle $\omega$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $AB$, and let $M$ be a point on $CD$ such that $DM = 2CM$. The line $AM$ intersects $BC$ at $E$, and the line $CM$ intersects $AB$ at $F$. The line $FE$ intersects $\omega$ again at $N$. Given that $\angle AMC = 90^\circ$, prove that quadrilateral $ADEF$ is cyclic if and only if $AN$ bisects $BC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be inscribed in circle $\omega$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$, and let $M$ be a point on $BD$ such that $BM = 2DM$. The line $AM$ intersects $BC$ at $E$, and the line $CM$ intersects $AB$ at $F$. The line $FE$ intersects $\omega$ again at $N$. Given that $\angle AMC = 90^\circ$, prove that quadrilateral $ADEF$ is cyclic if and only if $AN$ bisects $BC$.

positive_text:
Let $x_1, x_2, \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers defined recursively by
$$
x_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \frac{x_n}{2} & \text{if } x_n \text{ is even,} \\
2^k + \frac{x_n+1}{2} & \text{if } x_n \text{ is odd and } 2^{k-1} \le x_n < 2^k. 
\end{cases}
$$
Prove that for any initial value $x_1$, there exists an index $M$ such that for all $n > M$, $x_n = x_{n+2}$.

negatives.text:
Let $b_1, b_2, \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that
$$
b_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \frac{b_n}{2} & \text{if } b_n \text{ is even,} \\
2^r - \frac{b_n+1}{2} & \text{if } b_n \text{ is odd and } 2^{r-1} \le b_n < 2^r. 
\end{cases}
$$
Prove that for any starting value $b_1$, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n > N$, $b_n = b_{n+2}$.

Let $c_1, c_2, \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that
$$
c_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \frac{c_n}{2} & \text{if } c_n \text{ is even,} \\
3^r + \frac{c_n+1}{2} & \text{if } c_n \text{ is odd and } 3^{r-1} \le c_n < 3^r. 
\end{cases}
$$
Prove that for any starting value $c_1$, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n > N$, $c_n = c_{n+2}$.

Let $d_1, d_2, \dots$ be a sequence of positive integers such that
$$
d_{n+1} = \begin{cases} \frac{d_n}{2} & \text{if } d_n \text{ is even,} \\
2^r + \frac{d_n-1}{2} & \text{if } d_n \text{ is odd and } 2^{r-1} \le d_n < 2^r. 
\end{cases}
$$
Prove that for any starting value $d_1$, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n > N$, $d_n = d_{n+2}$.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = AC = BD$. Let $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at point $O$. Let $P$ be the second intersection of the circumcircles of triangles $ABC$ and $ADO$, and let $Q$ be the intersection of $AP$ with $BC$. Prove that $\angle COQ = \angle DOQ$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = BC = CD$. The lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet at point $O$, the circles $ABC$ and $CDO$ meet again at point $P$, and the lines $AP$ and $CD$ meet at point $Q$. Show that $\angle COQ = \angle DOQ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = AC = BD$. The lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet at point $O$, the circles $ABD$ and $ACO$ meet again at point $P$, and the lines $AP$ and $BC$ meet at point $Q$. Show that $\angle COQ = \angle DOQ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = AC = BD$. The lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet at point $O$, the circles $ABC$ and $ADO$ meet again at point $P$, and the lines $BP$ and $CD$ meet at point $Q$. Show that $\angle COQ = \angle DOQ$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle XYZ$ be an acute triangle inscribed in a circle $\Gamma$ with center $M$. The line $YM$ intersects $XZ$ at $Y_1$, and the line $ZM$ intersects $XY$ at $Z_1$. The line $Y_1Z_1$ intersects $\Gamma$ at points $R$ and $S$. If $XR = XS$, prove that $XY = XZ$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle inscribed in circle $\omega$ with center $O$. Line $BO$ intersects $AC$ at $B_1$, and line $CO$ intersects $AB$ at $C_1$. Line $B_1C_1$ intersects the circle again at $P$ and $Q$. If $BP = CQ$, prove that $AB = AC$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute triangle inscribed in circle $\omega$ with center $O$. Line $BO$ intersects $AC$ at $B_1$, and line $CO$ intersects $AB$ at $C_1$. Line $B_1C_1$ intersects the circle again at $P$ and $Q$. If $OP = OQ$, prove that $AB = AC$.

positive_text: \text{In a cyclic quadrilateral } WXYZ, \text{ triangle } WXY \text{ is equilateral. Diagonals } WY \text{ and } XZ \text{ intersect at } P. \text{ If } XP = 19 \text{ and } PZ = 6, \text{ find the possible values of } WZ.

negatives.text: \text{Quadrilateral } ABCD \text{ is cyclic such that } AB = BC = CD. \text{ Diagonals } AC \text{ and } BD \text{ intersect at } E. \text{ Given that } BE = 19 \text{ and } ED = 6, \text{ find the possible values of } AD.

\text{Quadrilateral } ABCD \text{ is cyclic such that } AB = BC = CA. \text{ Diagonals } AC \text{ and } BD \text{ intersect at } E. \text{ Given that } BE = 19 \text{ and } ED = 6, \text{ find the possible values of } AB.

\text{Quadrilateral } ABCD \text{ is cyclic such that } AB = BC = CA. \text{ Diagonals } AC \text{ and } BD \text{ intersect at } E. \text{ Given that } BE = 19 \text{ and } ED = 6, \text{ find the possible values of } AE.

positive_text: Triangle $PQR$ is isosceles with $PQ = PR = 3$ and right angle at $P$. Let $N$ be the midpoint of $QR$. Points $S$ and $T$ lie on $PR$ and $PQ$ respectively such that $PS > PT$ and $PSTN$ is cyclic. If triangle $NTS$ has area $2$, find the length of segment $SR$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, $AB = AC = 3$ and $\angle A = 60^\circ$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Points $D$ and $E$ lie on sides $AC$ and $AB$ respectively such that $AD > AE$ and $ADME$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. Given that triangle $EMD$ has area $2$, find the length of segment $CD$.

In triangle $ABC$, $AB = AC = 3$ and $\angle A = 90^\circ$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $BC$. Points $D$ and $E$ lie on sides $AC$ and $AB$ respectively such that $AD > AE$ and $ADME$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. Given that triangle $EMD$ has area $\frac{1}{2}$, find the length of segment $CD$.

positive_text: Determine all functions $ g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ satisfying $$ g(g(g(a)+b)+b) = a + b + g(b) $$ for all real numbers $ a, b $.

negatives.text: Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ such that $$ f(f(f(x)+y)+y) = x - y + f(y) $$ for all real $ x, y $.
Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ such that $$ f(f(f(x)+y)+y) = x + y^2 + f(y) $$ for all real $ x, y $.
Find all functions $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} $ such that $$ f(f(f(x)+y)+z) = x + y + f(z) $$ for all real $ x, y, z $.

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z > 0. \text{ Show that} \quad \frac{x^{3}}{x^{2}+x y+y^{2}}+\frac{y^{3}}{y^{2}+y z+z^{2}}+\frac{z^{3}}{z^{2}+z x+x^{2}} \geq \frac{x+y+z}{3}

negatives.text: \text{For positive real numbers } a, b, c, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{a^{3}}{a^{2}+b^{2}}+\frac{b^{3}}{b^{2}+c^{2}}+\frac{c^{3}}{c^{2}+a^{2}} \geq \frac{a+b+c}{3}
\text{Let } a, b, c > 0. \text{ Show that} \quad \frac{a^{3}}{a^{2}+2ab+b^{2}}+\frac{b^{3}}{b^{2}+2bc+c^{2}}+\frac{c^{3}}{c^{2}+2ca+a^{2}} \geq \frac{a+b+c}{3}
\text{For positive real numbers } a, b, c, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{a^{2}}{a^{2}+ab+b^{2}}+\frac{b^{2}}{b^{2}+bc+c^{2}}+\frac{c^{2}}{c^{2}+ca+a^{2}} \geq \frac{a+b+c}{3}

positive_text: Let $T = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$ be the set of non-negative integers. Find all strictly increasing functions $g: T \rightarrow T$ such that $k + g(g(k)) \leq 2 g(k)$ for all $k$ in $T$.

negatives.text: Let $S = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$. Find all strictly increasing functions $f: S \rightarrow S$ such that $n + f(n) \leq 2 f(f(n))$ for all $n$ in $S$.

positive_text: \text{Determine the area of the region in the plane defined by } x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 4|x| + 4|y|.

negatives.text: \text{Find the area of the set of points } (x, y) \text{ satisfying } x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 4x + 4y.
\text{Find the area of the region where } x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 4|x| - 4|y|.
\text{Find the area of the set of points } (x, y) \text{ such that } x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 4|x| + 4y.

positive_text: \text{Let } PQR \text{ be a triangle with orthocenter } H, \text{ incenter } I, \text{ and circumcenter } O. \text{ The circumcircle of } PQR \text{ is } \omega. \text{ Line } RI \text{ meets } \omega \text{ again at point } S \neq R. \text{ If } PQ = IS \text{ and } PH = HO, \text{ find the angles of triangle } PQR.

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with orthocenter } H, \text{ incenter } I, \text{ and circumcenter } O. \text{ The circumcircle of } ABC \text{ is } \omega. \text{ Line } CI \text{ meets } \omega \text{ again at } D \neq C. \text{ If } AB = ID \text{ and } BH = HO, \text{ find the angles of triangle } ABC.

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle with incenter } I, \text{ circumcenter } O, \text{ and circumcircle } \omega. \text{ Line } CI \text{ meets } \omega \text{ again at } D \neq C. \text{ If } BC = ID \text{ and } AH = OH, \text{ find the angles of triangle } ABC.

positive_text: Given a positive integer $ N $, consider all of its positive divisors. Let $ q\% $ represent the proportion of these divisors whose last digit is $ 3 $. For example, if $ N = 117 $, the divisors are $ 1, 3, 9, 13, 39, 117 $, and exactly two of them (namely $ 3 $ and $ 13 $) end in $ 3 $, so $ q = 33.33\cdots $. What is the largest possible value of $ q $, over all choices of $ N $?

negatives.text: For a positive integer $ n $, consider all its divisors (including $ 1 $ and itself). Suppose that $ p\% $ of these divisors have their unit digit equal to $ 7 $. For example, $ n = 117 $ has six divisors, and none of them end in $ 7 $. What is the maximum possible value of $ p $?

Let $ n $ be a positive integer and consider all of its divisors. Suppose that $ p\% $ of these divisors are prime numbers ending in $ 3 $. For example, $ n = 117 $ has six divisors, and one of them (namely $ 13 $) is a prime ending in $ 3 $. What is the maximum possible value of $ p $?

For a positive integer $ n $, consider all its divisors (including $ 1 $ and itself). Suppose that $ p\% $ of these divisors have their unit digit equal to $ 3 $. What is the maximum possible value of $ p $ when $ n $ is a power of $ 3 $?

positive_text: Let $\triangle XYZ$ be a triangle with $XY < YZ$, and let $\Gamma$ be its circumcircle. Let $P$ be the midpoint of the arc $\overparen{ZX}$ not containing $Y$, and let $Q$ be a point on $\Gamma$ such that $PQ \perp YZ$. Let $X'$ and $Y'$ be the points where the incircle of $\triangle XYZ$ touches $YZ$ and $ZX$, respectively. Prove that the lines $XQ$, $YP$, and $X'Y'$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < BC$, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be its circumcircle. Let $K$ be the midpoint of the arc $\overparen{AB}$ not containing $C$, and let $T$ be a point on $\mathcal{C}$ such that $KT \perp AC$. Let $A'$, $B'$ be the intouch points on $BC$, $AC$. Prove that the lines $AT$, $CK$, $A'B'$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < BC$, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be its circumcircle. Let $K$ be the midpoint of the arc $\overparen{CA}$ not containing $B$, and let $T$ be a point on $\mathcal{C}$ such that $KT$ is parallel to $BC$. Let $A'$, $B'$ be the intouch points on $BC$, $AC$. Prove that the lines $AT$, $BK$, $A'B'$ are concurrent.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < BC$, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be its circumcircle. Let $K$ be the midpoint of the arc $\overparen{CA}$ not containing $B$, and let $T$ be a point on $\mathcal{C}$ such that $KT$ is perpendicular to $BC$. Let $A'$, $B'$ be the points where the A-excircle and B-excircle touch $BC$, $AC$, respectively. Prove that the lines $AT$, $BK$, $A'B'$ are concurrent.

positive_text: \text{Let } \triangle ABC \text{ be given with } M \text{ the midpoint of } BC, \text{ and } D \text{ the foot of the perpendicular from } M \text{ to } AC. \text{ If } E \text{ is the midpoint of } MD, \text{ show that } AE \perp BD \text{ if and only if } AB = AC.

negatives.text: \text{Let } \triangle ABC \text{ have } M \text{ as the midpoint of } BC, \text{ and let } D \text{ be the projection of } M \text{ onto } AB. \text{ Let } E \text{ be the midpoint of } MD. \text{ Prove that } AE \perp BD \text{ if and only if } AB = AC.

\text{In } \triangle ABC, \text{ let } M \text{ be the midpoint of } AB, \text{ and } D \text{ be the foot of the perpendicular from } M \text{ to } AC. \text{ Let } E \text{ be the midpoint of } MD. \text{ Prove that } AE \perp BD \text{ if and only if } AB = AC.

\text{Let } \triangle ABC \text{ be given, with } M \text{ the midpoint of } BC, \text{ and } D \text{ the projection of } M \text{ onto } AC. \text{ Let } E \text{ be the midpoint of } CD. \text{ Prove that } AE \perp BD \text{ if and only if } AB = AC.

positive_text: Let $ PQRSTU $ be an equiangular hexagon with total side length $ 21 $. If $ PQ = 3 $, $ RS = 4 $, and $ TU = 5 $, determine the area of hexagon $ PQRSTU $.

negatives.text: Let $ ABCDEF $ be an equiangular hexagon with perimeter $ 21 $. Given that $ AB = 3 $, $ BC = 4 $, and $ EF = 5 $, compute the area of hexagon $ ABCDEF $.
Let $ ABCDEF $ be an equiangular hexagon with perimeter $ 21 $. Given that $ AB = 3 $, $ CD = 4 $, and $ FA = 5 $, compute the area of hexagon $ ABCDEF $.
Let $ ABCDEF $ be an equiangular hexagon with perimeter $ 21 $. Given that $ AB = 3 $, $ CD = 4 $, and $ EF = 5 $, compute the length of diagonal $ AD $.

positive_text: Let $PQR$ be a triangle with incenter $J$, and let $X, Y, Z$ be the midpoints of sides $QR, RP, PQ$, respectively. Lines $QJ$ and $YX$ meet at $U$, and lines $RJ$ and $ZX$ meet at $V$. Line $UV$ meets sides $PQ$ and $PR$ at $M$ and $N$, respectively. Prove that $PM = PN$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$, and let $D, E, F$ be the midpoints of sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. Lines $BI$ and $DF$ meet at $P$, and lines $CI$ and $DE$ meet at $Q$. Line $PQ$ meets sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $T$ and $S$, respectively. Prove that $AS = AT$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with centroid $G$, and let $D, E, F$ be the midpoints of sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. Lines $BG$ and $DE$ meet at $P$, and lines $CG$ and $DF$ meet at $Q$. Line $PQ$ meets sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $T$ and $S$, respectively. Prove that $AS = AT$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$, and let $D, E, F$ be the midpoints of sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. Lines $BI$ and $DE$ meet at $P$, and lines $CI$ and $DF$ meet at $Q$. Line $PQ$ meets the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at points $T$ and $S$. Prove that $AS = AT$.

positive_text: Points $X$, $Y$, $Z$ lie on a line in this order. A circle $\Gamma$ passes through $Y$ and $Z$, and a line $\ell$, not parallel to $YZ$ and passing through $X$, intersects $\Gamma$ at $P$ and $Q$. The internal angle bisectors of $\angle ZPY$ and $\angle ZQY$ meet the segment $YZ$ at $R$ and $S$. Show that $XR \cdot XS = XY \cdot XZ$.
\text{Find all ordered triples } (x, y, z) \text{ of positive integers such that } 5^{x} + 3^{y} = 2^{z} + 32

negatives.text: \text{Find all ordered triples } (a, b, c) \text{ of positive integers such that } 5^{a} + 3^{b} + 2^{c} = 32
\text{Find all ordered triples } (a, b, c) \text{ of positive integers such that } 5^{a} - 3^{b} - 2^{c} = 32
\text{Find all ordered triples } (a, b, c) \text{ of positive integers such that } 5^{a} + 3^{b} - 2^{c} = 31

positive_text:
Let $b_{1}$, $b_{2}$, $b_{3}$, $b_{4}$, $b_{5}$ be nonzero real numbers. Consider the polynomial
$$
Q(X) = \prod_{j=1}^{5} \left( b_{j} X^{4} + b_{j+1} X^{3} + b_{j+2} X^{2} + b_{j+3} X + b_{j+4} \right),
$$
with indices taken modulo 5. Show that $Q(X)$ has at least one root with negative real part.

negatives.text:
Let $d_{1}$, $d_{2}$, $d_{3}$, $d_{4}$, $d_{5}$ be nonzero real numbers. Consider the polynomial
$$
T(X) = \prod_{m=1}^{5} \left( d_{m} X^{4} + d_{m+1} X^{3} + d_{m+2} X^{2} + d_{m+3} X + d_{m+4} \right),
$$
with indices taken modulo 5. Prove that $T(X)$ has a root with imaginary part not zero.

Let $e_{1}$, $e_{2}$, $e_{3}$, $e_{4}$, $e_{5}$ be nonzero real numbers. Consider the polynomial
$$
U(X) = \prod_{n=1}^{5} \left( e_{n} X^{4} + e_{n+1} X^{3} + e_{n+2} X^{2} + e_{n+3} X + e_{n+4} \right),
$$
with indices taken modulo 5. Prove that $U(X)$ has a root with modulus less than 1.

positive_text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B \leq \angle C$, $I$ its incenter and $D$ the point where the angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$. Choose points $M$ and $N$ on segments $AB$ and $AC$ such that $BM = BD$ and $CN = CD$. Let the circumcircle of triangle $CMN$ intersect line $BC$ again at point $P$. Show that the points $D$, $I$, $M$, and $P$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B \geq \angle C$, $I$ its incenter and $D$ the point where the angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$. Let $M$ and $N$ be points on sides $AB$ and $AC$ such that $AM = AD$ and $AN = AD$. The circumcircle of triangle $CMN$ intersects line $BC$ again at point $P$. Prove that quadrilateral $DIM P$ is cyclic.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B \leq \angle C$, $I$ its incenter and $D$ the foot of the angle bisector of $\angle A$ on side $BC$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $BM = BD$ and $CN = CD$. The circumcircle of triangle $AMN$ intersects line $BC$ again at point $P$. Prove that quadrilateral $DIM P$ is cyclic.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle B \leq \angle C$, $I$ its incenter and $D$ the point where the angle bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $BM = BD$ and $CN = CD$. The circumcircle of triangle $CMN$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ again at point $P$. Prove that quadrilateral $DIM P$ is cyclic.

positive_text: Two circles $\gamma$ and $\delta$, with centers $P$ and $Q$ respectively, intersect at points $A$ and $B$. Let $U$ and $V$ be points on $\gamma$. Lines $UA$ and $VA$ intersect $\delta$ at $R$ and $S$, respectively, with $A$ lying between $U$ and $R$ and between $V$ and $S$. Let $N$ be the midpoint of $PQ$, $K$ be the midpoint of $UA$, and $L$ be the midpoint of $SA$. Show that $NK = NL$ if and only if $U, V, R$ and $S$ lie on a circle.

negatives.text: Two circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ intersect at points $A$ and $B$, with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $\omega_{1}$. The lines $XA$ and $YA$ intersect $\omega_{2}$ again at points $Z$ and $W$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $O_{1}O_{2}$, $S$ the midpoint of $XZ$, and $T$ the midpoint of $YW$. Prove that $MS = MT$ if and only if $X, Y, Z, W$ are concyclic.

Two circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ intersect at points $A$ and $B$, with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $\omega_{1}$. The lines $XA$ and $YA$ intersect $\omega_{2}$ again at points $Z$ and $W$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $O_{1}O_{2}$, $S$ the midpoint of $XA$, and $T$ the midpoint of $WA$. Prove that $MS = MT$ if and only if $X, Y, Z, W$ are concyclic and $A$ lies on the radical axis of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$.

Two circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ intersect at points $A$ and $B$, with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $\omega_{1}$. The lines $XA$ and $YA$ intersect $\omega_{2}$ again at points $Z$ and $W$, respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $O_{1}O_{2}$, $S$ the midpoint of $XA$, and $T$ the midpoint of $WA$. Prove that $MS = MT$ if and only if $X, Y, Z, W$ are concyclic and $O_{1}O_{2} = AB$.

positive_text: \text{Let } A \text{ be a non-empty set of rational numbers with at least two elements. Suppose that for any two distinct elements } a, b \in A, \text{ there exists an element } c \in A \text{ such that } \left|\frac{a - c}{b - c}\right| = 2 \text{ or } \left|\frac{b - c}{a - c}\right| = 2. \text{ Prove that } A \text{ is infinite.}

negatives.text: \text{Let } Y \text{ be a set of real numbers with at least two elements. Suppose that for any two distinct elements } y_1, y_2 \in Y, \text{ there exists an element } y_3 \in Y \text{ such that } \left|\frac{y_1 - y_3}{y_2 - y_3}\right| = 1 \text{ or } \left|\frac{y_2 - y_3}{y_1 - y_3}\right| = 1. \text{ Prove that } Y \text{ is infinite.}

\text{Let } W \text{ be a set of rational numbers with at least two elements. Suppose that for any two distinct elements } w_1, w_2 \in W, \text{ there exists an element } w_3 \in W \text{ such that } \left|\frac{w_1 - w_3}{w_2 - w_3}\right| < 2 \text{ or } \left|\frac{w_2 - w_3}{w_1 - w_3}\right| < 2. \text{ Prove that } W \text{ is infinite.}

positive_text: Let $\left(b_{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ be a sequence of positive integers such that $b_{n}^{2}$ divides $b_{n-1} b_{n+1}$, for all $n \geq 1$. Prove that if there exists an integer $m \geq 2$ with $\gcd(b_{m}, b_{1}) = 1$, then $b_{1}$ divides $b_{0}$.

negatives.text: Let $\left(c_{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ be a sequence of positive integers such that $c_{n}^{3}$ divides $c_{n-1} c_{n+1}$, for all $n \geq 1$. Prove that if there exists an integer $m \geq 2$ with $\gcd(c_{m}, c_{1}) = 1$, then $c_{1}$ divides $c_{0}$.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ have $PQ < PR$, and let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $QR$. Let $N$ be the midpoint of $QR$, and define $Q'$ as the reflection of $Q$ over $S$. The line perpendicular to $QR$ at $Q'$ meets $PR$ at point $T$. Prove that if $QT$ and $PN$ are perpendicular, then triangle $PQR$ is right-angled.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and define $B'$ as the reflection of $B$ over $D$. The line perpendicular to $BC$ at $B'$ intersects $AB$ at point $P$. Prove that if $BP$ and $AM$ are perpendicular, then triangle $ABC$ is right-angled.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and define $B'$ as the reflection of $B$ over $D$. The line perpendicular to $AB$ at $B'$ intersects $AC$ at point $P$. Prove that if $BP$ and $AM$ are perpendicular, then triangle $ABC$ is right-angled.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $AB < AC$, and let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and define $B'$ as the reflection of $A$ over $D$. The line perpendicular to $BC$ at $B'$ intersects $AC$ at point $P$. Prove that if $BP$ and $AM$ are perpendicular, then triangle $ABC$ is right-angled.

positive_text: Let $p > q > r > s$ be positive integers such that $p^{2} + p r - r^{2} = q^{2} + q s - s^{2}$. Prove that $p q + r s$ is a composite number.

negatives.text: Let $a > b > c > d$ be positive integers such that $a^{2} + a c + c^{2} = b^{2} + b d + d^{2}$. Prove that $a b + c d$ is a composite number.
Let $a > b > c > d$ be positive integers such that $a^{2} + a c - c^{2} = b^{2} + b d - d^{2}$. Prove that $a c + b d$ is a composite number.

positive_text:
Let $n \geq 3$ and $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ be $n$ distinct integers. Show that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_{i} - a_{i+1})^2 \geq 4n - 6,
$$
where $a_{n+1} = a_{1}$.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geq 3$ and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be $n$ real numbers. Prove that
$$
\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(x_{2}-x_{3}\right)^{2}+\ldots+\left(x_{n}-x_{1}\right)^{2} \geq 4 n-6 .
$$

Let $n \geq 3$ and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be $n$ distinct integers. Prove that
$$
\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)+\left(x_{2}-x_{3}\right)+\ldots+\left(x_{n}-x_{1}\right) \geq 4 n-6 .
$$

Let $n \geq 3$ and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ be $n$ distinct integers. Prove that
$$
\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|+\left|x_{2}-x_{3}\right|+\ldots+\left|x_{n}-x_{1}\right| \geq 4 n-6 .
$$

positive_text: Let $p, q, r, s$ be four real numbers. Choose a rearrangement $(m, n, o, p)$ of $(p, q, r, s)$ and define $a_1 = |m-n|$, $b_1 = |n-o|$, $c_1 = |o-p|$, and $d_1 = |p-m|$. Repeat this process with the new set $a_1, b_1, c_1, d_1$ to get $a_2, b_2, c_2, d_2$, and so on. It is known that for some $k$, $a_k = p$, $b_k = q$, $c_k = r$, and $d_k = s$. Determine all such quadruples $(p, q, r, s)$.

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c, d$ be four real numbers. Define $x_1 = |a - b|$, $y_1 = |b - c|$, $z_1 = |c - d|$, and $w_1 = |a - c|$. Repeat this process with $x_1, y_1, z_1, w_1$ to form $x_2, y_2, z_2, w_2$, and so on. It is known that $x_n = a$, $y_n = b$, $z_n = c$, $w_n = d$ for some $n$. Find all such quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$.

Let $p, q, r, s$ be four real numbers. Choose a permutation $(a, b, c, d)$ of $(p, q, r, s)$ and define $x_1 = a - b$, $y_1 = b - c$, $z_1 = c - d$, and $w_1 = d - a$. Repeat the process with the resulting values to form $x_2, y_2, z_2, w_2$, and so on. It is known that $x_n = p$, $y_n = q$, $z_n = r$, $w_n = s$ for some $n$. Find all such quadruples $(p, q, r, s)$.

Let $a, b, c, d$ be four real numbers. Define $x_1 = |a - b|$, $y_1 = |b - c|$, $z_1 = |c - d|$, and $w_1 = |d - a|$. Repeat the process with $x_1, y_1, z_1, w_1$ to form $x_2, y_2, z_2, w_2$, and so on. It is known that $x_n = 0$, $y_n = 0$, $z_n = 0$, $w_n = 0$ for some $n$. Find all such quadruples $(a, b, c, d)$.

positive_text:
Let $k \geq 4$ be a positive integer and there exist $k$ positive integers placed in a circle such that:
- The product of any two numbers that are not next to each other is divisible by $2015 \cdot 2016$.
- The product of any two numbers that are next to each other is not divisible by $2015 \cdot 2016$.
Determine the largest possible value of $k$.

negatives.text:
Let $n \geq 4$ be a positive integer and there exist $n$ positive integers placed in a circle such that:
- The product of each pair of two adjacent numbers is divisible by $2015 \cdot 2016$.
- The product of each pair of two non-adjacent numbers is not divisible by $2015 \cdot 2016$.
Find the maximum value of $n$.

Let $n \geq 4$ be a positive integer and there exist $n$ positive integers placed in a circle such that:
- The sum of each pair of two non-adjacent numbers is divisible by $2015 \cdot 2016$.
- The sum of each pair of two adjacent numbers is not divisible by $2015 \cdot 2016$.
Find the maximum value of $n$.

positive_text:
In triangle $PQR$, the incircle ($J$) touches $PQ$, $PR$ at $S$, $T$ respectively. Let $\ell_{q}$, $\ell_{r}$ be the reflections of $PQ$, $PR$ over $RT$, $QS$ respectively. Let $L$ be the intersection of $\ell_{q}$ and $\ell_{r}$. 
1. Show that $JL \perp QR$.
2. If $J$ lies on the circle through $L$, $S$, $T$, prove that $QS + RT = QR$.

negatives.text:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $D$, $E$ the points where the $A$-mixtilinear incircle is tangent to $AB$, $AC$. Reflect $AB$, $AC$ over $CD$, $BE$ to get $\Delta_b$, $\Delta_c$. Let $K$ be their intersection. 
1. Prove that $IK \perp BC$.
2. If $I$ lies on $\triangle KDE$, prove that $BD + CE = BC$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $D$, $E$ the midpoints of $AB$, $AC$. Reflect $AB$, $AC$ over $CD$, $BE$ to get $\Delta_b$, $\Delta_c$. Let $K$ be their intersection. 
1. Prove that $IK \perp BC$.
2. If $I$ lies on $\triangle KDE$, prove that $BD + CE = BC$.

positive_text: Find all integers $ n \geq 3 $ such that a convex polygon with $ n $ sides can be triangulated with diagonals in such a way that each vertex is connected to an even number of diagonals in the triangulation.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $ n \geq 3 $ such that a convex $ n $-gon can be triangulated with diagonals in such a way that each vertex is connected to an odd number of diagonals in the triangulation.
Find all integers $ n \geq 3 $ such that a convex $ n $-gon can be triangulated with diagonals in such a way that the total number of diagonals used is even.
Find all positive integers $ n \geq 3 $ such that a convex $ n $-gon can be triangulated with diagonals in such a way that the number of diagonals incident to each vertex is divisible by 3.

positive_text: Find all pairs of positive integers ($a$, $b$) such that both equations $x^{2} - a x + b = 0$ and $x^{2} - b x + a = 0$ have integer roots.

negatives.text: Find all pairs of positive integers ($p$, $q$) such that both equations $x^{2} - p x - q = 0$ and $x^{2} - q x - p = 0$ have integral solutions.
Find all pairs of positive integers ($p$, $q$) such that both equations $x^{2} + p x + q = 0$ and $x^{2} + q x + p = 0$ have integral solutions.
Find all pairs of positive integers ($p$, $q$) such that both equations $x^{2} - p x + q = 0$ and $x^{2} - q x + p = 0$ have rational solutions.

positive_text:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be the set of real numbers. Determine all functions $g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\ g(a g(b)-b)+g(a b-a)+g(a+b)=2 a b
$$
holds for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be the set of real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
\ f(x f(y)+y)+f(x y+x)+f(x+y)=2 x y
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be the set of real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
\ f(x f(y)-y)+f(x y)+f(x+y)=2 x y
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be the set of real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
\ f(x f(y)-y)+f(x y-x)+f(x y)=2 x y
$$
for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text:
Let triangle $PQR$ be acute, with $G$ as its orthocenter and $M$ as the midpoint of $QR$. Let the lines $PG$ and $RG$ intersect $RQ$ and $PQ$ at points $U$ and $V$ respectively. The circles $(MVU)$ and $(MUP)$ intersect again at a point $N$.

1. Prove that $N$, $M$, and $P$ are collinear, and that the lines $GN$, $UV$, and $QR$ concur.

2. Let $W$ be the foot of the angle bisector of $\angle QPR$ onto $QR$. The circle $(PNW)$ intersects the circumcircle of $\triangle PQR$ again at $X$ and intersects line $QR$ at $Y$ outside segment $QR$. Suppose that $PX$ and $PY$ intersect the circumcircle of triangle $PUV$ again at $Z$ and $T$ respectively. Prove that $TZ = TN$.

negatives.text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, with $H$ as its orthocenter and $I$ the midpoint of $BC$. Let the lines $AH$, $CH$ intersect $BC$, $AB$ at $E$, $F$ respectively. The circles $(IBF)$ and $(ICE)$ meet again at $D$.

1. Prove that $D$, $I$, $A$ are collinear and $HD$, $EF$, $BC$ are concurrent.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, with $H$ as its orthocenter and $I$ the midpoint of $BC$. The lines $BH$, $CH$ intersect $AC$, $AB$ at $E$, $F$ respectively. The circles $(IEF)$ and $(IBF)$ meet again at $D$.

1. Prove that $D$, $I$, $A$ are collinear and $HD$, $EF$, $BC$ are concurrent.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute, with $H$ as its orthocenter and $I$ the midpoint of $BC$. The lines $BH$, $CH$ intersect $AC$, $AB$ at $E$, $F$ respectively. The circles $(IBF)$ and $(ICE)$ meet again at $D$.

1. Prove that $D$, $H$, $A$ are collinear and $ID$, $EF$, $BC$ are concurrent.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with acute triangles $ACD$ and $BCD$. Let $AB$ and $CD$ intersect at $P$, and let $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $Q$. If the circumcircles of triangles $ADQ$ and $BCQ$ intersect again at $R$, prove that $PR \perp QR$. Furthermore, if $T$ is a point such that $\triangle TAB \sim \triangle RDC$, prove that $TA + RB = TB + RA$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with triangles $ACD$, $BCD$ acute. Suppose lines $AB$ and $CD$ intersect at $S$, and let $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$. The circles $(ABE)$ and $(CDE)$ intersect again at $F$. Prove that $SF \perp EF$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with triangles $ACD$, $BCD$ acute. Suppose $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $S$, and $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $E$. The circles $(ADE)$ and $(BDE)$ intersect again at $F$. Prove that $SF \perp EF$.

Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with triangles $ACD$, $BCD$ acute. Suppose $AB$ and $CD$ intersect at $S$, and $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $E$. The circles $(ADE)$ and $(BCE)$ intersect again at $F$. Prove that $SE \perp EF$.

positive_text: Let $\{a_{n}\}$ be a sequence defined by $a_{1}=2$ and $$a_{n+1}=a_{n}^{2}-a_{n}+1$$ for $n \geq 1$. Show that $$1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{n-1}}}<\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{a_{k}}<1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{n}}}$$ for all $n \geq 1$.

negatives.text: Let $\{a_{n}\}$ be a sequence defined by $a_{1}=2$ and $$a_{n+1}=a_{n}^{2}-a_{n}-1$$ for $n \geq 1$. Prove that $$1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{n-1}}}<\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{a_{k}}<1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{n}}}$$ for all $n \geq 1$.

Let $\{a_{n}\}$ be a sequence defined by $a_{1}=2$ and $$a_{n+1}=a_{n}^{3}-a_{n}+1$$ for $n \geq 1$. Prove that $$1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{n-1}}}<\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{a_{k}}<1-\frac{1}{2^{2^{n}}}$$ for all $n \geq 1$.

Let $\{a_{n}\}$ be a sequence defined by $a_{1}=2$ and $$a_{n+1}=a_{n}^{2}-a_{n}+1$$ for $n \geq 1$. Prove that $$1-\frac{1}{2^{n}}<\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{a_{k}}<1-\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}$$ for all $n \geq 1$.

positive_text:
Determine all functions $g: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
g\left(2 a^{3}+g(b)\right)=b+2 a^{2} g(a),
$$
for all real numbers $a, b$.

negatives.text:
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
f\left(2 x^{3}+f(y)\right)=y+2 x f(x),
$$
for all real numbers $x, y$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
f\left(2 x^{3}+f(y)\right)=y^{2}+2 x^{2} f(x),
$$
for all real numbers $x, y$.

Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
f\left(2 x^{3}+f(y)\right)=y+2 x^{2} f(x^{2}),
$$
for all real numbers $x, y$.

positive_text:
Let $a, b, c$ be non-zero real numbers satisfying
$$
a = 2 - \frac{b}{c}, \quad b = 2 - \frac{c}{a}, \quad c = 2 - \frac{a}{b}.
$$
Compute all possible values of $S = a + b + c$.

negatives.text:
Let $x, y, z$ be non-zero real numbers such that
$$
x = 1 - \frac{y}{z}, \quad y = 1 - \frac{z}{x}, \quad z = 1 - \frac{x}{y}.
$$
Find all possible values of $T = x + y + z$.

Suppose $x, y, z$ are non-zero real numbers such that
$$
x = 2 + \frac{y}{z}, \quad y = 2 + \frac{z}{x}, \quad z = 2 + \frac{x}{y}.
$$
Find all possible values of $T = x + y + z$.

Let $x, y, z$ be non-zero real numbers with
$$
x = 2 - \frac{y}{z}, \quad y = 2 - \frac{z}{x}, \quad z = 2 - \frac{x}{y}.
$$
Find all possible values of $T = xyz$.

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z \geq 0 \text{ with } x + y + z = 1. \text{ Prove that} \quad \frac{\sqrt{x}}{y + 1} + \frac{\sqrt{y}}{z + 1} + \frac{\sqrt{z}}{x + 1} > \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z}).

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c \geq 0 \text{ satisfy } a + b + c = 1. \text{ Prove that} \quad \frac{\sqrt{a}}{b + 1} + \frac{\sqrt{b}}{c + 1} + \frac{\sqrt{c}}{a + 1} > \frac{1}{2}(a + b + c).

\text{Let } a, b, c \geq 0 \text{ satisfy } a + b + c = 1. \text{ Prove that} \quad \frac{\sqrt{a}}{b + 2} + \frac{\sqrt{b}}{c + 2} + \frac{\sqrt{c}}{a + 2} > \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c}).

\text{Let } a, b, c \geq 0 \text{ satisfy } a + b + c = 1. \text{ Prove that} \quad \frac{\sqrt{a}}{b + 1} + \frac{\sqrt{b}}{c + 1} + \frac{\sqrt{c}}{a + 1} < \frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{c}).

positive_text: \text{Prove that there are no positive integers } a, b, c \text{ such that } (4a + 5b)(3a + 4b) = 7^{c}

negatives.text: \text{Prove that there are no positive integers } x, y, z \text{ such that } (3x + 4y)(4x + 5y) = 5^{z}
\text{Prove that there are no positive integers } x, y, z \text{ such that } (3x + 4y)(4x + 5y) = 7^{z+1}
\text{Prove that there are no positive integers } x, y, z \text{ such that } (3x + 4y)(4x + 5y) = 7^{z} + 1

positive_text: Let $PQRSTU$ be a convex hexagon with $PR = SU$, $RT = UQ$, and $TP = QS$. Show that the lines joining the midpoints of opposite sides of the hexagon $PQRSTU$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon with $AC = DF$, $CE = FB$, and $EA = BD + 1$. Prove that the lines connecting the midpoints of opposite sides of the hexagon $ABCDEF$ intersect in one point.

positive_text:
Let sequences $\left(a_{n}\right)$ and $\left(b_{n}\right)$ satisfy $a_{1}=b_{1}=1$ and
$$
a_{n+1}=\frac{a_{n}+2}{a_{n}+1} \quad \text{ and } \quad b_{n+1}=\frac{b_{n}^{2}+2}{2 b_{n}} \text{ for } n=1,2, \ldots .
$$
Prove that $b_{n+1}=a_{2^{n}}$ for all $n \geq 0$.

negatives.text:
Let sequences $\left(a_{n}\right)$ and $\left(b_{n}\right)$ satisfy $a_{1}=b_{1}=1$ and
$$
a_{n+1}=\frac{a_{n}+2}{a_{n}+1} \quad \text{ and } \quad b_{n+1}=\frac{b_{n}^{2}-2}{2 b_{n}} \text{ for } n=1,2, \ldots .
$$
Prove that $b_{n+1}=a_{2^{n}}$ for all $n \geq 0$.

Let sequences $\left(a_{n}\right)$ and $\left(b_{n}\right)$ satisfy $a_{1}=b_{1}=1$ and
$$
a_{n+1}=\frac{a_{n}+2}{a_{n}+1} \quad \text{ and } \quad b_{n+1}=\frac{b_{n}^{2}+2}{b_{n}} \text{ for } n=1,2, \ldots .
$$
Prove that $b_{n+1}=a_{2^{n}}$ for all $n \geq 0$.

Let sequences $\left(a_{n}\right)$ and $\left(b_{n}\right)$ satisfy $a_{1}=b_{1}=1$ and
$$
a_{n+1}=\frac{a_{n}+1}{a_{n}+2} \quad \text{ and } \quad b_{n+1}=\frac{b_{n}^{2}+2}{2 b_{n}} \text{ for } n=1,2, \ldots .
$$
Prove that $b_{n+1}=a_{2^{n}}$ for all $n \geq 0$.

positive_text: The triangle $DEF$ ($DE > DF$) is inscribed in the circle $\Omega'$. On the sides $DE$ and $DF$, the points $R$ and $S$ are selected, respectively, so that $DR = FS$. The lines $RS$ and $EF$ intersect at point $L$. Let $U$ be the incenter of triangle $DRL$, and $V$ the excenter of triangle $FSL$ tangent to side $FS$. Prove that the midpoint of the $\operatorname{arc} DEF$ of the circle $\Omega'$ is equidistant from $U$ and $V$.

negatives.text: The triangle $ABC$ ($AB > BC$) is inscribed in the circle $\Omega$. On the sides $AB$ and $BC$, the points $M$ and $N$ are chosen, respectively, so that $AM = BN$. The lines $MN$ and $AC$ intersect at point $K$. Let $P$ be the incenter of triangle $AMK$, and $Q$ the incenter of triangle $CNK$. Prove that the midpoint of the $\operatorname{arc} ABC$ of the circle $\Omega$ is equidistant from $P$ and $Q$.

The triangle $ABC$ ($AB > BC$) is inscribed in the circle $\Omega$. On the sides $AB$ and $BC$, the points $M$ and $N$ are chosen, respectively, so that $AM = CN$. The lines $MN$ and $AB$ intersect at point $K$. Let $P$ be the incenter of triangle $AMK$, and $Q$ the excenter of triangle $CNK$ tangent to side $CN$. Prove that the midpoint of the $\operatorname{arc} ABC$ of the circle $\Omega$ is equidistant from $P$ and $Q$.

The triangle $ABC$ ($AB > BC$) is inscribed in the circle $\Omega$. On the sides $AB$ and $BC$, the points $M$ and $N$ are chosen, respectively, so that $AM = CN$. The lines $MN$ and $AC$ intersect at point $K$. Let $P$ be the incenter of triangle $AMK$, and $Q$ the excenter of triangle $CNK$ tangent to side $CK$. Prove that the midpoint of the $\operatorname{arc} ABC$ of the circle $\Omega$ is equidistant from $P$ and $Q$.

positive_text: Let $PQRS$ be a rectangle with $PQ$ and $RS$ as the vertical sides. A point $T$ lies on segment $RS$, and the incircle of triangle $PQT$ is tangent to $PQ$, $PT$, and $QT$ at points $A$, $U$, and $V$ respectively. The line $VU$ intersects $QR$ and $PS$ at points $X$ and $Y$, and lines $AX$ and $AY$ intersect the incircle again at points $M$ and $N$. Prove that $AM = AN$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $\angle A = \angle B = 90^\circ$ and let $E$ be a point on side $CD$. Let the circle $\omega$ be tangent to $AB$, $AE$, and $BE$ at points $P$, $F$, and $K$, but it is not necessarily the incircle of triangle $ABE$. Let $KF$ intersect $BC$ and $AD$ at points $M$ and $N$ respectively, and let $PM$ and $PN$ intersect $\omega$ again at points $H$ and $T$. Prove that $PH = PT$.

Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid with $\angle A = \angle B = 90^\circ$ and let $E$ be a point on side $CD$. Let the circle $\omega$ be the incircle of triangle $ABE$, tangent to $AB$, $AE$, and $BE$ at points $P$, $F$, and $K$. Let $KF$ intersect $BC$ and $AD$ at points $M$ and $N$, and let $PM$ and $PN$ intersect $\omega$ again at points $H$ and $T$. Prove that $HM = TN$.

positive_text: Let $PQRS$ be a quadrilateral with right angles at $P$ and $Q$, and $PQ = PS$. Let $T$ be the midpoint of $PS$, and suppose that $SR = QR + PS$ with $PS > QR$. Prove that $\angle PSR = 2\angle QPT$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $\angle A = 90^\circ$, $\angle B = 45^\circ$, and $AB = AD$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of $AD$, and suppose that $CD = BC + AD$, $AD > BC$. Prove that $\angle ADC = 2\angle ABE$.
Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $\angle A = \angle B = 90^\circ$, $AB = 2AD$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of $AD$, and suppose that $CD = BC + AD$, $AD > BC$. Prove that $\angle ADC = 2\angle ABE$.
Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with $\angle A = \angle B = 90^\circ$, $AB = AD$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of $AB$, and suppose that $CD = BC + AD$, $AD > BC$. Prove that $\angle ADC = 2\angle ABE$.

positive_text: Suppose $N$ teams each select a subset of $5$ distinct integers from the set $\{1, 2, \dots, 23\}$, with the condition that any two teams have at most $3$ integers in common. Is it necessarily true that $N \le 2020$? Now consider the same setup, but with the set $\{1, 2, \dots, 25\}$ instead.

negatives.text: Suppose $N$ people each choose $5$ elements from a $23$-element set such that any two people share at most $4$ chosen elements. Does this mean that $N \le 2020$? Answer the same question with $25$ instead of $23$.

Suppose $N$ people each choose $4$ elements from a $23$-element set such that any two people share at most $3$ chosen elements. Does this mean that $N \le 2020$? Answer the same question with $25$ instead of $23$.

Suppose $N$ people each choose $5$ elements from a $23$-element set such that any two people share at least $3$ chosen elements. Does this mean that $N \le 2020$? Answer the same question with $25$ instead of $23$.

positive_text: Suppose $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive odd integers with $\gcd(a, b, c) = 1$ and $a^2 + b^2 + c^2$ is a multiple of $a + b + c$. Show that $a + b + c - 2$ is not congruent to $0$ modulo $3$.

negatives.text: Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be positive odd integers such that $\gcd(x, y, z) = 1$ and $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ is divisible by $x + y + z$. Prove that $x + y + z - 1$ is not divisible by $3$.
Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be positive integers such that $\gcd(x, y, z) = 1$ and $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ is divisible by $x + y + z$. Prove that $x + y + z - 2$ is not divisible by $3$.
Let $x$, $y$ and $z$ be odd positive integers such that $\gcd(x, y, z) = 1$ and $x^3 + y^3 + z^3$ is divisible by $x + y + z$. Prove that $x + y + z - 2$ is not divisible by $3$.

positive_text: Define a positive integer $x$ as distant from squares and cubes if for all integers $k$, both $|x - k^2| > 10^6$ and $|x - k^3| > 10^6$ hold. Show that there are infinitely many positive integers $n$ for which $2^n$ is distant from squares and cubes.

negatives.text: Call a positive integer $x$ to be remote from squares and cubes if each integer $k$ satisfies both $|x - k^2| > 10^6$ and $|x - k^3| > 10^6$. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $n!$ is remote from squares and cubes.

Call a positive integer $x$ to be remote from squares and cubes if each integer $k$ satisfies both $|x - k^2| > 10^6$ and $|x - k^3| > 10^6$. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $2^n + 1$ is remote from squares and cubes.

Call a positive integer $x$ to be remote from squares and cubes if each integer $k$ satisfies both $|x - k^2| > 10^6$ and $|x - k^3| > 10^6$. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $2^n$ is remote from squares and fourth powers.

positive_text: Let $G$ be the set of all vectors $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2020})$ with $x_i \in \{-1, 1\}$ for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, 2020$. Show that there exists a subset $T$ of $G$ with $|T| = 2020$, such that for every vector $v \in G$, there exists $w \in T$ for which the dot product $v \cdot w = 0$.

negatives.text: Let $F$ be the set of all sequences $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2020})$ with $a_i \in \{-1, 1\}$ for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, 2020$. Prove that there exists a set $S$, such that $S \subset F$, $|S| = 2020$ and for any $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2020}) \in F$ there exists $(b_1, b_2, \dots, b_{2020}) \in S$, such that $\sum_{i=1}^{2020} a_i b_i = 1$.

Let $F$ be the set of all sequences $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2020})$ with $a_i \in \{-1, 1\}$ for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, 2020$. Prove that there exists a set $S$, such that $S \subset F$, $|S| = 2020$ and for any $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2020}) \in F$ there exists $(b_1, b_2, \dots, b_{2020}) \in S$, such that $\sum_{i=1}^{2020} a_i b_i = 2$.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ not be isosceles, with incenter $I$ and circumradius $R$. Let $PS$ be the external bisector of $\angle QPR$ meeting side $QR$ at $S$. Let $T$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $QR$ such that $IS \perp IT$. Prove that $OT = 3R$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be scalene with incenter $I$ and circumradius $R$. Let $AL$ be the internal angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meeting $BC$ at $L$. Let $K$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ such that $IL \perp IK$. Prove that $OK = 3R$.

positive_text: Let $P$ be the midpoint of $AC$ in triangle $ABC$. A point $K$ lies on segment $BP$ such that $CK = CP$. It is given that $\angle CBP = 2\angle ABP$. Prove that $BC = PK$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, point $K$ lies on the median $BM$ such that $CM = 2CK$. It is also given that $\angle CBM = 2\angle ABM$. Prove that $BC = KM$.
Let $K$ be a point on the median $BM$ in triangle $ABC$ such that $CM = CK$. Suppose that $\angle CBM = 2\angle BAC$. Prove that $BC = KM$.
In triangle $ABC$, let $K$ lie on the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ such that $CK = CM$. Given that $\angle CBM = 2\angle ABM$, prove that $BC = KM$.

positive_text:
For each non-constant polynomial $Q(x)$ with integer coefficients, define
$$
N_{Q(x)} = \max_{x \in [1; 2022]} |Q(x)|.
$$
1. Find the minimum value of $N_{Q(x)}$ when $\deg Q(x) = 1$.
2. Suppose that $Q(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ with $\deg Q(x) = m$ and $2 \le m \le 2022$. Prove that $N_{Q(x)} \ge 1011$.

negatives.text:
For each non-constant polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients, define
$$
M_{P(x)} = \max_{x \in [0; 2020]} |P(x)|.
$$
1. Find the minimum value of $M_{P(x)}$ when $\deg P(x) = 1$.
2. Suppose that $P(x) \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ with $\deg P(x) = n$ and $2 \le n \le 2021$. Prove that $M_{P(x)} \ge 1010$.

positive_text: Let $P, Q, R, S$ be four points in that order on a straight line $\ell$ with $PQ = RS$. Let $(\Gamma_1)$ be a circle through $P, Q$ with tangents $p, q$ at $P, Q$, respectively. Let $(\Gamma_2)$ be a circle through $R, S$ with tangents $r, s$ at $R, S$, respectively. If $p$ meets $r, s$ at $X, Y$, and $q$ meets $r, s$ at $Z, W$, show that $X, Y, Z, W$ lie on a circle $(\Omega)$ and that the common external tangents of $(\Gamma_1)$ and $(\Gamma_2)$ meet on $(\Omega)$.

negatives.text: Let $A, B, C, D$ be points on the line $d$ in that order and $AB = CD$. Let $(P)$ be a circle through $A, B$ with tangents $a, b$ at $A, B$, and $(Q)$ a circle through $C, D$ with tangents $c, d$ at $C, D$. Suppose that $a$ intersects $c, d$ at $K, L$ and $b$ intersects $c, d$ at $M, N$. Prove that $K, L, M, N$ lie on a straight line.

Let $A, B, C, D$ be points on the line $d$ in that order and $AB = 2CD$. Let $(P)$ be a circle through $A, B$ with tangents $a, b$ at $A, B$, and $(Q)$ a circle through $C, D$ with tangents $c, d$ at $C, D$. Suppose that $a$ intersects $c, d$ at $K, L$ and $b$ intersects $c, d$ at $M, N$. Prove that $K, L, M, N$ lie on a circle.

Let $A, B, C, D$ be points on the line $d$ in that order and $AB = CD$. Let $(P)$ be a circle through $A, B$ with tangents $a, b$ at $A, B$, and $(Q)$ a circle through $C, D$ with tangents $c, d$ at $C, D$. Suppose that $a$ intersects $c, d$ at $K, L$ and $b$ intersects $c, d$ at $M, N$. Prove that $K, L, M, N$ lie on a circle and that the common internal tangents of $(P), (Q)$ meet on that circle.

positive_text: Let $ O $ be the center of the circle passing through the vertices of triangle $ ABC $. Points $ X $ and $ Y $ lie on segment $ BC $, with $ AX = BX $ and $ AY = CY $. Show that the circumcircle of triangle $ AXY $ also passes through the centers of the circumcircles of triangles $ AOB $ and $ AOC $.

negatives.text: Let $ O $ be the circumcenter of triangle $ ABC $. Points $ X $ and $ Y $ lie on side $ BC $ such that $ AX = AY $ and $ BX = CY $. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $ AXY $ passes through the circumcenters of triangles $ AOB $ and $ AOC $.

Let $ O $ be the circumcenter of triangle $ ABC $. Points $ X $ and $ Y $ lie on side $ BC $ such that $ AX = CX $ and $ AY = BY $. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $ AXY $ passes through the circumcenters of triangles $ AOB $ and $ AOC $.

Let $ O $ be the circumcenter of triangle $ ABC $. Points $ X $ and $ Y $ lie on side $ BC $ such that $ AX = BX $ and $ AY = CY $. Prove that the circumcircle of triangle $ AXY $ passes through the incenter of triangle $ ABC $.

positive_text: In triangle $XYZ$, with $XY > XZ$, two circles $o_Y$ and $o_Z$ lie inside angle $YXZ$. Circle $o_Y$ is tangent to $XY$ at $Y$, and circle $o_Z$ is tangent to $XZ$ at $Z$. A tangent from $Z$ to $o_Y$, not coinciding with $XZ$, meets $XY$ at $K$, while a tangent from $Y$ to $o_Z$, not coinciding with $XY$, meets $XZ$ at $L$. The line $KL$ and the angle bisector of $YXZ$ intersect side $YZ$ at $P$ and $M$, respectively. Prove that $YP = ZM$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, with $AB > AC$, circles $o_B$ and $o_C$ are inscribed in angle $BAC$ with $o_B$ tangent to $AB$ at $B$ and $o_C$ tangent to $AC$ at $C$. A tangent from $C$ to $o_B$, not coinciding with $AC$, intersects $AB$ at $K$, and a tangent from $B$ to $o_C$, not coinciding with $AB$, intersects $AC$ at $L$. Line $KL$ and the external angle bisector of $BAC$ intersect $BC$ at points $P$ and $M$, respectively. Prove that $BP = CM$.

In triangle $ABC$, with $AB > AC$, circles $o_B$ and $o_C$ are inscribed in angle $BAC$ with $o_B$ tangent to $AB$ at $B$ and $o_C$ tangent to $AC$ at $C$. A tangent from $B$ to $o_C$, not coinciding with $AB$, intersects $AC$ at $K$, and a tangent from $C$ to $o_B$, not coinciding with $AC$, intersects $AB$ at $L$. Line $KL$ and the angle bisector of $BAC$ intersect $BC$ at points $P$ and $M$, respectively. Prove that $BP = CM$.

positive_text:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers with $a > b$. Show that
$$
\operatorname{lcm}(a, b) + \operatorname{lcm}(a + 1, b + 1) > \frac{2ab}{\sqrt{a - b}}.
$$

negatives.text:
Prove that for any 2 positive integers $m$ and $n$ with $m > n$ holds the following inequality
$$
\operatorname{lcm}(m, n) + \operatorname{lcm}(m - 1, n - 1) > \frac{2mn}{\sqrt{m - n}}.
$$

Prove that for any 2 positive integers $m$ and $n$ with $m > n$ holds the following inequality
$$
\operatorname{lcm}(m, n) + \operatorname{lcm}(m + 1, n + 1) > \frac{2mn}{\sqrt{m + n}}.
$$

Prove that for any 2 positive integers $m$ and $n$ with $m > n$ holds the following inequality
$$
\operatorname{lcm}(m, n) + \operatorname{lcm}(m + 1, n + 1) > \frac{2mn}{\sqrt{m - n}} + 1.
$$

positive_text: A convex polygon with $ n $ sides is partitioned into $ m $ four-sided regions, $ k $ of which are concave. Show that $$ m \geq k + \frac{n-2}{2}. $$

negatives.text: Let a convex $ s $-gon be divided into $ q $ quadrilaterals, $ b $ of which are non-convex. Prove that $$ q \geq b + \frac{s - 4}{2}. $$
Let a convex polygon with $ s $ sides be divided into $ q $ quadrilaterals, $ b $ of which are non-convex. Prove that $$ q \geq 2b + \frac{s - 2}{2}. $$

positive_text: Let $b_0 = 2$ and $b_{n+1} = b_n^2 + b_n - 1$ for $n \ge 0$. Show that $\gcd(b_n, 2n + 1) = 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

negatives.text: Define $e_0 = 2$ and $e_{n+1} = e_n^2 + e_n - 1$ for $n \ge 0$. Prove that $\gcd(e_n, n + 1) = 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Let $f_0 = 2$ and $f_{n+1} = f_n^2 + f_n - 1$ for $n \ge 0$. Prove that $\gcd(f_n, 2n - 1) = 1$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

positive_text: In triangle $\triangle XYZ$, point $G$ lies on segment $YZ$ and point $Q$ lies on segment $XG$. A line $m$ through $G$ intersects $XY$, $QY$ at $R$, $S$ respectively, and intersects the extensions of $XZ$ and $QZ$ at $T$, $U$ respectively. Given $GS = GT$, prove that $GR = GU$.

negatives.text: In triangle $\triangle ABC$, point $D$ lies on segment $BC$ and point $P$ lies on segment $AD$. A line $\ell$ through $D$ intersects $AB$, $PB$ at $M$, $E$ respectively, and intersects the extensions of $AC$ and $PC$ at $F$, $N$ respectively. Given $DE = EF$, prove that $DM = DN$.

positive_text: Let the quadratic curve $ y = x^2 + ax + b $ intersect both the $ x $-axis and the $ y $-axis at three distinct points. Determine the circumcircle of the triangle formed by these three points. Show that there exists a fixed point that lies on this circle for all real values of $ a $ and $ b $. Find that fixed point.

negatives.text: Let the parabola $ y = x^2 + px + q $ intersect the coordinate axes in three distinct points. Consider the incircle of the triangle formed by these points. Prove that there is a point that belongs to that incircle for all real values of $ p $ and $ q $. Find that point.

Let the cubic curve $ y = x^3 + px + q $ intersect the coordinate axes in three distinct points. Consider the circumcircle of the triangle formed by these points. Prove that there is a point that belongs to that circle for all real values of $ p $ and $ q $. Find that point.

Let the parabola $ y = x^2 + px + q $ intersect the coordinate axes in three distinct points. Consider the circumcircle of the triangle formed by these points. Prove that there is a point that lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the vertex of the parabola and the y-intercept, regardless of $ p $ and $ q $. Find that point.

positive_text: A rectangular board $B$ is subdivided into smaller rectangles with sides aligned to the sides of $B$. Let $P$ be the union of all edges from all rectangles in the subdivision, and let $M$ be the set of all maximal connected segments in $P$. Let $I$ be the set of all points where four rectangles meet. Let $m$ be the number of elements in $M$, $i$ the number of points in $I$, and $r$ the total number of rectangles in the subdivision. Prove that $m + i = r + 3$.

negatives.text: A rectangle $R$ is partitioned into smaller rectangles whose sides are parallel with the sides of $R$. Let $B$ be the set of all boundary points of all the rectangles in the partition, including the boundary of $R$. Let $S$ be the set of all (closed) segments whose points belong to $B$. Let a maximal segment be a segment in $S$ which is not a proper subset of any other segment in $S$. Let an intersection point be a point in which 3 rectangles of the partition meet. Let $m$ be the number of maximal segments, $i$ the number of intersection points and $r$ the number of rectangles. Prove that $m + i = r + 3$.

A rectangle $R$ is partitioned into smaller rectangles whose sides are parallel with the sides of $R$. Let $B$ be the set of all boundary points of all the rectangles in the partition, including the boundary of $R$. Let $S$ be the set of all (open) segments whose points belong to $B$. Let a maximal segment be a segment in $S$ which is not a proper subset of any other segment in $S$. Let an intersection point be a point in which 4 rectangles of the partition meet. Let $m$ be the number of maximal segments, $i$ the number of intersection points and $r$ the number of rectangles. Prove that $m + i = r + 3$.

A rectangle $R$ is partitioned into smaller rectangles whose sides are parallel with the sides of $R$. Let $B$ be the set of all boundary points of all the rectangles in the partition, including the boundary of $R$. Let $S$ be the set of all (closed) segments whose points belong to $B$. Let a maximal segment be a segment in $S$ which is not a proper subset of any other segment in $S$. Let an intersection point be a point in which 4 rectangles of the partition meet. Let $m$ be the number of maximal segments, $i$ the number of intersection points and $r$ the number of rectangles. Prove that $m + i = r + 2$.

positive_text: Let $(b_k)$ be a sequence defined by $b_1 = \frac{1}{2}$ and $b_{n+1} = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^n b_i$ for all $n \ge 1$. Show that $b_{100} > 0.99$.

negatives.text: Let $(e_k)$ be a sequence defined by $e_1 = \frac{1}{2}$ and $e_{n+1} = 1 - (a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n)$ for all $n \ge 1$. Prove that $e_{100} > 0.99$.
Let $(g_k)$ be a sequence defined by $g_1 = \frac{1}{2}$ and $g_{n+1} = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^n g_i$ for all $n \ge 1$. Prove that $g_{100} > 0.99$.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ be acute with circumcenter $O$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $Q'$ and $R'$ be the reflections of $Q$ over line $PR$ and $R$ over line $PQ$, respectively. Let $K$ be the circumcenter of triangle $H Q' R'$, $D$ the midpoint of $KP$, and $T$ the intersection of line $OD$ with the line perpendicular to $PQ$ at $P$. Prove that $KP = KT$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, let $O$ be the circumcenter and $H$ the orthocenter. Reflect $B$ over $AB$ and $C$ over $AC$ to get points $B'$ and $C'$. Let $K$ be the circumcenter of triangle $HB'C'$, $D$ the midpoint of $KC$, and $S$ the intersection of line $OD$ with the perpendicular to $AB$ at $A$. Prove that $KA = KS$.

In triangle $ABC$, let $O$ be the circumcenter and $H$ the centroid. Reflect $B$ over $AC$ and $C$ over $AB$ to get points $B'$ and $C'$. Let $K$ be the circumcenter of triangle $HB'C'$, $D$ the midpoint of $KB$, and $S$ the intersection of line $OD$ with the perpendicular to $AB$ at $A$. Prove that $KA = KS$.

In triangle $ABC$, let $O$ be the circumcenter and $H$ the orthocenter. Reflect $B$ over $AC$ and $C$ over $AB$ to get points $B'$ and $C'$. Let $K$ be the circumcenter of triangle $HB'C'$, $D$ the midpoint of $KH$, and $S$ the intersection of line $OD$ with the perpendicular to $AB$ at $A$. Prove that $KA = KS$.

positive_text: Determine all positive real numbers $\beta$ such that there exists a sequence $ (a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots) $ of positive real numbers with the recurrence $ a_{n+2} = \sqrt{\beta a_{n+1} - a_n} $ for all $ n \ge 1 $.

negatives.text: Find all real $\alpha > 0$ for which there exists a sequence $ (x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots) $ of positive real numbers such that $ x_{n+2} = \sqrt{\alpha x_n - x_{n+1}} $ for all $ n \ge 1 $.
Find all real $\alpha > 0$ for which there exists a sequence $ (x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots) $ of positive real numbers such that $ x_{n+2} = \sqrt{\alpha x_{n+1} - x_n^2} $ for all $ n \ge 1 $.

positive_text:
Let $k \ge 3$ be an integer and let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k$ be real numbers in the interval $[0, 1]$. Let $t = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_k$, with $t \ge 3$. Prove that there exist integers $p$ and $q$ with $1 \le p < q \le k$ such that
$$
2^{q-p} a_p a_q > 2^{t-3}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer and let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be real numbers in the interval $[0, 1]$. Let $s = x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n$, with $s \ge 3$. Prove that there exist integers $i$ and $j$ with $1 \le i < j \le n$ such that
$$
2^{j-i} x_i x_j > 2^{s-2}.
$$

Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer and let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be real numbers in the interval $[0, 1]$. Let $s = x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n$, with $s \ge 3$. Prove that there exist integers $i$ and $j$ with $1 \le i < j \le n$ such that
$$
2^{j+i} x_i x_j > 2^{s-3}.
$$

Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer and let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be real numbers in the interval $[0, 1]$. Let $s = x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n$, with $s \ge 3$. Prove that there exist integers $i$ and $j$ with $1 \le i < j \le n$ such that
$$
2^{j-i} (x_i + x_j) > 2^{s-3}.
$$

positive_text: \text{Find the smallest } k > 0 \text{ such that } |a - kb| + |b - kc| + |c - ka| \geq 7 \text{ for all real } a, b, c \text{ with } a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 21.

negatives.text: \text{Find the least } k > 0 \text{ such that } |x - ky| + |y - kz| + |z - kx| \geq 7 \text{ for all real } x, y, z \text{ with } x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 21 \text{ and } x + y + z = 0.
\text{Find the least } k > 0 \text{ such that } |x - ky| + |y - kz| + |z - kx| \leq 7 \text{ for all real } x, y, z \text{ with } x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 21.
\text{Find the least } k > 0 \text{ such that } |x - ky| + |y - kz| + |z - kx| \geq 7 \text{ for all real } x, y, z \text{ with } x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 21 \text{ and } x, y, z \in \mathbb{Z}^+.

positive_text: Let $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality $x^2 g(x - a^2) \geq (x + 2a + 1) g(x)$ for all real numbers $x$ and $a$. Determine the value of $g(2022)$.

negatives.text: Let $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality $x^2 h(x - y^2) \leq (x + 2y + 1) h(x)$ for all real numbers $x$ and $y$. Find $h(2022)$.
Let $k : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality $x^2 k(x - y^2) \geq (x - 2y + 1) k(x)$ for all real numbers $x$ and $y$. Find $k(2022)$.
Let $m : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the inequality $x^2 m(x - y^2) \geq (x + 2y + 1)^2 m(x)$ for all real numbers $x$ and $y$. Find $m(2022)$.

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y > 0 \text{ such that } x + y + \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} = 5. \text{ Prove that } 1 \le x + y \le 4.

negatives.text: \text{Positive numbers } a, b \text{ satisfy } a + b + \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} = 6. \text{ Prove that } 1 \le a + b \le 4.
\text{Positive numbers } a, b \text{ satisfy } a + b + \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} = 5. \text{ Prove that } 2 \le a + b \le 5.
\text{Positive numbers } a, b \text{ satisfy } a + b + \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} = 5. \text{ Prove that } 1 \le ab \le 4.

positive_text: Determine all odd integers $ m $ for which the count of positive integers $ a $ satisfying $ a < \frac{m}{4} $ and $ \gcd(a, m) = 1 $ is odd.

negatives.text: Find all odd integers $ n $ such that the number of integers $ k $ with $ 0 < k < \frac{n}{2} $ and $ \gcd(n, k) = 1 $ is odd.
Find all odd integers $ n $ such that the number of integers $ k $ with $ 0 < k < \frac{n}{4} $ and $ \gcd(k, n) = 2 $ is odd.
Find all odd integers $ n $ such that the number of integers $ k $ with $ 0 < k < \frac{n}{4} $ and $ \gcd(n, k) = 1 $ is even.

positive_text: Let $XYZ$ be an acute, non-isosceles triangle with circumcircle $(O)$ and circumradius $R$. Denote $U$, $V$, $W$ as midpoints of segments $YZ$, $ZX$, $XY$ respectively. Let $(\omega)$ be the circle passing through $X$, $O$ and tangent to $OU$. Circle $(\omega)$ meets $XY$, $XZ$ at $E$, $F$. Denote $I$ as the midpoint of segment $EF$ and $K$ as the intersection of $EF$, $VW$. Prove that $R = 2IK$ and $\triangle UIO$ is an isosceles triangle.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be an acute, non-isosceles triangle with circumcircle $(O)$ and circumradius $R$. Denote $M$, $N$, $P$ as midpoints of segments $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ respectively. Let $(\omega)$ be the circle passing through $A$, $O$ and tangent to $OM$. Circle $(\omega)$ meets $AB$, $AC$ at $E$, $F$. Denote $I$ as the midpoint of segment $EF$ and $K$ as the intersection of $EF$, $MP$. Prove that $R = 2IK$ and $\triangle IMO$ is an isosceles triangle.

Let $ABC$ be an acute, non-isosceles triangle with circumcircle $(O)$ and circumradius $R$. Denote $M$, $N$, $P$ as midpoints of segments $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ respectively. Let $(\omega)$ be the circle passing through $A$, $O$ and tangent to $OM$. Circle $(\omega)$ meets $AB$, $AC$ at $E$, $F$. Denote $I$ as the midpoint of segment $EF$ and $K$ as the intersection of $EF$, $NP$. Prove that $R = 3IK$ and $\triangle IMO$ is an isosceles triangle.

positive_text: Let $x, y, z$ be nonnegative real numbers with $x \ge y \ge z$. Prove that $$ x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz \ge \frac{9}{2}(x - y)(y^2 - z^2). $$

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c$ be nonnegative real numbers with $a \ge b \ge c$. Prove that $$ a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc \ge \frac{9}{2}(a + b)(b^2 - c^2). $$
Let $a, b, c$ be nonnegative real numbers such that $a \ge b \ge c$. Prove that $$ a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc \ge \frac{9}{2}(a - b)(b - c)^2. $$
Let $a, b, c$ be nonnegative real numbers with $a \ge b \ge c$. Prove that $$ a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc \ge \frac{9}{2}(a - b)(b^3 - c^3). $$

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there do not exist positive integers $x$ and $y$ such that $$ n = \frac{x}{y} + \frac{x+1}{y+1}. $$

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $n$ that cannot be written in the form $$ n = \frac{a}{b} + \frac{a+1}{b-1}, $$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with $b > 1$.
Determine all positive integers $n$ for which there do not exist positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $$ n = \frac{a^2}{b^2} + \frac{(a+1)^2}{(b+1)^2}. $$
Find all positive integers $n$ that cannot be written in the form $$ n = \frac{a}{b} + \frac{a-1}{b-1}, $$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with $a > 1$ and $b > 1$.

positive_text: Let $PQR$ be a triangle inscribed in a circle $(M)$ with angle $\angle P = 45^\circ$ and $PQ < PR$. Let $PS, PT$ be the angle bisector and the height of triangle $PQR$ with $S, T$ on $QR$. If $MS$ intersects $PT$ at $U$ and $N$ is the circumcenter of triangle $UQR$, prove that $TN \parallel PS$.

negatives.text: Let $ABC$ be a triangle inscribed in circle $(O)$ with angle $\angle A = 60^\circ$ and $AB < AC$. Let $AD, AH$ be the angle bisector and altitude of triangle $ABC$ with $D, H$ on $BC$. Suppose that $OD$ intersects $AH$ at $E$ and $K$ is the circumcenter of triangle $EBC$. Prove that $HK \parallel AD$.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle inscribed in circle $(O)$ with angle $\angle A = 45^\circ$ and $AB < AC$. Let $AD, AH$ be the angle bisector and altitude of triangle $ABC$ with $D, H$ on $BC$. Suppose that $OH$ intersects $AD$ at $E$ and $K$ is the circumcenter of triangle $EBC$. Prove that $HK \parallel AD$.

positive_text:
Let $x_1 \le x_2 \le \dots \le x_{50}$ be real numbers with
(i) $x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_{50} = 0,$
(ii) $\sum_{i=1}^{50} |x_i| = 624.$
Determine the smallest possible value of $D = x_{50} - x_1$ and the largest possible value of $P = x_1x_2 \dots x_{50}$.

negatives.text:
Let $a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_{50}$ be real numbers with
(i) $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_{50} = 0,$
(ii) $\sum_{i=1}^{50} a_i^2 = 624.$
Find the minimum value of $S = a_{50} - a_1$ and the maximum value of $T = a_1a_2 \dots a_{50}$.

Let $a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_{50}$ be real numbers with
(i) $a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_{50} = 624,$
(ii) $\sum_{i=1}^{50} |a_i| = 624.$
Find the minimum value of $S = a_{50} - a_1$ and the maximum value of $T = a_1a_2 \dots a_{50}$.

positive_text:
Determine all integers $n < 2027$ such that:
(i) For each positive divisor $d$ of $n$, the set $\{1^d, 2^d, \dots, 2026^d\}$ forms a complete residue system modulo $2027$.
(ii) $\tau(n)^2$ divides $n$, where $\tau(n)$ is the number of positive divisors of $n$.

negatives.text:
Find all positive integers $n < 2027$ such that:
(i) For every positive divisor $d$ of $n$, the numbers $1^d, 2^d, \dots, 2026^d$ all have distinct remainders when divided by $2027$.
(ii) $\tau(n) \mid n$.

Find all positive integers $n < 2027$ such that:
(i) For every positive divisor $d$ of $n$, the numbers $1^d, 2^d, \dots, 2026^d$ all have distinct remainders when divided by $2027$.
(ii) $\tau(n) + 2 \mid n$.

Find all positive integers $n < 2027$ such that:
(i) For every positive divisor $d$ of $n$, the numbers $1^d, 2^d, \dots, 2026^d$ all have distinct remainders when divided by $2027$.
(ii) $\tau(n)^2 > n$.

positive_text:
Determine all non-negative real numbers $ c \ge 0 $ for which there exists a function $ f : (0, +\infty) \to (0, +\infty) $ satisfying
$$
f(y^2 f(x) + y + c) = x f(x + y^2)
$$
for all positive real numbers $ x $ and $ y $.

negatives.text:
Find all non-negative real numbers $ c \ge 0 $ such that there exists a function $ f : (0, +\infty) \to (0, +\infty) $ with the property
$$
f(y^2 f(x) + y + c) = x f(x + y^2) + 1
$$
for all $ x, y > 0 $.

Find all non-negative real numbers $ c \ge 0 $ such that there exists a function $ f : (0, +\infty) \to (0, +\infty) $ with the property
$$
f(y^2 f(x) + y + c) = x f(x + y)
$$
for all $ x, y > 0 $.

positive_text: Let $ H $ be a planar graph with all vertices having degree $ \ge 5 $. Show that there is at least one edge $ \{u, v\} $ in $ H $ with $ \deg(u) + \deg(v) \le 11 $.

negatives.text: Suppose $ G $ is a planar graph with minimum degree $ \ge 5 $. Prove that $ G $ contains an edge $ \{x, y\} $ such that $ \deg(x) + \deg(y) \le 10 $.
Suppose $ G $ is a planar graph with minimum degree $ \ge 5 $. Prove that $ G $ contains a vertex $ x $ such that $ \deg(x) \le 11 $.
Suppose $ G $ is a planar graph with minimum degree $ \ge 5 $. Prove that $ G $ contains an edge $ \{x, y\} $ such that $ \deg(x) + \deg(y) $ is even.

positive_text: Let triangle $ ABC $ have $ AB < BC $, and let $ D $ be a point on $ AC $ such that $ AB = BD $. Let the incircle of triangle $ ABC $ touch sides $ AB $ and $ AC $ at points $ K $ and $ L $, respectively. Let $ J $ be the incenter of triangle $ BCD $. Prove that line $ KL $ divides $ AJ $ in half.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ ABC $ have $ AB < BC $, and let $ D $ be a point on $ AC $ such that $ AB = CD $. Let the incircle of triangle $ ABC $ touch sides $ AB $ and $ AC $ at points $ K $ and $ L $, respectively. Let $ J $ be the incenter of triangle $ BCD $. Prove that line $ KL $ bisects segment $ AJ $.

Let triangle $ ABC $ have $ AB < BC $, and let $ D $ be a point on $ AC $ such that $ AB = BD $. Let the incircle of triangle $ ABC $ touch sides $ AB $ and $ BC $ at points $ K $ and $ L $, respectively. Let $ J $ be the incenter of triangle $ BCD $. Prove that line $ KL $ bisects segment $ AJ $.

Let triangle $ ABC $ have $ AB < BC $, and let $ D $ be a point on $ AB $ such that $ AB = BD $. Let the incircle of triangle $ ABC $ touch sides $ AB $ and $ AC $ at points $ K $ and $ L $, respectively. Let $ J $ be the incenter of triangle $ BCD $. Prove that line $ KL $ bisects segment $ AJ $.

positive_text: Наћи све природне бројеве $a$ и $k$ такве да важи $$a^{3} + 2a + 1 = 2^{k}$$

negatives.text: Наћи све природне бројеве $x$ и $n$ такве да важи $$x^{3} - 2x + 1 = 2^{n}$$
Наћи све природне бројеве $x$ и $n$ такве да важи $$x^{3} + 2x + 1 = 3^{n}$$
Наћи све природне бројеве $x$ и $n$ такве да важи $$x^{3} + 2x + 1 = 2^{n} + 1$$

positive_text:
Let $ k $ be a positive integer. For every function $ f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N} $, define a sequence of functions $ (g_{m})_{m \geq 1} $ by $ g_{1} = f $ and $ g_{m+1} = f \circ g_{m} $. A function $ f $ is said to be $ k $-stable if for all $ n \in \mathbb{N} $, the relation
$$
g_{k}(n) = f(n)^k
$$
holds.

a) For which $ k $ is there an injective $ k $-stable function $ f $?

b) For which $ k $ is there an arbitrary $ k $-stable function $ f $?

negatives.text:
Let $ k $ be a positive integer. For every function $ f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N} $, define $ f_{1} = f $, and $ f_{m+1} = f \circ f_{m} $ for $ m \geq 1 $. A function $ f $ is $ k $-final if for all $ n \in \mathbb{N} $, the relation
$$
f_{k}(n) = f(n)^{k+1}
$$
holds.

a) For which $ k $ is there an injective $ k $-final function $ f $?

b) For which $ k $ is there an arbitrary $ k $-final function $ f $?

Let $ k $ be a positive integer. For every function $ f: \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{N} $, define $ f_{1} = f $, and $ f_{m+1} = f \circ f_{m} $ for $ m \geq 1 $. A function $ f $ is $ k $-final if for all $ n \in \mathbb{N} $, the relation
$$
f_{k}(n) = f(n)^k + 1
$$
holds.

a) For which $ k $ is there an injective $ k $-final function $ f $?

b) For which $ k $ is there an arbitrary $ k $-final function $ f $?

positive_text: \text{Let } n \text{ be a positive integer. For positive real numbers } a, b, c \text{ such that } a + b + c = 1, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{a^{n+2}}{a^{n+1} + b^{n} + c^{n}} + \frac{b^{n+2}}{b^{n+1} + c^{n} + a^{n}} + \frac{c^{n+2}}{c^{n+1} + a^{n} + b^{n}} \geqslant \frac{1}{7}. \text{ When is equality achieved?}

negatives.text: \text{Let } k \text{ be a natural number. For positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ with } x + y + z = 1, \text{ prove or disprove that} \quad \frac{x^{k+2}}{x^{k+1} + y^{k} + z^{k}} + \frac{y^{k+2}}{y^{k+1} + z^{k} + x^{k}} + \frac{z^{k+2}}{z^{k+1} + x^{k} + y^{k}} < \frac{1}{7}.

\text{Let } k \text{ be a natural number. For positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ with } x + y + z = 1, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{x^{k+2}}{x^{k+1} + y^{k+1} + z^{k+1}} + \frac{y^{k+2}}{y^{k+1} + z^{k+1} + x^{k+1}} + \frac{z^{k+2}}{z^{k+1} + x^{k+1} + y^{k+1}} \geqslant \frac{1}{7}.

\text{Let } k \text{ be a natural number. For positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ with } x + y + z = 1, \text{ prove that} \quad \frac{x^{k+1}}{x^{k+1} + y^{k} + z^{k}} + \frac{y^{k+1}}{y^{k+1} + z^{k} + x^{k}} + \frac{z^{k+1}}{z^{k+1} + x^{k} + y^{k}} \geqslant \frac{1}{7}.

positive_text: \text{У скупу целих бројева решити једначину} \quad a^{x} + b^{4} = c^{z}, \quad \text{где је } a = 12, b = y, c = 2008.

negatives.text: \text{У скупу целих бројева решити једначину} \quad 12^{x} - y^{4} = 2008^{z}.
\text{У скупу целих бројева решити једначину} \quad 12^{x} + y^{3} = 2008^{z}.
\text{У скупу природних бројева решити једначину} \quad 12^{x} + y^{4} = 2008^{z}.

positive_text:
Доказати да за позитивне реалне бројеве $x, y$ и $z$, такве да је $x+y+z=1$, важи неједнакост
$$
\frac{1}{yz + x + \frac{1}{x}} + \frac{1}{zx + y + \frac{1}{y}} + \frac{1}{xy + z + \frac{1}{z}} \leqslant \frac{27}{31}
$$

negatives.text:
Доказати да за позитивне реалне бројеве $a, b$ и $c$, такве да је $a+b+c=1$, важи неједнакост
$$
\frac{1}{bc + a + \frac{1}{a}} + \frac{1}{ca + b + \frac{1}{b}} + \frac{1}{ab + c + \frac{1}{c}} \geqslant \frac{27}{31}
$$

Доказати да за позитивне реалне бројеве $a, b$ и $c$, такве да је $a+b+c=1$, важи неједнакост
$$
\frac{1}{bc + a + a} + \frac{1}{ca + b + b} + \frac{1}{ab + c + c} \leqslant \frac{27}{31}
$$

Доказати да за позитивне реалне бројеве $a, b$ и $c$, такве да је $abc=1$, важи неједнакост
$$
\frac{1}{bc + a + \frac{1}{a}} + \frac{1}{ca + b + \frac{1}{b}} + \frac{1}{ab + c + \frac{1}{c}} \leqslant \frac{27}{31}
$$

positive_text: Define the sequence $\left(x_{n}\right)_{n \geqslant 1}$ with $x_{1} = 3$, $x_{2} = 11$, and $x_{n} = 4x_{n-1} - x_{n-2}$ for $n \geqslant 3$. Show that each term $x_{n}$ can be written in the form $p^{2} + 2q^{2}$, where $p$ and $q$ are positive integers.

negatives.text: Let the sequence $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \geqslant 1}$ be defined by $a_{1} = 3$, $a_{2} = 11$, and $a_{n} = 4a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}$ for $n \geqslant 3$. Prove that every term of the sequence is of the form $a^{2} + 2b^{2}$ for some positive integers $a$ and $b$.

Define the sequence $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \geqslant 1}$ with $a_{1} = 3$, $a_{2} = 11$, and $a_{n} = 4a_{n-1} - a_{n-2}$ for $n \geqslant 3$. Show that each term $a_{n}$ can be written in the form $a^{2} + b^{2}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers.

Let the sequence $\left(a_{n}\right)_{n \geqslant 1}$ be defined by $a_{1} = 3$, $a_{2} = 11$, and $a_{n} = 3a_{n-1} - a_{n-2}$ for $n \geqslant 3$. Prove that every term of the sequence is of the form $a^{2} + 2b^{2}$ for some positive integers $a$ and $b$.

positive_text: Нека је $FGHIJ$ конвексан петоугао у коме је $FG = 1$, $\angle JFG = \angle FGH = 120^\circ$, $\angle HIJ = 60^\circ$ и $\angle FHJ = 30^\circ$. Доказати да је површина петоугла $FGHIJ$ мања од $\sqrt{3}$.

negatives.text: Нека је $JKLMN$ конвексан петоугао у коме је $JK = 1$, $\angle NJK = \angle JKL = 120^\circ$, $\angle LMN = 60^\circ$ и $\angle JLN = 90^\circ$. Доказати да је површина петоугла $JKLMN$ мања од $\sqrt{3}$.
