positive_text: Let $K$ be a point on the segment $QR$ of an acute triangle $PQR$. Let $O$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle PQR$ and $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $PK$. Let $\Omega_1, \Omega_2$ be the circumcircles of $\triangle PQM, \triangle PRM$, respectively. Let $m$ be the line parallel to $QR$ and passing through $M$. $m$ intersects $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ at $S$ and $T$, different from $M$, respectively. $m$ intersects $PQ$ and $PR$ at $G$ and $H$, respectively. Two lines $SB$ and $TC$ meet at $L$. Show that $KQ = KR$ if and only if $LG = LH$.

negatives.text: Let $P$ be a point on the side $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$ and $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $H$ to $AP$. Let $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2$ be the circumcircles of $\triangle ABD, \triangle ACD$, respectively. Let $l$ be the line perpendicular to $BC$ and passing through $D$. $l$ intersects $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ at $X$ and $Y$, different from $D$, respectively. $l$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Two lines $XB$ and $YC$ meet at $Z$. Show that $BP = CP$ if and only if $ZE = ZF$.

Let $P$ be a point on the side $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$ and $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $H$ to $AP$. Let $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2$ be the circumcircles of $\triangle ABD, \triangle ACD$, respectively. Let $l$ be the line parallel to $BC$ and passing through $D$. $l$ intersects $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ at $X$ and $Y$, different from $D$, respectively. $l$ intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at $E$ and $F$, respectively. Two lines $XB$ and $YC$ meet at $Z$. Show that $BP = CP$ if and only if $ZB = ZC$.

positive_text: Determine all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty) $ such that for all real numbers $ x, y, z, w $ with $ xy + yz + zw = 0 $, it holds that $$ f(x - y) + f(z - w) = f(x) + f(y + z) + f(w) $$.

negatives.text: Find all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty) $ such that for all real numbers $ a, b, c, d $ with $ ab + bc + cd = 0 $, it holds that $$ f(a + b) + f(c + d) = f(a) + f(b + c) + f(d) $$.
Determine all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty) $ such that for all real numbers $ a, b, c, d $ with $ ab + bc + cd = 0 $, it holds that $$ f(a - b) + f(c - d) = f(a) + f(b - c) + f(d) $$.
Find all functions $ f : \mathbb{R} \to [0, \infty) $ such that for all real numbers $ a, b, c, d $ with $ ab + bc + cd = 1 $, it holds that $$ f(a - b) + f(c - d) = f(a) + f(b + c) + f(d) $$.

positive_text: Determine the maximum of $\left(a^2 - bc\right)\left(b^2 - ca\right)\left(c^2 - ab\right)$, where $a, b, c$ are real numbers such that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1$.

negatives.text: Find the maximum value of $\left(x^2 + yz\right)\left(y^2 + zx\right)\left(z^2 + xy\right)$ given that $x, y, z$ are real numbers satisfying $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$.
Find the maximum value of $\left(x^2 - yz\right)\left(y^2 - zx\right)\left(z^2 - xy\right)$ given that $x, y, z$ are real numbers satisfying $x + y + z = 1$.
Find the maximum value of $\left(x^2 - y^2\right)\left(y^2 - z^2\right)\left(z^2 - x^2\right)$ given that $x, y, z$ are real numbers satisfying $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$.

positive_text:
Let $\omega$ be the incircle of triangle $XYZ$, tangent to $YZ$, $XZ$, and $XY$ at $P$, $Q$, and $R$, respectively. Let line $RQ$ intersect $XI$, $YI$, $YZ$, and $PI$ at points $U$, $V$, $S$, and $T$, respectively, where $I$ is the incenter of $\triangle XYZ$. Suppose the line through the midpoint of $VZ$ and $S$ meets $XU$ at a point $W$. Prove that
$$
WT = \frac{XY \cdot UT}{XI}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Let line $EF$ meet $BI$, $CI$, and $BC$ at points $K$, $L$, and $M$, respectively, with $I$ being the incenter of $\triangle ABC$. Suppose the line through the midpoint of $CL$ and $M$ intersects $BK$ at point $P$. Prove that
$$
PQ = \frac{AB \cdot KQ}{BI}.
$$

Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $AC$, and $AB$ at $D$, $E$, and $F$, respectively. Let line $EF$ meet $BI$, $CI$, and $BC$ at points $K$, $L$, and $M$, respectively, with $I$ being the incenter of $\triangle ABC$. Suppose the line through the midpoint of $CL$ and $M$ intersects $CK$ at point $P$. Prove that
$$
PQ = \frac{AB \cdot KQ}{CI}.
$$

positive_text: Let triangle $UVW$ be acute with $UV < UW$. Points $R$ and $S$ lie on the segments $UV$ and $UW$ respectively. Let $Q$ be a point such that $QV = QR$ and $QW = QS$. Let $Z$ be a point on the interior of arc $UW$ of the circumcircle of triangle $UVW$ that does not contain $V$. The line $ZU$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $RSU$ again at $T$. Prove that $QZ = QT$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB < AC$. Points $D, E$ lie on the interiors of $AB, AC$, respectively. Let $P$ be a point satisfying $PB = PE$, $PC = PD$. Let $X$ be a point on the interior of arc $AC$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$ which does not include the point $B$. The line $XA$ meets again the circumcircle of $ADE$ at $Y$. Show that $PX = PY$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be acute with $AB < AC$. Points $D, E$ lie on the interiors of $AB, AC$, respectively. Let $P$ be a point satisfying $PB = PD$, $PC = PE$. Let $X$ be a point on the interior of arc $AB$ of the circumcircle of $ABC$ which does not include the point $C$. The line $XA$ meets again the circumcircle of $ADE$ at $Y$. Show that $PX = PY$.

positive_text: Let $\mathbb{R}^+$ be the set of positive real numbers. Suppose $g : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ satisfies the condition that for every $a > 0$, there are finitely many $b > 0$ such that $$(a + g(b))(b + g(a)) \leq 4.$$ Prove that $g(m) > g(n)$ for all $m, n > 0$ with $m < n$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathbb{R}^+$ be the set of positive real numbers. Suppose $h : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ satisfies the condition that for every $x > 0$, there are finitely many $y > 0$ such that $$(x + h(y))(y + h(x)) < 4.$$ Prove that $h(x) > h(y)$ for all $x, y > 0$ with $x < y$.

Let $\mathbb{R}^+$ be the set of positive real numbers. Suppose $p : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ satisfies the condition that for every $x > 0$, there are finitely many $y > 0$ such that $$(x + p(y))(y + p(x)) \leq 4x.$$ Prove that $p(x) > p(y)$ for all $x, y > 0$ with $x < y$.

positive_text: Prove that there exists a constant $K$ such that for all primes $p > K$, the number of integers $x$ with $1 \le x \le p$ and $x^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ is at most $\frac{p}{2^{2024}}$.

negatives.text: Prove that there exists a constant $K$ such that for all primes $p > K$, the number of integers $x$ with $1 \le x \le p$ and $x^{p} \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$ is at most $\frac{p}{2^{2024}}$.
Prove that there exists a constant $K$ such that for all primes $p > K$, the number of integers $x$ with $1 \le x \le p$ and $x^{p-1} - 1$ divisible by $p$ is at most $\frac{p}{2^{2024}}$.

positive_text: Let $G$ be a graph with $n > 1$ vertices, no loops or multiple edges. Suppose that between any two distinct vertices, there is exactly one path connecting them. Prove that $G$ has $n - 1$ edges.

negatives.text: Let $n > 1$ points be connected by edges such that between any two points there is a path. Prove that there are $n - 1$ edges.
Given $n > 1$ points, some pairs connected by an edge. Suppose there is a unique path of length 2 between any two points. Prove that there are $n - 1$ edges.
Let $n > 1$ points be connected such that between any two points there is at least one path and at most two paths. Prove that there are $n - 1$ edges.

positive_text: Let $AB = BC$ and let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AC$. A point $H$ is selected on side $BC$ so that segment $MH$ is perpendicular to $BC$. If $P$ is the midpoint of $MH$, prove that segment $AH$ is perpendicular to segment $BP$.

negatives.text: Let $AB = BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$. A point $H$ is selected on side $BC$ so that $MH$ is perpendicular to $BC$. If $P$ is the midpoint of $CH$, prove that $AH$ is perpendicular to $BP$.
Let $AB = BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$. A point $H$ is selected on side $BC$ so that $MH$ is parallel to $BC$. If $P$ is the midpoint of $MH$, prove that $AH$ is perpendicular to $BP$.

Let $AB = BC$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $AC$. A point $H$ is selected on side $BC$ so that $MH$ is perpendicular to $BC$. If $P$ is the midpoint of $MB$, prove that $AH$ is perpendicular to $BP$.

positive_text: On a circle, we begin by marking two diametrically opposite points and labeling them both $1$. For each subsequent step, we add new points at the midpoint of each arc between two adjacent labeled points from the previous step, and label each new point with the sum of the two adjacent labels. What is the total of all labels on the circle after step $n$?

negatives.text: We begin with two points on a circle labeled $1$, placed at opposite ends of a diameter. At each subsequent step, we place new points at the midpoint of each arc between adjacent points and label them with the product of the two adjacent labels. What is the total sum of the labels after step $n$?

Two points are placed on a circle at opposite ends of a diameter and labeled $1$. At step $n > 1$, a new point is placed at the midpoint of each arc between two adjacent points from step $n - 1$, and it is labeled with the sum of the labels at the two adjacent points. However, only the new points are labeled, and the original labels are removed. What is the total sum of the labels after step $n$?

We place two points on a circle at opposite ends of a diameter and label them both $1$. At step $n > 1$, we place new points at the midpoint of each arc between two adjacent points from the previous step and label them with the sum of the labels at the two adjacent points. However, after placing the labels, we remove all the labels from the circle. What is the total sum of the labels after step $n$?

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ be given. A line through $R$ is drawn parallel to the bisector of $\angle Q$, intersecting the bisector of $\angle P$ at $S$. Another line through $R$ is drawn parallel to the bisector of $\angle P$, intersecting the bisector of $\angle Q$ at $T$. Show that if $ST \parallel PQ$, then $RP = RQ$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be given. A line through $C$ is drawn parallel to the bisector of $\angle B$, intersecting the side $AB$ at $D$. Another line through $C$ is drawn parallel to the bisector of $\angle A$, intersecting the side $AB$ at $E$. Show that if $DE \parallel AB$, then $CA = CB$.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $m$ be natural numbers such that for all natural numbers $z$ with $z 
e y$, $y - z$ divides $x - z^m$. Prove that $x = y^m$.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers such that for every natural number $k$ not equal to $b$, $b - k$ divides $a + k^n$. Prove that $a = b^n$.
Let $a$, $b$, $n$ be natural numbers such that for every natural number $k$ not equal to $b$, $b - k$ divides $a - (k + 1)^n$. Prove that $a = b^n$.

positive_text: Let $PQRS$ be a tangential quadrilateral with $PQ$ parallel to $RS$, and $QR = SP$. The diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ intersect at $T$. Let $r_1$, $r_2$, $r_3$, and $r_4$ be the inradii of triangles $PQT$, $QRT$, $RST$, and $SPT$ respectively. Prove that $\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_3} = \frac{1}{r_2} + \frac{1}{r_4}$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with $AB$ parallel to $CD$, and $BC = AD$. The diagonals $AC$, $BD$ intersect at $E$. Let $r_1$, $r_2$, $r_3$, $r_4$ be the inradii of triangles $ABE$, $BCE$, $CDE$, $DAE$ respectively. Prove that $\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_3} = \frac{1}{r_2} + \frac{1}{r_4}$.

Let $ABCD$ be a tangential quadrilateral with $AB$ parallel to $CD$, and $BC = 2AD$. The diagonals $AC$, $BD$ intersect at $E$. Let $r_1$, $r_2$, $r_3$, $r_4$ be the inradii of triangles $ABE$, $BCE$, $CDE$, $DAE$ respectively. Prove that $\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_3} = \frac{1}{r_2} + \frac{1}{r_4}$.

Let $ABCD$ be a tangential quadrilateral with $AB$ perpendicular to $CD$, and $BC = AD$. The diagonals $AC$, $BD$ intersect at $E$. Let $r_1$, $r_2$, $r_3$, $r_4$ be the inradii of triangles $ABE$, $BCE$, $CDE$, $DAE$ respectively. Prove that $\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_3} = \frac{1}{r_2} + \frac{1}{r_4}$.

positive_text: Suppose $a$, $b$, and $p$ are positive integers with $p > 1$. Prove that the equation $a(a + 1) = b^p$ has no solutions.

negatives.text: Let $p$, $q$, and $s$ be natural numbers with $s > 1$. Prove that $p(p + 2) = q^s$ has no solutions.

positive_text: Let $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ be real numbers. Show that there exist integers $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ with $|x_i - y_i| < 1$ such that for every subset $S \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, the inequality $\left|\sum_{i \in S} x_i - \sum_{i \in S} y_i\right| < \frac{n + 1}{4}$ holds.

negatives.text: Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers. Show that there exist integers $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ with $|a_i - b_i| < 1$ such that for every subset $S \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, the inequality $\left|\sum_{i \in S} a_i - \sum_{i \in S} b_i\right| < \frac{n}{4}$ holds.
Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers. Show that there exist integers $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ with $|a_i - b_i| < 1$ such that the total sum $\sum a_i - \sum b_i$ is less than $(n + 1)/4$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers. Show that there exist integers $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ with $|a_i - b_i| < 2$ such that for every subset $S \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, the inequality $\left|\sum_{i \in S} a_i - \sum_{i \in S} b_i\right| < \frac{n + 1}{4}$ holds.

positive_text: A creature crawls over the surface of a spherical world at a maximum speed of $u$. A drone flies over the surface at a speed of $v$. Show that the drone can always locate the creature if $v > 10u$.

negatives.text: An alien moves on the surface of a planet with speed not exceeding $u$. A spaceship searches for the alien with speed $v$. Prove the spaceship can always find the alien if $v > 5u$.

An alien moves on the surface of a planet with speed not exceeding $u$. A spaceship searches for the alien with speed $v$. Prove the spaceship can always find the alien if $v > 10u$ and the planet is flat.

An alien moves on the surface of a planet with speed not exceeding $u$. A spaceship searches for the alien with speed $v$. Prove the spaceship can always find the alien if $v > 10u$ and the alien is stationary.

positive_text:
a. Points $M$ and $N$ lie on segment $XY$ with $XM = NY$. Prove that for any point $Q$ in the plane: $QX + QY \geq QM + QN$.

b. Suppose four points $X$, $M$, $N$, $Y$ satisfy the condition that for all points $Q$ in the plane, $QX + QY \geq QM + QN$. Prove that $M$ and $N$ lie on segment $XY$ with $XM = NY$.

negatives.text:
a. $B$ and $C$ are on the segment $AD$ with $AB = 2CD$. Prove that for any point $P$ in the plane: $PA + PD \geq PB + PC$.

b. Given four points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ on the plane such that for any point $P$ on the plane we have $PA + PD \geq PB + PC$. Prove that $B$ and $C$ are on the segment $AD$ with $AB = 2CD$.

a. $B$ and $C$ are on the segment $AD$ with $AB = CD$, but $AD = 10$. Prove that for any point $P$ on the segment $AD$: $PA + PD \geq PB + PC$.

b. Given four points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ on the plane such that for any point $P$ on the segment $AD$ we have $PA + PD \geq PB + PC$. Prove that $B$ and $C$ are on the segment $AD$ with $AB = CD$.

a. $B$ and $C$ are on the segment $AD$ with $AB = CD$. Prove that for any point $P$ in the plane: $PA + PD \leq PB + PC$.

b. Given four points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ on the plane such that for any point $P$ on the plane we have $PA + PD \leq PB + PC$. Prove that $B$ and $C$ are on the segment $AD$ with $AB = CD$.

positive_text: Let $G$ be a graph with at least three vertices such that for every triple of distinct vertices $X$, $Y$, $Z$, there exists a path from $X$ to $Y$ that does not include $Z$. Prove that for any two distinct vertices $X$ and $Y$, there exist two vertex-disjoint paths from $X$ to $Y$.

negatives.text: Let $G$ be a graph with at least three vertices such that for every triple of vertices $A$, $B$, $C$, there exists a path from $A$ to $B$ that does not include $C$. Prove that for any two distinct vertices $A$ and $B$, there exist two edge-disjoint paths from $A$ to $B$.

Let $G$ be a graph with at least three vertices such that for every pair of vertices $A$, $B$, there exists a path from $A$ to $B$ that does not include a third vertex $C$, for some vertex $C$. Prove that for any two distinct vertices $A$ and $B$, there exist two vertex-disjoint paths from $A$ to $B$.

positive_text: Determine all integer values of $a$, $b$ such that $a(a + 1) = b(b^3 + b^2 + b + 1)$.

negatives.text: Find all integers $x$, $y$ satisfying $x^{2} - x = y^{4} + y^{3} + y^{2} + y$.
Find all integers $x$, $y$ satisfying $x^{2} + x = y^{4} + y^{3} + y^{2} + y + 1$.
Find all integers $x$, $y$ satisfying $x^{2} + x = y^{4} + y^{3} + y^{2} + y$ for $y > 0$.

positive_text: Show that there are infinitely many primes $p$ for which there exist positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $a^2 + a + 1 = p b$.

negatives.text: Prove that we can find positive integers $x$, $y$ satisfying $x^{2} - x + 1 = p y$ for an infinite number of primes $p$.
Prove that we can find positive integers $x$, $y$ satisfying $x^{3} + x + 1 = p y$ for an infinite number of primes $p$.
Prove that we can find positive integers $x$, $y$ satisfying $x^{2} + x + 1 = p y$ for an infinite number of composite numbers $p$.

positive_text: Let $\{x_i\}$ and $\{y_i\}$ be rearrangements of $\{1, 1/2, \dots, 1/n\}$. Suppose $x_1 + y_1 \geq x_2 + y_2 \geq \ldots \geq x_n + y_n$. Prove that for each $k$ from $1$ to $n$, $x_k + y_k \geq \dfrac{4}{k}$.

negatives.text: Let $\{a_i\}$ and $\{b_i\}$ be permutations of $\{1, 1/2, \dots, 1/n\}$. Suppose $a_1 + b_1 > a_2 + b_2 > \ldots > a_n + b_n$. Prove that for all $m$ with $1 \leq m \leq n$, $a_m + b_m \geq \dfrac{3}{m}$.

positive_text: Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence defined by $x_1 = 1$ and $x_{n+1} = x_n + \frac{1}{x_n}$ for all $n \geq 1$. Show that $x_{100} > 14$.

negatives.text: Let $\{b_n\}$ be a sequence defined by $b_1 = 1$ and $b_{n+1} = b_n + \frac{1}{b_n^2}$ for all $n \geq 1$. Prove that $b_{100} > 14$.
Let $\{c_n\}$ be a sequence defined by $c_1 = 1$ and $c_{n+1} = c_n - \frac{1}{c_n}$ for all $n \geq 1$. Prove that $c_{100} < 14$.
Let $\{d_n\}$ be a sequence defined by $d_1 = 1$ and $d_{n+1} = d_n + \frac{1}{d_n}$ for $n \geq 1$. Prove that $d_{100} < 14$.

positive_text: Consider the cubic equation $x^{3} + p x^{2} + q x + r = 0$, where $p$, $q$, and $r$ are integers to be chosen in turn: first, one of them is chosen by Player A; then, one of the remaining by Player B; and finally, the last by Player A. Player A wants the equation to have three integer roots (possibly repeated), while Player B wants to prevent this. Who has a winning strategy?

negatives.text: Given the equation $x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x + c = 0$, players alternate choosing values for the coefficients $a$, $b$, and $c$ in any order they choose, all being integers. The first player wants the equation to have three real roots, while the second wants to prevent this. Who wins?

Consider the equation $x^{3} + a x^{2} + b x + c = 0$. The first player picks one coefficient to set to zero, the second player picks a different coefficient to set to zero, and the first player picks the last coefficient to be an integer. The first player wants the equation to have three integer roots, while the second wants to prevent this. Who wins?

Given the quadratic equation $x^{2} + a x + b = 0$, the first player chooses a value for $a$, then the second player chooses a value for $b$. The first player wants the equation to have two integer roots, while the second wants to prevent this. Who wins?

positive_text: Let a regular polygon with $ n $ sides be inscribed in a circle of radius $ R $. Define $ d_n $ as the perpendicular distance from the circle's center to the midpoint of a side. Show that $ (n + 1) d_{n + 1} - n d_n > R $.

negatives.text: A regular $ n $-gon is inscribed in a circle of radius $ R $. The distance from the center of the circle to a vertex is $ h_n $. Prove that $ (n + 1) h_{n + 1} - n h_n > R $.
A regular $ n $-gon is inscribed in a circle of radius $ R $. The distance from the center of the circle to the center of a side is $ h_n $. Prove that $ (n - 1) h_{n - 1} - n h_n > R $.
A regular $ n $-gon is inscribed in a circle of radius $ R $. The distance from the center of the circle to the center of a side is $ h_n $. Prove that $ (n + 1) h_{n + 1} - n h_n = R $.

positive_text: Consider a binary string $S$ such that all consecutive 5-length substrings are distinct. Furthermore, adding a 0 or 1 to either the beginning or the end of $S$ causes a repeat of a 5-length substring. Prove that the first 4 characters of $S$ match the last 4 characters.

negatives.text: Let $S$ be a finite sequence of 0s and 1s such that for any $i < j$, the sequences of length 5 beginning at position $i$ and position $j$ are different. Furthermore, if you replace a digit in $S$ with the opposite digit (0 to 1 or 1 to 0), the uniqueness of 5-length substrings is lost. Prove that the first 4 digits of the sequence are the same as the last 4 digits.

positive_text: Let $x, y, z, w$ be positive real numbers. Prove that it is impossible for all of the following to be true simultaneously: $x + y < z + w$; $(x + y)(z + w) < xy + zw$; $(x + y)zw < xy(z + w)$.

negatives.text: Let $a, b, c, d$ be positive real numbers. Prove that at least one of the following inequalities does not hold: $a + b < c + d$; $(a + b)(c + d) < ab + cd$; $a + b)cd < cd(a + b)$.
Let $a, b, c, d$ be positive real numbers. Prove that at least one of the following inequalities does not hold: $a + b < c + d$; $(a + b)(c + d) < ab + cd$; $(a + b)(c + d) < ab(c + d)$.
Let $a, b, c$ be positive real numbers. Prove that at least one of the following inequalities does not hold: $a + b < c$; $(a + b)c < ab + c$; $(a + b)c < ab(c)$.

positive_text: \text{Let } m \text{ be a positive integer. Show that } \sum \frac{1}{ab} = \frac{1}{2}, \text{ where the sum is over all pairs } (a,b) \text{ with } 0 < a < b \leq m, \gcd(a,b) = 1, \text{ and } a + b > m.

negatives.text: \text{Let } k \text{ be a positive integer. Show that } \sum \frac{1}{ab} = \frac{1}{2}, \text{ where the sum is over all pairs } (a,b) \text{ with } 0 < a < b \leq k, \gcd(a,b) = 1, \text{ and } a + b < k.

\text{Let } p \text{ be a positive integer. Show that } \sum \frac{1}{ab} = \frac{1}{2}, \text{ where the sum is over all pairs } (a,b) \text{ with } 0 < a < b \leq p, \gcd(a,b) = 1, \text{ and } a + b = p + 1.

positive_text: In triangle $ PQR $, let $ J $ be the incenter, and let $ N $ be the midpoint of side $ QR $. The segment $ JN $ intersects the height from $ P $ to $ QR $ at point $ F $. Prove that $ PF = r $, where $ r $ is the inradius of triangle $ PQR $.

negatives.text: In triangle $ ABC $, let $ I $ be the incenter, and let $ M $ be the midpoint of side $ BC $. The segment $ IM $ intersects the median from $ A $ to $ BC $ at point $ E $. Prove that $ AE = r $, where $ r $ is the inradius of triangle $ ABC $.

In triangle $ ABC $, let $ I $ be the incenter, and let $ M $ be the midpoint of side $ BC $. The segment $ IM $ intersects the perpendicular bisector of $ BC $ at point $ E $. Prove that $ AE = r $, where $ r $ is the inradius of triangle $ ABC $.

In triangle $ ABC $, let $ I $ be the incenter, and let $ M $ be the midpoint of side $ BC $. The segment $ IM $ intersects the angle bisector from $ A $ to $ BC $ at point $ E $. Prove that $ AE = r $, where $ r $ is the inradius of triangle $ ABC $.

positive_text: Let $ X $ and $ Y $ be adjacent nodes in a circular graph of 12 nodes. Initially, node $ X $ is labeled $ - $, and all other nodes are labeled $ + $. In one move, you can flip the signs of $ n $ consecutive nodes. Show that you cannot achieve a configuration where $ Y $ is labeled $ - $ and all other nodes are labeled $ + $ if all moves use $ n = 6 $. Show that the same is true if all moves use $ n = 3 $ or if all moves use $ n = 4 $.

negatives.text: Let $ A $ and $ B $ be adjacent vertices of a regular $ 12 $-gon. Initially, vertex $ A $ is marked $ - $, and all other vertices are marked $ + $. In each move, you can flip the signs of $ n $ adjacent vertices. Show that you cannot achieve a configuration where $ B $ is marked $ - $ and all other vertices are marked $ + $ if all moves use $ n = 5 $.

Let $ A $ and $ B $ be adjacent vertices of a regular $ 12 $-gon. Initially, vertex $ A $ is marked $ - $, and all other vertices are marked $ + $. In each move, you can flip the signs of $ n $ adjacent vertices. Show that you cannot achieve a configuration where $ B $ is marked $ - $ and all other vertices are marked $ + $ if all moves use $ n = 6 $, but you can flip the signs of any $ n $ adjacent vertices, not just consecutive ones.

positive_text: You are given three positive integers $a, b, c$. At each step, if two of the numbers satisfy $x \leq y$, you can replace them with $2x$ and $y - x$. Prove that it is always possible to reach a state where one of the numbers is zero.

Let $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ be real numbers such that $$(s - q)^2 < (r - p)(sp - rq).$$ Prove that the equations $x^2 + px + q = 0$ and $x^2 + rx + s = 0$ have real roots and that the roots of each are interlaced with those of the other.

negatives.text: Let $a$, $b$, $A$, $B$ be real numbers such that $$(B - b)^2 > (A - a)(Ba - Ab).$$ Prove that the quadratics $x^2 + ax + b = 0$ and $x^2 + Ax + B = 0$ have real roots and between the roots of each there is a root of the other.
Let $a$, $b$, $A$, $B$ be real numbers such that $$(B - b)^2 < (A - a)(Ba - Ab).$$ Prove that the quadratics $x^2 + ax + b = 0$ and $x^2 + Ax + B = 0$ have no real roots.

positive_text: A number is assigned to each corner of a regular $n$-gon. A move consists of identifying four consecutive corners labeled $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ (in order), such that $(p - s)(q - r) < 0$, and swapping $q$ and $r$. Prove that the number of such moves is finite.

negatives.text: A number is placed at each vertex of a regular $n$-gon. A move is to find four consecutive vertices $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ such that $(a - d)(b - c) > 0$, and then swap $b$ and $c$. Show that only finitely many moves are possible.

A number is placed at each vertex of a regular $n$-gon. A move is to find four consecutive vertices $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ such that $(a - d)(b - c) = 0$, and then swap $b$ and $c$. Show that only finitely many moves are possible.

A number is placed at each vertex of a regular $n$-gon. A move is to find four consecutive vertices $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ such that $(a - d)(b - c) < 0$, and then swap $a$ and $d$. Show that only finitely many moves are possible.

positive_text: Let $ c $, $ p $, and $ q $ be positive integers with $ c > 1 $. Show that if $ c^p + 1 $ divides $ c^q + 1 $, then $ p $ divides $ q $. Furthermore, suppose that the positive integer $ d $ is relatively prime to $ c $. Show that if $ c^p + d^p $ divides $ c^q + d^q $, then $ p $ divides $ q $.

negatives.text: Let $ a $, $ m $, and $ n $ be positive integers with $ a > 1 $. Show that if $ a^m - 1 $ divides $ a^n - 1 $, then $ m $ divides $ n $.
Let $ a $, $ m $, and $ n $ be positive integers with $ a > 1 $. Show that if $ a^m + 1 $ divides $ a^n - 1 $, then $ m $ divides $ n $.
Let $ a $, $ m $, and $ n $ be positive integers with $ a > 1 $. Suppose that $ a^m + m $ divides $ a^n + n $. Show that $ m $ divides $ n $.

positive_text: In triangle $\triangle XYZ$, with sides $x \geq y \geq z$ and area $1$, prove that $y^2 \geq 2$

negatives.text: A triangle has area $1$, and sides $a \geq b \geq c$. Prove that $a^2 \geq 2$
A triangle has area $1$, and sides $a \geq b \geq c$. Prove that $b^2 > 2$

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z, w, v \text{ be positive real numbers. Show that } (x + y + z + w + v)^2 \geq 4(xy + yz + zw + wv + vx)

negatives.text: \text{Let } a, b, c, d, e \text{ be positive real numbers. Show that } (a + b + c + d + e)^2 \geq 4(ac + bd + ce + da + eb)
\text{Let } a, b, c, d, e \text{ be positive real numbers. Show that } (a + b + c + d + e)^2 \geq 5(ab + bc + cd + de + ea)
\text{Let } a, b, c, d, e \text{ be positive real numbers. Show that } (a + b + c + d + e)^2 \geq 4(ab + bc + cd + de + ca)

positive_text: Let $G$ be a complete graph with $n > 4$ vertices. Prove that there exists an orientation of the edges such that for any pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, there is a directed path of length at most 2 from $u$ to $v$.

negatives.text: Given $n > 4$ points, show that you can place an arrow between each pair of points, so that given any point you can reach any other point by travelling along either one or two arrows, in any direction.

Given $n > 4$ points, show that you can place an arrow between each pair of points, so that given any point you can reach any other point by travelling along at least three arrows in the direction of the arrow.

Given $n > 4$ points, show that you can place an arrow between each pair of points, so that given any point you can reach any other point by travelling along either one or two arrows, but each arrow can be traversed only once.

positive_text: \text{Suppose } f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \text{ satisfies } |f(x)| \leq 1 \text{ for all } x \in [-1, 1]. \text{ Prove that } |cx^2 + bx + a| \leq 2 \text{ for all } x \in [-1, 1].

negatives.text: \text{Let } p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \text{ with } |p(x)| \leq 1 \text{ for all } |x| \leq 1. \text{ Prove that } |cx^2 - bx + a| \leq 2 \text{ for all } |x| \leq 1.
\text{Let } p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \text{ with } |p(x)| \leq 1 \text{ for all } |x| \leq 1. \text{ Prove that } |cx^2 + bx + a| \leq 2 \text{ for all } |x| \leq 2.
\text{Let } p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \text{ with } |p(x)| \leq 1 \text{ for all } |x| \leq 1. \text{ Prove that } |cx^3 + bx^2 + a| \leq 2 \text{ for all } |x| \leq 1.

positive_text: In a single-elimination tournament with 1024 participants labeled $1$ to $1024$, each round halves the number of players until a winner is determined. If player $m$ faces player $n$ and $m < n - 2$, then $m$ always defeats $n$. What is the maximum possible label of the tournament winner?

negatives.text: In a single-elimination tournament with 1024 players labeled $1$ to $1024$, if $m$ plays $n$ and $m < n - 1$, then $m$ always wins. What is the largest possible number for the winner?
In a single-elimination tournament with 1024 players labeled $1$ to $1024$, if $m$ plays $n$ and $m > n - 2$, then $m$ always wins. What is the largest possible number for the winner?
In a single-elimination tournament with 1024 players labeled $1$ to $1024$, if $m$ plays $n$ and $m < n$, then $m$ always wins. What is the largest possible number for the winner?

positive_text: Let $f(x) = m x^2 + n x + k$. Suppose the equation $f(x) = x$ has no real solutions. Show that the equation $f(f(x)) = 0$ also has no real solutions.

negatives.text: Let $p(x) = a x^2 + b x + c$. If $p(x) = -x$ has no real roots, prove that $p(p(x)) = 0$ has no real roots.
Define $p(x) = a x^2 + b x + c$. Suppose $p(x) = x$ has exactly one real root. Prove that $p(p(x)) = 0$ has no real roots.
Let $p(x) = a x^2 + b x + c$. If $p(x) = x$ has no real roots, prove that $p(p(x)) = x$ has no real roots.

positive_text: In triangle $PQR$, $\angle R = 90^\circ$ and $PR = QR$. Let $S$ lie on $RP$ and $T$ on $RQ$ with $RS = RT$. Drop perpendiculars from $S$ and $R$ to $QT$; let these perpendiculars intersect $PQ$ at $M$ and $N$ respectively. Prove that $MN = NQ$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, $\angle C = 90^\circ$ and $AC = BC$. Take points $D$ on $CA$ and $E$ on $CB$ such that $CD = CE$. Let the perpendiculars from $D$ and $C$ to $BE$ meet $AB$ at $K$ and $L$ respectively. Show that $KL = LB$.

In triangle $ABC$, $\angle C = 90^\circ$ and $AC = 2BC$. Take points $D$ on $CA$ and $E$ on $CB$ such that $CD = CE$. Let the perpendiculars from $D$ and $C$ to $AE$ meet $AB$ at $K$ and $L$ respectively. Show that $KL = LB$.

In triangle $ABC$, $\angle C = 90^\circ$ and $AC = BC$. Take points $D$ on $CA$ and $E$ on $CB$ such that $CD = 2CE$. Let the perpendiculars from $D$ and $C$ to $AE$ meet $AB$ at $K$ and $L$ respectively. Show that $KL = LB$.

positive_text: Suppose $ g $ is a function from $[0, 1]$ to the non-negative reals with $ g(1) = 1 $, and for any $ x, y $ in $[0, 1]$ with $ x + y \leq 1 $, we have $ g(x + y) \geq g(x) + g(y) $. Prove that $ g(x) \leq 2x $ for all $ x $. Does it follow that $ g(x) \leq 1.9x $ for all $ x $?
Determine all real values of $p$, $q$, $r$ for which $p x + q y + r z + q x + r y + p z + r x + p y + q z = x + y + z$ holds for every real $x$, $y$, $z$.

negatives.text: Find all real $a$, $b$, $c$ such that $a x^2 + b y^2 + c z^2 + b x^2 + c y^2 + a z^2 + c x^2 + a y^2 + b z^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ for all real $x$, $y$, $z$.
Find all real $a$, $b$, $c$ such that $a x + b y + c z + b x + c y + a z + c x + a y + b z = x^2 + y + z$ for all real $x$, $y$, $z$.
Find all real $a$, $b$, $c$ such that $a x + b y + c z + b x + c y + a z + c x + a y + b z = x + y^2 + z$ for all real $x$, $y$, $z$.

positive_text: \text{Let square } WXYZ \text{ have side length } s. \text{ Point R lies on WX and point S lies on XY such that } XR = XS. \text{ Point T is on RZ such that } \angle XTY = 90^\circ. \text{ Prove that } \angle ZTS = 90^\circ.

negatives.text: \text{ABCD is a square. P is on AB and Q is on BC such that } BP = 2BQ. \text{ H lies on PC such that } \angle BHC = 90^\circ. \text{ Show that } \angle DHQ = 90^\circ.
\text{ABCD is a square. P is on AB and Q is on CD such that } BP = BQ. \text{ H lies on PC such that } \angle BHC = 90^\circ. \text{ Show that } \angle DHQ = 90^\circ.
\text{ABCD is a square. P is on AB and Q is on BC such that } BP = BQ. \text{ H lies on PD such that } \angle BHC = 90^\circ. \text{ Show that } \angle DHQ = 90^\circ.

positive_text: \text{Let } x_i, y_j \text{ be real numbers and } p_i, q_j > 0. \text{ Define } f_{ij} = \frac{x_i + y_j}{p_i + q_j}. \text{ Let } F_i = \max_{0 \leq j \leq n} f_{ij}, \text{ and } G_j = \min_{1 \leq i \leq n} f_{ij}. \text{ Prove that there exists some } f_{ij} \text{ with } 1 \leq i, j \leq n \text{ such that } f_{ij} = F_i = G_j.

negatives.text: \text{Let } a_i, b_j, c_i, d_j \in \mathbb{R}, \text{ with } c_i + d_j > 0. \text{ Define } e_{ij} = \frac{a_i + b_j}{c_i + d_j}. \text{ Let } M_i = \max_{1 \leq j \leq n} e_{ij}, \text{ and } m_j = \max_{1 \leq i \leq n} e_{ij}. \text{ Prove that there exists some } e_{ij} \text{ with } 1 \leq i, j \leq n \text{ such that } e_{ij} = M_i = m_j.

\text{Let } a_i, b_j, c_i, d_j > 0, \text{ and define } e_{ij} = \frac{a_i + b_j}{c_i + d_j}. \text{ Let } M_i = \max_{0 \leq j \leq n} e_{ij}, \text{ and } m_j = \min_{1 \leq i \leq n} e_{ij}. \text{ Prove that there exists some } e_{ij} \text{ with } 1 \leq i, j \leq n \text{ such that } e_{ij} = M_i \cdot m_j.

\text{Let } a_i, b_j, c_i, d_j > 0, \text{ and define } e_{ij} = \frac{a_i + b_j}{c_i + d_j}. \text{ Let } M_i = \max_{0 \leq j \leq n} e_{ij}, \text{ and } m_j = \min_{1 \leq i \leq n} e_{ij}. \text{ Prove that there exists some } e_{ij} \text{ with } 1 \leq i, j \leq n \text{ such that } e_{ij} = M_i + m_j.

positive_text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers placed in a circle such that their sum is zero and one of them equals $1$. Prove that:

1. Two adjacent numbers differ by at least $\frac{n}{4}$.
2. There is an index $i$ such that $\left|a_i - \frac{a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}}{2}\right| \geq \frac{8}{n^2}$.
3. Improve the constant $8$ to some $k > 8$.
4. For $n = 30$, show $k = \frac{1800}{113}$ is valid.
5. Provide an example of $30$ such numbers where the deviation from the mean of neighbors is at most $\frac{2}{113}$.

negatives.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ be real numbers arranged in a circle with sum $0$, and suppose one of them is $1$. Prove that:

1. Two adjacent numbers differ by at least $\frac{n}{2}$.
2. There is an index $i$ such that $\left|a_i - \frac{a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}}{2}\right| \geq \frac{4}{n^2}$.
3. Improve the constant $4$ to some $k > 4$.
4. For $n = 30$, show $k = \frac{900}{113}$ is valid.
5. Construct an example of $30$ such numbers where the deviation from the mean of neighbors is at most $\frac{1}{113}$.

positive_text: Suppose we have a regular $n$-gon, with each vertex assigned a value of $+1$ or $-1$. You are allowed to flip the signs of all vertices that lie on a regular $k$-gon, where $1 < k \leq n$. For instance, in a regular $6$-gon, flipping $\{1, 4\}$, $\{2, 5\}$, $\{3, 6\}$, $\{1, 3, 5\}$, $\{2, 4, 6\}$, or the full set $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ are all valid moves. Prove that for $n = 15$, $n = 30$, and for any $n > 2$, there exists at least one configuration of signs that cannot be transformed to all $+1$ using these moves. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum number of configurations such that no configuration can be obtained from another via any sequence of moves. Compute $f(200)$ and show it equals $2^{80}$.

negatives.text: Suppose we have a regular $n$-gon, with each vertex assigned a value of $+1$ or $-1$. You are allowed to flip the signs of all vertices that lie on a regular $k$-gon, where $1 < k < n$. For instance, in a regular $6$-gon, flipping $\{1, 4\}$, $\{2, 5\}$, $\{3, 6\}$, $\{1, 3, 5\}$, $\{2, 4, 6\}$ are valid moves, but you cannot flip the full set $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$. Prove that for $n = 15$, $n = 30$, and for any $n > 2$, there exists at least one configuration of signs that cannot be transformed to all $+1$ using these moves. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum number of configurations such that no configuration can be obtained from another via any sequence of moves. Compute $f(200)$.

Suppose we have a regular $n$-gon, with each vertex assigned a value of $+1$ or $-1$. You are allowed to flip the signs of all vertices that lie on a regular $k$-gon, where $1 < k \leq n$. For instance, in a regular $6$-gon, flipping $\{1, 4\}$, $\{2, 5\}$, $\{3, 6\}$, $\{1, 3, 5\}$, $\{2, 4, 6\}$ or $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ are all valid moves. Prove that for $n = 15$, $n = 30$, and for any $n > 2$, there exists at least one configuration of signs that cannot be transformed to all $+1$ using these moves. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum number of configurations such that no configuration can be obtained from another via any sequence of moves. Compute $f(200)$ and show it equals $2^{80}$, assuming that all moves commute.

positive_text: Three cyclists travel along straight, distinct paths at constant velocities. At $t = 0$, their positions do not lie on a straight line. Show that there are at most two positive times $t$ for which their positions are collinear.

negatives.text: Three people are walking along straight roads at constant speed. At time $t = 0$, they are not collinear. Prove that they will be collinear for $t > 0$ at most once.
Three men are walking along straight roads at constant speed. At time $t = 0$, they are not collinear. Prove that they will be collinear for $t > 0$ at most three times.
Three men are walking along straight roads at constant speed. At time $t = 0$, they are not collinear. Prove that they will be collinear for $t > 0$ at most twice, assuming one man is stationary.

positive_text: Let $m > 3$ be an integer. Let $T$ be the set of integer grid points $(x, y)$ with $0 \leq x, y < m$. Prove that it is possible to select $m$ points from $T$ such that no three are on the same straight line and no four form the vertices of a parallelogram.

negatives.text: Let $n > 3$ be an integer. Let $S$ be the set of lattice points $(a, b)$ with $0 < a, b < n$. Show that we can choose $n$ points of $S$ so that no three chosen points are collinear and no four chosen points form a parallelogram.

Let $n > 3$ be an integer. Let $S$ be the set of lattice points $(a, b)$ with $0 \leq a, b < n$. Show that we can choose $n$ points of $S$ so that no three chosen points are collinear and no four chosen points form a square.

Let $n > 3$ be an integer. Let $S$ be the set of lattice points $(a, b)$ with $0 \leq a, b < n$. Show that we can choose $n$ points of $S$ so that no four chosen points are collinear and no three chosen points form a parallelogram.

positive_text: Define $y_n = (\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2} + 1)^n$. Suppose $y_n = p_n + q_n \sqrt{2} + r_n \sqrt{3} + s_n \sqrt{6}$, with $p_n, q_n, r_n, s_n$ integers. Determine $\lim_{n \to \infty} q_n / p_n$, $\lim_{n \to \infty} r_n / p_n$, and $\lim_{n \to \infty} s_n / p_n$.

negatives.text: Let $w_n = (1 + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{6})^n$. Write $w_n = a_n + b_n \sqrt{2} + c_n \sqrt{6} + d_n \sqrt{12}$, where $a_n, b_n, c_n, d_n$ are integers. Compute $\lim_{n \to \infty} b_n / a_n$, $\lim_{n \to \infty} c_n / a_n$, and $\lim_{n \to \infty} d_n / a_n$.

Let $u_n = (1 + \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3})^n$. Express $u_n = a_n + b_n \sqrt{2} + c_n \sqrt{3} + d_n \sqrt{6}$, where $a_n, b_n, c_n, d_n$ are integers. Determine $\lim_{n \to \infty} b_n / a_n$, $\lim_{n \to \infty} c_n / a_n$, and $\lim_{n \to \infty} d_n / a_n$.

positive_text: Two players take turns removing tokens from two piles. Let the sizes of the piles be $a$ and $b$, with $a > b$. On a turn, a player removes any positive multiple of $b$ from pile $a$. The first player to reduce one of the piles to zero wins. Prove that if $a > 2b$, the first player can always win. Determine all values of $k$ such that if $a > k b$, the first player has a guaranteed win.

negatives.text: Two players play a game with two piles of tokens. On each turn, a player may remove a number of tokens from the larger pile that is a multiple of the smaller pile. The player who removes the last token wins. Show that if $m > 2n$, the first player can always win.

Two players take turns removing tokens from two piles of sizes $m$ and $n$, where $m > n$. On a turn, a player removes a number of tokens from the larger pile equal to a multiple of the smaller pile. The player who cannot make a move loses. Prove that if $m > 2n$, the first player has a winning strategy.

Two players play a game with two piles of tokens of size $m$ and $n$, where $m > n$. On each turn, a player may remove a number of tokens from the larger pile equal to any multiple of the number in the smaller pile. The game ends when one pile is empty. If $m > 2n$, show that the second player can always win.

positive_text: Prove that there exists an infinite sequence of real numbers $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $\ldots$ such that all $|a_k| < 100$ and for all integers $i > j$, $|a_i - a_j| > \frac{1}{i - j}$.

negatives.text: Prove that there exists an infinite sequence $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$, $\ldots$ of real numbers with $|x_n| < 1$ and for all $m > n$, $|x_m - x_n| < \frac{1}{m - n}$.
Show that there is an infinite sequence $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$, $\ldots$ such that $|x_n| < 1$ and for any $m > n$, $|x_m - x_n| > \frac{1}{m^2 - n^2}$.
Prove that there exists an infinite sequence $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$, $\ldots$ of real numbers such that $|x_n| < 1$ and for any $m > n$, $|x_m - x_n| > \frac{1}{\log(m - n)}$.

positive_text: Define the function $f(x) = x^2 + x + 1$. Prove that for all positive integers $k$, the sequence $a_1 = k$, $a_{n+1} = f(a_n)$ consists of pairwise relatively prime terms.

negatives.text: Let $q(x) = x^2 - x + 1$. Show that for every positive integer $n$, the numbers $n$, $q(n)$, $q(q(n))$, $q(q(q(n)))$, ... are relatively prime.
Let $r(x) = x^2 + x + 2$. Show that for every positive integer $n$, the numbers $n$, $r(n)$, $r(r(n))$, $r(r(r(n)))$, ... are relatively prime.
Let $s(x) = x^2 + x + 1$. Show that for every positive integer $n$, the numbers $n$, $s(n)$, $s(n) + 1$, $s(n) + 2$, ... are relatively prime.

positive_text: Prove that there exists a constant $ c $ such that the graph of $ y = c \sin x $ contains $ 1978 $ squares of distinct side lengths with all four vertices lying on the graph.

Let $T_0 = \{(7, 23)\}$. At each step, we may perform the following operations: if $(2a, 2b) \in T_n$, then we may add $(a, b)$; if $(a, b) \in T_n$, we may add $(a+1, b+1)$; if $(a, b), (b, c) \in T_n$, we may add $(a, c)$. Is it possible to get $(1, 50)$ and $(1, 100)$ in the set? If the initial pair is $(a, b)$ with $a < b$, for which values of $n$ can $(1, n)$ be generated?

negatives.text: Let $T_0 = \{(5, 19)\}$. At each step, we may perform the following operations: if $(a, 2b) \in T_n$, then we may add $(a, b)$; if $(a, b) \in T_n$, we may add $(a+1, b+1)$; if $(a, b), (b, c) \in T_n$, we may add $(a, c)$. Is it possible to get $(1, 50)$ and $(1, 100)$ in the set? If the initial pair is $(a, b)$ with $a < b$, for which values of $n$ can $(1, n)$ be generated?

Let $T_0 = \{(5, 19)\}$. At each step, we may perform the following operations: if $(2a, 2b) \in T_n$, then we may add $(a, b)$; if $(a, b) \in T_n$, we may add $(a+1, b+1)$; if $(a, b), (a, c) \in T_n$, we may add $(a, c)$. Is it possible to get $(1, 50)$ and $(1, 100)$ in the set? If the initial pair is $(a, b)$ with $a < b$, for which values of $n$ can $(1, n)$ be generated?

positive_text:
Find a sequence $b_{1}$, $b_{2}$, ..., $b_{25}$ of 0s and 1s such that all the following sums are odd:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}
 & b_{1}^{2} + b_{2}^{2} + \ldots + b_{25}^{2} \\
 & b_{1}b_{2} + b_{2}b_{3} + \ldots + b_{24}b_{25} \\
 & b_{1}b_{3} + b_{2}b_{4} + \ldots + b_{23}b_{25} \\
 & \ldots \\
 & b_{1}b_{24} + b_{2}b_{25}
\end{array}
$$
Show that such a sequence can be extended to one of length $n > 1000$.

negatives.text:
Find a sequence $c_{1}$, $c_{2}$, ..., $c_{25}$ of 0s and 1s such that the following sums are all even:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}
 & c_{1}c_{1} + c_{2}c_{2} + \ldots + c_{25}c_{25} \\
 & c_{1}c_{2} + c_{2}c_{3} + \ldots + c_{24}c_{25} \\
 & c_{1}c_{3} + c_{2}c_{4} + \ldots + c_{23}c_{25} \\
 & \ldots \\
 & c_{1}c_{24} + c_{2}c_{25}
\end{array}
$$
Show that such a sequence exists.

positive_text:
\text{Let } p \text{ and } q \text{ be real numbers. Find real } m \text{ and } n \text{ satisfying:}\\
(m - n)(m^2 - n^2)^{1/2} = p(1 - m^2 + n^2)^{1/2}\\
(n - m)(m^2 - n^2)^{1/2} = q(1 - m^2 + n^2)^{1/2}.

negatives.text:
\text{Let } a \text{ and } b \text{ be real numbers. Find real } x \text{ and } y \text{ satisfying:}\\
(x - y)(x^2 - y^2)^{1/2} = a(1 + x^2 - y^2)^{1/2}\\
(y - x)(x^2 - y^2)^{1/2} = b(1 + x^2 - y^2)^{1/2}.

\text{Let } a \text{ and } b \text{ be real numbers. Find real } x \text{ and } y \text{ satisfying:}\\
(x - y)(x^2 - y^2) = a(1 - x^2 + y^2)^{1/2}\\
(y - x)(x^2 - y^2) = b(1 - x^2 + y^2)^{1/2}.

\text{Let } a \text{ and } b \text{ be real numbers. Find real } x \text{ and } y \text{ satisfying:}\\
(x + y)(x^2 - y^2)^{1/2} = a(1 - x^2 + y^2)^{1/2}\\
(y + x)(x^2 - y^2)^{1/2} = b(1 - x^2 + y^2)^{1/2}.

positive_text: Define $g(k)$ as $k$ plus the sum of its digits. Does there exist an integer $k$ such that $g(k) = 1980$? Prove that for any positive integer $m$, there exists some integer $k$ such that $g(k) = m$ or $g(k) = m + 1$.

negatives.text: Define $h(k)$ as $k$ times the sum of its digits. Does there exist an integer $k$ such that $h(k) = 1980$? Prove that for any positive integer $m$, there exists some integer $k$ such that $h(k) = m$ or $h(k) = m + 1$.

Define $j(k)$ as $k$ minus the sum of its digits. Does there exist an integer $k$ such that $j(k) = 1980$? Prove that for any positive integer $m$, there exists some integer $k$ such that $j(k) = m$ or $j(k) = m + 1$.

Define $k(n)$ as the sum of $n$ and the product of its digits. Does there exist an integer $n$ such that $k(n) = 1980$? Prove that for any positive integer $m$, there exists some integer $n$ such that $k(n) = m$ or $k(n) = m + 1$.

positive_text: Let $\{b_n\}$ be a sequence of positive integers defined by $b_1 = k$ and $b_{n + 1} = b_n + $ the product of all digits in the base-10 representation of $b_n$. For instance, if $k = 5$, the sequence is $5, 10, 10, \ldots$. Does there exist a starting value $k$ such that the sequence $\{b_n\}$ is unbounded?

negatives.text: Define the sequence $\{c_n\}$ of positive integers by $c_1 = p$ and $c_{n + 1} = c_n + $ the sum of the digits of $c_n$. For example, if $p = 5$, the sequence is $5, 10, 11, 13, \ldots$. Is there a value of $p$ for which the sequence is unbounded?

Let $\{d_n\}$ be a sequence of positive integers defined by $d_1 = q$ and $d_{n + 1} = d_n + $ the product of the digits of $d_n$ if $d_n$ is odd, and $d_{n + 1} = d_n$ otherwise. For example, if $q = 5$, the sequence is $5, 10, 10, \ldots$. Is there an $q$ such that the sequence $\{d_n\}$ is unbounded?

Define the sequence $\{e_n\}$ of positive integers with $e_1 = r$ and $e_{n + 1} = e_n + $ the product of the digits of $e_n$ only if the product is positive; otherwise, $e_{n + 1} = e_n$. For example, if $r = 5$, the sequence is $5, 10, 10, \ldots$. Is there an $r$ such that $\{e_n\}$ is unbounded?

positive_text: Given a cuboid with side lengths $a < b < c$, define $P = 4(a + b + c)$, $A = 2(ab + bc + ca)$, and $D = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$. Prove that $3a < \left(\frac{P}{4} - \sqrt{D^2 - \frac{A}{2}}\right)$ and $3c > \left(\frac{P}{4} + \sqrt{D^2 - \frac{A}{2}}\right)$.

negatives.text: Let $a < b < c$ be the edge lengths of a rectangular prism. Define $P = 4(a + b + c)$, $A = 2(ab + bc + ca)$, and $D = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$. Show that $3a < \left(\frac{P}{4} + \sqrt{D^2 - \frac{A}{2}}\right)$ and $3c > \left(\frac{P}{4} - \sqrt{D^2 - \frac{A}{2}}\right)$.

Let $a < b < c$ be the edge lengths of a rectangular prism. Define $P = 4(a + b + c)$, $A = 2(ab + bc + ca)$, and $D = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$. Show that $3a < \left(\frac{P}{4} - \sqrt{D^2 - A}\right)$ and $3c > \left(\frac{P}{4} + \sqrt{D^2 - A}\right)$.

Let $a < b < c$ be the edge lengths of a rectangular prism. Define $P = 4(a + b + c)$, $A = 2(ab + bc + ca)$, and $D = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$. Show that $3a < \left(\frac{P}{4} - \sqrt{D^2 - \frac{A}{2}}\right)$ and $3b > \left(\frac{P}{4} + \sqrt{D^2 - \frac{A}{2}}\right)$.

positive_text: \text{Let } WXYZ \text{ be a tetrahedron with } \angle YWZ = 90^\circ \text{ and } \angle XWY = 90^\circ. \text{ If } \theta \text{ is the angle between lines } YZ \text{ and } WX, \text{ prove that } \cos \theta < \dfrac{XZ}{YW}.
Let $PQRS$ be a convex quadrilateral. Let $X$ be the midpoint of $QR$ and $Y$ be the midpoint of $RS$. If $k = PX + PY$, prove that the area of $PQRS$ is less than $\frac{k^2}{2}$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $CD$. If $k = AM - AN$, prove that the area of $ABCD$ is less than $\frac{k^2}{2}$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $CD$. If $k = AM + AN$, prove that the area of $ABCD$ is greater than $\frac{k^2}{2}$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$ and $N$ be the midpoint of $CD$. If $k = AM + AN$, prove that the perimeter of $ABCD$ is less than $\frac{k^2}{2}$.

positive_text: Find positive integers $x$, $y$, and $z$ such that $x^4 - y^3 = z^2$.

negatives.text: Are there any solutions in positive integers to $a^4 = b^3 - c^2$?
Are there any solutions in positive integers to $a^3 = b^3 + c^2$?
Are there any solutions in positive integers to $a^4 = b^2 + c^2$?

positive_text: \text{Find all real solutions to:}\\\sin a + 2\sin (a + b + c) = 0\\\sin b + 3\sin (a + b + c) = 0\\\sin c + 4\sin (a + b + c) = 0

negatives.text: \text{Find all real solutions to:}\\\sin x + 2\cos (x + y + z) = 0\\\sin y + 3\cos (x + y + z) = 0\\\sin z + 4\cos (x + y + z) = 0
\text{Find all real solutions to:}\\\sin x + 2\sin (x + y) = 0\\\sin y + 3\sin (x + y) = 0\\\sin z + 4\sin (x + y) = 0
\text{Find all real solutions to:}\\\sin x + 2\sin (2x + y + z) = 0\\\sin y + 3\sin (2x + y + z) = 0\\\sin z + 4\sin (2x + y + z) = 0

positive_text:
Let $\{b_n\}$ be a sequence of positive integers satisfying:

(1) $b_n \leq n^{3/2}$ for all $n$, and

(2) $a - b$ divides $b_a - b_b$ for all integers $a > b$.

Determine the explicit form of $b_n$.

negatives.text:
Let $\{c_n\}$ be a sequence of positive integers such that:

(1) $c_n \leq n^{3/2}$ for all $n$, and

(2) $m + n$ divides $c_m - c_n$ for all $m > n$.

Find $c_n$.

Let $\{d_n\}$ be a sequence of positive integers satisfying:

(1) $d_n \leq n^{3/2}$ for all $n$, and

(2) $m - n$ divides $d_m + d_n$ for all $m > n$.

Find $d_n$.

positive_text: Determine all pairs of positive integers $(a, b)$ such that $a^{3} - b^{3} - ab = 61$.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $(x, y)$ satisfying $x^{3} - y^{3} = xy - 61$.
Find all positive integers $(x, y)$ such that $x^{3} + y^{3} = xy + 61$.
Find all positive integers $(x, y)$ satisfying $x^{2} - y^{2} = xy + 61$.

positive_text: \text{Let } PQR \text{ be a triangle. Point } P' \text{ is on } QR \text{ such that } \frac{QP'}{QR} = \frac{1}{4}. \text{ Point } Q' \text{ is on } RP \text{ with } \frac{RQ'}{RP} = \frac{1}{4}, \text{ and point } R' \text{ is on } PQ \text{ with } \frac{PR'}{PQ} = \frac{1}{4}. \text{ Prove that the perimeter of triangle } P'Q'R' \text{ is between } \frac{1}{2} \text{ and } \frac{3}{4} \text{ of the perimeter of triangle } PQR.

negatives.text: \text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle. Let } A' \text{ lie on side } BC \text{ with } \frac{BA'}{BC} = \frac{1}{3}. \text{ Similarly, let } B' \text{ lie on side } CA \text{ with } \frac{CB'}{CA} = \frac{1}{3}, \text{ and let } C' \text{ lie on side } AB \text{ with } \frac{AC'}{AB} = \frac{1}{3}. \text{ Prove that the perimeter of triangle } A'B'C' \text{ is between } \frac{1}{2} \text{ and } \frac{3}{4} \text{ of the perimeter of triangle } ABC.

\text{Let } ABC \text{ be a triangle. Let } A' \text{ lie on side } BC \text{ with } \frac{BA'}{BC} = \frac{1}{4}. \text{ Similarly, let } B' \text{ lie on side } CA \text{ with } \frac{CB'}{CA} = \frac{1}{4}, \text{ and let } C' \text{ lie on side } AB \text{ with } \frac{AC'}{AB} = \frac{1}{4}. \text{ Prove that the area of triangle } A'B'C' \text{ is between } \frac{1}{2} \text{ and } \frac{3}{4} \text{ of the area of triangle } ABC.

positive_text: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers such that $a^3 + b^3 = a - b$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 < 1$.

negatives.text: Let $x$ and $y$ be positive real numbers such that $x^3 - y^3 = x - y$. Prove that $x^2 + y^2 < 1$.
Suppose $x$ and $y$ are positive real numbers with $x^3 + y^3 = x + y$. Show that $x^2 + y^2 < 1$.
Given positive real numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfying $x^3 + y^3 = x - y$, prove that $x^2 - y^2 < 1$.

positive_text: Find integers $a$ and $k$ such that $a$ is the product of $k$ consecutive positive integers and also the product of $k + 2$ consecutive positive integers. Prove that $k = 2$ is not possible.

negatives.text: Find integers $a$ and $k$ such that $a$ is the product of $k$ consecutive positive integers and also the product of $k + 1$ consecutive positive integers. Prove that $k = 2$ is not possible.
Find integers $a$ and $k$ such that $a$ is the product of $k$ consecutive positive integers and also the product of $k + 2$ consecutive negative integers. Prove that $k = 2$ is not possible.

positive_text: Suppose that for all real numbers $\theta$, the inequality $p \cos \theta + q \cos 3\theta > 1$ is false. Prove that $|q| \leq 1$.

negatives.text: The reals $a$ and $b$ are such that $a \cos x + b \sin 3x > 1$ has no real solutions. Show that $|b| \leq 1$.
The reals $a$ and $b$ are such that $a \cos x + b \cos 2x > 1$ has no real solutions. Show that $|b| \leq 1$.

positive_text:
Do there exist polynomials $a(x)$, $b(x)$, $c(x)$ such that
$$
a(a_1)^3 + b(b_1)^3 + c(c_1)^3 = 1
$$
for all real numbers $x$, $y$, $z$, where $a_1 = x - y + z$, $b_1 = y - z - 1$, $c_1 = z - x + 1$?

negatives.text:
Do there exist polynomials $p(x)$, $q(x)$, $r(x)$ such that
$$
 p(x - y + z)^3 + q(y - z + 1)^3 + r(z - x + 1)^3 = 1
$$
for all $x$, $y$, $z$?

Do there exist polynomials $p(x)$, $q(x)$, $r(x)$ such that
$$
 p(x - y + z)^3 + q(y - z - 1)^3 + r(z - x + 1)^3 = x + y + z
$$
for all $x$, $y$, $z$?

Do there exist polynomials $p(x)$, $q(x)$, $r(x)$ such that
$$
 p(x - y + z)^3 + q(y - z - 1)^3 + r(z - x + 1)^3 = 1
$$
for all $x$, $y$, $z$ with $x + y + z = 0$?

positive_text: Let $ 0 < a, b, c < \frac{\pi}{2} $. Suppose $ \cos a = a $, $ \sin(\cos b) = b $, and $ \cos(\sin c) = c $. Rank $ a, b, c $ from smallest to largest.

negatives.text: Let $ 0 < a, b, c < \frac{\pi}{2} $. Suppose $ \sin a = a $, $ \sin(\cos b) = b $, and $ \cos(\sin c) = c $. Rank $ a, b, c $ from smallest to largest.
Let $ 0 < a, b, c < \pi $. Suppose $ \cos a = a $, $ \sin(\cos b) = b $, and $ \cos(\sin c) = c $. Rank $ a, b, c $ from smallest to largest.

positive_text: Let $ A $ be a union of $ m $ disjoint open intervals on $ \mathbb{R} $. Suppose that for every $ d < 1 $, there are two points in $ A $ with distance exactly $ d $. Prove that the total length of the intervals in $ A $ is at least $ \frac{1}{m} $.

negatives.text: Let $ Y $ be a union of $ k $ disjoint intervals of the real line. Suppose that for every $ h > 1 $, there exist two points in $ Y $ with distance $ h $. Show that the sum of the lengths of the intervals in $ Y $ is at least $ \frac{1}{k} $.

Let $ Z $ be a union of $ k $ disjoint intervals on the real line. Suppose that for every $ h < 1 $, there exist at least three points in $ Z $ such that the distances between each pair are $ h $. Show that the total length of the intervals in $ Z $ is at least $ \frac{1}{k} $.

Let $ W $ be a union of $ k $ disjoint intervals on the real line. Suppose that for every $ h < 1 $, there exist two points in $ W $ with distance less than $ h $. Show that the sum of the lengths of the intervals in $ W $ is at least $ \frac{1}{k} $.

positive_text: Let $ y $ be a real number whose base-10 expansion contains each digit from 0 to 9 at least once. Define $ g(k) $ to be the number of unique $ k $-digit subsequents in the decimal expansion of $ y $. Prove that if there exists some $ k $ such that $ g(k) \leq k + 8 $, then $ y $ is rational.

negatives.text: Let $ x $ be a real number whose decimal representation includes all the digits at least once. Define $ f(n) $ to be the number of distinct $ n $-digit segments in the decimal representation. Show that if for all $ n $, $ f(n) \leq n + 8 $, then $ x $ is rational.

Let $ x $ be a real number whose decimal representation includes all the digits at least once. Define $ f(n) $ to be the number of distinct $ n $-digit segments in the decimal representation. Show that if for some $ n $, $ f(n) \leq n + 9 $, then $ x $ is rational.

Let $ x $ be a real number whose decimal representation includes all the digits at least once. Define $ f(n) $ to be the number of distinct $ n $-digit segments in the decimal representation. Show that if for some $ n $, $ f(n) \leq n + 8 $, then $ x $ is irrational.

positive_text: Let $a_1 < a_2 < \ldots < a_n$ be real numbers. Suppose $\{b_i\}$ is a permutation of $\{a_i\}$ and that $a_1 + b_1 < a_2 + b_2 < \ldots < a_n + b_n$. Show that $a_i = b_i$ for all $i$.

negatives.text: Let $a_1 < a_2 < \ldots < a_n$ be real numbers. Suppose $\{b_i\}$ is a permutation of $\{a_i\}$ and that $a_1 \cdot b_1 < a_2 \cdot b_2 < \ldots < a_n \cdot b_n$. Show that $a_i = b_i$ for all $i$.
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \ldots < a_n$ be real numbers. Suppose $\{b_i\}$ is a permutation of $\{a_i\}$ and that $a_1 - b_1 < a_2 - b_2 < \ldots < a_n - b_n$. Show that $a_i = b_i$ for all $i$.

positive_text: \text{Let } a, b, c \text{ be positive real numbers such that } a^2 + a b + \dfrac{b^2}{3} = 25, \dfrac{b^2}{3} + c^2 = 9, c^2 + c a + a^2 = 16. \text{ Compute } a b + 2 b c + 3 c a.

negatives.text: \text{Let } x, y, z \text{ be positive real numbers such that } x^2 - x y + \dfrac{y^2}{3} = 25, \dfrac{y^2}{3} + z^2 = 9, z^2 + z x + x^2 = 16. \text{ Find the value of } x y + 2 y z + 3 z x.
\text{Given } x, y, z \text{ positive reals with } x^2 + x y + y^2 = 25, \dfrac{y^2}{3} + z^2 = 9, z^2 + z x + x^2 = 16, \text{ compute } x y + 2 y z + 3 z x.

positive_text: A circular disk of radius $ r $ moves so that the center traces a polygon with perimeter $ p $, and the polygon has an incircle of radius $ R > r $. What is the area of the region swept out by the disk?

negatives.text: The center of a coin of radius $ r $ traces out a polygon with perimeter $ p $, which has a circumcircle of radius $ R > r $. What is the area of the figure traced out by the coin?
The center of a coin of radius $ r $ traces out a polygon with perimeter $ p $, which has an incircle of radius $ r $. What is the area of the figure traced out by the coin?

positive_text: \text{Points } W, X, Y \text{ and } Z \text{ lie on a straight path in that order. Prove that if } P \text{ is not on the path then } |PW| + |PZ| + ||WX| - |YZ|| > |PX| + |PY|

negatives.text: \text{Points } A, B, C, D \text{ lie on a line in that order. Prove that if } X \text{ does not lie on the line then } |XA| + |XD| - ||AB| - |CD|| > |XB| + |XC|
\text{Points } A, B, C, D \text{ lie on a line in that order. Prove that if } X \text{ lies on the line then } |XA| + |XD| + ||AB| - |CD|| > |XB| + |XC|
\text{Points } A, B, C, D \text{ lie on a line in that order. Prove that if } X \text{ is not on the line then } |XA| + |XD| + ||AB| + |CD|| > |XB| + |XC|

positive_text: A sequence $\{a_n\}$ is given by $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 1$, and $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1}^2 - \frac{a_n}{2}$. Prove that $\{a_n\}$ is convergent and determine its limit.

negatives.text: The real sequence $\{x_n\}$ is defined by $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 1$, and $x_{n+2} = x_{n+1}^2 + \frac{x_n}{2}$. Prove that the sequence converges and find its limit.
A real sequence $\{x_n\}$ is defined by $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 1$, and $x_{n+2} = x_{n+1}^3 - \frac{x_n}{2}$. Prove that the sequence converges and find its limit.
Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence of real numbers defined by $x_1 = 1$, $x_2 = 1$, and $x_{n+2} = x_{n+1}^2 - x_n^2$. Prove that the sequence converges and find its limit.

positive_text: Prove that $\dfrac{(x + y)^2}{2} + \dfrac{x + y}{4} \geq x\sqrt{y} + y\sqrt{x}$ for all $x, y > 0$.

negatives.text: Show that $\dfrac{(a + b)^2}{2} + \dfrac{a + b}{4} \geq a\sqrt[3]{b} + b\sqrt[3]{a}$ for all positive $a$ and $b$.
Prove that $\dfrac{(a + b)^2}{2} + \dfrac{a + b}{4} \geq a\sqrt{b} + b\sqrt{a}$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.
Show that $\dfrac{(a + b)^2}{2} - \dfrac{a + b}{4} \geq a\sqrt{b} + b\sqrt{a}$ for all positive $a$ and $b$.

positive_text: Let $\alpha$ be a real number and define $C = \cos^2 \alpha$, $D = \sin^2 \alpha$. Prove that for all positive real numbers $p$ and $q$, the inequality $p^C q^D < p + q$ holds.

negatives.text: Let $A = \cos^2 a$, $B = \sin^2 a$. Show that for all real $a$ and positive $x$, $y$ we have $x^A y^B \leq x + y$.
Let $A = \cos a$, $B = \sin a$. Show that for all real $a$ and positive $x$, $y$ we have $x^A y^B < x + y$.

positive_text: Let $\{b_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence such that $b_{4k+1} = 1$, $b_{4k+3} = 0$, and $b_{2k} = b_k$ for all $k \geq 1$. Prove that the sequence $\{b_n\}$ is not periodic.

negatives.text: Let $\{e_n\}$ be a sequence such that $e_{4n + 1} = 1$, $e_{4n + 3} = 1$, and $e_{2n} = e_n$. Show that the sequence is not periodic.
Let $\{f_n\}$ be a sequence with $f_{2n} = f_n$, $f_{4n + 1} = 1$, and $f_{4n + 2} = 0$. Show that the sequence is not periodic.
Define a sequence $\{g_n\}$ with $g_{2n} = g_n$, $g_{4n + 1} = 1$, and $g_{4n + 3} = 0$. Show that the sequence is periodic.

positive_text: Six points $P, Q, R, S, T, U$ lie equally spaced on the circumference of a circle in that order, with $PU$ as a diameter. The center is $O$. The lines $OR$ and $OS$ intersect the segment $QT$ at points $M$ and $N$ respectively. Prove that $MN + RS = OP$.

negatives.text: The points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ are equally spaced on the circumference of a circle (in that order) and $AF$ is a diameter. The center is $O$. $OC$ and $OD$ meet $BD$ at $M$ and $N$ respectively. Show that $MN + CD = OA$.

The points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ are equally spaced on the circumference of a circle (in that order) and $AF$ is a diameter. The center is $O$. $OC$ and $OD$ meet $BE$ at $M$ and $N$ respectively. Show that $MN + DE = OA$.

The points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$, $E$, $F$ are equally spaced on the circumference of a circle (in that order) and $AF$ is a diameter. The center is $O$. $OC$ and $OD$ meet $BE$ at $M$ and $N$ respectively. Show that $MN - CD = OA$.

positive_text: Let $ a $ be a real number. Define $ a_0 = 1 + \sqrt{1 + a} $, $ a_1 = 2 + \frac{a}{a_0} $, $ a_2 = 2 + \frac{a}{a_1} $, $ \ldots $, $ a_{1985} = 2 + \frac{a}{a_{1984}} $. Find all solutions to $ a_{1985} = a $.

negatives.text: Let $ x $ be a real number. Define $ x_0 = 1 + \sqrt{1 - x} $, $ x_1 = 2 + \frac{x}{x_0} $, $ x_2 = 2 + \frac{x}{x_1} $, $ \ldots $, $ x_{1985} = 2 + \frac{x}{x_{1984}} $. Find all solutions to $ x_{1985} = x $.

Let $ x $ be a real number. Define $ x_0 = 1 + \sqrt{1 + x} $, $ x_1 = 2 + \frac{x^2}{x_0} $, $ x_2 = 2 + \frac{x^2}{x_1} $, $ \ldots $, $ x_{1985} = 2 + \frac{x^2}{x_{1984}} $. Find all solutions to $ x_{1985} = x $.

Let $ x $ be a real number. Define $ x_0 = 1 + \sqrt{1 + x} $, $ x_1 = 2 + \frac{x}{x_0} $, $ x_2 = 2 + \frac{x}{x_1} $, $ \ldots $, $ x_{1985} = 2 + \frac{x}{x_{1984}} $. Find all solutions to $ x_{1985} = x^2 $.

positive_text: On a large grid of square tiles, prove that for any $n > 12$, there exists a rectangle with more than $n$ tiles that cannot be subdivided into a rectangle of exactly $n$ tiles by cutting along the grid lines.

negatives.text: Given a large sheet of squared paper, show that for $n > 12$ you can cut along the grid lines to get a rectangle of exactly $n$ unit squares such that it is also possible to cut it into a rectangle of $n + 1$ unit squares.

Given a large sheet of squared paper, show that for $n > 12$ you can cut along the grid lines to get a rectangle of more than $n$ unit squares such that it is impossible to cut it into a square of $n$ unit squares.

Given a large sheet of squared paper, show that for $n > 12$ you can cut along the grid lines to get a rectangle of more than $n$ unit squares such that it is impossible to cut it into a rectangle of $n$ unit squares using a single straight cut.

positive_text: Let $ q(x) = dx^2 + ex + f $, where $ d > 100 $. Determine the maximum number of integer values of $ x $ for which $ q(x) < 50 $.

negatives.text: Let $ p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c $, where $ a < 100 $. What is the maximum number of integer values of $ x $ for which $ p(x) < 50 $?
The quadratic $ p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c $ has $ a > 100 $. What is the maximum number of integer values of $ x $ for which $ p(x) > 50 $?
Let $ p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c $ with $ a > 100 $. Determine the maximum number of integer values of $ x $ for which $ |p(x)| < 50 $.

positive_text: Determine all values of $(a, b)$ for which $|\sin a - \sin b| + \sin a \sin b \leq 0$.

negatives.text: Find all pairs $(x, y)$ such that $|\sin x - \sin y| + \sin x + \sin y \leq 0$.
Find all pairs $(x, y)$ such that $|\cos x - \cos y| + \cos x \cos y \leq 0$.
Find all pairs $(x, y)$ such that $|\sin x + \sin y| + \sin x \sin y \leq 0$.

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $x$, $y$, $z$ such that $x^2 + y = z$, where $x$ is an $m$-digit repdigit with $m > 1$, $y$ is an $m$-digit repdigit, and $z$ is a $2m$-digit repdigit.

negatives.text: Find all positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ so that $a^2 + b = c$ and $a$ has $n > 1$ decimal digits all the same, $b$ has $n$ decimal digits all the same, and $c$ has $n$ decimal digits all the same.
