positive_text: Let $ n $ be a positive integer and $ k \ge 2 $ be an integer. Define $ F_k(n) $ as the highest power $ r $ such that $ k^r $ divides $ n! $. Show that there are infinitely many values of $ n $ for which $ F_{10}(n) > F_9(n) $ and infinitely many for which $ F_{10}(n) < F_9(n) $.

negatives.text: Let $ n $ be a positive integer and define $ G_k(n) $ as the greatest exponent $ r $ such that $ k^r $ divides $ n $. Prove that there are infinitely many $ n $ for which $ G_{10}(n) > G_9(n) $ and infinitely many for which $ G_{10}(n) < G_9(n) $.

Let $ n $ be a positive integer and define $ H_k(n) $ as the greatest exponent $ r $ such that $ k^r $ divides $ 2n $. Prove that there are infinitely many $ n $ for which $ H_{10}(n) > H_9(n) $ and infinitely many for which $ H_{10}(n) < H_9(n) $.

Let $ n $ be a positive integer and define $ J_k(n) $ as the greatest exponent $ r $ such that $ k^r $ divides $ n! $. Prove that there are infinitely many $ n $ for which $ J_{10}(n) > J_8(n) $ and infinitely many for which $ J_{10}(n) < J_8(n) $.

positive_text: Let $\mathbb{R}_+$ be the set of positive real numbers. Find all functions $g : \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}_+$ such that $$ g(a + b + ab) + g\left(\frac{1}{a}\right) g\left(\frac{1}{b}\right) = 1 $$ for every $a, b \in \mathbb{R}_+$.

negatives.text: Let $\mathbb{R}_+$ be the set of positive real numbers. Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}_+$ such that $$ f(xy + x + y) + f\left(\frac{1}{x + 1}\right) f\left(\frac{1}{y + 1}\right) = 1 $$ for every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}_+$.

Let $\mathbb{R}_+$ be the set of positive real numbers. Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}_+$ such that $$ f(xy + x + y) + f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) = x $$ for every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}_+$.

Let $\mathbb{R}_+$ be the set of positive real numbers. Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}_+$ such that $$ f(x^2 + y^2 + xy) + f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) f\left(\frac{1}{y}\right) = 1 $$ for every $x, y \in \mathbb{R}_+$.

positive_text:
Show that there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for all $n$, with $M = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$, we can find three permutations $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_M$; $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_M$; and $z_1, z_2, \dots, z_M$ of $1, 2, \dots, M$ such that
$$
\left| \sqrt{x_j} + \sqrt{y_j} + \sqrt{z_j} - 2\sqrt{M} \right| < C
$$
for all $j = 1, 2, \dots, M$.

negatives.text:
Prove that there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for all $n$, with $M = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$, we can find two permutations $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_M$; $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_M$ of $1, 2, \dots, M$ such that
$$
\left| \sqrt{x_j} + \sqrt{y_j} - 2\sqrt{M} \right| < C
$$
for all $j = 1, 2, \dots, M$.

Prove that there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for all $n$, with $M = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$, we can find three permutations $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_M$; $y_1, y_2, \dots, y_M$; and $z_1, z_2, \dots, z_M$ of $1, 2, \dots, M$ such that
$$
\left| \sqrt{x_j} + \sqrt{y_j} + \sqrt{z_j} - 2\sqrt{M} \right| < C
$$
for all $j = 1, 2, \dots, M$, and additionally $x_j + y_j + z_j = M$ for all $j$.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 3$ be a positive integer. There are $n$ competitors from $k$ different teams, labeled from 1 to $n$. In any head-to-head match, the competitor with the smaller label always wins. It is given that for any permutation $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, the winners of the $n-1$ matches $a_1$ vs $a_2$, $a_2$ vs $a_3$, $\dots$, $a_{n-1}$ vs $a_n$ will include at least one competitor from each of the $k$ teams. Prove that $n \ge 2^k$.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be a positive integer. There are $n$ players from $k$ different teams, labeled from 1 to $n$. In any match, the player with the smaller label wins. It is known that for any permutation $\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, the winners of the $n-1$ matches $a_1$ vs $a_2$, $a_2$ vs $a_3$, $\dots$, $a_{n-1}$ vs $a_n$ will include at least one player from each of the $k-1$ teams. Prove that $n \ge 2^k$.

positive_text:
Let $\phi = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$. Determine all continuous functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying, for all real numbers $p, q, r$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(\phi p + q) + f(\phi q + r) + f(\phi r + p) \\
&= \phi f(p + q + r) + 2f(p) + 2f(q) + 2f(r).
\end{aligned}$$

negatives.text:
Let $\alpha = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$. Find all continuous functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, for all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(\alpha x + y) + f(\alpha y + z) + f(\alpha z + x) \\
&= \alpha f(x + y + z) + 2f(x + y + z) + 2f(x) + 2f(y) + 2f(z).
\end{aligned}$$

Let $\alpha = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$. Find all continuous functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, for all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(\alpha x + y) + f(\alpha y + z) + f(\alpha z + x) \\
&= 2f(x + y + z) + 2f(x) + 2f(y) + 2f(z).
\end{aligned}$$

Let $\alpha = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$. Find all continuous functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, for all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(\alpha x + y) + f(\alpha y + z) + f(\alpha z + x) \\
&= \alpha f(x) + 2f(x) + 2f(y) + 2f(z).
\end{aligned}$$

positive_text:
Let $ g: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty) $ be a function satisfying
$$
(g(a b))^2 = g(a^2)g(b^2)
$$
for all $ a, b > 0 $ with $ a^2b^3 > 2024 $. Prove that $(g(a b))^2 = g(a^2)g(b^2)$ for all $ a, b > 0 $.

negatives.text:
Let $ h: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+ $ be a function satisfying
$$
(h(xy))^2 = h(x^3)h(y^2)
$$
for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+ $ with $ x^2y^3 > 2008 $. Prove that $(h(xy))^2 = h(x^3)h(y^2)$ for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+ $.

Let $ k: \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+ $ be a function satisfying
$$
(k(xy))^3 = k(x^2)k(y^2)
$$
for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+ $ with $ x^2y^3 > 2008 $. Prove that $(k(xy))^3 = k(x^2)k(y^2)$ for all $ x, y \in \mathbb{R}^+ $.

positive_text: \text{Let } x, y, z > 0. \text{ Prove that } \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 - \sqrt{2} xy} + \sqrt{y^2 + z^2 - \sqrt{2} yz} \geq \sqrt{x^2 + z^2}.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that } \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + \sqrt{2} ab} + \sqrt{b^2 + c^2 + \sqrt{2} bc} \geq \sqrt{a^2 + c^2} \text{ for all positive real numbers } a, b, c.
\text{Prove that } \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 - ab} + \sqrt{b^2 + c^2 - bc} \geq \sqrt{a^2 + c^2} \text{ for all positive real numbers } a, b, c.
\text{Prove that } \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 - \sqrt{2} ab} + \sqrt{c^2 + d^2 - \sqrt{2} cd} \geq \sqrt{a^2 + c^2} \text{ for all positive real numbers } a, b, c, d.

positive_text: Let $\{b_n\}_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of positive integers such that $b_n b_{n+3} = b_{n+2} b_{n+5}$ for all positive integers $n$. Compute the greatest integer that divides $\sum_{k=1}^{2550} b_{2k-1} b_{2k}$ for all such sequences.

negatives.text: Let $\{c_n\}_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of positive integers with $c_n c_{n+3} + c_{n+2} c_{n+5} = 0$ for all positive integers $n$. Determine the largest integer that always divides $\sum_{k=1}^{2550} c_{2k} c_{2k-1}$.

Let $\{d_n\}_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of positive integers with $d_n d_{n+3} = d_{n+1} d_{n+4}$ for all positive integers $n$. Determine the largest integer that always divides $\sum_{k=1}^{2550} d_{2k} d_{2k-1}$.

Let $\{e_n\}_{n \ge 1}$ be a sequence of positive integers with $e_n e_{n+3} = e_{n+1} e_{n+5}$ for all positive integers $n$. Determine the largest integer that always divides $\sum_{k=1}^{2550} e_{2k} e_{2k-1}$.

positive_text: Let $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|g(a + b)| = |g(a) + g(b)|$ for all real numbers $a, b$. Prove that $g(a + b) = g(a) + g(b)$ for all $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$.

negatives.text: Let $h: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|h(x + y)| = |h(x) - h(y)|$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $h(x + y) = h(x) - h(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.
Let $p: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|p(x + y)| = |p(x)| + |p(y)|$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that $p(x + y) = p(x) + p(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ADE$ be a triangle with $AD \leq AE$ and let $Q$ be a point inside the triangle lying on the bisector of $\angle DAE$. Points $F, G$ are on the segments $QE, QD$ respectively such that $\angle QDF = \angle QEG$. The line $DF$ meets $AE$ at $M$, and the line $EG$ meets $AD$ at $N$. Prove that $DM \leq EN$.

negatives.text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$ and let $P$ be a point on the external bisector of $\angle BAC$. Let $D, E$ be points on the segments $PC, PB$ respectively such that $\angle PBD = \angle PCE$. The line $BD$ meets $AC$ at $X$, and the line $CE$ meets $AB$ at $Y$. Prove that $BX < CY$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB \leq AC$ and let $P$ be a point on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. Let $D, E$ be points on the segments $PC, PB$ respectively such that $\angle PBD = 2\angle PCE$. The line $BD$ meets $AC$ at $X$, and the line $CE$ meets $AB$ at $Y$. Prove that $BX \leq CY$.

positive_text: Let $\omega$ be the incircle of triangle $ABC$, touching side $BC$ at $D$ and side $AC$ at $E$. Construct a line perpendicular to $BC$ through $D$ that intersects $\omega$ at point $P$, the one closer to $A$. The line $AP$ intersects $BC$ at $M$. Let $N$ lie on $AC$ so that $CN = AE$. Then $BN$ intersects $\omega$ at point $Q$ closer to $B$ and intersects $AM$ at $R$. Prove that the area of triangle $ABR$ equals the area of quadrilateral $PQMN$.

negatives.text: Let $\omega$ be the incircle of triangle $ABC$, tangent to $BC$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively. Draw a line perpendicular to $BC$ at $D$ to meet $\omega$ at point $P$ closer to $A$. The line $AP$ intersects $AC$ at $M$. Let $N$ be a point on $AC$ such that $CN = AE$. Then $BN$ intersects $\omega$ at point $Q$ closer to $B$ and intersects $AM$ at point $R$. Show that the area of triangle $ABR$ equals the area of quadrilateral $PQMN$.

Let $\omega$ be the incircle of triangle $ABC$, tangent to $BC$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$, respectively. Draw a line perpendicular to $BC$ at $D$ to meet $\omega$ at point $P$ closer to $A$. The line $AP$ intersects $BC$ at $M$. Let $N$ be a point on $AC$ such that $CN = AC$. Then $BN$ intersects $\omega$ at point $Q$ closer to $B$ and intersects $AM$ at point $R$. Show that the area of triangle $ABR$ equals the area of quadrilateral $PQMN$.

positive_text: Let $q(x) = x^{2013} + c_{2012}x^{2012} + c_{2011}x^{2011} + \dots + c_1x + c_0$ be a polynomial with real coefficients. All the roots of $q(x)$ are $$ -d_{1006}, -d_{1005}, \dots, -d_1, 0, d_1, \dots, d_{1005}, d_{1006} $$ where $d_1, d_2, \dots, d_{1006}$ are positive real numbers with product equal to $1$. Prove that $c_3c_{2011} \geq 1012036$.

negatives.text: Let $r(x) = x^{2013} + b_{2012}x^{2012} + b_{2011}x^{2011} + \dots + b_1x + b_0$ be a polynomial with real coefficients. Suppose that all the roots of $r(x)$ are $$ -c_{1006}, -c_{1005}, \dots, -c_1, 0, c_1, \dots, c_{1005}, c_{1006} $$ where $c_1, c_2, \dots, c_{1006}$ are positive real numbers with product equal to $\frac{1}{2}$. Show that $b_3b_{2011} \geq 1012036$.

Let $s(x) = x^{2013} + d_{2012}x^{2012} + d_{2011}x^{2011} + \dots + d_1x + d_0$ be a polynomial with real coefficients. Suppose that all the roots of $s(x)$ are $$ -e_{1006}, -e_{1005}, \dots, -e_1, 0, e_1, \dots, e_{1005}, e_{1006} $$ where $e_1, e_2, \dots, e_{1006}$ are positive real numbers with product equal to $1$. Show that $d_2d_{2010} \geq 1012036$.

positive_text: \text{Let } A = (0, a) \text{ and } B = (b, 0), \text{ where } a, b \in \mathbb{Z}^+. \text{ A person moves from } A \text{ to } B \text{ by taking unit-length steps either right or down, staying within the first quadrant. At each step, the person computes the distance to the axis perpendicular to the direction of the step. If the step increases the distance to the origin, this value is added; otherwise, it is subtracted. Prove that the total sum of all such values is zero after the person reaches } B.

negatives.text: \text{Let } M \text{ and } N \text{ be positive integers. Mr. Pisut starts walking from } (0, N) \text{ to } (M, 0) \text{ by taking unit-length steps either right or down. At each step, he records the distance to the origin. Prove that the sum of all such recorded distances is zero after he reaches } (M, 0).

\text{Let } M \text{ and } N \text{ be positive integers. Mr. Pisut starts walking from } (0, N) \text{ to } (M, 0) \text{ by taking unit-length steps either right or down. At each step, he records the distance to the axis to which his step is parallel. If the step takes him farther away from the origin, he records the distance as a positive value; otherwise it is recorded in negative. Prove that the product of all distances recorded is zero after he finishes his walk.}

positive_text: Let $k$ be a positive integer. We wish to create a set of tokens, each labeled with a factorial number $a!$, such that every integer $s$ from $1$ up to $k!$ can be expressed as a sum of distinct elements from the set. What is the minimum number of tokens needed in the set?

negatives.text: Let $n$ be a positive integer. We want to make a set of cards, each with a number of the form $m!$ written on it. For any positive integer $t$ such that $1 \le t < n!$, we can express $t$ as a sum of some of the numbers on the cards. What is the smallest number of cards needed?

Let $n$ be a positive integer. We want to make a set of cards, each labeled with a number of the form $2^m$. For any positive integer $t$ such that $1 \le t \le n!$, we can express $t$ as a sum of some of the numbers on the cards. What is the smallest number of cards needed?

Let $n$ be a positive integer. We want to make a set of cards, each with a number of the form $m!$. For any positive integer $t$ such that $1 \le t \le n!$, we can express $t$ as a product of some of the numbers on the cards. What is the smallest number of cards needed?

positive_text: Let triangle $XYZ$ be such that $XY \neq XZ$. The bisector of $\angle YXZ$ meets side $YZ$ at point $M$ and intersects the perpendicular bisector of $YZ$ at point $N$. Prove that $\frac{MN}{XN} = \left(\frac{YZ}{XY+XZ}\right)^2$.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ be such that $AB \neq AC$. Let the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersect $BC$ at $P$, and intersect the perpendicular bisector of segment $AB$ at $Q$. Prove that $\frac{PQ}{AQ} = \left(\frac{BC}{AB+AC}\right)^2$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be such that $AB \neq AC$. Let the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersect $BC$ at $P$, and intersect the perpendicular bisector of segment $BC$ at $Q$. Prove that $\frac{PQ}{AQ} = \left(\frac{AB}{AC+BC}\right)^2$.

Let triangle $ABC$ be such that $AB \neq AC$. Let the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ intersect $BC$ at $P$, and intersect the perpendicular bisector of segment $BC$ at $Q$. Prove that $\frac{PQ}{AQ} = \left(\frac{BC}{AB - AC}\right)^2$.

positive_text: Let $ p $ be a prime number greater than or equal to 5. Prove that there exists an integer $ a $ between 1 and $ p $, inclusive, for which the equation $$ x^2 - y^{\frac{p-1}{2}} = a $$ has no integer solutions.

negatives.text: Let $ p $ be a prime number greater than or equal to 5. Prove that for every integer $ t \in \{1, 2, \ldots, p\} $, the equation $$ x^2 = y^{\frac{p-1}{2}} + t $$ has at least one integer solution.

Let $ p $ be a prime number greater than or equal to 5. Prove that there exists an integer $ t \in \{1, 2, \ldots, p\} $ such that the equation $$ x^2 = y^{\frac{p+1}{2}} + t $$ has no integer solutions.

Let $ p $ be a prime number greater than or equal to 5. Prove that there exists an integer $ t \in \{1, 2, \ldots, p\} $ such that the equation $$ x^2 = y^{\frac{p-1}{2}} - t $$ has no integer solutions.

positive_text: Let $ a $ and $ b $ be positive integers. Prove that if $ a^{4b+1} - 1 $ is a prime number then there exists a non-negative integer $ k $ such that $ b = 2^k $.

negatives.text: Let $ m $ and $ n $ be positive integers. Prove that if $ m^{4n-1} - 1 $ is a prime number then there exists an integer $ t \ge 0 $ such that $ n = 2^t $.
Let $ m $ and $ n $ be positive integers. Prove that if $ m^{4n+1} + 1 $ is a prime number then there exists an integer $ t \ge 0 $ such that $ n = 2^t $.
Let $ m $ and $ n $ be positive integers. Prove that if $ m^{4n+1} - 1 $ is a prime number then there exists an integer $ t \ge 0 $ such that $ m = 2^t $.

positive_text: Is there a mapping $ g: \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Q} $ such that for each rational number $ q $, there is a unique pair $ (a, b) $ of positive integers with $ q = g(a) + \frac{1}{b} $?

negatives.text: Does there exist a function $ f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Q} $ such that for any rational number $ r $, there exists exactly one ordered pair $ (m, n) $ of positive integers satisfying the equation $ r = f(m) - \frac{1}{n} $?

positive_text:
Suppose $f$ and $g$ are real-valued functions on the grid $\{1, 2, ..., 2000\} 	imes \{1, 2, ..., 2000\}$. Suppose there exist two subsets $A$ and $B$ of size 1000 each such that $f(x, y) = g(x, y)$ for all $x

otin B$. What is the maximum number of pairs $(x, y)$ where $f(x, y) 
e g(x, y)$?

negatives.text: Let $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ be functions on $\{1, 2, ..., 2000\}^2$. Suppose there exist subsets $X, Y$ of size 1000 such that $f(x, y) = g(x, y)$ for all $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$. What is the maximum number of pairs $(x, y)$ where $f(x, y) \ne g(x, y)$?

Let $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ be real functions on the square $\{1, 2, ..., 2000\}^2$. Suppose there exists a single 1000-element subset $X$ such that $f(x, y) = g(x, y)$ for all $x \notin X$ and all $y$. What is the maximum number of pairs $(x, y)$ where $f(x, y) \ne g(x, y)$?

Suppose $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ are real functions on $\{1, 2, ..., 2000\}^2$. Suppose there exist subsets $X, Y$ of size 1000 such that $f(x, y) = g(x, y)$ for all $x \in X$ and $y \notin Y$. What is the maximum number of pairs $(x, y)$ where $f(x, y) \ne g(x, y)$?

positive_text: Find all integer solutions $(a, b)$ to the equation $$ 5^a = b^4 + 4b + 1 $$

negatives.text: Find all integer pairs $(x, y)$ satisfying $$ 5^x = y^4 + 4y + 2 $$
Find all integer pairs $(x, y)$ satisfying $$ 5^x = y^4 + 4y^2 + 1 $$

positive_text: \text{Prove that } \sqrt{p^4 + r^4} + \sqrt{p^4 + s^4} + \sqrt{q^4 + r^4} + \sqrt{q^4 + s^4} \ge 2\sqrt{2}(ps + qr) \text{ for all real numbers } p, q, r, s.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that } \sqrt{a^4 + c^4} + \sqrt{a^4 + d^4} + \sqrt{b^4 + c^4} + \sqrt{b^4 + d^4} \ge 2\sqrt{2}(ad - bc) \text{ for all real numbers } a, b, c, d.
\text{Prove that } \sqrt{a^2 + c^2} + \sqrt{a^2 + d^2} + \sqrt{b^2 + c^2} + \sqrt{b^2 + d^2} \ge 2\sqrt{2}(ad + bc) \text{ for all real numbers } a, b, c, d.
\text{Prove that } \sqrt{a^4 + c^4} + \sqrt{a^4 + d^4} + \sqrt{b^4 + c^4} + \sqrt{b^4 + d^4} \ge 2\sqrt{2}(ac + bd) \text{ for all real numbers } a, b, c, d.

positive_text: Let there be $ n+1 $ cities in a country. Each pair of cities may have multiple two-way flights, meaning a flight from city $ A $ to city $ B $ and vice versa can occur on the same day. For each city $ A $ that is not the capital, the number of take-offs $ d_A $ from $ A $ in one day satisfies $ d_A \le n $. Additionally, for any two non-capital cities $ A $ and $ B $, if there is no two-way flight between $ A $ and $ B $, then $ d_A + d_B \le n $. The capital has no such restrictions. Determine the maximum number of two-way flights possible in a day, and describe all such optimal configurations.

negatives.text: In a country with $ n+1 $ cities, there are two-way flights between some of these cities. A two-way flight between cities $ A $ and $ B $ means there is a flight from $ A $ to $ B $ and vice versa on the same day. Let $ d_A $ be the number of take-offs from city $ A $. For all cities $ A $ except for the capital, one has $ d_A \le n $. Moreover, for any two cities $ A $, $ B $ (excluding the capital), one has $ d_A + d_B \le n $, if there is a two-way flight between $ A $ and $ B $. There is no restriction on the number of flights from the capital. Find the maximum number of two-way flights possible in a day and describe all such optimal configurations.

positive_text: Let $C$ and $D$ be two distinct points on a circle $\Omega$. For a point $Q$ moving along $\Omega$ (excluding $C$ and $D$), determine the set of all points $N$ such that $QN$ lies along the ray opposite to the angle bisector of $\angle CQD$ and $NQ = CQ + QD$.

negatives.text: Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct points on a circle $\Gamma$. For a variable point $P$ different from $A$ and $B$ on $\Gamma$, find the geometric locus of the point $M$ such that $PM$ is the angle bisector of $\angle APB$ and $MP = AP + PB$.

Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct points on a circle $\Gamma$. For a variable point $P$ different from $A$ and $B$ on $\Gamma$, find the geometric locus of the point $M$ such that $PM$ is the opposite ray to the angle bisector of $\angle APB$ and $MP = |AP - PB|$.

Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct points on a circle $\Gamma$. For a variable point $P$ different from $A$ and $B$ on $\Gamma$, find the geometric locus of the point $M$ such that $PM$ is the opposite ray to the angle bisector of $\angle APB$ and $MP = AP + PB + AB$.

positive_text: Define a sequence $\{y_n\}$ with initial terms $y_1 = p$, $y_2 = q$ and recurrence $y_n = 2008y_{n-1} - y_{n-2}$ for all $n \ge 3$. Show that there exist positive integers $p$ and $q$ such that $1 + 2006y_ny_{n+1}$ is a perfect square for every $n \ge 1$.

negatives.text: Let $\{z_n\}$ be a sequence defined by $z_1 = a$, $z_2 = b$ and $z_n = 2008z_{n-1} - z_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 3$. Prove that there exist positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $1 + 2007z_nz_{n+1}$ is a perfect square for all $n \ge 1$.

Consider the sequence $\{w_n\}$ with $w_1 = a$, $w_2 = b$ and $w_n = 2008w_{n-1} + w_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 3$. Prove that there are positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $1 + 2006w_nw_{n+1}$ is a perfect square for all $n \ge 1$.

Let $\{u_n\}$ be defined by $u_1 = a$, $u_2 = b$ and $u_n = 2008u_{n-1} - u_{n-2}$ for $n \ge 3$. Show that there are positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $1 + 2006u_nu_{n}$ is a perfect square for all $n \ge 1$.

positive_text: Let $ n > 1 $ be an integer and $ q = 6n + 1 $ be a prime number. Let $ a = 2^q - 1 $. Show that $$\frac{2^a - 1}{127a}$$ is an integer.

negatives.text: Let $ k > 1 $ be an integer and $ p = 6k + 1 $ be a prime number. Define $ m = 2^p - 1 $. Prove that $$\frac{2^{m} - 2}{127m}$$ is an integer.
Let $ k > 1 $ be an integer and $ p = 6k + 1 $ be a prime number. Let $ m = 2^p - 1 $. Prove that $$\frac{2^{m + 1} - 1}{127m}$$ is an integer.
Let $ k > 1 $ be an integer and $ p = 6k + 1 $ be a prime number. Define $ m = 2^p + 1 $. Prove that $$\frac{2^m - 1}{127m}$$ is an integer.

positive_text: A graph of $2008$ vertices is a union of disjoint cycles. At time $t = 0$, a vertex is chosen and marked as infected. At time $t = 1$, a vertex adjacent to an uninfected vertex is chosen and marked as protected. For each positive integer $k$, at time $t = 2k$, the infection spreads to an uninfected and unprotected neighbor of an infected vertex (if one exists); at time $t = 2k + 1$, the protection spreads to an uninfected and uninfected neighbor of a protected vertex (if one exists). Determine the maximum number of vertices that can be infected, regardless of the configuration of the graph.

negatives.text: A graph of $2008$ vertices is a union of disjoint cycles. At time $t = 0$, a vertex is chosen and marked as infected. At time $t = 1$, a vertex is chosen and marked as protected. For each positive integer $k$, at time $t = 2k$, the infection spreads to an uninfected and unprotected vertex (not necessarily adjacent) of an infected vertex (if one exists); at time $t = 2k + 1$, the protection spreads to an uninfected and uninfected vertex (not necessarily adjacent) of a protected vertex (if one exists). Determine the maximum number of vertices that can be infected, regardless of the configuration of the graph.

A graph of $2008$ vertices is a union of disjoint paths. At time $t = 0$, a vertex is chosen and marked as infected. At time $t = 1$, a vertex is chosen and marked as protected. For each positive integer $k$, at time $t = 2k$, the infection spreads to an uninfected and unprotected neighbor of an infected vertex (if one exists); at time $t = 2k + 1$, the protection spreads to an uninfected and uninfected neighbor of a protected vertex (if one exists). Determine the maximum number of vertices that can be infected, regardless of the configuration of the graph.

positive_text: Let $ABCD$ be a tangential quadrilateral with incenter $I$ and inradius $r$. Let $X$ be the intersection of lines $AB$ and $CD$, let $Y$ be the intersection of lines $AD$ and $BC$, and let $Z$ be the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Show that $|IZ| \cdot d = r^2$, where $d$ is the distance from $I$ to the line $XY$.

negatives.text: Let $ABCD$ be a cyclic quadrilateral with circumcenter $O$ and circumradius $R$. Let $P$ be the intersection of lines $AB$ and $CD$, and $Q$ be the intersection of lines $AD$ and $BC$. Let $E$ be the intersection of diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Show that $|OE| \cdot d = R^2$, where $d$ is the distance from $O$ to the line $PQ$.

Let $ABCD$ be a tangential quadrilateral with incenter $O$ and inradius $r$. Let $P$ be the intersection of lines $AB$ and $CD$, and $Q$ be the intersection of lines $AD$ and $BC$. Let $E$ be the intersection of the midlines $AC$ and $BD$. Show that $|OE| \cdot d = r^2$, where $d$ is the distance from $O$ to the line $PQ$.

positive_text: Let the incircle of triangle $PQR$ touch sides $QR$, $PR$, and $PQ$ at points $X$, $Y$, and $Z$, respectively. Prove that $\sqrt{|PX|} + \sqrt{|QY|} + \sqrt{|RZ|} \le \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$.

negatives.text: Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$ touch sides $BC$, $AC$, and $AB$ at points $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$, respectively. Prove that $\sqrt{|AB_1|} + \sqrt{|BC_1|} + \sqrt{|CA_1|} \le \dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}$.

positive_text: In a gathering of $n \ge 4$ people, each pair may or may not be connected by a handshake. For any $n-1$ people, it is possible to arrange them in a circle such that adjacent people have shaken hands. However, arranging all $n$ people in such a circle is impossible. Determine the smallest possible value of $n$.

negatives.text: In a group of $n \ge 4$ students, each pair may or may not be friends. Any $n-1$ students can form a line so that adjacent students are friends, but all $n$ students cannot form such a line. Find the smallest possible value of $n$.

In a class of $n \ge 4$ students, some of whom are friends, any $n-1$ students can form a circle so that adjacent students are friends, and all $n$ students can also form such a circle. Find the smallest possible value of $n$.
In a group of $n \ge 4$ students, some of whom are friends, it is possible to form a circle of all $n$ students such that adjacent students are not friends. Find the smallest possible value of $n$.

positive_text: \text{Points } P, Q, R \text{ lie on the sides } XY, YZ, ZX \text{ of triangle } XYZ \text{ such that } XP = XR, YP = YQ \text{ and } PQ = PR. \text{ Let } J \text{ be the incenter of triangle } XYZ, \text{ and let } L \text{ be the intersection of line } YJ \text{ and the tangent to the circumcircle of triangle } XJY \text{ at } X. \text{ Prove that } XL = QL \text{ if } XL = XP.

negatives.text: \text{Points } D, E, F \text{ lie on the sides } AB, BC, CA \text{ of triangle } ABC \text{ such that } AD = AF, BD = BE \text{ and } DE = DF. \text{ Let } I \text{ be the incenter of triangle } ABC, \text{ and let } K \text{ be the intersection of line } CI \text{ and the tangent to the circumcircle of triangle } ABI \text{ at } A. \text{ Prove that } AK = EK \text{ if } AK = AD.

\text{Points } D, E, F \text{ lie on the sides } AB, BC, CA \text{ of triangle } ABC \text{ such that } AD = AF, BD = BE \text{ and } DE = DF. \text{ Let } I \text{ be the incenter of triangle } ABC, \text{ and let } K \text{ be the intersection of line } BI \text{ and the tangent to the circumcircle of triangle } ACI \text{ at } A. \text{ Prove that } AK = EK \text{ if } AK = AD.

positive_text:
Let $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be positive real numbers such that $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n = 1$. Prove that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{x_i}{\sqrt{x_i^4 + 3}} \le \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x_i}.
$$

negatives.text:
Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers with $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n = 1$. Show that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{a_i^2}{\sqrt{a_i^4 + 3}} \le \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_i}.
$$

Let $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers with $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n = 1$. Show that
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{a_i}{\sqrt{a_i^4 + 1}} \le \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_i}.
$$

positive_text: \text{Prove that } x^2 y^2 (x^2 + y^2 - 2) \geq (x + y)(xy - 1) \text{ for all positive real numbers } x \text{ and } y.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that } a^2 b^2 (a^2 + b^2 - 2) \geq (a + b)(ab + 1) \text{ for all positive real numbers } a \text{ and } b.
\text{Prove that } a^2 b^2 (a^2 + b^2 + 2) \geq (a + b)(ab - 1) \text{ for all positive real numbers } a \text{ and } b.
\text{Prove that } a^2 b^2 (a^2 + b^2 - 2) \geq (a + b)(ab - 1) \text{ for all real numbers } a \text{ and } b.

positive_text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $S = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. Suppose $B_1, B_2, \dots, B_k$ are subsets of $S$ such that for any distinct $i$ and $j$, exactly one of $B_i \cap B_j$, $B^c_i \cap B_j$, $B_i \cap B^c_j$, and $B^c_i \cap B^c_j$ is empty. What is the maximum possible value of $k$?

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $E = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. Suppose $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$ are subsets of $E$ such that for all $1 \le i < j \le k$, at least one of $A_i \cap A_j$, $A'_i \cap A_j$, $A_i \cap A'_j$, and $A'_i \cap A'_j$ is empty. Determine the maximum possible value of $k$.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $E = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. Suppose $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$ are subsets of $E$ such that for all $1 \le i < j \le k$, exactly one of $A_i \cup A_j$, $A'_i \cup A_j$, $A_i \cup A'_j$, and $A'_i \cup A'_j$ is empty. Determine the maximum possible value of $k$.

Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer and $E = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. Suppose $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_k$ are subsets of $E$ such that for all $1 \le i < j \le k$, exactly one of $A_i \cap A_j$, $A_i \cap A_j$, $A_i \cap A_j$, and $A_i \cap A_j$ is empty. Determine the maximum possible value of $k$.

positive_text: In triangle $PQR$, $|PQ| = |PR|$, and $M$ is the midpoint of segment $QR$. A perpendicular from $M$ to side $PR$ meets $PR$ at point $N$. The line $QN$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $PQM$ again at point $S$. If $T$ is the intersection of $MN$ and $PS$, prove that $|MT| = |TN|$.

negatives.text: In triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = |AC|$, and $D$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$. A line through $D$ is drawn to intersect $AC$ at $E$, but not necessarily perpendicularly. If $F$ is the second point of intersection of $BE$ with the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$, and $G$ is the intersection of $DE$ and $AF$, show that $|DG| = |GE|$.

In triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = |AC|$, and $D$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$. A perpendicular from $D$ to $AB$ intersects $AB$ at point $E$. Let $F$ be the second point where $BE$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABD$. If $G$ is the intersection of $DE$ and $AF$, prove that $|DG| = |GE|$.

In triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = |AC|$, and $D$ is the midpoint of $[BC]$. A perpendicular from $D$ to $AC$ intersects $AC$ at $E$. The line $BE$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ again at $F$. If $G$ is the intersection of $DE$ and $AF$, prove that $|DG| = |GE|$.

positive_text:
Prove that
$$
 x + y + z + \sqrt{3} \geq 8xyz \left( \frac{1}{x^2 + 1} + \frac{1}{y^2 + 1} + \frac{1}{z^2 + 1} \right)
$$
for all positive real numbers $x, y, z$ such that $xy + yz + zx \leq 1$.

negatives.text:
Prove that
$$
 a + b + c + \sqrt{3} \geq 4abc \left( \frac{1}{a^2 + 1} + \frac{1}{b^2 + 1} + \frac{1}{c^2 + 1} \right)
$$
for all positive real numbers $a, b, c$ satisfying $ab + bc + ca \leq 1$.

positive_text: \text{Prove that } \frac{1}{a + b^{20} + c^{11}} + \frac{1}{b + c^{20} + a^{11}} + \frac{1}{c + a^{20} + b^{11}} \le 1 \text{ for all positive real numbers } a, b, c \text{ such that } abc = 1.

negatives.text: \text{Let } x, y, z > 0 \text{ with } xyz = 1. \text{ Prove that } \frac{1}{x + y^{20} - z^{11}} + \frac{1}{y + z^{20} - x^{11}} + \frac{1}{z + x^{20} - y^{11}} \le 1.
\text{Let } x, y, z > 0 \text{ with } x + y + z = 1. \text{ Prove that } \frac{1}{x + y^{20} + z^{11}} + \frac{1}{y + z^{20} + x^{11}} + \frac{1}{z + x^{20} + y^{11}} \le 1.
\text{Let } x, y, z > 0 \text{ with } xyz = 1. \text{ Prove that } \frac{1}{x + y^{20} + z^{10}} + \frac{1}{y + z^{20} + x^{10}} + \frac{1}{z + x^{20} + y^{10}} \le 1.

positive_text: Let $ T_r(n) = 1^r + 2^r + \dots + n^r $, where $ r $ is a rational number and $ n $ is a positive integer. Determine all triples $ (p, q, k) $, where $ p $ and $ q $ are positive rational numbers and $ k $ is a positive integer, for which there exist infinitely many positive integers $ n $ such that $ T_p(n) = (T_q(n))^k $.

negatives.text: Let $ S_r(n) = 1^r + 2^r + \dots + n^r $, where $ r $ is a rational number and $ n $ is a positive integer. Find all triples $ (a, b, c) $, where $ a $ and $ b $ are positive rational numbers and $ c $ is a positive integer, for which there exist only finitely many positive integers $ n $ satisfying $ S_a(n) = (S_b(n))^c $.

Let $ S_r(n) = 1^r + 2^r + \dots + n^r $, where $ r $ is a rational number and $ n $ is a positive integer. Find all triples $ (a, b, c) $, where $ a $ and $ b $ are positive rational numbers and $ c $ is a positive integer, for which there exist infinitely many positive integers $ n $ satisfying $ S_{a+n}(n) = (S_b(n))^c $.

positive_text: \text{Find all triples } (a, b, q) \text{ satisfying } a^2 - 3ab + q^2b^2 = 12q \text{ where } a, b \text{ are integers and } q \text{ is a prime number}.

negatives.text: \text{Find all triples } (x, y, p) \text{ satisfying } x^2 - 3xy + p^2y^2 = -12p \text{ where } x, y \text{ are integers and } p \text{ is a prime number}.
\text{Find all triples } (x, y, p) \text{ satisfying } x^2 - 3xy + py^2 = 12p \text{ where } x, y \text{ are integers and } p \text{ is a prime number}.
\text{Find all triples } (x, y, p) \text{ satisfying } x^2 - 3xy + p^2y^2 = 12p^2 \text{ where } x, y \text{ are integers and } p \text{ is a prime number}.

positive_text: Let $S$ be the set of all $2012$-tuples $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{2012})$, with each $a_i$ chosen from $\{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$. A subset $X \subset S$ is decreasing if, for any $(a_1, \dots, a_{2012}) \in X$, all $(b_1, \dots, b_{2012})$ with $b_i \le a_i$ for all $i$ are also in $X$. A subset $Y \subset S$ is increasing if, for any $(a_1, \dots, a_{2012}) \in Y$, all $(b_1, \dots, b_{2012})$ with $b_i \ge a_i$ for all $i$ are also in $Y$. Determine the maximum value of $\frac{|X \cap Y|}{|X| \cdot |Y|}$, where $X$ and $Y$ are nonempty decreasing and increasing subsets, respectively.

negatives.text: Let $P$ be the set of all $2012$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, where $x_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$. A subset $A \subset P$ is decreasing if for any $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in A$, all $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ with $y_i < x_i$ for all $i$ are also in $A$. A subset $B \subset P$ is increasing if for any $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in B$, all $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ with $y_i > x_i$ for all $i$ are also in $B$. Find the maximum of $\frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| \cdot |B|}$.

Let $P$ be the set of all $2012$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, with each $x_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$. A subset $A \subset P$ is decreasing if for any $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in A$, all $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ with $y_i \le x_i$ for at least one $i$ are also in $A$. A subset $B \subset P$ is increasing if for any $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in B$, all $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ with $y_i \ge x_i$ for at least one $i$ are also in $B$. Find the maximum value of $\frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| \cdot |B|}$.

Let $P$ be the set of all $2012$-tuples $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012})$, where $x_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$. A subset $A \subset P$ is decreasing if for any $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in A$, all $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ with $y_i \le x_i$ for all $i$ are also in $A$. A subset $B \subset P$ is increasing if for any $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{2012}) \in B$, all $(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{2012})$ with $y_i \ge x_i$ for all $i$ are also in $B$. Find the maximum value of $\frac{|A \cap B|}{|A| + |B|}$.

positive_text: Two circles, $\omega_1$ with diameter $[AB]$ and $\omega_2$ centered at $A$, intersect at points $C$ and $D$. Let $E$ be a point on $\omega_2$, outside $\omega_1$, on the same side of $AB$ as $C$. Let $F$ be the second intersection of $BE$ with $\omega_2$. Suppose that a point $K$ lies on $\omega_1$, on the same side of the diameter through $C$ as $A$, and satisfies $2 \cdot CK \cdot AC = CE \cdot AB$. Let $L$ be the second intersection of $KF$ with $\omega_1$. Prove that the reflection of $D$ over line $BE$ lies on the circumcircle of triangle $LFC$.

Let triangle $PQR$ have $PR > PQ$. A circle $\gamma$ is tangent to $PQ$ and $PR$ at points $M$ and $N$ respectively, and intersects the circumcircle of $PQR$ at points $S$ and $T$. Let $U$ and $V$ be points on $PQ$ and $PR$ such that $$ \frac{PU}{PQ} = \frac{RN}{RM + RN} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{PV}{PR} = \frac{RM}{RM + RN}. $$ Prove that the lines $UV$, $QR$, and $ST$ are concurrent.

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $AC > AB$. A circle $\omega$ is tangent to the extensions of $AB$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$ respectively, and intersects the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$ and $L$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $$ \frac{AX}{AB} = \frac{CE}{BD - CE} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{AY}{AC} = \frac{BD}{BD - CE}. $$ Prove that the lines $XY$, $BC$, and $KL$ are concurrent.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $AC > AB$. A circle $\omega$ is tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$ respectively, and intersects the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$ and $L$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $$ \frac{AX}{AB} = \frac{CE^2}{BD^2 + CE^2} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{AY}{AC} = \frac{BD^2}{BD^2 + CE^2}. $$ Prove that the lines $XY$, $BC$, and $KL$ are concurrent.

Let triangle $ABC$ have $AC > AB$. A circle $\omega$ is tangent to the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$ respectively, and intersects the circumcircle of $ABC$ at $K$ and $L$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be points on $AB$ and $AC$ such that $$ \frac{AX}{AB} = \frac{CE}{BD + CE} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{AY}{AC} = \frac{CE}{BD + CE}. $$ Prove that the lines $XY$, $BC$, and $KL$ are concurrent.

positive_text: \text{Let } p > 1, q > 1, r > 1, s > 1, m, n \text{ be real numbers satisfying} \quad p^m + q^n = (p^2 + q^2)^m \text{ and } r^m + s^n = 2^n (rs)^{n/2}. \text{ Prove that } m < n.

negatives.text: \text{Let } a > 1, b > 1, c > 1, d > 1, x, y \text{ be real numbers satisfying} \quad a^x + b^x = (a^2 + b^2)^x \text{ and } c^x + d^y = 2^y (cd)^{y/2}. \text{ Prove that } x < y.

\text{Let } a > 1, b > 1, c > 1, d > 1, x, y \text{ be real numbers satisfying} \quad a^x + b^y = (a^2 + b^2)^x \text{ and } c^x + d^y = 2^x (cd)^{y/2}. \text{ Prove that } x < y.

positive_text: Let $ l $ be a line intersecting $ AB $ at $ F $, $ AC $ at $ D $, and $ BC $ at $ E $, and let it intersect the internal angle bisector of $ \angle BAC $ at point $ P $. Assume $ F $ lies on the extension of $ AB $ beyond $ B $, $ CD = CE $, and $ P $ is inside triangle $ ABC $. Prove that $$ FB \cdot FA + CP^2 = CF^2 \iff AD \cdot BE = PD^2. $$

negatives.text: Let $ l $ intersect $ AB $ at $ F $, $ AC $ at $ D $, and $ BC $ at $ E $, and intersect the external bisector of $ \angle BAC $ at $ P $. Suppose $ F $ is at the opposite side of $ A $ with respect to $ BC $, $ CD = CE $, and $ P $ is outside triangle $ ABC $. Prove that $$ FB \cdot FA + CP^2 = CF^2 \iff AD \cdot BE = PD^2. $$

Suppose $ F $ is at the opposite side of $ A $ with respect to $ BC $, $ CD = 2CE $, and $ P $ is in the interior of triangle $ ABC $. Prove that $$ FB \cdot FA + CP^2 = CF^2 \iff AD \cdot BE = PD^2. $$

positive_text: \text{Determine the smallest possible value of } \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z} \text{ for positive real numbers } x, y, z \text{ such that } xyz = 1, \quad x+y+z = 5 \text{ and} \quad (xy+2x+2y-9)(yz+2y+2z-9)(zx+2z+2x-9) \geq 0.

negatives.text: \text{Determine the smallest possible value of } \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} \text{ for positive real numbers } a, b, c \text{ such that } abc = 1, \quad a+b+c = 5 \text{ and} \quad (ab+2a+2b-9)(bc+2b+2c-9)(ca+2c+2a-9) \leq 0.

positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ be isosceles with $PQ = PR$. Let $S$ lie on the smaller arc $PR$ of the circumcircle $\Gamma$ of triangle $PQR$. Let $T$ be the reflection of $Q$ over the line $PS$. The line $QT$ meets $\Gamma$ again at $U$. The tangent at $U$ to $\Gamma$ intersects $PR$ at $M$, and the lines $SU$ and $PQ$ intersect at $N$. Prove that the points $M, N, T$ are collinear.

Let $E$ be the reflection of $B$ over the line $AD$. The line $BE$ intersects $\omega$ again at $F$. The tangent at $F$ to $\omega$ meets $AB$ at $K$, and the lines $DF$ and $AC$ intersect at $L$. positive_text: Let triangle $PQR$ have $|PQ| > |PR|$. Let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $QR$, $L$ be the point where the angle bisector of $\angle Q$ intersects $PS$, and $U$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ to $RL$. Let $T$ be the intersection of $AB$ with the line through $N$ parallel to $DM$. Prove that $BM$ is the internal bisector of $\angle TBC$.

positive_text:
Let triangle $PQR$ be right-angled at $R$. Let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to $PQ$. Define points $U$ and $V$ as the reflections of $S$ over $RP$ and $RQ$, respectively. Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be the circumcenters of triangles $UQR$ and $VPR$, respectively. Show that
$$
2|M_1M_2| = |PQ|.
$$

negatives.text:
Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$. Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the reflections of $D$ with respect to $AC$ and $AB$, respectively. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ECB$ and $FCA$, respectively. Prove that
$$
2|O_1O_2| = |AB|.
$$

Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$. Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the reflections of $D$ with respect to $AC$ and $BC$, respectively. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ECB$ and $FCA$, respectively. Prove that
$$
|O_1O_2| = |AB|.
$$

Let triangle $ABC$ be right-angled at $C$. Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $AB$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the reflections of $D$ with respect to $AC$ and $BC$, respectively. Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the circumcenters of triangles $ECA$ and $FCA$, respectively. Prove that
$$
2|O_1O_2| = |AB|.
$$

positive_text: Let $ p $ be an odd prime and $ k > 1 $, $ n $ be positive integers such that $ \frac{k^{pn} - 1}{k^n - 1} $ is a prime. Prove that $ pn \mid (p-1)^n + 1 $.

negatives.text: Let $ p $ be an odd prime and $ m > 1 $, $ n $ be positive integers such that $ \frac{m^{p+n} - 1}{m^n - 1} $ is a prime. Prove that $ p+n \mid (p-1)^n + 1 $.
Let $ p $ be an odd prime and $ m > 1 $, $ n $ be positive integers such that $ \frac{m^{pn} - 1}{m^n + 1} $ is a prime. Prove that $ pn \mid (p-1)^n + 1 $.

positive_text: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle where $\angle B < \angle C$, and let $K$ be the center of the $A$-excircle. If line $AK$ meets $BC$ at point $D$, and $E$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BKC$, prove that $$ \frac{1}{|KA|} = \frac{1}{|KD|} + \frac{1}{|KE|}. $$

negatives.text: Let triangle $ABC$ have $\angle B < \angle C$, and let $K$ be the center of the incircle. Suppose line $AK$ meets $BC$ at point $D$, and $E$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BKC$. Prove that $$ \frac{1}{|KA|} = \frac{1}{|KD|} + \frac{1}{|KE|}. $$

In triangle $ABC$ with $\angle B < \angle C$, let $K$ be the center of the $A$-excircle. The lines $BK$ and $AC$ intersect at $D$, and $E$ is the circumcenter of triangle $BKC$. Prove that $$ \frac{1}{|KB|} = \frac{1}{|KD|} + \frac{1}{|KE|}. $$

Let triangle $ABC$ with $\angle B < \angle C$ have $K$ as the center of the $A$-excircle. The line $AK$ meets $BC$ at $D$, and $E$ is the incenter of triangle $BKC$. Prove that $$ \frac{1}{|KA|} = \frac{1}{|KD|} + \frac{1}{|KE|}. $$

positive_text: \text{Determine all integer triples } (a, b, q) \text{ such that } |6a^2 - 17a - 39| = q^b \text{ where } q \text{ is a prime and } b \geq 1.

negatives.text: \text{Find all integer triples } (m, j, r) \text{ such that } |6m^2 + 17m - 39| = r^j \text{ where } r \text{ is a prime and } j \geq 1.
\text{Find all integer triples } (x, y, s) \text{ such that } |6x^2 - 17x - 39| = s^y + 1 \text{ where } s \text{ is a prime and } y \geq 1.
\text{Find all integer triples } (u, v, t) \text{ such that } |6u^2 - 17u + 39| = t^v \text{ where } t \text{ is a prime and } v \geq 1.

positive_text:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a collection of $n$ subsets of a universal set, each of size $k$, such that for any distinct $X, Y \in \mathcal{F}$, the symmetric difference $X \Delta Y$ is also in $\mathcal{F}$.

a) Is it possible that $n = 2023$? If so, what are all possible values of $k$?

b) Is it possible that $n = 1023$? If so, what are all possible values of $k$?

negatives.text:
Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a family of $n$ subsets of a universal set, each of size $k$, such that for any distinct $A, B \in \mathcal{S}$, the intersection $A \cap B$ is also in $\mathcal{S}$.

a) Is it possible that $n = 2023$? If so, what are all possible values of $k$?

b) Is it possible that $n = 1023$? If so, what are all possible values of $k$?

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a family of $n$ subsets of a universal set, each of size $k$, such that for any distinct $A, B \in \mathcal{S}$, the union $A \cup B$ is also in $\mathcal{S}$.

a) Is it possible that $n = 2023$? If so, what are all possible values of $k$?

b) Is it possible that $n = 1023$? If so, what are all possible values of $k$?

positive_text: Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer and $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ be real numbers. For each $1 \le k \le n$, define $$ y_k = \frac{x_k + \max\{x_{k+1}, x_{k+2}\}}{2}, $$ with indices taken modulo $n$, so $x_{n+1} = x_1$, $x_{n+2} = x_2$, and $y_{n+1} = y_1$. Find the smallest $\mu$ such that $$ \mu \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - x_{i+1})^{2024} \right] \geq \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - y_{i+1})^{2024} $$ for all $n \ge 3$ and real numbers $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$.

negatives.text: Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer and $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be real numbers. For each $1 \le k \le n$, define $$ b_k = \frac{a_k + a_{k+1}}{2}, $$ with $b_{n+1} = b_1$, $a_{n+1} = a_1$, $a_{n+2} = a_2$. Find the smallest $\lambda$ such that $$ \lambda \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_i - a_{i+1})^{2024} \right] \geq \sum_{i=1}^{n} (b_i - b_{i+1})^{2024} $$ holds for all $n \ge 3$ and real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$.

Let $n \ge 3$ be an integer and $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ be real numbers. For each $1 \le k \le n$, define $$ b_k = \frac{a_k + \max\{a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}\}}{2}, $$ with $b_{n+1} = b_1$, $a_{n+1} = a_1$, $a_{n+2} = a_2$. Find the smallest $\lambda$ such that $$ \lambda \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} |a_i - a_{i+1}|^{2024} \right] \geq \sum_{i=1}^{n} |b_i - b_{i+1}|^{2024} $$ holds for all $n \ge 3$ and real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$.

positive_text: Let $ \sigma(n) $ denote the sum of the positive divisors of $ n $. Consider a sequence $ (b_k)_{k=0}^{\infty} $ with $ b_0 = 1 $, and for $ k \geq 1 $, define $ b_k $ to be the least integer greater than 1 such that $$ \sigma(b_0 b_1 \cdots b_{k-1}) \mid \sigma(b_0 b_1 \cdots b_k). $$ Compute how many elements of this sequence divide $ 2024^{2024} $.

negatives.text: Let $ \sigma(n) $ be the sum of the positive divisors of $ n $. Define a sequence $ (e_i)_{i=0}^{\infty} $ with $ e_0 = 1 $, and for $ i \geq 1 $, define $ e_i $ as the smallest integer greater than 1 such that $$ \sigma(e_0 e_1 \cdots e_{i}) \mid \sigma(e_0 e_1 \cdots e_{i-1}). $$ How many of the terms of the sequence divide $ 2024^{2024} $?

Let $ \sigma(n) $ be the sum of the positive divisors of $ n $. Define a sequence $ (g_i)_{i=0}^{\infty} $ by $ g_0 = 1 $, and for $ i \geq 1 $, $ g_i $ is the smallest integer greater than 1 such that $$ \sigma(g_0 + g_1 + \cdots + g_{i-1}) \mid \sigma(g_0 + g_1 + \cdots + g_i). $$ How many of the terms of the sequence divide $ 2024^{2024} $?

positive_text:
Let $x, y, z \in [0; \frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfy the conditions
$$
\sin x + \sin y + \sin z = 1, \quad \sum_{\text{cyc}} \sin x \cos 2x = -1.
$$
Find the value of $\sin^2 x + \sin^2 y + \sin^2 z$.

negatives.text:
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0; \frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfy the conditions
$$
\sin \alpha + \sin \beta + \sin \gamma = 1, \quad \sin \alpha \cos^2 \alpha + \sin \beta \cos^2 \beta + \sin \gamma \cos^2 \gamma = -1.
$$
Find all the possible values of the expression $\sin^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \beta + \sin^2 \gamma$.

Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0; \pi]$ satisfy the conditions
$$
\sin \alpha + \sin \beta + \sin \gamma = 1, \quad \sin \alpha \cos 2\alpha + \sin \beta \cos 2\beta + \sin \gamma \cos 2\gamma = -1.
$$
Find all the possible values of the expression $\sin^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \beta + \sin^2 \gamma$.

Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in [0; \frac{\pi}{2}]$ satisfy the conditions
$$
\sin \alpha + \sin \beta + \sin \gamma = 1, \quad \sin^2 \alpha \cos 2\alpha + \sin^2 \beta \cos 2\beta + \sin^2 \gamma \cos 2\gamma = -1.
$$
Find all the possible values of the expression $\sin^2 \alpha + \sin^2 \beta + \sin^2 \gamma$.

positive_text: Let $P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n$ ($n \ge 3$) be $n$ points in the plane not all collinear. Define a function $g(X)$ for any point $X$ as the total distance from $X$ to all the $P_i$. Suppose there exists a point $A$ such that $g(A) \le g(X)$ for all points $X$. If there is another point $B$ with $g(A) = g(B)$, prove that $A = B$.

negatives.text: Given $n$ ($n \ge 3$) points in the plane not all collinear, define $f(M)$ as the sum of the squares of the distances from $M$ to each of these $n$ points. Suppose $M_1$ is a point minimizing $f(M)$. If there exists another point $M_2$ such that $f(M_1) = f(M_2)$, prove or disprove that $M_1 = M_2$.

Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ ($n \ge 3$) be points in the plane not all on a single line. Define $h(M)$ as the product of the distances from $M$ to each $A_i$. Suppose $M_1$ is a point minimizing $h(M)$. If there is a point $M_2$ such that $h(M_1) = h(M_2)$, prove that $M_1 = M_2$.

Let $n$ points be placed in the plane not all on a single line. For any point $P$, define $d(P)$ as the number of points among the $n$ that lie on the same line as $P$. Suppose there is a point $Q$ such that $d(Q) \ge d(P)$ for all other points $P$. If another point $R$ satisfies $d(Q) = d(R)$, prove that $Q = R$.

positive_text: \text{Prove that for all integers } n \ge 1, \quad \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k+2}{(k)! + (k+1)! + (k+2)!} < \frac{1}{2}.

negatives.text: \text{Prove that for every positive integer } n, \quad \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k+2}{k! + (k+1)! + (k+2)!} < 1.
\text{Prove that for every positive integer } n, \quad \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k+2}{k! + (k+1)! + (k+2)!} < \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{n}.
\text{Prove that for every positive integer } n, \quad \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k+2}{k! + (k+1)! + (k+2)!} < \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{n!}.

positive_text:
a) Determine all real numbers $x$ for which $$x^2 + \frac{1}{x(x + 2)} = 1$$
b) Determine all pairs of positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $$a^2 + b^2 + \frac{1}{a(a + 2)} + \frac{1}{b(b + 2)} = 2$$

negatives.text:
a) Solve for all real numbers $x$ such that $$x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 - 2x} = 1$$
b) Find all pairs of positive real numbers $x$ and $y$ such that $$x^2 + y^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 - 2x} + \frac{1}{y^2 - 2y} = 2$$

a) Find all real numbers $x$ such that $$x^2 + \frac{1}{(x + 1)^2} = 1$$
b) Find all pairs of positive real numbers $x$ and $y$ such that $$x^2 + y^2 + \frac{1}{(x + 1)^2} + \frac{1}{(y + 1)^2} = 2$$

a) Find all real numbers $x$ such that $$x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x + 1} = 1$$
b) Find all pairs of positive real numbers $x$ and $y$ such that $$x^2 + y^2 + \frac{1}{x^2 + 2x + 1} + \frac{1}{y^2 + 2y + 1} = 2$$

positive_text: \left( \frac{x+y}{z^2} + \frac{y+z}{x^2} + \frac{z+x}{y^2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{x^2}{y+z} + \frac{y^2}{z+x} + \frac{z^2}{x+y} \right) \ge 3 + \frac{x+y}{z} + \frac{y+z}{x} + \frac{z+x}{y}

negatives.text: \left( \frac{a+b}{c^2} + \frac{b+c}{a^2} + \frac{c+a}{b^2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{a^3}{b+c} + \frac{b^3}{c+a} + \frac{c^3}{a+b} \right) \ge 3 + \frac{a+b}{c} + \frac{b+c}{a} + \frac{c+a}{b}
\left( \frac{a+b}{c^2} + \frac{b+c}{a^2} + \frac{c+a}{b^2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{a^2}{b+c} + \frac{b^2}{c+a} + \frac{c^2}{a+b} \right) \ge 3 + \frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a}
\left( \frac{a-b}{c^2} + \frac{b-c}{a^2} + \frac{c-a}{b^2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{a^2}{b+c} + \frac{b^2}{c+a} + \frac{c^2}{a+b} \right) \ge 3 + \frac{a+b}{c} + \frac{b+c}{a} + \frac{c+a}{b}

positive_text: \text{Let } a + b + a - b = 1. \text{ Determine the minimum and maximum of } a^2 - 6a + b^2 - 6b.

negatives.text: \text{We know that } |x+y| + |x-y| = 2. \text{ Find the least and the greatest value of the expression } x^2 - 6x + y^2 - 6y.
\text{We know that } |x+y| + |x-y| = 1. \text{ Find the least and the greatest value of the expression } x^2 - 6x + y^2 + 6y.
\text{We know that } |x+y| + |x+y| = 1. \text{ Find the least and the greatest value of the expression } x^2 - 6x + y^2 - 6y.

positive_text: Side $AB$ of the parallelogram $ABCD$ is extended beyond the point $B$ and point $K$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle DAK$ is isosceles triangle with base $AK$. Side $AD$ is extended beyond the point $D$ and point $L$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle BDL$ is isosceles triangle with base $DL$. Bisectors of angles $\angle ABD$ and $\angle DAK$ intersect at point $Q$. Find radius of a circle circumscribed about triangle $KAL$, if $\angle AQD = \alpha$ and $KL = a$.

negatives.text: Side $BC$ of the parallelogram $ABCD$ is extended beyond the point $C$ and point $K$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle CDK$ is equilateral triangle with base $CK$. Side $DC$ is extended beyond the point $C$ and point $L$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle CBL$ is isosceles triangle with base $CL$. Bisectors of angles $\angle LBC$ and $\angle CDK$ intersect at point $Q$. Find radius of a circle circumscribed about triangle $ALK$, if $\angle BQD = \alpha$ and $KL = a$.

Side $BC$ of the parallelogram $ABCD$ is extended beyond the point $C$ and point $K$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle CDK$ is isosceles triangle with base $CK$. Side $DC$ is extended beyond the point $C$ and point $L$ is placed on the extension so that $\triangle CBL$ is isosceles triangle with base $CL$. Bisectors of angles $\angle LBC$ and $\angle CDK$ intersect at point $Q$. Find radius of a circle circumscribed about triangle $AKL$, if $\angle AQD = \alpha$ and $KL = a$.

positive_text: Determine the value of the parameter $\theta$ such that the equation $|x - \sin \theta| + |x - \frac{1}{2}| = \cos 3\theta$ has exactly one solution. What is this solution?

negatives.text: Determine the value of the parameter $\alpha$ such that the equation $|x - \frac{1}{2}| + |x - \sin \alpha| = \sin 3\alpha$ has exactly one solution. What is this solution?
Determine the value of the parameter $\alpha$ such that the equation $|x - \frac{1}{2}| + |x - \sin \alpha| = \cos 3\alpha$ has exactly two solutions. What are these solutions?
Determine the value of the parameter $\alpha$ such that the equation $|x - \frac{1}{2}| + |x - \sin \alpha| = -\cos 3\alpha$ has exactly one solution. What is this solution?

positive_text: Let $\{a_n\}$ be a sequence with $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 2$, and $a_{n+2} = a_{n+1} + a_n$ for all $n \geq 1$. Determine the maximum possible number of terms of $\{a_n\}$ that can appear as consecutive terms in an increasing arithmetic progression.

negatives.text: Let $\{b_n\}$ be a sequence with $b_1 = 1$, $b_2 = 2$, and $b_{n+2} = b_{n+1} + b_n + 1$ for all $n \geq 1$. What may be the greatest number of members of $\{b_n\}$ among the consecutive members of an increasing arithmetic progression?

Let $\{c_n\}$ be a sequence with $c_1 = 1$, $c_2 = 2$, and $c_{n+2} = c_{n+1} - c_n$ for all $n \geq 1$. What may be the greatest number of members of $\{c_n\}$ among the consecutive members of an increasing arithmetic progression?

Let $\{d_n\}$ be a sequence with $d_1 = 1$, $d_2 = 3$, and $d_{n+2} = d_{n+1} + d_n$ for all $n \geq 1$. What may be the greatest number of members of $\{d_n\}$ among the consecutive members of an increasing arithmetic progression?

positive_text: Suppose $\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{-a-b} = \frac{3}{2}$ for some real numbers $a$ and $b$ such that $a + b \ne 0$. What is a possible value of $\frac{1}{a^2} + \frac{1}{b^2} + \frac{1}{(a + b)^2}$?

negatives.text: Suppose $\frac{1}{x-y} + \frac{1}{y-z} + \frac{1}{x-z} = \frac{3}{2}$. What value may $\frac{1}{(x-y)^2} + \frac{1}{(y-z)^2} + \frac{1}{(x-z)^2}$ have?
Given $\frac{1}{x-y} + \frac{1}{y-z} + \frac{1}{z-x} = \frac{3}{2}$, what value may $\frac{1}{x-y} + \frac{1}{y-z} + \frac{1}{z-x}$ have?

positive_text: Let $ S(n) $ be the sum of the positive divisors of $ n $, and let $ T(n) $ count the number of positive integers less than $ n $ that are relatively prime to $ n $. Show that there are infinitely many values of $ n $ such that $ T(S(n)) > n $.

negatives.text: For every positive integer $ m $, denote by $ \sigma(m) $ the sum of all its divisors, and by $ \phi(m) $ the number of positive integers less than $ m $ and coprime with $ m $. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $ n $ for which $ \phi(\sigma(n)) < n $.

positive_text:
Determine all real-coefficient polynomials $Q(x)$ such that for all distinct positive integers $a, b, c, d$ with $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 2d^2$ and $\gcd(a, b, c, d) = 1$, the identity
$$
2Q^2(d) + 2Q(ab + bc + ca) = Q^2(a + b + c)
$$
holds.

negatives.text:
Find all polynomials $R(x)$ with real coefficients such that for all distinct natural numbers $p, q, r, s$ with $p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = 3s^2$ and $\gcd(p, q, r, s) = 1$, the following holds:
$$
2R^2(s) + 2R(pq + qr + rp) = R^2(p + q + r).
$$

Find all real-coefficient polynomials $S(x)$ such that for all distinct natural numbers $m, n, o, p$ with $m^2 + n^2 + o^2 = 2p^2$ and $\gcd(m, n, o, p) = 1$, the following identity holds:
$$
2S^2(p) + 2S(mn + no + om) = S^2(mn + no + om).
$$

Determine all real-coefficient polynomials $T(x)$ such that for all distinct natural numbers $u, v, w, x$ with $u^2 + v^2 + w^2 = 2x^2$ and $\gcd(u, v, w, x) = 1$, the following holds:
$$
2T(x)^2 + 2T(uv + vw + wu) = T(u + v + w)^2 + 1.
$$

positive_text: \frac{PA^2}{QR} + \frac{PB^2}{RP} + \frac{PC^2}{PQ} \ge \frac{PA + PB + PC}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ where } P \text{ is the point inside triangle } PQR \text{ such that } \angle QPR = \angle RPQ = \angle PQR = 120^\circ

negatives.text: \frac{AO^2}{BC} + \frac{BO^2}{CA} + \frac{CO^2}{AB} \ge \frac{AO + BO + CO}{\sqrt{2}} \text{ where } O \text{ is the point inside triangle } ABC \text{ such that } \angle AOB = \angle BOC = \angle COA = 120^\circ

\frac{AO^2}{BC} + \frac{BO^2}{CA} + \frac{CO^2}{AB} \ge \frac{AB + BC + CA}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ where } O \text{ is the point inside triangle } ABC \text{ such that } \angle AOB = \angle BOC = \angle COA = 120^\circ

\frac{AO^2}{BC} + \frac{BO^2}{CA} + \frac{CO^2}{AB} \ge \frac{AO + BO + CO}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ where } O \text{ is the point inside triangle } ABC \text{ such that } \angle AOB = \angle BOC = \angle COA = 90^\circ

positive_text: Determine how many positive integer pairs $(a, b)$ satisfy $(2^k)! = 2^a b$.

negatives.text: Find the number of positive integer pairs $(n, m)$ such that $(2^k + 1)! = 2^n m$.
Find the number of positive integer pairs $(n, m)$ such that $(2^k)! = 3^n m$.
Find the number of positive integer pairs $(n, m)$ such that $(2^{k^2})! = 2^n m$.

positive_text: Determine all positive integers $ n $ such that any polynomial $ f(x) $ with real coefficients can be expressed as a sum $ f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (a_i^2(x) + b_i^3(x)) $, where each $ a_i(x), b_i(x) $ is a polynomial with real coefficients.

negatives.text: Determine all positive integers $ n $ such that every polynomial $ f(x) $ with real coefficients can be written as $ f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (p_i^2(x) + q_i^2(x)) $ for some real-coefficient polynomials $ p_i(x), q_i(x) $.

Find all positive integers $ n $ such that every polynomial $ f(x) $ with real coefficients can be written as $ f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (p_i^3(x) + q_i^3(x)) $ for some real-coefficient polynomials $ p_i(x), q_i(x) $.

Determine all positive integers $ n $ such that every polynomial $ f(x) $ with real coefficients can be written as $ f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (p_i^2(x) + q_i^3(x)) $, where $ p_i(x), q_i(x) $ are real numbers, not polynomials.

positive_text: Given integers $x, y, z$ such that $xy + yz + zx = 1$, prove that $(1 + x^2)(1 + y^2)(1 + z^2)$ is a perfect square.

negatives.text: Given integers $a, b, c$ such that $ab + bc + ca = 2$, prove that $(1 + a^2)(1 + b^2)(1 + c^2)$ is a perfect square.
Given integers $a, b, c$ such that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1$, prove that $(1 + a^2)(1 + b^2)(1 + c^2)$ is a perfect square.

positive_text: \text{Sketch the graph of the equation: } \frac{a}{|a|} + \frac{|b|}{b} = 2b.

negatives.text: \text{Draw the graph of the equation: } \frac{x}{|x|} - \frac{|y|}{y} = 2y.
\text{Graph the equation: } \frac{x}{|x|} + \frac{|y|}{y} = -2y.
\text{Plot the graph of the equation: } \frac{x^2}{|x^2|} + \frac{|y|}{y} = 2y.

positive_text:
Let $x$, $y$, $z$ be nonnegative real numbers such that $x + y + z = 1$. Prove that
$$
(x - 1)^2 + (y - 1)^2 + (z - 1)^2 \geq 6\sqrt{xyz}.
$$
Is equality possible?

negatives.text:
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be nonnegative real numbers such that $a + b + c = 1$. Prove that
$$
(1 - a)^2 + (1 - b)^2 + (1 - c)^2 \geq 6\sqrt[3]{abc}.
$$
Is equality possible?

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be nonnegative real numbers such that $a + b + c = 1$. Prove that
$$
(1 - a)^2 + (1 - b)^2 + (1 - c)^2 \geq 6\sqrt{ab + bc + ca}.
$$
Is equality possible?
